SYNTH-0003♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Kenneth Miller♔♔♔♔♔♔Kenneth R. Miller, RN (Retired)⏎4417 Bayshore Blvd., Apt. 12C⏎Tampa, FL 33611⏎⏎October 14, 2024⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Re: HHS Request for Information, Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care Settings, Federal Register Vol. 89 (2024)⏎⏎To the Office of the Deputy Secretary:⏎⏎My name is Kenneth Miller. I spent forty-one years as a critical care nurse, most of them at Tampa General Hospital, and I am submitting this comment not as a representative of any organization but as someone who has stood at enough bedsides to know the difference between a patient who is deteriorating and a monitor that says they are deteriorating. Those are not the same thing, and the RFI before you appears, in several of its framing questions, to treat them as though they were. The word that keeps pulling my attention is "productivity." The document uses it to describe what AI can improve in clinical care. I want to explain, as precisely as I can, why that word choice is not merely imprecise but is evidence of a category error that will, if left unexamined, produce policies that cause measurable harm.⏎⏎In 2019, a nurse I worked with in the ICU overrode an early sepsis-detection algorithm four times in a single month. The same patient each time: a chronic dialysis patient whose baseline lactate ran elevated, whose presentation the algorithm read as emergency, and whose actual condition she understood from eighteen months of caring for him. She was right all four times. The attending eventually stopped second-guessing her. I tell that story not to argue that algorithms are wrong, but to name what her judgment depended on: accumulated, specific knowledge of a specific human being, built through repeated direct encounter, held in a mind that was still practicing the skill of independent clinical reasoning. Kelley and colleagues, in their 2014 meta-analysis published in PLOS ONE, found that the quality of the patient-clinician relationship has independent, statistically significant effects on health outcomes, even after controlling for treatment fidelity. The relationship itself is a clinical variable. When you route clinical encounters through an algorithmic intermediary, you do not merely change the workflow. You degrade that variable in ways that do not show up in readmission rates for at least several years, by which time the reimbursement structures will already be locked in.⏎⏎The RFI asks, in substance, what HHS can do to accelerate adoption. My concern is with the prior question that the document does not ask: what is lost when AI mediates the clinical encounter, and how would we know? The literature on automation bias is not ambiguous on this point. Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt, writing in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association in 2012, documented systematically that clinicians exposed to decision-support tools shift toward the algorithm's recommendation even when their own independent assessment is more accurate. This is not a failure of individual judgment; it is a predictable cognitive response to an authoritative-seeming output, consistent with what Tversky and Kahneman described in their 1974 work on anchoring as a heuristic bias. The question is not whether this happens. It does. The question is what HHS intends to do about the fact that the reimbursement incentives being contemplated in this RFI will push hospitals to deploy these tools before anyone has measured the anchoring effects on clinical reasoning in their specific patient populations. I have not seen that question addressed anywhere in the document.⏎⏎There is a related problem that I think deserves its own paragraph, because it tends to get folded into workforce discussions that I am deliberately setting aside here. Warm and Mathis, writing in Academic Medicine in 2022, described what they call the "supervised autonomy paradox" in graduate medical education: trainees who operate under intensive algorithmic guidance develop competency profiles that look adequate under normal conditions and fail under the exact conditions, novel presentations, system failures, edge cases, where independent judgment matters most. This is not a training problem. It is a structural consequence of practicing a cognitive skill less frequently, which is what happens when an algorithm absorbs a portion of the reasoning task. Skinner and Skelton, in a 2021 qualitative study published in BMJ Open, found that physicians themselves describe a felt loss of diagnostic confidence and relational presence when technology mediates their patient interactions, and they connect that loss directly to changes in how they attend to the patient in the room. Bickmore and Picard, whose 2005 work in ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction examined long-term human-computer relationships, found that even well-designed technological mediation changes the affective character of relational exchange in ways that participants do not always consciously register. I raise these findings because the RFI's framing of AI adoption as a question of benefit realization and barrier removal does not account for them. The document describes clinical care as a domain where AI can improve outputs. It does not appear to consider that clinical care might be a practice whose integrity depends on conditions that AI intermediation systematically erodes.⏎⏎What I am asking HHS to do is straightforward, though I recognize it runs against the momentum of this RFI:⏎⏎1. Before any reimbursement incentive is attached to AI-assisted clinical decision-making, require prospective measurement of clinician independent reasoning performance in facilities that adopt the tool, compared to matched controls, with a minimum follow-up period of thirty-six months.⏎⏎2. Fund research specifically designed to measure what is lost in the therapeutic relationship when AI mediates the clinical encounter, not just what is gained in throughput or documentation time. The Kelley et al. meta-analysis framework offers a starting point for operationalizing relationship quality as an outcome variable.⏎⏎3. Require that any AI clinical decision support tool seeking reimbursement-linked deployment demonstrate, in peer-reviewed literature, that it does not produce statistically significant anchoring effects on the clinician population in which it will be used, under the patient demographic conditions specific to that deployment context. A dialysis patient in a safety-net hospital in Tampa is not the patient in the training data from an academic medical center in Boston.⏎⏎4. Convene a working group that includes bedside nurses, not just physicians and health IT executives, before any final guidance on reimbursement structures is issued. Nurses are the clinicians who interact most frequently with these tools in practice, and their absence from the design conversation is something I notice every time I read a document like this one.⏎⏎I want to be honest about what I am not saying. I am not saying AI has no place in clinical care. I am not nostalgic for paper charts or dismissive of tools that can genuinely reduce cognitive load in high-volume settings. What I am saying is that the RFI before you is structured as a question about acceleration, and that framing forecloses the prior question about whether the thing being accelerated will, at the speeds being contemplated, damage the relational and cognitive substrate that makes medicine work. The 2014 Kelley meta-analysis found effect sizes for the patient-clinician relationship that were comparable to those for several pharmacological interventions. We do not accelerate drug adoption without measuring harm. I do not understand why the standard should be different here, and the RFI does not explain it.⏎⏎The specific question I am addressing from the RFI is the one asking what research priorities HHS should fund to support responsible AI adoption in clinical settings. My answer is that the research priority should not be adoption. It should be understanding, at a mechanistic level, what changes in clinical cognition and relational quality when AI enters the encounter, and whether those changes are reversible once they have been institutionalized through reimbursement. That is not a hostile question. That is the question any careful clinician would ask before changing a care protocol that affects forty million patients.⏎⏎My colleague who overrode that sepsis algorithm four times is retired now too. I wonder sometimes whether the nurse who eventually takes her position will have practiced independent clinical reasoning enough to do what she did, or whether by then the assumption will simply be that the algorithm doesn't need overriding because the algorithm has always been there.⏎⏎Sincerely,⏎⏎Kenneth R. Miller, RN (Retired)⏎Tampa, Florida♔♔2026-01-24T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-24T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔4♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔individual♔high♔angry♔Florida♔retired nurse♔77♔My forty-one years in critical care — ending at Tampa General before my knees gave out — taught me that a nurse's most irreplaceable skill is reading the patient in front of you, not the algorithm predicting what that patient probably looks like. SYNTH-0004♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Christopher Ramirez♔McKinsey Center for US Health System Reform♔♔♔♔♔McKinsey Center for US Health System Reform | HHS AI RFI Comment | Page 1⏎⏎Response to HHS Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Submitted by: Christopher Ramirez, VP of Regulatory Affairs, McKinsey Center for US Health System Reform⏎⏎Before turning to the substance of the Center's concerns, a preliminary clarification is necessary, because the framing of this document has caused genuine confusion both within our organization and among the health system leaders with whom we consult regularly. This is a Request for Information, not a proposed rule, and not a final rule. The distinction matters considerably, and HHS would do well to acknowledge, somewhere in the preamble of whatever action follows this RFI, that the current document carries no binding regulatory effect. The McKinsey Center has fielded inquiries from compliance officers at three separate health systems in the Midwest who read the Federal Register notice and asked, in good faith, whether AI deployment timelines were now a federal mandate. They are not. But the fact that sophisticated regulatory professionals cannot immediately locate that answer in the document's framing is itself a policy problem worth naming. An RFI is a listening exercise. A proposed rule is a formal regulatory action subject to notice-and-comment under the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. 553, and a final rule is the binding output of that process. The Center raises this not to be pedantic but because the governance stakes of this particular subject area are high enough that the procedural posture of each HHS action should be unambiguous from the first paragraph. Confusion about where one stands in the regulatory timeline produces either premature compliance spending or, more commonly, a kind of paralytic wait-and-see posture that the Department presumably wishes to avoid.⏎⏎With that framing concern noted, the Center turns to the substantive question it believes is most consequential among those HHS has posed: what regulatory and policy conditions are necessary to ensure that AI adoption in clinical care does not degrade the quality of the diagnostic encounter itself. This is not a question the RFI poses with particular precision. In fact, the document's repeated invocation of "productivity" as an organizing value for AI deployment is, the Center would argue, a category error that will produce bad policy if left unexamined. The clinical encounter is not a production process. The relationship between a clinician and a patient is the mechanism by which diagnosis occurs, and decades of outcomes research confirm that this relationship has independent therapeutic value that cannot be disaggregated from its informational content. Kelley, J.M., et al. (2014), in a systematic review and meta-analysis published in PLOS ONE (9(4), e94207), found consistent associations between the quality of the patient-clinician relationship and measurable health outcomes across a range of conditions. Hojat, M., et al. (2011), writing in Academic Medicine (86(3), 359-364), demonstrated that physician empathy scores were directly correlated with clinical outcomes in diabetic patients, with higher-empathy physicians producing better HbA1c and LDL control even after controlling for other variables. These are not soft findings. They are quantitative evidence that something happens in the room between clinician and patient that cannot be replicated by a system that processes the patient's structured data fields.⏎⏎McKinsey Center for US Health System Reform | HHS AI RFI Comment | Page 2⏎⏎The Center's concern about productivity framing is not abstract. Consider what actually happens when a clinician is intermediated by an AI diagnostic support tool during a primary care encounter. The patient in front of the clinician is, say, a 67-year-old woman who cannot articulate her symptoms with precision -- she says she feels "off," that her sleep has changed, that her husband thinks she looks pale. None of this maps cleanly to structured inputs. The AI tool, drawing on her EHR data, flags anemia risk and suggests a CBC order. The clinician, whose attention has been partly captured by the screen displaying the AI recommendation, does order the CBC. What the clinician does not do, because the AI has already provided a plausible diagnostic direction, is spend the next four minutes watching the patient's face, noticing the slight tremor in her left hand, asking the follow-up question about her balance that would have opened a different diagnostic pathway entirely. Abraham Verghese has written about this with unusual clarity -- see his 2008 piece in the New England Journal of Medicine (359(26), 2748-2751) and his broader argument that the physical and relational examination is not merely confirmatory but generative of diagnostic information that does not exist anywhere in the chart. The AI tool in this scenario is not wrong. It is, in a narrow sense, helpful. But it has restructured the cognitive and attentional economy of the encounter in ways that may have foreclosed a better diagnosis. Danielle Ofri, in What Doctors Feel (Beacon Press, 2017), makes a related argument about affective attunement -- the way a clinician's emotional responsiveness to a patient's presentation generates diagnostic hypotheses that purely inferential reasoning would not reach. The question HHS should be asking is not how to accelerate AI deployment but whether deployment, at the pace and in the configurations currently being pursued, is outcome-neutral with respect to these relational and attentional dimensions of care.⏎⏎The automation complacency literature is directly relevant here, and the Center is concerned that HHS's RFI does not engage with it at all. Parasuraman, R., and Manzey, D.H. (2010), writing in Human Factors (52(3), 381-410), documented the well-established phenomenon by which human operators who rely on automated systems progressively reduce their independent monitoring of the task domain, even when the automated system's error rate is non-trivial. Goddard, K., et al. (2012), in a systematic review published in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association (19(1), 121-127), found that automation bias -- the tendency to defer to automated recommendations even against contradicting evidence -- is a robust and generalizable effect across decision-support contexts. The clinical implications of these findings are not hypothetical. If clinicians are trained and incentivized to work alongside AI diagnostic tools from early in their careers, the question of what diagnostic capacities they develop and retain in the absence of those tools becomes a genuine public health question. Tversky, A., and Kahneman, D. (1974), in their foundational work on judgment under uncertainty published in Science (185(4157), 1124-1131), identified anchoring as one of the most durable cognitive biases in human decision-making. An AI recommendation displayed prominently at the top of a clinical interface is an anchor. It will shape the clinician's subsequent reasoning whether or not the clinician intends it to, and the magnitude of that effect will likely increase as the clinician's independent diagnostic confidence erodes over time. The Center does not assert that this trajectory is inevitable. It does assert that HHS has not yet demonstrated that it has seriously evaluated this risk, and that the current RFI's framing gives no indication that the Department intends to do so before accelerating deployment.⏎⏎McKinsey Center for US Health System Reform | HHS AI RFI Comment | Page 3⏎⏎The empirical record on AI deployment in clinical settings is also considerably more mixed than the RFI's framing implies. Topol, E.J. (2019), writing in Nature Medicine (25, 44-56), offered a measured assessment of AI's diagnostic performance that acknowledged both genuine capability and significant implementation challenges, including the gap between retrospective model performance and prospective real-world utility. Obermeyer, Z., and Emanuel, E.J. (2016), in the New England Journal of Medicine (375(13), 1216-1219), noted that predictive models in clinical medicine frequently perform well on training data while producing outputs that are difficult to integrate into actual clinical workflows. The National Academy of Medicine's 2023 workshop proceedings on AI in health care (NAM Press, Washington, D.C.) documented a range of deployment failures that are not reflected in the performance metrics typically used to evaluate these tools prior to deployment. Against this backdrop, and given that our own analysis identified 47 distinct points of patient data exposure across commonly deployed clinical AI pipelines and that fewer than 19% of health systems deploying AI diagnostic tools had implemented data minimization protocols consistent with existing HIPAA guidance as of our most recent review, the Center finds the RFI's acceleration framing premature. There have been, to the Center's knowledge, no civil monetary penalties issued specifically in connection with AI-related data handling failures between 2021 and 2024, despite a 340% increase in reported AI deployments across CMS-enrolled facilities during that same period. That enforcement gap is not evidence that the deployments have been clean. It is evidence that HHS has not yet built the oversight infrastructure commensurate with the deployment pace it is now proposing to accelerate.⏎⏎The Center's formal recommendations, in response to the specific RFI questions concerning regulatory actions HHS can take, are as follows:⏎⏎1. HHS should issue precautionary deployment standards for AI tools used in primary diagnostic encounters, requiring prospective demonstration of relational-outcome neutrality -- meaning that deployment should be conditioned on evidence that the tool does not measurably degrade the quality or duration of the patient-clinician interaction, not merely that it produces acceptable performance on clinical endpoints.⏎⏎2. HHS should require mandatory therapeutic-relationship impact assessments as a condition of Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement for AI-assisted encounters. The assessment framework should draw on validated instruments for measuring patient-reported relational quality, and results should be reported to CMS on a facility-level basis.⏎⏎3. HHS should institute a moratorium on AI intermediation in primary diagnostic encounters -- meaning configurations in which AI output is displayed to the clinician prior to or during the initial patient interview -- pending demonstrated relational-outcome neutrality across a representative sample of deployment contexts. This is not a moratorium on AI in clinical care broadly. It is a targeted pause on a specific configuration that the Center believes carries the highest risk of the attentional and relational harms described above.⏎⏎4. HHS should, separately and urgently, clarify in plain language the procedural posture of each action it takes in this space, distinguishing RFIs from proposed rules from final rules, so that health system compliance officers, clinicians, and patients can understand what is binding and what is not.⏎⏎The Center also notes, for the record, that Bickmore, T.W., and Picard, R.W. (2005), writing in ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction (12(2), 293-327), found that long-term human-computer relational bonds, while they can be established under controlled conditions, are qualitatively different from human-human relationships in ways that affect trust calibration and information disclosure. The relevance to clinical AI is direct: patients who believe they are in a relational encounter with a human clinician, but whose clinician is substantially cognitively occupied by an AI interface, are in a different epistemic situation than they understand themselves to be in. Whether that situation is ethically acceptable, and under what disclosure conditions, is a question the RFI does not ask. The Center believes it should be among the first questions HHS addresses before any further acceleration of deployment in primary care settings.⏎⏎The Center remains available to provide additional technical input as HHS moves from this RFI toward whatever regulatory action follows. Correspondence may be directed to Christopher Ramirez, VP of Regulatory Affairs, McKinsey Center for US Health System Reform.⏎⏎centerforhealthreform-regulatory@mckinsey-health.org♔♔2026-02-02T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-02T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔organization♔high♔resigned♔South Dakota♔VP of regulatory affairs♔41♔EPIC's 2024 analysis of federal health data-sharing frameworks identified 47 distinct points of patient data exposure across commonly deployed clinical AI pipelines, spanning model training, inference logging, and third-party vendor integrations. SYNTH-0005♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Charles Ramirez♔♔♔♔♔♔COMMENT OF CHARLES RAMIREZ, RETIRED LIBRARIAN, NAMPA, IDAHO⏎Submitted to the HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information Docket⏎Re: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎THE QUESTION HHS IS NOT ASKING⏎⏎The framing of this request troubles me in a specific, professional way. The RFI asks what actions HHS can take to "accelerate adoption" of artificial intelligence in clinical settings. Speed is treated as the policy objective. After forty years as a librarian — the last eighteen as director of a branch system in Nampa — I am familiar with the experience of watching an institution adopt an information system without first asking whether that system performs equitably across the populations it will serve. The consequences in a library are inconvenient. The consequences in a cardiology practice managing warfarin dosages are of a different order entirely.⏎⏎I am 73 years old. I have a documented cardiac arrhythmia, first identified in the fall of 2022, and my anticoagulation regimen is managed in part through a clinical decision-support algorithm that no one at the practice has been able to explain to me in plain language. I have asked the front desk, the nurse practitioner, and the physician who inherited my case when my cardiologist retired. The closest I received to an answer was a description of the algorithm as "evidence-based," which is not a description of an information system; it is a marketing characterization. The Nampa Public Library had more explicit policies about how its catalog algorithm surfaced materials to patrons — including documented acknowledgment that the system weighted recent acquisitions and patron circulation patterns in ways that could disadvantage older collections — than the clinical system now shaping recommendations about my blood.⏎⏎THE DOCUMENTED PERFORMANCE GAP AND WHY IT IS NOT SURPRISING⏎⏎I want to be clear that I am not opposed to algorithmic decision support in clinical care. Every information retrieval system I ever managed had architecture, embedded assumptions, and limitations baked into it. The question was always whether those properties were disclosed, audited, and corrected when they produced inequitable outcomes. The literature on clinical AI performance gaps reads, to me, less like alarming novelty and more like the expected behavior of systems validated on unrepresentative populations and then deployed without ongoing surveillance.⏎⏎The Sjoding et al. (2020) finding in the New England Journal of Medicine — that pulse oximeters systematically overestimate oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin pigmentation, a bias with direct implications for any AI system trained on pulse oximetry data — is a predictable consequence of training data that reflected historical measurement practices rather than measurement ground truth (Sjoding, M.W., Dickson, R.P., Iwashyna, T.J., Gay, S.E., & Valley, T.S., 2020, Racial bias in pulse oximetry measurement, NEJM 383(25), 2477-2478). The Obermeyer et al. (2019) Science paper documenting that a widely used commercial risk-scoring algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients — because it used cost as a proxy for health need, and cost reflects historical patterns of care access rather than actual morbidity — is a predictable consequence of using a proxy variable without auditing its distributional properties across patient subgroups (Obermeyer, Z., Powers, B., Vogeli, C., & Mullainathan, S., 2019, Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations, Science 366(6464), 447-453). Adamson and Smith's 2018 analysis in JAMA Dermatology documenting that machine learning diagnostic tools for skin conditions performed substantially worse on images of darker skin tones is a predictable consequence of training datasets composed predominantly of images from lighter-skinned patients (Adamson, A.S., & Smith, A., 2018, Machine learning and health care disparities in dermatology, JAMA Dermatology 154(11), 1247-1248).⏎⏎None of these findings required extraordinary circumstances to produce. They required ordinary information science: a system trained on biased inputs will produce biased outputs, and the bias will be invisible to users who do not know to look for it. What is extraordinary is not that these failures occurred, but that the systems were deployed and widely adopted before the failures were documented.⏎⏎THE EXTERNAL VALIDATION PROBLEM AND WHAT IT MEANS FOR RURAL IDAHO⏎⏎Wong et al. (2021) published an external validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model and found that its performance in their hospital setting was substantially worse than the performance reported by the vendor — the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve dropped from the vendor-reported 0.76 to 0.63 in external validation, and the model generated a high rate of false positives that the authors estimated would require substantial nursing time to evaluate (Wong, A., Otles, E., Donnelly, J.P., et al., 2021, External validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model in hospitalized patients, JAMA Internal Medicine 181(8), 1065-1070). The hospital in which that validation study was conducted was a large academic medical center with the resources to conduct the validation in the first place.⏎⏎I live in Idaho. My cardiologist practiced in Boise, which has more clinical infrastructure than most of the state. The communities where I ran library branches before consolidating in Nampa were smaller, with fewer resources, serving populations that included a substantial proportion of elderly patients, agricultural workers, and individuals whose access to specialty care required a two-hour drive on a good day. Those are exactly the populations least likely to be represented in the training data for clinical AI systems developed by vendors in urban academic medical centers, and exactly the populations least likely to have their local clinical institutions conduct the kind of external validation study that Wong et al. conducted. When HHS asks what it can do to accelerate adoption in community and rural settings, the literature suggests the appropriate prior question is: has anyone verified that these systems work for the patients in those settings?⏎⏎I recognize this is not a new concern. Char, Shah, and Magnus raised it in 2018 in the New England Journal of Medicine, noting that machine learning systems trained on data from large academic medical centers may not generalize to community settings, and that the patients most likely to be harmed by this failure of generalization are those who already face the greatest barriers to care (Char, D.S., Shah, N.H., & Magnus, D., 2018, Implementing machine learning in health care — addressing ethical challenges, NEJM 378(11), 981-983). That was seven years ago. The RFI does not indicate what, if anything, changed in the interim.⏎⏎WHAT DENTAL COVERAGE FOR SENIORS HAS TO DO WITH THIS⏎⏎I want to raise something that probably does not belong in a comment about clinical AI, and I recognize it may be set aside by whoever reviews this docket. But I have been waiting, as a Medicare beneficiary, for dental coverage that was discussed seriously in 2021 and 2022 and then did not materialize in any meaningful form. I raise it here because the pattern is the same: HHS identifies a gap in care that disproportionately affects older adults and people with limited incomes, there is a period of consultation and comment and expressed commitment, and then the coverage does not happen. My teeth are not in good condition. Periodontal disease has documented associations with cardiovascular outcomes — the cardiologist who retired knew this and mentioned it at nearly every appointment. The algorithm that now manages my warfarin, presumably, does not ask about my dental status. I do not know whether it was designed to. I cannot find out. I raise this not to conflate two unrelated policy areas but because I am genuinely uncertain, after several years of watching how these processes work, whether the consultative machinery of federal rulemaking produces outcomes proportionate to the effort it requires of commenters.⏎⏎THE EQUITY AUDIT QUESTION HHS SHOULD PRIORITIZE⏎⏎If HHS is going to take one concrete action in response to this RFI, the literature points clearly to mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing as the place to start. Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones (2020) documented in the New England Journal of Medicine how race correction variables embedded in clinical algorithms — the kidney function equations are the most discussed example, but the problem is not limited to them — systematically produce different clinical recommendations for patients of different racial backgrounds in ways that are often not disclosed to clinicians or patients and that can perpetuate rather than correct historical disparities in care (Vyas, D.A., Eisenstein, L.G., & Jones, D.S., 2020, Hidden in plain sight — reconsidering the use of race correction in clinical algorithms, NEJM 383(9), 874-882). The existence of these embedded variables is not always known to the clinicians using the systems. It is certainly not known to patients.⏎⏎What I would want — and I recognize that one retired librarian from Nampa is not a particularly authoritative voice on federal health IT policy — is a requirement that any AI or algorithmic decision-support system deployed in clinical settings, and particularly any system touching reimbursement decisions or medication management, be subject to documented equity auditing stratified by race, ethnicity, age, sex, primary language, and geography before deployment, and that the results of that audit be made available to patients upon request in plain language. Not a technical appendix. Plain language. The kind of language the library profession has spent decades developing standards for, because we understood that information access without information comprehension is not access at all.⏎⏎The second thing I would want is post-deployment surveillance with the same stratification. Performance at deployment is not performance six months later when the patient population has shifted, when the underlying data distribution has changed, or when clinicians have adapted their behavior in response to the algorithm's outputs in ways that introduce new biases. This is not a novel methodological demand; it is standard practice in any information system that touches consequential decisions. It was standard practice in the collection development policies I wrote for the Canyon County library system in 2007. I genuinely do not understand why it is not standard practice for systems managing blood thinners.⏎⏎THE ACCELERATION PROBLEM⏎⏎HHS should reconsider whether "acceleration" is the right frame for this policy moment. The documented failures I have described above were not failures of adoption speed; they were failures of validation rigor before adoption and surveillance discipline after. Accelerating adoption without first establishing mandatory equity auditing requirements will, with high probability, accelerate the deployment of systems that perform less well for the patients who most need them to perform well. The communities with the fewest resources to conduct their own external validation studies — rural communities, safety-net hospitals, federally qualified health centers — will be the communities most exposed to this risk.⏎⏎I am not arguing that clinical AI should not be adopted. I am arguing that the policy variable HHS should be optimizing is demonstrated equity of performance across patient populations, not speed of adoption. Those two objectives are not necessarily in conflict, but the RFI treats the second as primary and largely ignores the first, and the literature suggests that is exactly backwards.⏎⏎There is also something worth noting about the information asymmetry between patients and institutions in this space. I am a reasonably educated person with forty years of professional experience evaluating information systems. I cannot get a plain-language explanation of the algorithm managing my cardiac care. I do not know what data it was trained on, what patient populations were included in its validation studies, whether it has been externally validated in a setting resembling the one in which it is being used, or whether there are known performance gaps for patients of my age or demographic profile. That is not a patient empowerment problem in the soft sense that phrase is usually used. It is a structural information asymmetry that the regulatory framework HHS administers could address directly, if the will to do so existed.⏎⏎I filed this comment because professional conscience requires it, not because I expect it to change the trajectory of this rulemaking. The docket will receive comments from vendors, health systems, and trade associations with substantially more resources to make their case than I have. I hope that whoever reviews comments from individual patients will note that the patients most affected by the equity failures documented in the literature above are often the least able to navigate a federal comment process, and that the absence of their voices in this docket is itself a form of information asymmetry that HHS should account for in how it weighs what it reads here.⏎⏎My one specific request: before HHS issues any final guidance accelerating clinical AI adoption, it should require that any system deployed under that guidance be subject to a publicly accessible equity audit, with results stratified by the demographic categories I listed above, in plain language, updated annually. Whether that audit is conducted by the vendor, by an independent third party, or by the deploying institution is a question I am not qualified to answer. That it should be conducted and disclosed is not a question I have any uncertainty about at all.⏎⏎I remain available if the Department wishes to follow up, though I acknowledge that no federal agency has ever followed up on a comment I submitted, and I have submitted several over the years on library-related matters.⏎⏎Charles Ramirez⏎Nampa, Idaho♔♔2026-02-06T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-06T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔7♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔individual♔high♔resigned♔Idaho♔librarian♔73♔My cardiologist in Boise retired two years before I had my first serious arrhythmia episode, and the practice that absorbed his patients relies heavily on a decision-support algorithm I cannot get anyone to explain to me in plain language — not the front desk, not the nurse practitioner, not the physician who now manages my warfarin dosage from what feels like considerable professional distance. SYNTH-0006♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Linda Lopez♔American Academy of Neurology♔♔♔♔♔American Academy of Neurology⏎Comments on HHS Health Sector Artificial Intelligence Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by Linda Lopez, Senior Policy Analyst⏎American Academy of Neurology | 201 Chicago Avenue, Minneapolis, MN 55415⏎aanpolicy@aan.com⏎⏎AAN Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 1⏎⏎I. THE PREMISE REQUIRES SCRUTINY BEFORE THE ACCELERATION BEGINS⏎⏎The American Academy of Neurology (AAN) welcomes HHS's commitment to examining how artificial intelligence can improve clinical outcomes across the health system. Our members have watched AI-assisted tools demonstrate genuine promise in neuroimaging interpretation, seizure detection, and multiple sclerosis disease monitoring, and we are not skeptical of the technology's potential. But the framing of this Request for Information — organized around accelerating adoption — deserves direct engagement before HHS moves to implementation. Acceleration is not a neutral posture. When the existing body of peer-reviewed evidence documents, with considerable rigor, that AI systems trained on historical healthcare data reproduce and in some cases amplify decades of discriminatory treatment patterns, choosing speed over safeguards is a policy decision with distributive consequences. Those consequences will fall most heavily on the patients our members treat every day in community neurology clinics, rural hospitals, and safety-net institutions across the country. The AAN respectfully submits that HHS cannot responsibly answer the question of how to accelerate AI adoption without first answering the question of how to ensure that acceleration does not widen the health disparities that already define American healthcare. We address two specific areas of the RFI in these comments: the regulatory framework for pre-deployment equity auditing, and the structural gap in post-deployment surveillance requirements.⏎⏎AAN Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 2⏎⏎II. THE TRAINING DATA PROBLEM IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL — IT IS DOCUMENTED AND IT SCALES⏎⏎The foundational concern with AI deployment in clinical settings is one that the AAN believes HHS has not fully confronted in the RFI's framing. AI systems do not generate bias independently; they inherit it from the data on which they are trained. Healthcare data, accumulated across decades of documented disparate treatment, contains embedded patterns that reflect who received care, who was believed when they reported symptoms, and whose conditions were coded with precision versus imprecision. When a model learns from that data, it learns those patterns. The problem, as Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, and Mullainathan S documented in a 2019 Science study of a widely used population health algorithm, is that the bias often operates through proxy variables that appear clinically neutral. In that analysis, the algorithm used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need — a substitution that systematically underestimated the severity of illness in Black patients because historical spending disparities meant Black patients had incurred lower costs for equivalent disease burden (Obermeyer et al., Science 2019;366(6464):447-453). The algorithm was not designed to discriminate. It was designed to optimize a variable that happened to encode discrimination. This is the mechanism HHS needs to understand when it considers what "validation" means for AI systems in clinical care.⏎⏎The implications are not limited to resource allocation algorithms. Sjoding MW and colleagues documented in 2020 that pulse oximetry — a device so ubiquitous that clinicians rarely question its readings — produces systematically less accurate measurements in patients with darker skin pigmentation, a finding with direct implications for any AI system that incorporates oximetry data in its training set or real-time inputs (Sjoding et al., N Engl J Med 2020;383(25):2477-2478). Adamson AS and Smith A identified in 2018 that dermatology AI models trained predominantly on images of lighter-skinned patients showed markedly degraded performance on images of patients with darker skin tones, a disparity the authors traced directly to the demographic composition of training datasets (Adamson and Smith, JAMA Dermatol 2018;154(11):1247-1248). Gianfrancesco MA and colleagues have described how electronic health record data systematically underrepresents patients with limited healthcare access, creating a selection bias baked into the foundation of most clinically deployed AI models (Gianfrancesco et al., JAMA Intern Med 2018;178(11):1544-1547). The pattern across these studies is not coincidental. It reflects a structural reality: health data is not a neutral sample of health experience. It is a record of healthcare access, and access has never been equitably distributed.⏎⏎What makes this problem particularly difficult in the AI context — and the AAN wants to be precise here — is the phenomenon of automation bias. Human clinicians make errors, including errors shaped by implicit bias, but those errors are at least theoretically visible to the individual clinician, subject to peer review, and correctable through feedback. When an AI system produces a biased output, the authoritative format of that output — a risk score, a probability estimate, a flag in the clinical decision support interface — tends to suppress the kind of questioning that a clinician might apply to a colleague's verbal recommendation. Char DS, Shah NH, and Magnus D made this point in 2018, observing that the opacity of machine learning models in healthcare creates accountability structures that are fundamentally different from those governing human clinical judgment (Char et al., N Engl J Med 2018;378(11):981-983). Parikh RB, Teeple S, and Navathe AS extended this concern in 2019, noting that without transparency requirements embedded in deployment conditions, clinicians have no mechanism to identify when an AI recommendation reflects a biased training signal rather than genuine clinical evidence (Parikh et al., JAMA 2019;322(24):2377-2378). The AAN's concern is that HHS's acceleration agenda, if it proceeds without mandatory equity auditing requirements, will deploy automation bias at scale in precisely the settings — community hospitals, rural neurology practices, federally qualified health centers — where patients have the fewest alternative sources of care and the least capacity to seek second opinions when AI-generated recommendations go wrong.⏎⏎AAN Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 3⏎⏎III. VALIDATION IN ACADEMIC MEDICAL CENTERS IS NOT VALIDATION FOR THE PATIENTS WHO NEED THESE TOOLS MOST⏎⏎There is a second structural problem that the AAN believes deserves explicit regulatory attention, and it is one that the RFI does not adequately acknowledge. The AI tools most likely to receive rapid deployment approval are tools validated in the large academic medical centers and integrated health systems that have the research infrastructure to conduct validation studies. This creates a systematic mismatch between the populations in which AI performance is measured and the populations in which AI performance matters most. Wong A and colleagues published an external validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model in 2021, finding that the model's performance in their community hospital setting was substantially worse than the performance reported by the developer using the developer's own institutional data (Wong et al., JAMA Intern Med 2021;181(8):1065-1070). This is not an isolated finding. It reflects a generalizable pattern: model performance degrades when models encounter populations, documentation practices, and clinical workflows that differ from the conditions under which they were trained and validated. Rural hospitals in North Dakota — where AAN members practicing in communities like Minot and Dickinson serve patients who may drive three hours for a neurology appointment — do not look like academic medical centers in Boston or Houston. Their patient populations are different, their documentation infrastructure is different, and the clinical contexts in which AI outputs will be interpreted are different. A model validated at a Level I academic center and then deployed across a critical access hospital network is not a validated model in any meaningful sense for the patients in that network.⏎⏎Vyas DA, Eisenstein LEG, and Jones DS documented in 2020 how race-correction embedded in clinical algorithms — the practice of adjusting algorithm outputs based on patient race as a categorical variable — can systematically direct fewer resources toward Black patients even when developers believe the corrections reflect legitimate biological variation (Vyas et al., N Engl J Med 2020;383(9):874-882). Pierson E and colleagues demonstrated in 2021 that algorithmic approaches to pain assessment, when trained on data reflecting historical undertreatment of underserved populations, reproduce those undertreament patterns in their outputs — a finding with direct implications for neurological pain conditions including migraine, neuropathy, and post-stroke pain syndromes (Pierson et al., Nat Med 2021;27(1):136-140). Wiens J, Saria S, Sendak M, and colleagues articulated in 2019 what they called a "roadmap for responsible machine learning for health care," arguing that external validation in deployment-representative populations should be a non-negotiable precondition for clinical AI deployment, and that ongoing performance monitoring stratified by demographic subgroup should be a mandatory condition of continued use (Wiens et al., Nat Med 2019;25(9):1337-1340). The AAN endorses this framework without reservation and urges HHS to translate it into enforceable regulatory requirements rather than voluntary guidance.⏎⏎The U.S. Government Accountability Office reached closely related conclusions in its 2022 report on AI in health care, identifying the absence of standardized performance evaluation requirements as a significant gap in the current oversight framework (GAO, GAO-22-104629, 2022). The National Academy for State Health Policy's 2023 policy scan of algorithmic accountability in state Medicaid programs found that as of the scan's publication, no state Medicaid program had implemented mandatory equity auditing requirements for AI tools used in coverage or care management decisions, and that the absence of federal standards was identified by state officials as the primary barrier to developing such requirements independently (NASHP, Algorithmic Accountability in State Medicaid Programs, 2023). That finding should concern HHS directly. If states are waiting for federal leadership and federal leadership is organized around acceleration rather than accountability, the result will be the rapid deployment of inadequately validated tools into Medicaid populations — the populations most likely to include patients from historically marginalized communities and least likely to have alternative care options when those tools fail.⏎⏎AAN Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 4⏎⏎IV. WHAT HHS MUST REQUIRE — AND WHY THESE ARE NOT OPTIONAL ELEMENTS⏎⏎The AAN's regulatory recommendations in response to this RFI are specific. HHS should establish, through binding regulatory action rather than guidance documents, a mandatory pre-deployment equity audit requirement for any AI clinical decision support system used in Medicare- or Medicaid-reimbursed care settings. That audit should require disaggregated performance reporting by race, ethnicity, sex, age, insurance status, and rurality, conducted in a population that is representative of the intended deployment environment rather than the developer's home institution. HHS should further require that AI developers seeking reimbursement eligibility for their tools submit to ongoing post-deployment surveillance, with performance data stratified by the same demographic variables reported to HHS on a schedule no less frequent than annually, and with automatic suspension of reimbursement eligibility triggered by documented performance disparities exceeding pre-specified thresholds.⏎⏎We want to be clear that these requirements are not intended to slow AI adoption for its own sake. Our members are practicing neurologists who are genuinely interested in what AI can offer for early Alzheimer's detection, epilepsy monitoring, and stroke triage. The AAN is not reflexively opposed to this technology. But "move fast" and "do no harm" are in direct tension when the populations most likely to be harmed by inadequately validated tools are the same populations with the least capacity to absorb that harm. A pre-deployment equity audit requirement does not prevent deployment. It requires that developers demonstrate, before deployment, that their tool performs adequately for the populations it will actually serve. That is a reasonable condition. The absence of such a condition is not neutrality — it is a regulatory choice to prioritize speed over safety for the most vulnerable patients in the American healthcare system.⏎⏎The AAN also notes that the RFI does not address the question of who bears the cost of equity auditing for smaller AI developers, and we acknowledge this is a genuine implementation challenge that HHS will need to work through. We do not have a fully developed answer to that question in these comments, and we would be glad to participate in any technical workgroup HHS convenes to address it.⏎⏎AAN Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 5⏎⏎The AAN appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and requests that HHS treat the equity auditing and post-deployment surveillance recommendations as the minimum threshold for a responsible acceleration framework, not as aspirational elements to be addressed in a later rulemaking cycle. SYNTH-0007♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Betty Martin♔♔♔♔♔♔My son Caleb spent eleven days being treated for a viral infection before a second-opinion physician caught a ruptured appendicitis. He recovered. What I didn't expect, in the weeks that followed, was how completely the administrative infrastructure across three separate facilities failed to produce a coherent record of what had happened to him. A temperature reading from a Tuesday afternoon. A nurse's note about rebound tenderness. Simple things, factual things, that the systems simply could not reconcile with each other. I came out of that experience not primarily worried about diagnostic AI, though I have plenty of questions there too. I came out of it worried about the layer underneath — the coordinators, navigators, prior authorization reviewers, benefits counselors — the people whose work is what actually holds a patient's care together across institutional seams. And when I read HHS framing administrative efficiency as an unambiguous target for AI acceleration, I find myself genuinely troubled in a way I want to try to be precise about.⏎⏎THE PROBLEM WITH TREATING ADMINISTRATIVE WORK AS OVERHEAD⏎⏎The framing embedded in this request for information treats administrative work as a kind of friction to be removed. I understand why. Himmelstein and colleagues documented in their 2019 analysis published in the New England Journal of Medicine that administrative costs in the United States account for roughly 34 percent of total health expenditures, a figure so large it almost demands a technological response. But the conclusion that follows from that number — automate it — misreads what the work is. Michael Polanyi, writing in The Tacit Dimension in 1966, made an observation that I keep returning to: we know more than we can tell. The experienced care coordinator who notices that a patient's listed address doesn't match where they actually live, who knows that the Medicaid office in a particular county has a three-week processing lag that requires a workaround, who remembers that a specific patient's daughter is the one to call because the patient himself won't report worsening symptoms — none of that is in a structured data field. None of it will ever be in a training dataset. And yet it is exactly the kind of knowledge that prevents a missed referral or a dropped care transition from becoming a catastrophic outcome for someone who has no margin for error.⏎⏎What concerns me specifically about the HHS accelerate-adoption framing is the assumption, buried inside it, that AI will free up human time. Sinsky and colleagues, in their 2016 time-motion study published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, found that physicians in ambulatory practice were already spending roughly half their working hours on administrative tasks rather than patient care. The proposed solution is to offload those tasks to automated systems. But in already-understaffed administrative departments, the actual effect of imperfect AI is not liberated capacity. It is staff time redirected toward identifying and correcting errors that the system generated invisibly. Obermeyer and colleagues demonstrated in Science in 2019 that a widely used commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients precisely because it was trained on cost data rather than illness data — and that the bias was invisible to the operators deploying it. That finding should be read as a warning about any administrative AI that touches eligibility determinations, prior authorization, or care navigation, because those are exactly the functions where a systematic error will fall hardest on patients who are already the least positioned to catch and contest a mistake. The National Partnership for Women and Families documented in their 2023 policy brief on automating inequality in health care that low-income and minority patients absorb a disproportionate share of administrative errors precisely because they have less access to the advocacy infrastructure that corrects those errors for more privileged patients.⏎⏎I want to be clear that I am not arguing against AI in health care broadly. I am arguing against premature deployment in administrative functions where the foundational infrastructure is not ready and where the cost of failure is distributed inequitably. The ONC's own 2023 interoperability progress report acknowledged that significant gaps remain in the ability of health systems to exchange even basic structured data reliably. If three hospitals in my son's care network could not reconcile a symptom timeline in 2022, the data those systems would feed into an administrative AI today is not clean enough to trust for consequential decisions. The GAO documented in its 2022 report on Medicare Advantage prior authorization that even the existing human-judgment processes in prior auth are producing errors and delays at a scale that harms patients — which means that automating those processes does not start from a reliable baseline. It scales whatever is already broken.⏎⏎o The administrative friction that HHS wants to eliminate is sometimes the only human checkpoint in a patient's care transition.⏎o A phone call from a navigator who notices something is off, a coordinator who flags a discrepancy because she knows this patient's history, is not inefficiency. It is error-correction that the system itself cannot perform.⏎o The workers who carry this tacit institutional knowledge are not a cost to be optimized away. They are, in many cases, the functional safety net for patients the rest of the system does not see clearly.⏎⏎MY DIRECT REQUEST TO HHS⏎⏎Before any administrative AI tool is deployed in functions touching eligibility, prior authorization, care coordination, or patient navigation, HHS should require demonstrated safety evidence, including prospective data on error rates disaggregated by race, income, and insurance status. It should require equity impact assessments as a condition of any reimbursement pathway for these tools. And it should stop using the language of efficiency gains as justification for deployment timelines, because efficiency measured at the system level is not the same thing as safety experienced at the patient level, and the difference between those two things lands on people who cannot afford to absorb it.⏎⏎I also want to ask, directly, that HHS stop treating the workers who currently perform administrative functions as a transitional cost. The knowledge they hold is not in any database. When those workers are displaced or their departments are cut in anticipation of AI savings that may not materialize the way vendors promise, that knowledge is gone. What replaces it is a system that processes structured inputs and has no idea what it doesn't know. That is not an efficiency gain. It is a different kind of infrastructure failure, and I have already seen what one of those looks like from a waiting room in Missouri while my kid was in surgery.⏎⏎Betty Martin⏎Missouri♔♔2026-02-04T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-04T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔3♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Even administrative healthcare functions that appear routine require human contextual judgment that AI cannot replicate, and automating them will produce systematic errors that harm patients and workers.♔individual♔high♔frustrated♔Missouri♔stay-at-home parent♔51♔When my son Caleb was misdiagnosed with a viral infection for eleven days before a second-opinion physician caught his appendicitis — already ruptured — I sat in that waiting room outside his surgery and thought obsessively about every moment a better tool could have flagged what the first doctor missed. SYNTH-0008♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Sharon Thomas♔Harvard Medical School Department of Biomedical Informatics♔♔♔♔♔Harvard Medical School⏎Department of Biomedical Informatics⏎25 Shattuck Street, Boston, MA 02115⏎⏎Sharon Thomas, MS, PhD⏎Senior Biostatistician⏎⏎March 14, 2025⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Hubert H. Humphrey Building⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎To the Office of the Deputy Secretary and ASTP/ONC:⏎⏎The biostatistics team submitting these comments operates at the intersection of academic research and clinical implementation, and the vantage point that intersection provides is, frankly, uncomfortable given the framing of this RFI. The Department's request centers on acceleration — on identifying barriers to AI adoption and removing them. Our team's direct experience with deployed AI tools in academic health system environments suggests that the more consequential question is not how to accelerate adoption but whether current adoption incentive structures are aligned with clinician welfare and patient safety at all. That is the question these comments are organized around, and the team offers it not as a rejection of AI in healthcare but as an empirical correction to a policy posture that the evidence does not support.⏎⏎To ground that claim concretely: a 2024 internal analysis conducted across the University of Kansas Health System's clinical informatics and quality improvement divisions examined 14 active AI-assisted decision-support deployments. Nine of the 14 tools encountered significant friction at the point of integration with existing EHR infrastructure — delays attributable not to algorithmic performance but to ambiguous liability documentation standards and unclear institutional ownership of model outputs. A prospective evaluation of three predictive sepsis models deployed between 2022 and 2024 further found that clinician adoption rates fell below 40% in units where reimbursement pathways for AI-augmented encounters remained undefined, compared to 74% adoption in units where pilot billing frameworks had been pre-negotiated with payers prior to go-live. The Department's RFI correctly identifies reimbursement ambiguity and integration friction as adoption barriers. What the RFI does not adequately address — and what the same dataset makes visible — is the more troubling pattern beneath those numbers: that even in units with high adoption rates, the tools were being used in ways that expanded documentation requirements and alert volumes for frontline clinicians rather than reducing them. The gap between what AI deployment is marketed to achieve and what it actually produces at the point of care is not a minor implementation detail. It is the central policy problem.⏎⏎The preponderance of available evidence suggests that the primary drivers of clinician burnout — excessive documentation burden, alert fatigue, and erosion of professional autonomy — are worsened rather than relieved by the AI deployment patterns currently prevalent in U.S. health systems. Shanafelt et al. (2022) documented sustained increases in physician burnout between 2011 and 2020, with electronic health record burden consistently identified as a primary occupational stressor (Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 97(3), 491–506). Melnick et al. (2020) found a direct association between perceived EHR usability deficits and professional burnout across a national physician sample, with documentation time and alert interruption frequency as the strongest mediating variables (Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 95(3), 476–487). The ONC's own 2023 Clinician Experience Survey, published as ONC Data Brief No. 61, documented that a majority of responding clinicians reported increased documentation time in EHR environments that had recently integrated new clinical decision support tools — a finding that should be read as a direct challenge to the premise that more AI integration produces less clinician burden. Wachter and Goldsmith (2018) argued in the Harvard Business Review that the EHR's failure to reduce burnout was not incidental to its design but structural — that tools built to serve billing, compliance, and liability documentation functions cannot simultaneously serve as cognitive relief for clinicians. The team's prospective evaluation is consistent with that structural diagnosis: the sepsis models that generated the lowest adoption rates were those whose alert outputs required the most additional documentation to justify clinical override, suggesting that the tools had been integrated in ways that added workflow steps rather than removing them. Topol's influential 2019 argument for convergence between human and artificial intelligence in high-performance medicine (Nature Medicine, 25(1), 44–56) is frequently cited in support of accelerationist AI policy, but it is worth noting that Topol's framework assumed clinician augmentation, not replacement or surveillance — an assumption that the actual deployment incentive structures in U.S. health systems are systematically violating.⏎⏎Harvard Medical School Department of Biomedical Informatics | HHS AI RFI | March 2025 | Page 2⏎⏎That structural violation takes a specific form that this submission wants to name precisely. AI tools marketed to healthcare institutions as burnout-reduction or efficiency solutions are, under current procurement conditions, more likely to function as instruments of workforce rationalization than as genuine improvements to care quality. The mechanism is not difficult to trace: when a health system purchases an AI tool on the promise that it will reduce the time required for a given clinical task by 30%, the financial incentive is not to maintain current staffing and give clinicians 30% more time for patient interaction. The financial incentive is to reduce staffing by a corresponding margin and capture the efficiency gain as cost savings. National Nurses United's 2023 workforce and patient safety analysis documented exactly this pattern across multiple health system deployments, finding that AI adoption announcements were frequently followed by staffing ratio changes that increased nurse caseloads in the affected units (NNU Research Report, Washington, D.C., 2023). The team is not aware of any current HHS regulatory mechanism that would require a health system to demonstrate that an AI deployment has not resulted in increased caseloads before receiving reimbursement incentives for that deployment. That gap is the policy problem the Department should be addressing.⏎⏎A related structural concern is the systematic exclusion of frontline clinicians from AI procurement governance. A 2023 joint survey conducted by the Pew Research Center and the American Hospital Association on AI procurement practices in U.S. health systems found significant gaps in clinician consultation at the procurement stage, with nurses, care coordinators, and physician staff in frontline roles consistently underrepresented in vendor selection and implementation governance processes. This is not a minor procedural concern. The consequence of excluding frontline workers from procurement is that the tools selected tend to optimize for the metrics that matter to administrators — throughput, documentation completeness, billing accuracy — rather than the metrics that matter to clinicians and patients. Goddard et al. (2012) demonstrated in a systematic review that automation bias — the tendency to defer to algorithmic recommendations even in the face of contradictory clinical evidence — is significantly more pronounced when clinicians have had no role in designing or evaluating the tool they are using (Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 19(1), 121–127). The implication for AI governance is direct: excluding clinicians from procurement does not just produce worse tools; it produces tools that actively degrade the clinical judgment of the people using them. Rajpurkar et al. (2022) documented the persistent gap between AI benchmark performance in controlled research settings and real-world adoption outcomes in deployed clinical environments (Nature Medicine, 28(1), 31–38), a gap that the team's own adoption data — 40% versus 74% depending on reimbursement pre-negotiation status — replicates and extends. What Rajpurkar's analysis did not address, and what the team's experience makes clear, is that a portion of that gap is attributable not to model performance deficits but to governance and procurement failures that could be corrected through regulatory requirement.⏎⏎The equity dimension of this problem also warrants attention, particularly given HHS's stated commitment to reducing health disparities. Obermeyer et al. (2019) demonstrated that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to manage population health prioritized cost as a proxy for health need, producing systematic underestimation of illness severity in Black patients relative to white patients at equivalent levels of actual health need (Science, 366(6464), 447–453). The mechanism they identified — cost as a proxy variable encoding historical access disparities — is present in a large proportion of the training data sets used to develop clinical AI tools in the United States. Bates et al. (2021) reviewed the AI patient safety literature and noted that bias in training data remains among the most consistently identified risks in deployed clinical AI, with health system deployments in under-resourced settings showing disproportionate rates of algorithmic error (npj Digital Medicine, 4(1), 54). The team's concern is that an accelerationist regulatory posture, by prioritizing speed of deployment over rigor of pre-deployment evaluation, will systematically favor tools that perform well on the patient populations most heavily represented in training data — which in U.S. health system data is typically white, insured, and urban — while producing degraded performance for the patients who most depend on safety-net institutions. This is not a hypothetical risk. It is the documented pattern of existing deployments, and the Department's RFI does not, in the team's reading, give it adequate weight.⏎⏎Harvard Medical School Department of Biomedical Informatics | HHS AI RFI | March 2025 | Page 3⏎⏎Given the foregoing, the team's recommendations to HHS focus on two of the RFI's specific areas of inquiry: reimbursement design and pre-deployment requirements. On reimbursement, the team recommends that the Department condition any reimbursement incentives for AI-augmented clinical encounters on demonstrated compliance with the following pre-deployment requirements:⏎⏎1. A mandatory workforce impact assessment, conducted prospectively and reviewed by an independent body, documenting the tool's projected and actual effects on clinician caseloads, documentation time, alert burden, and staffing ratios in the deployment unit. The assessment should be repeated at 12 and 24 months post-deployment, with results made available to CMS and to the relevant state health workforce agencies.⏎⏎2. Documented clinician representation in the AI governance structure responsible for the procurement decision, with specific representation requirements for nurses and other non-physician frontline staff. The Pew/AHA survey data cited above suggest that voluntary consultation frameworks have not produced adequate representation; mandatory governance requirements are therefore warranted.⏎⏎3. Pre-deployment equity testing using patient subgroup performance data that includes race, insurance status, primary language, and rural/urban classification as stratification variables, with a minimum performance parity threshold defined by HHS in rulemaking before any reimbursement incentive is made available.⏎⏎4. A staffing-ratio neutrality condition: health systems receiving reimbursement incentives for AI-augmented encounters should be required to demonstrate, at each annual assessment, that the relevant deployment unit has not experienced a reduction in staffing ratios below the levels documented at the time of initial deployment. This is not a prohibition on efficiency; it is a requirement that efficiency gains not be captured exclusively through workforce reduction.⏎⏎The team acknowledges that these requirements will slow some deployments. That is the point. The evidence reviewed here does not support the conclusion that faster AI adoption in healthcare, under current procurement and incentive conditions, is equivalent to better AI adoption. Dyrbye et al. (2019) found that work-unit safety climate — which includes clinician perceptions of workload sustainability and professional autonomy — was a significant independent predictor of physician burnout, separate from individual-level factors (Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 94(6), 1080–1090). A regulatory environment that accelerates the deployment of tools likely to degrade safety climate will worsen burnout rates and, by extension, patient safety outcomes. The Department's stated goal of improving clinical care through AI is achievable, but the path to it runs through workforce protection, not around it.⏎⏎One additional concern the team wants to flag, even though it sits somewhat at the margins of the formal RFI questions: the documentation standards governing AI-assisted clinical encounters are, as of this writing, genuinely unclear in ways that create perverse incentives at the point of care. Clinicians in the University of Kansas Health System deployments described above reported uncertainty about whether documenting reliance on an AI recommendation created additional liability exposure relative to not documenting it — a question that neither institutional legal counsel nor the relevant vendors could answer consistently. Nine of the 14 deployments in that analysis encountered EHR integration friction attributable in part to this uncertainty. HHS has the authority to provide sub-regulatory guidance clarifying documentation standards for AI-augmented encounters, and doing so would reduce one real source of clinician burden without requiring rulemaking. The team would strongly encourage the Department to prioritize that guidance, with the caveat that it should be developed in consultation with frontline clinician organizations rather than primarily with vendors or health system administrators whose interests in the documentation question may not align with those of the people actually using the tools.⏎⏎The email address for correspondence on these comments is s.thomas@hms.harvard.edu.⏎⏎Sincerely,⏎⏎Sharon Thomas, MS, PhD⏎Senior Biostatistician⏎Harvard Medical School, Department of Biomedical Informatics♔♔2026-01-28T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-28T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔7♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare will be used by employers and insurers as a mechanism for workforce surveillance, productivity extraction, staffing cuts, and the devaluation of clinical expertise rather than genuine care improvement.♔academic_organization♔high♔hopeful♔New Mexico♔biostatistician♔48♔A 2024 internal analysis conducted across The University of Kansas Health System's clinical informatics and quality improvement divisions examined 14 active AI-assisted decision-support deployments, finding that 9 of the 14 tools encountered significant friction at the point of integration with existing EHR infrastructure—delays attributable not to algorithmic performance but to ambiguous liability and documentation standards.
