SYNTH-0009♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Michael Hall♔American Urological Association♔♔♔♔♔American Urological Association⏎Comments Submitted to the Docket⏎HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎89 Fed. Reg. 102456 (Dec. 18, 2024)⏎Submitted by: Michael Hall, Senior Policy Analyst⏎American Urological Association⏎⏎AUA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-OD-2024-0019 | Page 1⏎⏎⏎THE ACCOUNTABILITY VACUUM PRECEDING PROPOSED ACCELERATION⏎⏎The American Urological Association (AUA) submits these comments in response to the Department's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. The AUA represents more than 24,000 urologic surgeons and physicians across the United States, a substantial portion of whom are now practicing in environments where AI-assisted clinical decision support tools are operationally present whether or not those physicians sought them out or were trained to use them. The AUA's 2024 member survey, conducted in coordination with a regional policy review panel convened across three summits held during calendar year 2024, found that 58% of responding physicians reported access to at least one AI-assisted clinical tool in their practice setting. Fewer than a quarter of those physicians reported receiving any formal guidance from payers or federal agencies on liability standards, documentation requirements, or reimbursement pathways associated with AI-generated clinical recommendations. The AUA raises this data not as background context but as the central empirical fact the Department should be confronting in this rulemaking proceeding: the acceleration the RFI proposes has, in meaningful respects, already occurred, and the accountability infrastructure that should have preceded it does not exist.⏎⏎The Department's RFI, at 89 Fed. Reg. 102456, frames its inquiry around regulatory facilitation, reimbursement pathway development, and interoperability improvements to bring AI tools more fully into clinical workflows. The AUA does not dispute that these are legitimate areas of federal interest. What the AUA disputes, with considerable professional urgency, is the premise embedded in that framing — that the primary constraints on beneficial AI adoption are technical and financial rather than legal and structural. Price, Gerke, and Cohen, writing in JAMA in 2019, identified the liability exposure facing physicians who rely on AI-generated recommendations as both legally unsettled and practically asymmetric: the physician bears clinical accountability under existing malpractice doctrine while the vendor retains significant insulation through product liability frameworks that were not designed with clinical decision support in mind (Price WN II, Gerke S, Cohen IG, "Potential Liability for Physicians Using Artificial Intelligence," JAMA, 2019;322(18):1765–1766). That observation was made five years ago. The legal landscape has not materially changed. The deployment of AI tools into clinical settings has accelerated dramatically in the interim. The AUA's member physicians are the ones absorbing the resulting risk.⏎⏎⏎AUA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-OD-2024-0019 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE STRUCTURAL DESIGN OF LIABILITY DIFFUSION⏎⏎The liability problem the AUA is describing is not, the organization wishes to be precise about this, simply a gap in existing doctrine that further regulatory guidance could patch. It is a structural feature of how AI intermediation in clinical care is currently architected. When an AI-assisted clinical error causes patient harm, three credible deflection narratives become simultaneously available to the parties involved:⏎⏎1. The treating clinician asserts that the AI tool generated the recommendation and that the clinician's own judgment was exercised appropriately given the information available.⏎⏎2. The hospital or health system asserts that the tool was implemented according to vendor specifications and that any failure reflects either the vendor's algorithm or the clinician's misapplication of the output.⏎⏎3. The AI vendor asserts that the tool performed within its validated parameters, that the training data disclosed its limitations, and that responsibility for clinical integration rests with the deploying institution.⏎⏎This is not a hypothetical sequence. Delvaux, Ketterer, and colleagues, in a comparative review published in the Journal of Law and the Biosciences, documented precisely this deflection architecture across multiple national liability frameworks and concluded that no existing legal system has produced a coherent mechanism for compelling accountability to any single party when AI intermediates a clinical decision (Delvaux N, Ketterer F, Detollenaere J, et al., "Liability Frameworks for Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Settings: A Comparative Review," Journal of Law and the Biosciences, 2023;10(1):lsad004). The result, as the AUA understands it from the lived professional experience of its members, is that injured patients face a system in which every party possesses a credible deflection narrative and no party faces a structural incentive to accept responsibility. Traditional malpractice doctrine, as Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert documented in JAMA in 2020, functions on the foundational assumption that a human decision-maker can be identified and that the quality of that decision can be evaluated against a professional standard of care (Mello MM, Frakes MD, Blumenkranz E, Studdert DM, "Malpractice Liability and Health Care Quality," JAMA, 2020;323(4):352–366). AI intermediation disrupts both assumptions. The decision-maker is partially algorithmic and therefore not subject to the same standard-of-care analysis. The quality of the AI's contribution is often opaque even to the clinician who relied on it, a problem Obermeyer and Emanuel flagged in their 2016 New England Journal of Medicine analysis of machine learning in clinical medicine, where they noted that the interpretability constraints of high-performance predictive models create accountability problems that technical validation alone cannot resolve (Obermeyer Z, Emanuel EJ, "Predicting the Future — Big Data, Machine Learning, and Clinical Medicine," N Engl J Med, 2016;375:1216–1219).⏎⏎The AUA raises this not to argue against AI adoption categorically. The organization's member physicians are using these tools now, and many report genuine clinical value from them, particularly in diagnostic imaging review and pathology flagging applications relevant to urologic oncology. Topol's 2019 analysis in Nature Medicine documented meaningful performance gains in AI-assisted diagnostic accuracy that the AUA does not dismiss (Topol EJ, "High-Performance Medicine: The Convergence of Human and Artificial Intelligence," Nature Medicine, 2019;25:44–56). The argument is different: clinical benefit does not eliminate the need for accountability infrastructure, and the Department's RFI treats the two as separable questions when they are in fact structurally linked.⏎⏎⏎AUA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-OD-2024-0019 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE PROBLEM OF INSTITUTIONAL LOCK-IN AND AUDIT IMPOSSIBILITY⏎⏎The AUA is particularly concerned with one dimension of the acceleration question that the RFI does not address at all, which is the relationship between deployment scale and the feasibility of post-deployment accountability enforcement. Sendak, Elish, Gao, and colleagues, writing in the proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency in 2020, documented the degree to which AI systems embedded in clinical workflows generate operational dependencies that make those systems difficult to audit, challenge, or remove without disrupting care delivery (Sendak MP, Elish MC, Gao M, et al., "The Human Body Is a Black Box: Supporting Clinical Decision-Making with Deep Learning," Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, 2020:99–109). This is not a theoretical concern. It reflects a well-documented pattern in health information technology implementation more broadly, where systems that become load-bearing infrastructure within clinical workflows acquire a form of institutional protection that insulates them from the kind of critical scrutiny that should accompany any tool influencing patient care decisions. When CMS billing infrastructure or reimbursement incentives are layered on top of AI tool deployment, as the RFI contemplates, that lock-in becomes significantly harder to reverse. A hospital system that has structured its documentation workflows, its prior authorization submissions, and its quality reporting around an AI tool that is later found to produce systematically biased outputs — and Hoffman and Podgurski's 2019 Yale Journal of Health Policy, Law, and Ethics analysis documented the scope of this risk in clinical AI contexts — faces an enforcement environment in which the cost of compliance with any corrective mandate is prohibitive enough to create enormous regulatory resistance (Hoffman S, Podgurski A, "Artificial Intelligence and Discrimination in Health Care," Yale Journal of Health Policy, Law, and Ethics, 2019;19(3):1–51).⏎⏎The AUA is not arguing that the Department should refuse to develop reimbursement pathways for AI-assisted clinical services. The organization understands that reimbursement signals are among the most powerful levers available to HHS for shaping clinical practice, and the AUA's rural and independent practice members — who face disproportionate implementation cost barriers that the 2024 regional summits documented with particular consistency — would benefit from reimbursement structures that make validated tools accessible outside of large academic health system environments. What the AUA is arguing is that the sequence matters enormously. Embedding these tools before accountability frameworks exist does not merely leave a gap to be filled later. It actively produces conditions in which later accountability enforcement becomes structurally impractical.⏎⏎The European AI Act framework, analyzed by Cohen, Evgeniou, Gerke, and Minssen in the Harvard Law Review Forum in 2022, adopted a precondition model for high-risk AI applications — requiring demonstrated conformity assessment and clear accountability assignment before deployment rather than after — precisely because the European regulatory drafters recognized that post-deployment enforcement of accountability standards against embedded systems is a qualitatively different and substantially harder problem than pre-deployment accountability assignment (Cohen IG, Evgeniou T, Gerke S, Minssen T, "The European Artificial Intelligence Act and the Future of AI Governance," Harvard Law Review Forum, 2022;135:232–261). The United States has not adopted an equivalent framework for clinical AI. The RFI does not propose one. The AUA believes this is the most consequential omission in the Department's current approach.⏎⏎⏎AUA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-OD-2024-0019 | Page 4⏎⏎⏎THE PHYSICIAN-PATIENT RELATIONSHIP AND THE MORAL DIMENSION⏎⏎The AUA also wishes to register, briefly but clearly, that the accountability concern here is not reducible to litigation risk or regulatory compliance exposure. The American Medical Association's policy framework on augmented intelligence, AMA Policy H-480.940 (2023), affirms that AI tools in clinical settings must be designed and deployed in ways that preserve physician accountability to patients and that the physician-patient relationship requires an identifiable human being who is answerable for clinical decisions. This is a foundational ethical commitment, not merely a policy preference. Patients who are harmed in AI-assisted clinical encounters have a right to a specific, answerable human being who bears responsibility for the care they received. The structural diffusion of accountability that the current deployment model produces is not merely a litigation inconvenience — it represents a failure of the basic moral architecture of the physician-patient relationship. Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen, in their 2020 Academic Press analysis of ethical and legal challenges in AI-driven healthcare, framed this concern as one that regulatory frameworks must treat as a first-order constraint rather than a downstream consideration (Gerke S, Minssen T, Cohen G, "Ethical and Legal Challenges of Artificial Intelligence-Driven Healthcare," Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare, Academic Press, 2020:295–336). The AUA agrees with that framing entirely.⏎⏎The National Academy for State Health Policy's February 2024 review of state legislative and regulatory action on healthcare AI documented that at least fourteen states had introduced or enacted legislation in 2023 addressing AI accountability in clinical settings, reflecting a growing recognition at the state level that federal inaction on this question is producing a fragmented and potentially inconsistent accountability environment (National Academy for State Health Policy, "State Legislative and Regulatory Action on Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: 2023 Year in Review," NASHP Report, February 2024). The AUA notes that state-level variation in AI accountability standards creates additional compliance complexity for multi-state physician practices and health systems, and that a coherent federal framework — one the RFI is positioned to initiate but has not yet proposed — would serve the interests of both patients and providers more effectively than the current patchwork.⏎⏎⏎AUA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-OD-2024-0019 | Page 5⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY REQUEST⏎⏎The AUA respectfully requests that HHS condition any regulatory facilitation or reimbursement pathway development for AI-assisted clinical tools on prior demonstration of a clear, enforceable accountability framework that satisfies the following requirements:⏎⏎1. Identification of a responsible human party — whether clinician, institution, or vendor — who bears primary accountability for AI-assisted clinical decisions that result in patient harm, with no exception granted on the basis of algorithmic complexity or system novelty.⏎⏎2. Enforceable vendor disclosure obligations requiring that AI tool developers provide deploying institutions and treating clinicians with sufficient information about model limitations, known failure modes, and validation populations to permit meaningful clinical judgment about when AI output should and should not be relied upon.⏎⏎3. Pre-deployment audit requirements for AI tools classified as high-risk under any HHS risk stratification framework, conducted by entities with no financial relationship to the tool's developer, with results made available to CMS and ONC prior to reimbursement eligibility determination.⏎⏎4. A structured post-market surveillance mechanism that does not depend on voluntary vendor reporting and that creates enforceable obligations to remove or restrict AI tools found to produce systematically biased or harmful outputs — regardless of the operational disruption that removal may cause to deploying institutions.⏎⏎The AUA recognizes that these requirements would slow the acceleration the RFI envisions. That is, from the organization's perspective, precisely the point. The member physicians of the AUA are already operating in an accountability vacuum with respect to AI tools they are actively using in clinical practice. Scaling that vacuum before⏎⏎AUA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-OD-2024-0019 | Page 6⏎⏎remediation exists does not serve patients, does not serve physicians, and does not serve the long-term credibility of federal health AI policy. The AUA would welcome the opportunity to engage further with ASTP/ONC staff on the development of a pre-deployment accountability framework and can make available the member survey data and regional summit findings referenced in these comments upon request.⏎⏎mhall@auanet.org⏎www.auanet.org/policy♔♔2026-01-18T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-18T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔7♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔supportive♔New Hampshire♔senior policy analyst♔61♔A 2024 TMA member survey of 4,200 practicing physicians across Texas found that 58% had access to at least one AI-assisted clinical tool in their practice setting, yet fewer than a quarter reported receiving any formal guidance from payers or federal agencies on liability standards, documentation requirements, or reimbursement pathways associated with AI-generated clinical recommendations. SYNTH-0010♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Joseph Sanchez♔Leidos Health♔♔♔♔♔Leidos Health | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 1⏎⏎⏎Leidos Health submits this comment in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care settings. Leidos Health provides compliance infrastructure, operational oversight, and regulatory advisory services across a substantial portfolio of long-term care and post-acute facilities. The specific operational data referenced herein draws from compliance monitoring conducted in partnership with Tapestryhealth's Compliance Division, whose 2024 Cross-Facility Workflow and AI Readiness Audit (March 2024) spans 47 long-term care facilities serving approximately 9,200 residents. That audit provides the evidentiary basis for this submission. This comment addresses the Department's solicitation primarily on the question of regulatory accountability frameworks as a precondition for adoption, because our compliance team's field experience is that the absence of a coherent accountability architecture is a more immediate adoption barrier than cost or infrastructure constraints. Whether HHS ultimately agrees with that framing or not, we believe the doctrinal gaps described below warrant serious attention before any accelerated adoption pathway is formalized.⏎⏎⏎ACCOUNTABILITY DIFFUSION AS A SYSTEMS-DESIGN PROBLEM⏎⏎⏎The 2024 Tapestryhealth audit found that 81% of facility administrators operating under value-based care arrangements reported uncertainty about whether AI-generated clinical recommendations would be defensible under current survey and certification standards, including the participation requirements codified at 42 C.F.R. Part 483 (2023 ed.). That figure does not reflect technophobia or budget constraints. It reflects a rational compliance posture in the face of genuinely unresolved legal questions about causal attribution when an adverse clinical outcome follows an AI-assisted recommendation. The existing tort framework, as analyzed by Brown and Krause in their examination of algorithmic physician liability (Journal of Law and the Biosciences, 2021, 8(1):lsab019), does not map cleanly onto multi-party AI deployment chains where the treating clinician, the deploying facility, the EHR vendor, and the AI model developer each hold partial information and partial control. The respondeat superior doctrine and conventional duty-of-care analysis were not designed for this architecture. Price and Gerke made a related observation in their 2019 JAMA piece on physician liability for AI use (322(18):1765-1766), noting that physicians who rely on AI outputs without adequate interpretive context may face liability exposure that neither they nor their institutions fully understand at the point of deployment.⏎⏎Leidos Health | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎This is not a theoretical concern for our compliance team. When facility administrators in our portfolio are asked why they have not piloted AI-driven risk stratification tools despite expressed interest, they cite the following (drawn directly from the March 2024 audit summary):⏎⏎1.  Absence of explicit ONC or CMS guidance on which entity in the deployment chain bears primary liability for a care decision influenced by an AI recommendation.⏎2.  No established standard for what constitutes adequate clinical override documentation when a clinician departs from an AI-generated recommendation, and whether that documentation satisfies the survey and certification requirements under 42 C.F.R. Part 483.⏎3.  Uncertainty about whether AI-generated outputs used in care planning constitute "clinical decision support" for reimbursement purposes under current CMS definitions, a gap the ONC's 2023 Report to Congress (Annual Update on the Adoption of Health Information Technology) acknowledged without resolving.⏎4.  The absence of any post-market surveillance obligation on AI vendors that would give facility compliance officers recourse when model drift degrades performance after initial deployment.⏎⏎Cohen, Amarasingham, Shah, and colleagues identified the foundational version of this problem in their 2014 Health Affairs analysis of complex predictive analytics in health care (33(7):1139-1147), observing that the legal and ethical frameworks governing clinical decision-making had not been updated to account for probabilistic algorithmic outputs. A decade later, the gap has widened rather than closed. Pasquale's analysis of algorithmic opacity (The Black Box Society, Harvard University Press, 2015) remains relevant here: when the reasoning process of a clinical AI tool is not accessible to the compliance officer, the treating clinician, or the facility administrator, the standard accountability mechanisms that survey and certification processes depend on cannot function as designed. The GAO reached a similar structural conclusion in GAO-21-7SP (November 2020), finding that the benefits of health care AI tools are materially constrained by the absence of governance frameworks that specify accountability at each point in the deployment chain.⏎⏎Sawicki's 2022 analysis in the Northwestern University Law Review (117(3):801-858) argues, persuasively in our view, that courts are poorly positioned to resolve these questions through common-law development alone, and that regulatory intervention is warranted to specify the duty of care applicable to AI-assisted clinical decisions. The American Health Law Association's 2023 briefing paper on AI accountability and governance frameworks in health care reached a functionally identical conclusion. Tapestryhealth's compliance team concurs. The infrastructural lock-in dynamics described by Gillespie, Boczkowski, and Foot in their MIT Press volume on media technologies (2014) apply with some force here: once facilities adopt AI tools without a specified accountability framework in place, the organizational and contractual dependencies that follow make retroactive governance significantly harder to impose.⏎⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD REQUIRE⏎⏎⏎Our recommendation is specific. HHS should require, as a precondition for any AI deployment pathway receiving federal recognition, reimbursement eligibility, or safe harbor treatment, that the deploying entity file a fully specified accountability chain document that identifies:⏎⏎o  The legal entity responsible for post-market surveillance and model drift reporting.⏎o  The clinical override documentation standard that satisfies 42 C.F.R. Part 483 compliance for AI-assisted care planning decisions.⏎o  The contractual mechanism by which the facility can obtain model performance data sufficient to discharge its duty of care under applicable survey and certification standards.⏎⏎This is not a request for a future rulemaking priority. It is a request that HHS treat an enforceable accountability chain as a threshold requirement before any deployment pathway is opened. The 68% of clinical staff in our portfolio who currently spend more than 30% of their shift time on documentation tasks that AI tools could reduce will not benefit from accelerated adoption if the facilities employing them cannot absorb the compliance risk of deployment. The sequencing matters. Governance architecture should precede, not follow, the acceleration the Department is⏎⏎Leidos Health | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 3⏎⏎seeking. Facilities operating under value-based arrangements in particular, where AI-driven risk stratification has the clearest near-term clinical utility, are currently unable to move forward without clearer CMS guidance on whether AI-generated risk scores constitute defensible clinical documentation for purposes of both care planning and reimbursement eligibility determinations.⏎⏎leidos-health-hhs-ai-rfi-2024@leidos.com⏎⏎Joseph Sanchez, Chief Compliance Officer, Leidos Health♔♔2026-02-06T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-06T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔3♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔organization♔high♔concerned♔Maine♔compliance officer♔44♔Tapestryhealth's internal compliance monitoring data, drawn from operational oversight across 47 long-term care facilities serving approximately 9,200 residents, reveals that 68% of clinical staff report spending more than 30% of their shift time on documentation and administrative tasks that AI-assisted tools could materially reduce. SYNTH-0012♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Charles Mitchell♔American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network♔♔♔♔♔American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network⏎250 Williams Street NW⏎Atlanta, GA 30303⏎⏎Charles Mitchell, Research Director, ACS CAN Utah Chapter⏎Salt Lake City, UT 84101⏎⏎Submitted electronically via regulations.gov⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL-RFI⏎⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎200 Independence Avenue SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎ACS CAN COMMENTS | HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎⏎THE RELATIONAL FOUNDATIONS OF CLINICAL CARE⏎⏎Consider a patient ACS CAN staff encountered during field work at the Huntsman Cancer Institute in Salt Lake City in March of this year: an elderly woman, seventy-three years old, referred for what her primary care chart described as "fatigue and mild anorexia." She could not name her symptoms in the language her physician used. She sat with her hands folded in her lap and described feeling "like the light had gone dim." No algorithm would have scored that phrase as a flag for depression complicating early-stage pancreatic disease. Her physician, who had seen her for eleven years, heard something in it. He ordered the imaging that found the mass. The therapeutic relationship — that accumulated, attentive, relational presence — was itself a diagnostic instrument, and no clinical decision support system running on her prior claims data would have reproduced what it produced in that examination room.⏎⏎ACS CAN raises this not as anecdote but as illustration of a category of clinical knowledge that the HHS Request for Information, published in the Federal Register in 2024, does not adequately theorize. The RFI repeatedly frames its goals in terms of "accelerating adoption," "enhancing productivity," and reducing "friction" in clinical workflows. ACS CAN understands why that language is chosen — it speaks to the administrative and economic realities that genuinely impede beneficial technology deployment. But the framing carries philosophical commitments that deserve scrutiny, because when productivity becomes the organizing value of clinical care, the things that cannot be measured as productivity tend to get treated as inefficiencies. And some of those things are, in the precise sense used by Michael Balint in his foundational 1957 work The Doctor, His Patient and the Illness, the medicine itself. Balint argued that the physician's attention — not merely technical competence, but relational presence — functions as a pharmacologically active substance in the therapeutic encounter. That argument has since accumulated a substantial evidence base, and the RFI's framing does not engage it.⏎⏎ACS CAN COMMENTS | HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE MEASURABLE CLINICAL VALUE OF RELATIONAL PRESENCE⏎⏎The claim that the therapeutic relationship carries independent clinical value is not sentimental. It is documented. Kelley and colleagues, in a 2014 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials published in PLOS ONE, found that the quality of the patient-clinician relationship produced measurable improvements in objective health outcomes — not patient satisfaction scores, not subjective wellbeing ratings, but outcomes (Kelley JM, Kraft-Todd G, Schapira L, et al., "The influence of the patient-clinician relationship on healthcare outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials," PLOS ONE, 2014;9(4):e94207). Epstein and Street, writing in the Annals of Family Medicine in 2011, described patient-centered care not as a stylistic preference but as a values-laden orientation that generates distinct clinical pathways — pathways that depend on the clinician's capacity to read context, navigate ambiguity, and respond to what is not said (Epstein RM, Street RL Jr., "The values and value of patient-centered care," Annals of Family Medicine, 2011;9(2):100–103). Street and colleagues, in a 2009 paper in Patient Education and Counseling, mapped specific communication behaviors — eliciting concerns, acknowledging emotion, expressing partnership — to downstream health outcomes through at least five distinct causal pathways (Street RL Jr., Makoul G, Arora NK, Epstein RM, "How does communication heal? Pathways linking clinician-patient communication to health outcomes," Patient Education and Counseling, 2009;74(3):295–301). This is not a literature that frames communication as supplementary to "real" medicine. It frames communication as a clinical mechanism.⏎⏎What AI intermediation does to these mechanisms is not a theoretical question. It is an empirical one, and the evidence available is not reassuring. Zulman and colleagues, publishing in JAMA in January 2020, documented the specific physician behaviors — sustained attention, deliberate acknowledgment, shared deliberation — that preserve connection in clinical encounters, and observed that screen-mediated interactions systematically interrupt several of them (Zulman DM, Haverfield MC, Shaw JG, et al., "Practices to foster physician presence and connection with patients in the clinical encounter," JAMA, 2020;323(1):70–81). The clinical encounter is a fragile ecology. When a physician's attention is divided between a patient's face and an algorithmic recommendation displayed on a monitor, the division is not neutral. The patient registers it. In oncology settings specifically — which are ACS CAN's primary domain of concern — the stakes of that registration are not trivial. A patient receiving a cancer diagnosis, or discussing a treatment plan that involves significant toxicity, or trying to decide whether to pursue a clinical trial, is not engaged in an information-retrieval transaction. That patient is navigating existential terrain, and the clinician who is half-watching a screen is not fully present for the navigation. ACS CAN is not aware of any evidence that AI-augmented oncology consultations have been evaluated for their effect on this dimension of care, and the RFI does not ask about it.⏎⏎ACS CAN COMMENTS | HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE DESKILLING PROBLEM AND ITS LONG HORIZON⏎⏎ACS CAN wants to be precise about what the deskilling concern is and is not. It is not technophobia. The organization has supported, and continues to support, careful integration of AI tools in radiology, pathology, and genomic interpretation — domains where pattern-recognition support demonstrably extends human capacity without restructuring the relational encounter. The concern is specifically about what happens to clinical reasoning capacity when algorithmic recommendations become the default starting point for clinical judgment, and when that pattern persists across years of training and practice.⏎⏎The human factors research on this question is well-developed and consistently sobering. Parasuraman and Manzey, in a 2010 paper in Human Factors, documented "automation complacency" — the systematic tendency of human operators who work alongside automated systems to reduce their own cognitive monitoring, trusting the system's outputs in ways that degrade their capacity for independent assessment (Parasuraman R, Manzey DH, "Complacency and bias in human use of automation: an attentional integration," Human Factors, 2010;52(3):381–410). Skitka, Mosier, and Burdick, in a 1999 paper in the International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, demonstrated that automation bias — the tendency to follow automated recommendations even when they conflict with available evidence — is robust, persistent, and not reliably corrected by training (Skitka LJ, Mosier KL, Burdick M, "Does automation bias decision-making?" International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 1999;51(5):991–1006). These findings come from aviation, nuclear power, and process control — domains where the human-automation interface has been studied for decades. Medicine is newer to this literature, and that relative newness is itself a problem, because it means the field is deploying at scale before the longitudinal data on cognitive effects are available.⏎⏎ACS CAN COMMENTS | HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎Hoff, in a 2011 study in Health Care Management Review examining primary care physicians' adaptation to two specific workflow innovations, found evidence of progressive skill atrophy in domains where algorithmic support was consistently available — physicians became less confident and less accurate in those domains over time, not more (Hoff T, "Deskilling and adaptation among primary care physicians using two work innovations," Health Care Management Review, 2011;36(4):338–348). This is not a dramatic finding. It is a quiet one, and that is part of what makes it worrying. The atrophy is not perceptible in individual encounters. It accumulates over years of practice, and by the time it becomes visible — in the physician who cannot interpret an EKG without algorithmic prompting, or the oncologist who has lost the habit of sitting with diagnostic uncertainty before ordering the next test — the profession's capacity for independent judgment has already been restructured in ways that are not easily reversed.⏎⏎Verghese, Shah, and Harrington, writing in JAMA in 2018, put the concern plainly: the physician's clinical reasoning is itself a form of knowledge that must be practiced to be maintained, and systems that routinely substitute algorithmic outputs for that reasoning are not augmenting the physician but gradually replacing a function that the physician must exercise to remain capable of exercising it (Verghese A, Shah NH, Harrington RA, "What this computer needs is a physician: humanism and artificial intelligence," JAMA, 2018;319(1):19–20). The RFI's language of "agentic supervisory approaches" — in which clinicians are positioned as monitors of AI-generated recommendations rather than independent reasoners — is precisely the model that the deskilling literature identifies as highest-risk. ACS CAN is concerned that HHS is considering the rapid deployment of that model without adequate engagement with this body of evidence.⏎⏎ACS CAN COMMENTS | HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI RFI | Page 5⏎⏎⏎WHERE THE RFI'S FRAMING GOES WRONG — AND WHAT A DIFFERENT FRAMING WOULD REQUIRE⏎⏎ACS CAN wants to be fair to the RFI. The document does acknowledge the importance of "patient-centered" outcomes, and it does note that clinician trust is a factor in adoption. Topol's 2019 paper in Nature Medicine, which the RFI's framing echoes in several places, genuinely argued that AI could liberate clinicians to spend more time on the relational dimensions of care by automating routine cognitive labor (Topol EJ, "High-performance medicine: the convergence of human and artificial intelligence," Nature Medicine, 2019;25(1):44–56). That argument is not implausible in principle. The problem is that it assumes a particular implementation pathway — one in which time freed from algorithmic tasks is reliably reallocated to relational engagement — and there is very little evidence that this reallocation actually occurs in practice. What the evidence suggests instead is that time freed from one cognitive task in a clinical workflow tends to be absorbed by documentation, administrative overhead, and the supervision of additional algorithmic outputs. The relational dividend that Topol describes has not been demonstrated at scale.⏎⏎The deeper problem with the RFI's framing is that it treats the question of "accelerating adoption" as separable from the question of what is being adopted, and at what stage of relational-safety validation. Wachter and Cassel, writing in JAMA in 2020, argued that the medical profession needs to develop rigorous frameworks for evaluating AI tools not only on technical performance metrics but on their effects on the clinical encounter as a whole — including the relational dimensions that do not appear in accuracy benchmarks (Wachter RM, Cassel CK, "Leavening the lump: making AI work for clinicians and patients," JAMA, 2020;323(18):1801–1802). ACS CAN endorses that argument and observes that the RFI does not propose any such framework. The RFI asks about reimbursement pathways, regulatory streamlining, and research investment. It does not ask how HHS would know whether a deployed AI tool was eroding the relational dimensions of care in the settings where it was operating.⏎⏎ACS CAN COMMENTS | HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI RFI | Page 6⏎⏎There is also a concern that ACS CAN wants to flag about the implicit model of clinical cognition that underlies the RFI's approach. The document's enthusiasm for AI-augmented decision support reflects, in part, a view of clinical reasoning as essentially a pattern-recognition and probability-estimation task — a view that Tversky and Kahneman's foundational 1974 work on judgment under uncertainty would recognize as a useful but partial description of how humans actually reason (Tversky A, Kahneman D, "Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases," Science, 1974;185(4157):1124–1131). Clinical reasoning is not only probabilistic inference. It involves narrative interpretation, contextual weighting, and what might be called the tolerance of productive ambiguity — the capacity to sit with an incomplete picture and continue attending to the patient while the picture develops. This last capacity is particularly at risk when algorithmic systems are designed to reduce ambiguity by forcing early categorization. Consider the oncology context again: a patient presenting with vague constitutional symptoms who is in a high-anxiety state about a family history of cancer needs a clinician who can hold the uncertainty open long enough to establish a therapeutic alliance before the diagnostic workup proceeds. An AI system that flags "low probability of malignancy — recommend watchful waiting" and generates a discharge summary template is not supporting that clinical process. It is short-circuiting it.⏎⏎ACS CAN COMMENTS | HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI RFI | Page 7⏎⏎⏎WHAT ACS CAN IS ASKING HHS TO DO⏎⏎ACS CAN's specific request to HHS is this: before the Department moves forward with reimbursement and regulatory frameworks designed to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care settings, it should commission or require relational-safety evaluation as a precondition for deployment support. This means developing, through a transparent public process with clinician and patient input, a set of validated metrics for assessing the effect of AI clinical decision support tools on the relational dimensions of the clinical encounter — metrics that go beyond patient satisfaction surveys and include direct observation of communicative behavior, longitudinal tracking of clinician reasoning patterns, and patient-reported measures of felt presence and therapeutic trust.⏎⏎ACS CAN recognizes that this is a harder and slower ask than the RFI's current orientation suggests HHS wants to hear. The Department is clearly under pressure — from industry, from health systems, from parts of the physician community — to move quickly. ACS CAN does not dismiss those pressures. The administrative burdens that AI tools can reduce are real, and the diagnostic capabilities that some tools extend are genuine. But the history of medical technology adoption is not uniformly encouraging on the question of whether moving quickly produces better outcomes than moving carefully. The deskilling findings in Hoff's 2011 study were not visible in the short-term evaluations of the workflow innovations he examined. They emerged over time, in longitudinal data. A reimbursement framework that rewards AI-augmented encounters without any mechanism for tracking their relational effects will not generate that longitudinal data, and by the time the effects are visible in outcome measures, a generation of clinicians will have trained in an environment that systematically undervalued the relational capacities that the evidence base says are clinically active.⏎⏎ACS CAN COMMENTS | HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI RFI | Page 8⏎⏎Think about a father ACS CAN staff observed in a pediatric oncology waiting room in Primary Children's Hospital, also in Salt Lake City, translating for his eight-year-old daughter during a consultation with an oncologist. The translation was imperfect — he was simplifying, softening, and also, it became clear, masking his own terror in the effort of rendering the physician's words into something his daughter could hold. The oncologist noticed. She stopped. She addressed the father directly, in English, and said: "I can see this is very hard for you." That pause, that address, that acknowledgment — it did not appear in any billing code. It did not generate a productivity metric. What it did was keep the father present and functional for the remainder of the consultation, which meant that the treatment plan that emerged from that consultation was one the family actually understood and could execute.⏎⏎ACS CAN is not arguing that AI tools cannot coexist with moments like that one. The argument is that the policy framework HHS is developing will shape the conditions under which such moments are possible or impossible, and that a framework organized around productivity acceleration and adoption speed is not a framework that will protect those conditions. The relational safety evaluation ACS CAN is requesting is not an obstacle to beneficial AI integration. It is the precondition for knowing whether what is being integrated is beneficial in the full sense that medicine requires — not merely technically accurate, not merely efficient, but genuinely present to the patient as a person navigating illness.⏎⏎ACS CAN COMMENTS | HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI RFI | Page 9⏎⏎ACS CAN would welcome the opportunity to contribute to the development of relational-safety metrics through any stakeholder process HHS convenes. The organization's research staff have been engaged in outcome measurement in oncology care settings for more than a decade, and the methodological questions involved in operationalizing concepts like "felt presence" and "therapeutic trust" are tractable — they have been addressed, partially and imperfectly, in the communication research literature that this comment has cited. What has not been done is translate that literature into regulatory standards with teeth. That translation is what ACS CAN is asking HHS to undertake, and to undertake it before, not after, the reimbursement infrastructure for AI-augmented care is locked in place. Once the financial incentives are structured, the behavioral patterns follow, and the behavioral patterns are much harder to revise than the regulations that created them. The Department's Q4 2024 stakeholder convening schedule, to the extent it remains open, would be an appropriate venue for beginning that work, and ACS CAN requests that a session specifically addressing relational-safety standards be included on that agenda.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Charles Mitchell⏎Research Director, ACS CAN Utah Chapter⏎American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network⏎⏎cmitchell@acscan.org⏎801-555-0147⏎⏎ACS CAN COMMENTS | HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI RFI | Page 10♔♔2026-02-11T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-11T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔9♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔concerned♔Utah♔research director♔36♔A 2024 TMA member survey of 4,200 Texas physicians found that 58% reported using at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or clinical decision-support tool in their practice, yet 73% of those users cited fragmented reimbursement pathways as the primary barrier to broader implementation. I am here because the RFI HHS has issued asks the right questions about acceleration and says almost nothing coherent about what gets lost when you automate the people who actually hold the system together.⏎⏎THE ADMINISTRATIVE KNOWLEDGE PROBLEM⏎⏎The RFI frames administrative labor as friction. I want to be precise about why that framing is wrong in a way that matters for patient outcomes.⏎⏎Care coordinators, patient navigators, and benefits counselors are not doing clerical work. They are doing something closer to what Michael Polanyi described in The Tacit Dimension (1966) as embodied, non-transferable expertise — the kind of knowledge that cannot be fully articulated because it is accumulated through practice, failure, and relationship. A care coordinator at a community health center in Providence knows that Mrs. Souza on the third floor will not follow up with a specialist unless someone calls her daughter first, and that the Medicaid transportation benefit has a 72-hour advance notice requirement that the hospital's discharge planning software does not account for, and that the particular social worker at the Cranston office who handles housing exceptions is only reachable on Tuesday mornings. None of that is in a structured data field. None of it will survive the conversion to a training set.⏎⏎HHS should ask itself: what happens to that knowledge when the position is eliminated or its scope is narrowed to reviewing AI-generated outputs? The answer, based on the research, is that errors multiply silently. Ash, Berg, and Coiera documented exactly this pattern in their 2004 study in JAMIA — when health information systems automate coordination tasks, they do not eliminate errors, they transform them into a different category of error that is harder to detect because it appears to have already been handled. The system says the referral was sent. The referral was not received. The patient does not know to ask.⏎⏎I want to be direct about the efficiency argument as well. Sinsky et al. (2016) found that physicians in ambulatory practice were already spending nearly two hours on administrative tasks for every one hour of direct patient care, and that was before the current generation of AI-assisted documentation tools added a new layer of error-correction labor. The argument that AI will reduce administrative burden assumes that AI outputs require no human review. Every practitioner I have spoken with in Rhode Island says the opposite is true in their current experience — the tools generate plausible-sounding errors that take longer to catch than the original task would have taken. The GAO's 2023 report on AI in health care (GAO-23-105980) noted that implementation challenges and unintended consequences remain poorly documented, which is a polite way of saying we do not actually know what these tools cost in human labor once the error-correction load is counted.⏎⏎WHAT HHS IS NOT ACCOUNTING FOR⏎⏎There is a specific population question here that the RFI does not address with anything like adequate seriousness. Obermeyer and colleagues demonstrated in Science in 2019 that a widely-used health management algorithm systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients because it used cost as a proxy for health need — a proxy that encodes decades of unequal access. The National Partnership for Women and Families documented in 2022 that administrative AI deployed in care coordination and benefits navigation contexts reproduces similar disparities, specifically for patients with limited English proficiency, patients in rural areas, and elderly patients with complex medication regimens. My mother is 81, Latina, and was on anticoagulation therapy. I do not think it is a coincidence that the algorithm got her wrong.⏎⏎The people who catch these errors are the navigators and coordinators who know the patient. Atul Gawande wrote in The New Yorker in 2018 about how the introduction of EHR systems degraded the quality of physician attention by redirecting cognitive load toward documentation compliance — and he was writing about physicians, who have institutional protection and professional standing. Patient navigators do not have that protection. When their positions are automated or restructured around AI oversight, the institutional knowledge walks out with them and there is no audit trail for what was lost.⏎⏎My specific demands are these:⏎⏎1. Any administrative AI deployed in care coordination, patient navigation, or benefits counseling must be subject to mandatory pre-deployment equity audits, stratified by race, ethnicity, language preference, age, and insurance status. Not voluntary. Not post-market. Before deployment.⏎⏎2. Human accountability must be preserved at every decision point that affects a patient's care trajectory. An AI recommendation is not a decision. A credentialed human being must be responsible for the final determination, and that responsibility must be documented and auditable.⏎⏎3. HHS must require that any institution deploying administrative AI demonstrate, with evidence, that it has not reduced the number of human care coordinators or patient navigators as a condition of receiving any federal incentive payment tied to that deployment. The efficiency savings cannot be extracted from the workforce that catches the errors.⏎⏎4. The tacit knowledge problem must be treated as a safety problem, not a training data problem. You cannot solve it by collecting more data. The knowledge is relational and contextual and it degrades when the relationships are severed.⏎⏎I work in customer service. I am not a health policy expert. SYNTH-0017♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Sharon Lewis♔Carnegie Mellon University Block Center for Technology and Society♔♔♔♔♔Sharon Lewis, Associate Professor⏎Carnegie Mellon University Block Center for Technology and Society⏎Pittsburgh, PA 15213⏎⏎Submitted to: HHS Office of the Deputy Secretary / ASTP-ONC⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎The data are worth sitting with for a moment before the policy argument begins. A 2024 survey encompassing responses from 2,847 cardiologists across academic medical centers, community hospitals, and outpatient practices found that 68% had encountered at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or clinical decision-support tool in their practice setting within the prior twelve months, yet only 23% reported receiving any formal training on the clinical validation evidence underlying those tools. A subsequent analysis of cardiology-specific AI deployments identified more than 140 commercially available algorithms targeting cardiovascular indications, of which fewer than 30% had been evaluated in prospective trials reflecting the demographic diversity of U.S. patient populations. The gap between those two figures — between the pace of deployment and the evidentiary infrastructure that would make deployment safe — is not an implementation problem that better incentives will fix. It is a structural feature of a market that has been allowed to move faster than the epistemological frameworks needed to govern it. HHS's Request for Information proceeds from the premise that the central problem facing AI adoption in clinical care is friction, and that the appropriate federal response is to reduce that friction through regulatory accommodation, reimbursement reform, and accelerated research-and-development pathways. This comment respectfully argues that this framing is mistaken in a way that matters, and that the consequences of institutionalizing it will be difficult to reverse once the reimbursement architecture has been built.⏎⏎The argument here is not that AI has no legitimate role in clinical medicine. Topol's 2019 synthesis in Nature Medicine of high-performance medicine applications makes a genuinely compelling case for specific, narrow tasks where pattern recognition at scale outperforms individual clinician judgment — certain image-classification problems in dermatology and radiology being the clearest examples (Topol, E.J., 2019, Nature Medicine, 25(1), 44–56). The argument, rather, is that the acceleration model HHS is proposing treats these narrow successes as generalizable evidence for a broader transformation of how clinical care is organized and compensated, and that this generalization is not warranted by the evidence and carries costs that the RFI does not adequately account for. Obermeyer and Emanuel, writing in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2016, were careful to note that machine learning's predictive power is most reliable in well-specified, data-rich domains and degrades sharply in the presence of the ambiguity, missing data, and contextual complexity that characterize most actual clinical encounters (Obermeyer, Z., & Emanuel, E.J., 2016, NEJM, 375(13), 1216–1219). That caveat has not become less true in the intervening years, even as the marketing language surrounding clinical AI has become considerably more confident.⏎⏎Consider a clinical encounter that occurred in the context of a cardiology practice in Arkansas, during a period when this researcher was embedded in a community hospital as part of a larger study on AI tool integration. The patient was a sixty-three-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes who presented with what her referring physician had documented as "atypical chest discomfort, likely musculoskeletal." Her ECG and initial biomarker panel were within normal limits. Every available algorithmic risk-stratification tool — and there were three in use at this facility — rated her as low-risk and flagged her for expedited discharge. The cardiologist on service that afternoon, a clinician with twenty-two years of practice, did something that no clinical decision-support system can do: she noticed. She noticed the way the patient sat in the chair, the slightly too-careful quality of her breathing, the way she answered questions about her symptoms with a specificity that suggested she had been rehearsing them, as if she did not expect to be believed. The cardiologist asked a question that was not on any intake form: "Has anyone in your family died young from heart problems?" The patient's daughter, who had been sitting quietly in the corner, said, "Her mother and two sisters." The patient was admitted. She had a left anterior descending artery lesion that required urgent intervention the following morning. None of the algorithms had been wrong, exactly — her presentation genuinely was atypical and her initial values genuinely were unremarkable. But none of them had been sufficient, either, and the thing that was sufficient was not pattern recognition. It was presence. Cassell's observation, in The Nature of Suffering and the Goals of Medicine, that illness is irreducibly personal — that what is wrong with a patient cannot be fully captured in any set of physiological parameters, however comprehensive — is not a romantic claim about the art of medicine (Cassell, E.J., 1991, Oxford University Press). It is a description of a structural feature of the clinical encounter that AI systems are not designed to address and that HHS's acceleration framework does not appear to take seriously.⏎⏎The therapeutic relationship is not merely a pleasant feature of good clinical care that can be traded off against efficiency gains. Kelley and colleagues, in a 2014 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials published in PLOS ONE, found that the quality of the patient-clinician relationship had measurable, independent effects on health outcomes across a range of conditions, including adherence, symptom resolution, and patient-reported functional status (Kelley, J.M., Kraft-Todd, G., Schapira, L., Kossowsky, J., & Riess, H., 2014, PLOS ONE, 9(4), e94207). Roter and Hall's foundational work on clinical communication, now in its second edition, documents the mechanisms through which the relational dimensions of the medical encounter — attentiveness, empathy, the willingness to tolerate ambiguity in the patient's account of their experience — produce clinical information that structured data collection cannot replicate (Roter, D.L., & Hall, J.A., 2006, Praeger Publishers). What the HHS acceleration model does not reckon with is the possibility that AI intermediation, even when the algorithms perform as advertised, may degrade these relational dynamics in ways that are not visible in the short-term outcome metrics that reimbursement reform tends to favor. If a clinician's attention is organized around monitoring and responding to algorithmic recommendations rather than around the patient in front of them, the nature of the encounter changes, and not in ways that are easily reversed once the practice patterns have been established.⏎⏎The deskilling concern deserves more attention than the RFI appears to give it. Hoff's 2011 study in Health Care Management Review of primary care physicians using two work innovations found that algorithmic decision-support tools, when used routinely, produced measurable deskilling effects — physicians became less confident in and less accurate at clinical judgments they had previously made independently, and this effect persisted even after the tools were removed from the workflow (Hoff, T., 2011, Health Care Management Review, 36(4), 338–348). Parasuraman and Manzey's work on automation complacency in Human Factors documents the cognitive mechanisms through which this happens: when a system provides reliable-seeming outputs, human operators progressively reduce their independent monitoring of the situation, and this attentional withdrawal is not easily reversed on demand (Parasuraman, R., & Manzey, D.H., 2010, Human Factors, 52(3), 381–410). The concern is not hypothetical. The survey data cited at the opening of this comment — 68% exposure to AI tools, 23% formal training on validation evidence — describes a clinical workforce that is already being shaped by tools it does not fully understand, in a policy environment that is now proposing to accelerate that process. Tversky and Kahneman's work on heuristics and biases is relevant here in an underappreciated way: the classic finding is that humans are susceptible to systematic cognitive errors when relying on simplified decision rules (Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D., 1974, Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131). What AI deployment at scale does is not eliminate these biases but institutionalize new ones, with the additional problem that the heuristic is now embedded in a system that produces confident-looking numerical outputs, which are substantially harder for clinicians to interrogate than their own intuitions.⏎⏎Regarding the specific RFI questions on reimbursement policy and regulatory pathways, the concern here is with the proposed approach of using Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement incentives to drive adoption of AI clinical decision-support tools. The logic is legible: if you want widespread adoption, tie it to payment. But this mechanism has a history of producing adoption without appropriate implementation, and the clinical AI context has features that make this risk particularly acute. Shortliffe and Sepúlveda, writing in JAMA in 2018, noted that the history of clinical decision support is littered with tools that were widely deployed and then quietly abandoned because their alert fatigue costs and workflow disruption effects outweighed their clinical benefits — and those tools were far simpler than current AI systems (Shortliffe, E.H., & Sepúlveda, M.J., 2018, JAMA, 320(21), 2199–2200). Reimbursement-driven adoption of the current generation of cardiovascular AI algorithms — more than 140 commercially available tools, fewer than 30% prospectively validated in demographically representative populations — would produce a clinical environment in which tools of uncertain equity performance are embedded in billing workflows, which is a substantially harder problem to unwind than a voluntary pilot that fails.⏎⏎The equity dimension of the validation gap warrants explicit attention in this comment, in part because it connects directly to HHS's stated commitment to health equity and in part because it is the dimension of the AI deployment problem that is most likely to be obscured by aggregate performance metrics. Dzau, Ginsburg, and Chopra, writing in JAMA in 2021, observed that the promise of precision medicine — including AI-assisted precision medicine — depends critically on whether the training data and validation populations reflect the diversity of patients who will ultimately be affected by the technology (Dzau, V.J., Ginsburg, G.S., & Chopra, A., 2021, JAMA, 326(18), 1844–1845). In cardiovascular medicine specifically, the demographic composition of the training datasets underlying most commercially deployed algorithms has been documented to underrepresent Black patients, women, and patients with comorbidity profiles common in lower-income populations. An algorithm that performs well in aggregate but performs poorly in the populations that already face the greatest barriers to equitable care is not a neutral tool — it is a mechanism for encoding and scaling existing disparities. Bickmore and colleagues' work on health literacy and patient-clinician communication is relevant here as well: patients with lower health literacy are more likely to defer to technologically mediated recommendations they do not understand, and less likely to raise concerns that might prompt a clinician to override an algorithmic output (Bickmore, T.W., Pfeifer, L.M., & Jack, B.W., 2009, Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 1265–1274). The combination of an undertested algorithm, a deskilled clinician, and a patient who does not know they can push back is not a hypothetical worst case. It is a reasonably predictable consequence of the acceleration model if implemented without the evidentiary and equity safeguards that the RFI treats as secondary concerns.⏎⏎Carnegie Mellon University Block Center for Technology and Society Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎Verghese, Shah, and Harrington's 2018 JAMA commentary on humanism and artificial intelligence makes an argument that this comment wants to extend: what the computer needs is a physician not because the computer cannot process information efficiently, but because the goals of medicine are not reducible to information processing (Verghese, A., Shah, N.H., & Harrington, R.A., 2018, JAMA, 319(1), 19–20). The RFI's framing of clinical care as a domain where AI can "accelerate adoption" and reduce "friction" implicitly treats the relational and interpretive dimensions of clinical medicine as inefficiencies — as things that slow down the flow of information rather than as constitutive features of what medicine is for. This is not a technophobic position. It is a position about what clinical care is, and what it is not. The policy consequence of getting this wrong is not that AI tools will fail to perform as advertised on narrow benchmarks — some of them will perform well on narrow benchmarks — but that the clinical infrastructure built around those benchmarks will progressively crowd out the human capacities that cannot be benchmarked: the capacity to notice what is not in the data, to hear what the patient cannot say directly, to make a judgment that is not reducible to the features the algorithm was trained on.⏎⏎What HHS should do instead of the acceleration model is not obvious, and this comment does not want to pretend otherwise. There is a legitimate case for federal action to support the development of prospectively validated, demographically representative AI tools for specific, well-defined clinical tasks — the kind of narrow, evidence-grounded deployment that Topol's more careful passages actually describe, rather than the broader transformation that his work is sometimes invoked to justify. There is a case for requiring pre-deployment equity audits as a condition of Medicare reimbursement eligibility, for funding independent post-market surveillance infrastructure, and for mandating clinician training on validation evidence as a condition of institutional AI deployment — the 77% training gap documented in the survey data cited above represents a failure of implementation governance that reimbursement incentives alone will not fix. What there is not a case for is treating the pace of AI adoption as itself a policy goal, as if the primary problem in clinical AI is that too few algorithms are being used by too few clinicians. The primary problem is that the algorithms being deployed have not been adequately tested in the populations they will affect, the clinicians using them have not been adequately trained to evaluate their outputs critically, and the policy framework governing their deployment is oriented toward removing barriers rather than ensuring that the barriers being removed are the right ones. The fact that a tool is technically impressive and commercially available is not, by itself, a reason to build a reimbursement architecture around it. The question of whether that tool should be used in a particular clinical context, by a particular clinician, with a particular patient, is a question that requires human judgment — the kind that is produced by training, experience, and the ongoing practice of actually being present with patients — and the progressive displacement of that judgment by algorithmic recommendation-following is not a problem that post-deployment monitoring will catch in time to matter.⏎⏎One additional note, which is perhaps more logistical than philosophical but feels worth raising: the RFI asks about regulatory pathways for AI tools, but it does not appear to specify how HHS will handle the situation in which a tool that has received favorable regulatory treatment based on performance data from one patient population is subsequently deployed in a substantially different population. The FDA's current framework for AI-based Software as a Medical Device has provisions for post-market performance monitoring, but the enforcement mechanisms are weak and the reporting requirements are inconsistent across tool categories. If HHS is going to build a reimbursement architecture around AI clinical decision-support adoption, the question of what happens when a tool's real-world performance diverges from its validation data — particularly in populations that were underrepresented in that validation data — needs a clearer answer than the RFI currently provides, and the answer cannot simply be that the market will correct for this over time.♔♔2026-01-17T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-17T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔8♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔academic_organization♔high♔resigned♔Arkansas♔associate professor♔45♔A 2024 ACC member survey encompassing responses from 2,847 cardiologists across academic medical centers, community hospitals, and outpatient practices found that 68% had encountered at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or clinical decision-support tool in their practice setting within the prior 12 months, yet only 23% reported receiving any formal training on the clinical validation evidence underlying those tools. SYNTH-0019♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Rebecca Harris♔♔♔♔♔♔Submitted via the Federal eRulemaking Portal: http://www.regulations.gov⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎My husband Raymond was hospitalized at Ruby Memorial in Morgantown in the fall of 2019, his second cardiac event in three years. The hospitalist managing his care that week had fourteen patients across two floors — I know because I counted the names on the whiteboard outside the nurses' station, and I stood there looking at that list for a long time. That physician was running. Not metaphorically. Physically moving between rooms at a pace that made me tired just watching. And it was a second-year pharmacy student, doing her rotation rounds more or less by chance, who caught a medication interaction on Raymond's chart that the hospitalist had missed.⏎⏎I want to be honest about what that moment teaches, because I have thought about it a great deal since HHS published this request for information. The easy lesson — the one that fits most cleanly into the framing of this RFI — is that an AI-assisted clinical decision support tool would have caught that interaction automatically, would have flagged it before anyone had to be lucky. And that is probably true. I am not writing to dispute it. What I want to push back on, carefully and with some specificity, is the larger architecture of assumptions that surrounds that easy lesson, because I think HHS is asking the wrong question, and I think the consequences of asking the wrong question in this domain are serious enough to warrant saying so plainly.⏎⏎The RFI asks, essentially, what regulatory and reimbursement barriers are preventing faster AI adoption in clinical settings. That framing treats adoption speed as the variable to be optimized and assumes that the clinical benefits of AI tools are well enough established that the main work remaining is removing friction. I am not a clinician or a health policy researcher, but I have read enough of the relevant literature to be worried about this assumption. Abraham Verghese and his co-authors wrote in JAMA in 2018 that the physician-patient encounter is not simply a data collection event, and that the physical and relational dimensions of that encounter carry diagnostic and therapeutic weight that no pattern-recognition system currently captures (Verghese, Shah, and Harrington, "What This Computer Needs Is a Physician," JAMA 319(1), 2018). What concerned them was not AI accuracy on specific tasks but the risk that instrumenting the encounter around algorithmic outputs would progressively erode the clinician's capacity to read what cannot be coded: the way a patient's eyes move when they are frightened and cannot find words, the particular quality of silence when a family member knows something the patient hasn't said, the physical presentation that doesn't match the chief complaint. These are not romantic notions about medicine. They are diagnostic data. Losing access to them because a clinician has been trained to wait for the algorithm's recommendation before forming a judgment is a real clinical risk, and it does not show up in accuracy benchmarks.⏎⏎There is a body of research on what Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt called "automation bias" — the tendency for human decision-makers to over-rely on automated recommendations even when those recommendations are wrong — published in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association in 2012. Their systematic review found that automation bias is not a personality flaw in particular clinicians; it is a predictable cognitive response to working alongside systems that are usually right. The more accurate an AI decision-support tool becomes on average, the more dangerous its errors become, because the clinician's independent judgment has been progressively offloaded onto the system. Tversky and Kahneman's foundational work on heuristics and biases (Science, 185(4157), 1974) gives us the underlying cognitive architecture here: people anchor on the first number, the first recommendation, the first framing they encounter, and adjustment away from that anchor is systematically insufficient. When the anchor is an algorithmic output, the implications for clinical reasoning are not trivial. I genuinely don't understand why HHS's framing of this RFI doesn't grapple more seriously with this literature, given that it's not obscure.⏎⏎What I keep coming back to is the question of what the therapeutic relationship is actually worth, clinically, not just ethically. Kelley and colleagues published a systematic review and meta-analysis in PLOS ONE in 2014 examining the influence of the patient-clinician relationship on health outcomes, and they found measurable effects on a range of outcomes including symptom resolution, medication adherence, and patient-reported functional status (Kelley et al., "The Influence of the Patient-Clinician Relationship on Healthcare Outcomes," PLOS ONE 9(4), e94207, 2014). Epstein and Street, writing in the Annals of Family Medicine in 2011, made the related point that patient-centered care is not a style preference but a clinical mechanism — that the quality of communication and relational attunement in an encounter affects physiological outcomes through pathways that include reduced anxiety, improved self-management, and more accurate symptom reporting (Epstein and Street, "The Values and Value of Patient-Centered Care," Annals of Family Medicine 9(2), 2011). When AI systems are inserted into the encounter in ways that redirect clinician attention toward screen-mediated recommendation-following rather than toward the patient, these mechanisms are disrupted. The algorithm may be technically correct and the patient may still be worse off. HHS's productivity-centered framing, with its emphasis on efficiency gains and adoption rates, is structurally incapable of seeing this kind of harm because it doesn't appear in the metrics that framework is designed to measure.⏎⏎I want to say something about Eric Topol's 2019 piece in Nature Medicine, "High-Performance Medicine: The Convergence of Human and Artificial Intelligence," because it is often cited as a kind of authoritative endorsement of rapid AI integration in clinical care, and I think that reading is selective. Topol is genuinely enthusiastic about specific AI applications, particularly in medical imaging and genomics, where the task is well-defined and the relational dimensions of the encounter are not the primary variable. But he also writes with considerable care about the risk of relational displacement, about the ways that efficiency-driven AI deployment could reduce the physician to a technician executing algorithmic recommendations, and about the importance of preserving what he calls the "human dimensions" of care as a precondition for beneficial AI integration, not an afterthought. That part of his argument tends not to make it into the policy summaries. The version of Topol that gets cited in RFIs like this one is the optimistic version, the convergence framing, and the cautions get left behind. That selective reading concerns me.⏎⏎Here is what I would ask HHS to sit with. Raymond's pharmacy student caught that interaction because she was paying attention, because she was in the room, because she read the chart with her own eyes and her own judgment and had not yet been trained to wait for a system to tell her what to notice. If a clinical decision support tool had been running and had not flagged the interaction — for whatever reason, a gap in its training data, an unusual combination of factors, a dosing parameter it wasn't calibrated for — would she have looked as carefully? I don't know. I genuinely don't. And I think "I don't know" is the honest answer, and I think honest answers deserve more weight in regulatory processes than they usually get. The RFI as written asks how to remove barriers to AI adoption. The question I would ask HHS to consider instead is what conditions must be met, what evidence must exist, what safeguards must be demonstrated, before a given AI application belongs in the clinical encounter at all. Not as a barrier to innovation. As a condition of responsible medicine. Those are different questions, and which one you ask determines what you learn from the answers.⏎⏎I recognize that I am not submitting a technical white paper here, and I recognize that HHS will receive comments from organizations with far more institutional resources than I have. The appendix I had intended to attach, which would have included additional citations and a longer treatment of the automation bias literature in nursing contexts specifically, is not complete in time for this submission deadline and I am submitting without it.
