SYNTH-0021♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Rebecca Johnson♔American Nurses Association♔♔♔♔♔American Nurses Association / GLI Research Network⏎Submitted to HHS Docket — Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Rebecca Johnson, Research Director⏎Organization: American Nurses Association (in collaboration with GLI affiliated hepatology network)⏎Albuquerque, NM 87102⏎⏎rjohnson@ana-network.org⏎⏎---⏎⏎ADMINISTRATIVE AI AND THE DEVALUATION OF TACIT EXPERTISE: WHY HHS MUST SLOW DOWN BEFORE IT SCALES UP⏎⏎The framing problem in this RFI is not subtle. HHS has structured its questions around acceleration — what regulatory, reimbursement, and R&D actions can hasten AI adoption — without first establishing a meaningful threshold of evidence that the thing being accelerated does not harm the populations most dependent on the administrative infrastructure being automated. GLI's 2024 landscape analysis, conducted across 47 affiliated hepatology centers, found that 63% had piloted at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or care coordination tool within the prior 18 months, yet fewer than 20% had successfully integrated those tools into routine clinical workflows. The two most commonly cited barriers were reimbursement uncertainty and interoperability failures. But the third finding, which has received considerably less attention from HHS in the design of this RFI, was this: member facilities serving high proportions of Medicaid-enrolled patients with chronic liver disease reported the largest implementation gaps, and in qualitative follow-up interviews, clinical and administrative staff at those facilities described a pattern in which AI-generated outputs were wrong in ways that were invisible to the system but consequential for patients. That is the problem GLI is asking HHS to take seriously.⏎⏎ANA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎The intellectual framework the Department appears to be operating from treats administrative healthcare work — care coordination, patient navigation, benefits counseling, prior authorization review — as essentially clerical: structured, repeatable, documentable, and therefore automatable. This is empirically incorrect. Michael Polanyi's foundational work on tacit knowledge (The Tacit Dimension, 1966) established that a significant portion of skilled expert work consists of knowledge that practitioners cannot fully articulate, because it is embedded in contextual judgment built through repeated exposure to specific, local conditions. This is not an abstraction. A care coordinator at a federally qualified health center in Bernalillo County, New Mexico, knows that the county's Medicaid transportation broker — as of the most recent contract cycle — runs a roughly two-week backlog for non-emergency medical transport, and she routes around that by submitting requests fourteen days in advance and flagging appointments that cannot be rescheduled. An AI system trained on national claims data or even regional utilization patterns will not know this. It will generate a transportation referral that looks correct in the record and will fail the patient without any error code, any alert, any flag. As Ash, Berg, and Coiera documented in their 2004 analysis of health IT-related errors in JAMIA, the most dangerous category of system-generated error is not the error that crashes — it is the error that completes silently and looks like success.⏎⏎GLI's annual member survey, drawing on responses from more than 300 hepatologists, advanced practice providers, and health system administrators, identified the absence of clear HHS guidance on AI-generated clinical decision support as the primary obstacle to broader adoption. But the survey data also surfaced something the RFI does not directly address: the administrative roles adjacent to clinical care are already severely understaffed. Donelan et al. (2019, Mayo Clinic Proceedings) documented physician burnout patterns tied directly to administrative burden accumulation, and Sinsky et al. (2016, Annals of Internal Medicine) found that physicians in ambulatory settings were spending roughly two hours on administrative tasks for every hour of direct patient care. The workforce absorbing the errors that AI systems generate in administrative functions is not a workforce with excess capacity. The efficiency argument for administrative AI assumes a baseline of adequate staffing. That baseline does not exist in safety-net settings. When an AI system generates an incorrect eligibility determination or drops an attachment in a prior authorization portal — and there are known bugs in at least two major commercial insurer portals that do exactly this — a human worker must catch it, diagnose it, and remediate it. That remediation work is not counted in the efficiency calculus. It is invisible, like the error itself.⏎⏎ANA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎The equity implications of this dynamic are not speculative. Obermeyer et al. (2019, Science) demonstrated with considerable rigor that a widely deployed health management algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients by using cost as a proxy for illness — a design choice that encoded existing structural inequities into the tool's outputs. Barocas and Selbst (2016, California Law Review) have argued more broadly that automated systems do not merely reflect existing disparities; they amplify them, because the errors they generate fall disproportionately on populations whose data is least well-represented in training corpora and who have the fewest resources to self-advocate when the system produces a wrong answer. GLI's member facilities serving Medicaid-enrolled patients with chronic liver disease are precisely this population. The National Partnership for Women and Families documented in 2023 that care coordinators and patient navigators function as critical infrastructure for underserved populations — not as supplementary services, but as the mechanism by which those populations access care at all. Automating that infrastructure with tools that have not been evaluated for equity-specific failure modes is not acceleration. It is a policy choice about whose errors are acceptable.⏎⏎GLI is also asking HHS to reconsider the premise that administrative friction is uniformly waste. A 2022 Health Affairs analysis on administrative complexity and health equity found that safety-net providers, despite higher administrative burden, were more likely to catch coverage gaps, benefits errors, and eligibility lapses precisely because the human beings doing that work were applying contextual judgment at each step. Shortell et al. (2021, Annual Review of Public Health) have written on organizational learning in health systems, and their work supports the view that institutional knowledge — the kind that lives in people, not in systems — is a form of safety infrastructure. Removing it in the name of efficiency, without demonstrating that the replacement performs at least as well on equity outcomes, is a decision that will not show up in aggregate quality metrics until the damage is done. Jacobs et al. (2021, ACM FAccT) documented a persistent gap between the design assumptions of AI tools and the actual complexity of administrative healthcare environments. The evidence base for caution here is not thin.⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY RECOMMENDATION⏎⏎GLI and ANA jointly urge HHS to take the following actions before authorizing or incentivizing AI automation of administrative healthcare functions:⏎⏎1. Commission independent, peer-reviewed research specifically characterizing the tacit knowledge content of administrative healthcare roles — care coordination, patient navigation, benefits counseling, and prior authorization review — across safety-net and Medicaid-serving settings. This research should use ethnographic and cognitive task analysis methodologies, not survey instruments, because the knowledge in question is by definition not fully articulable by the workers who hold it.⏎⏎2. Establish a non-inferiority standard for equity outcomes as a precondition for CMS reimbursement of AI-assisted administrative tools. Specifically, any tool seeking reimbursement authorization should be required to demonstrate, in a population that includes at least 30% Medicaid enrollees, that error rates for eligibility determinations, referral completions, and benefits communications are statistically non-inferior to the human baseline. The rigor standards applied to clinical interventions — as discussed, for instance, in Bhatt and Mehta's 2016 NEJM analysis of adaptive trial designs — should apply here. There is no coherent justification for a lower evidentiary threshold in administrative AI simply because the harm pathway is less direct.⏎⏎3. Require that any AI tool deployed in administrative functions in federally funded facilities include a mandatory human review checkpoint for any output that affects a patient's access to care — not as a general principle, but as a specific, auditable workflow requirement with documentation standards.⏎⏎ANA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎GLI recognizes that HHS is under real pressure to demonstrate that the Department can move quickly on AI adoption, and that the efficiency gains in some clinical AI applications are genuine. Garg et al. (2005, JAMA) found mixed but sometimes meaningful effects of computerized clinical decision support on practitioner performance and patient outcomes, and that evidence base has strengthened in certain domains since. The case for accelerating AI in, say, imaging interpretation or sepsis prediction is materially different from the case for automating the work of a patient navigator who knows which community health worker at the FQHC in Rio Rancho speaks the patient's Diné dialect and can get them on the phone in twenty minutes. Those are not the same kind of work, and HHS should stop treating them as if they are.⏎⏎The comment period for this RFI closes before GLI's Q3 member survey data will be fully analyzed, which means the Department will be making initial policy decisions without the benefit of updated implementation data from our network. SYNTH-0022♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Lisa Sanchez♔Stryker Corporation♔♔♔♔♔Lisa Sanchez, Health IT Director⏎Stryker Corporation⏎Portland, Oregon 97201⏎⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL⏎⏎⏎PRELIMINARY NOTE ON INSTITUTIONAL STANDING⏎⏎Stryker Corporation's health IT operations maintain active operational data on clinical documentation burden across 847 client records analyzed during the 2023-2024 caseload period. That analysis found administrative documentation — progress notes, treatment plans, prior authorization submissions — consuming an average of 4.2 hours per clinician per week, which is 11% of total billable capacity. A structured survey of 34 licensed clinical social workers operating within our practice networks, conducted in the same period, found that 79% identified AI-assisted documentation as their single highest-priority technology need. Clinicians further reported that documentation overhead directly reduced session availability by an estimated 6-9 client contact hours per month per provider. These numbers are not offered here to demonstrate enthusiasm for AI deployment. They are offered because the Department needs to understand what the actual problem is before it issues policy that will predictably make the problem worse.⏎⏎⏎RESPONSE TO RFI QUESTION: REGULATORY AND REIMBURSEMENT ACTIONS TO ACCELERATE AI ADOPTION⏎⏎The Department's posture in this RFI is accelerationist. The framing — what regulatory, reimbursement, and R&D actions can HHS take to accelerate adoption — presupposes that the primary obstacle to beneficial AI in clinical care is insufficient institutional momentum, and that federal policy should function as an accelerant. That framing is wrong, and Stryker's operational data, combined with the published clinical literature, gives the Department specific and concrete reasons to reconsider it.⏎⏎The burnout literature is unambiguous about what is actually driving clinician attrition and care degradation. Shanafelt et al. (2022), published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, documented that physician burnout rates increased from 38.2% in 2011 to 62.8% by 2021, with EHR burden and loss of professional autonomy identified as primary structural drivers. Melnick et al. (2020), also in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, found a direct association between perceived EHR usability problems and professional burnout among U.S. physicians, with the burden concentrated in documentation tasks. Sinsky et al. (2016), in the Annals of Internal Medicine, found that physicians in ambulatory practice spent 49.2% of their total work time on EHR and desk work, and only 27% in direct face-to-face patient contact. Overhage and McCallie (2020), also in Annals of Internal Medicine, found that physician time spent in the EHR during outpatient encounters averaged 16 minutes per visit, with documentation consuming the majority of that time. The documentation burden is real, it is severe, and it is causally linked to burnout. Stryker's own survey data, showing 79% of clinical social workers prioritizing AI documentation tools, is consistent with this literature.⏎⏎The problem is what health systems are actually doing with AI tools marketed as solutions to this problem. National Nurses United's 2023 research report, "Safeguards for Safe Staffing: AI and Nurse Staffing in U.S. Hospitals," documented systematic patterns in which AI-enabled productivity monitoring was used by hospital administrators to justify staffing reductions rather than workload relief. The American Hospital Association's 2023 workforce survey found that technology adoption decisions in health systems are concentrated at the administrative level, with frontline clinical staff structurally excluded from procurement processes. This is not an aberration. It is the predictable consequence of deploying efficiency tools in institutions whose financial incentives reward throughput over workforce sustainability.⏎⏎Stryker Corporation's position is that the Department's accelerationist framing will hand health system administrators a policy mandate to do exactly this at scale.⏎⏎⏎Stryker Corporation Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE WORKFORCE HARM IS A PATIENT HARM⏎⏎The causal chain here is specific and it needs to be stated plainly. Dyrbye et al. (2019), in the Journal of Nursing Administration, found direct relationships between work-unit safety climate, burnout severity, and measurable patient safety outcomes. Wachter and Goldsmith (2018), writing in Harvard Business Review, argued that EHR-related burnout is producing a workforce crisis with direct downstream effects on care quality, and that technology interventions that increase documentation load or reduce professional autonomy will worsen outcomes regardless of their efficiency claims. Bates et al. (2021), in npj Digital Medicine, acknowledged that AI has genuine potential to reduce documentation burden but cautioned that deployment design, governance structures, and institutional incentive alignment determine whether that potential is realized or inverted. The causal mechanism is not complicated: clinicians who are surveilled, overextended, and stripped of professional judgment make more errors, leave the workforce faster, and produce worse outcomes for the patients in front of them. This is an outcomes argument, not a values argument.⏎⏎The Department should also be clear-eyed about what AI-driven productivity monitoring does to professional autonomy specifically. Ajunwa, Crawford, and Ford (2017), in the California Law Review, documented how algorithmic workplace surveillance systematically erodes worker discretion and devalues professional expertise in ways that are structurally distinct from traditional management oversight. In clinical settings, where professional judgment is the mechanism of care, this degradation is not an HR problem. It is a safety problem. When a licensed clinical social worker's session notes are analyzed by an AI system whose output feeds into a productivity dashboard reviewed by an administrator with no clinical training, the clinician's professional authority over their own documentation is compromised. Topol (2019), writing in Nature Medicine, argued that the most beneficial AI deployments in medicine are those that augment physician judgment rather than replace or override it — a design principle that is structurally incompatible with the surveillance and throughput-optimization models currently being deployed in U.S. health systems.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS WITH THE RFI'S FRAMING AND SCOPE⏎⏎The RFI asks what actions HHS can take to accelerate adoption. Stryker's response is that the Department has asked the wrong question, and the right question is: under what governance conditions, with what demonstrated safeguards, and subject to what accountability mechanisms, should AI deployment in clinical settings receive federal support or reimbursement recognition?⏎⏎The following conditions are the minimum acceptable threshold:⏎⏎1. Mandatory frontline worker consultation in procurement. Any AI tool deployed in a clinical or administrative setting that receives federal reimbursement support or is deployed in a federally-funded health system must have documented evidence of frontline clinician consultation prior to procurement. "Consultation" means structured input from the workers who will use the system, with documented responses to that input — not a checkbox informational session conducted after the contract is signed.⏎⏎2. Demonstrated workforce safety standards before deployment. HHS should require that AI vendors demonstrate, with independently audited data, that their tools do not increase documentation burden, alert fatigue, or productivity surveillance load on frontline workers. The burden of demonstration falls on the vendor and the deploying institution, not on the workforce.⏎⏎3. Explicit prohibition on using AI productivity data to justify staffing reductions. Any health system that uses AI-generated productivity metrics as a basis for reducing clinical staffing ratios, eliminating administrative support roles, or increasing caseload thresholds should be ineligible for federal AI adoption incentives. This prohibition needs to be explicit, not implied.⏎⏎4. Equity and disparate impact review. AI tools deployed in clinical settings serving populations protected under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act must be subject to prospective disparate impact analysis, with findings made available to CMS and ONC prior to system-wide deployment.⏎⏎5. Incident reporting and accountability. HHS should establish a mandatory reporting mechanism for AI-related workforce harms, analogous to adverse event reporting in patient safety contexts. Workforce harm that produces patient harm should trigger the same regulatory accountability as other clinical safety failures.⏎⏎⏎Stryker Corporation Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎The Department may read these conditions as obstacles to the adoption the RFI is designed to accelerate. Stryker's position is that deployment without these conditions is not adoption — it is imposition, and the distinction matters for outcomes. The 34 licensed clinical social workers in our survey network who identified AI documentation tools as their highest-priority need are not asking for tools selected by their administrators and optimized for throughput. They are asking for tools that actually reduce the 4.2 hours per week they spend on documentation that doesn't require their clinical expertise. Those are not the same request, and federal policy that treats them as equivalent will produce predictable harm.⏎⏎There is a version of AI deployment in clinical settings that would genuinely help the workforce and improve patient outcomes. Bates et al. (2021) identified ambient documentation, intelligent prior authorization processing, and context-aware clinical decision support as areas with real potential for burden reduction without autonomy erosion. Realizing that potential requires governance structures that the current market will not produce on its own, because the institutions making procurement decisions are not the ones bearing the cost of bad deployments. The clinicians and patients are.⏎⏎The Department has an opportunity to establish those governance structures now, before accelerated adoption locks in deployment patterns that will take years to reverse. What concerns Stryker, given the current framing of this RFI, is that the Department may instead issue guidance that treats adoption speed as the primary metric of success — and that health system administrators, who have every financial incentive to read that guidance as permission to impose AI on their workforces, will do exactly that. The NNU's 2023 findings on nurse staffing suggest this pattern is already well underway in hospitals. Extending federal reimbursement incentives to AI adoption without the governance conditions described above will accelerate that pattern, not correct it.⏎⏎Stryker Corporation respectfully requests that HHS convene a formal comment period specifically addressing AI workforce governance standards, separate from this RFI, and that any interim guidance issued on AI adoption reimbursement include an explicit prohibition on using AI productivity outputs as a basis for staffing decisions pending development of those standards. The specific mechanism for the staffing prohibition — whether regulatory, through conditions of participation, or through CMS reimbursement policy — is a detail worth working through carefully, and Stryker would welcome the opportunity to participate in that process.⏎⏎Contact for follow-up:⏎Lisa Sanchez, Health IT Director⏎lsanchez@stryker.com⏎(503) 555-0194♔♔2026-02-26T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-26T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare will be used by employers and insurers as a mechanism for workforce surveillance, productivity extraction, staffing cuts, and the devaluation of clinical expertise rather than genuine care improvement.♔organization♔high♔angry♔Oregon♔health IT director♔42♔A cross-sectional analysis conducted across our 2023–2024 clinical caseload of 847 active client records found that administrative documentation—including progress notes, treatment plans, and prior authorization submissions—consumed an average of 4.2 hours per clinician per week, representing nearly 11% of total billable capacity. SYNTH-0023♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Sharon Ramirez♔Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine♔♔♔♔♔Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine⏎Department of Preventive Medicine — Biostatistics Division⏎Submitted via regulations.gov | HHS-2024-AI-RFI⏎⏎Sharon Ramirez, M.S., Biostatistician⏎Collaborative Research Network, 47-Site Clinical Trial Consortium⏎⏎---⏎⏎Northwestern Feinberg Biostatistics Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎---⏎⏎I. SCOPE AND FRAMING OF THESE COMMENTS⏎⏎These comments are submitted in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings, published in the Federal Register in 2024. The submission addresses a comparatively narrow but, from a methodological standpoint, quite pressing subset of the RFI's scope: the Department's apparent failure to distinguish between AI tools deployed in support of clinical decision-making and AI tools deployed in support of coverage determination and prior authorization by insurance entities. The RFI, as drafted, treats acceleration as a posture that applies uniformly across these deployment contexts. The evidence assembled through the submitter's institutional work — and through the published literature on insurance AI specifically — does not support that uniform posture. On the contrary, the evidence suggests that the insurance authorization context presents a configuration of incentive misalignment, training objective misspecification, and post-deployment performance drift that is structurally distinct from the clinical AI context and that warrants a regulatory response calibrated to that distinction, rather than the general acceleration framework HHS appears to be contemplating.⏎⏎The submitter's institutional vantage point is worth briefly describing, because it bears directly on the credibility of what follows. Beginning in 2023 and concluding in Q2 of 2024, the Logos Research Centre Biostatistics Working Group conducted a cross-site audit of AI validation practices across 47 affiliated clinical research sites, ultimately published as an internal technical report (Logos Research Centre Biostatistics Working Group, "AI Methodology Standards in Clinical Trial Environments: A Cross-Site Audit of Validation Practices Across 47 Affiliated Research Sites," Internal Technical Report Q2-2024, unpublished). The findings were, to put it plainly, not reassuring. Eighty-three percent of data teams reported integrating at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or predictive modeling tool into active study protocols. Fewer than thirty percent of those implementations had undergone formal prospective validation against pre-specified statistical benchmarks prior to deployment. A systematic review of 214 peer-reviewed manuscripts published between 2021 and 2023, conducted in parallel with the site audit, found that only 38% of publications reported adequate pre-registration of model performance thresholds. These figures describe research-grade environments — environments with institutional review boards, data safety monitoring committees, and professional statistical oversight. The insurance prior authorization context has none of those structural safeguards and adds to the absence of safeguards a set of financial incentives that actively push model outputs toward denial rather than clinical appropriateness. The gap between what the research literature documents and what HHS's RFI appears to assume is, in this submitter's assessment, quite wide.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Northwestern Feinberg Biostatistics Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎II. THE MISCHARACTERIZATION OF INSURANCE AI AS CLINICAL AI⏎⏎It would appear that the RFI's framing of AI in the health sector proceeds from an implicit model in which AI tools are primarily aids to clinicians — tools that help practitioners diagnose more accurately, flag drug interactions, or predict patient deterioration. This is a reasonable description of one class of AI deployment. It is not a reasonable description of the AI tools that, by volume of patient encounters affected, are probably the most prevalent form of health-sector AI in operation today: the automated prior authorization and claims adjudication systems deployed by major insurers, including but not limited to UnitedHealth Group, Cigna, and Humana. These systems do not assist clinicians. They override clinician judgment, and they do so at scale, using models whose training labels encode cost-containment objectives rather than clinical appropriateness criteria. The distinction is not semantic. It is a distinction between training objective alignment and training objective misspecification, and it has direct consequences for the harm distribution of model errors.⏎⏎The Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations documented this dynamic in considerable detail in its November 2023 report, "Denial, Delay, Deny: How Medicare Advantage Insurers Use AI to Override Physician Judgment." The Subcommittee found that UnitedHealth Group's nH Predict algorithm, deployed to adjudicate post-acute care authorizations for Medicare Advantage beneficiaries, generated denial rates that, according to reporting by Mukherjee and Ross in STAT News on November 14, 2023, reached approximately 90% for elderly patients seeking skilled nursing facility care following hospitalization. Ninety percent. That figure is not a performance metric consistent with a model trained to identify clinically inappropriate care requests. It is a figure consistent with a model trained — whether explicitly or through the structure of its reward signal — to minimize authorization approvals. The distinction between those two training objectives is precisely the kind of methodological issue that pre-deployment prospective validation against pre-specified clinical appropriateness benchmarks would be designed to detect. No such validation appears to have occurred prior to the deployment of nH Predict, and HHS's RFI does not propose to require it.⏎⏎One is compelled to note, parenthetically, that the phenomenon being described here is not unique to insurance AI. The broader problem of training objective misspecification in health AI is well-documented. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan, writing in Science in 2019, identified a commercially deployed algorithm used to manage the health of populations — an algorithm affecting an estimated 70 million people, as further described in Obermeyer and Mullainathan's 2019 proceedings paper at the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency — that had been trained to predict healthcare costs as a proxy for health need, producing systematic underestimation of need among Black patients whose historical healthcare utilization was depressed by access barriers rather than by lower underlying disease burden (Obermeyer et al., "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations," Science, 366(6464), 447-453, 2019). The insurance AI context replicates and amplifies this structural vulnerability: when the training label is cost rather than clinical appropriateness, the model will produce outputs that are systematically miscalibrated relative to the clinical construct the payer nominally claims the model is measuring.⏎⏎---⏎⏎III. THE APPEALS INFRASTRUCTURE AS A STATISTICAL PROBLEM⏎⏎Northwestern Feinberg Biostatistics Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎---⏎⏎The second dimension of this problem that the RFI appears not to have considered is the statistical structure of the appeals process through which AI-generated denials are nominally contestable. This is not a rhetorical observation about the fairness of the system. It is a quantitative observation about the population-level distribution of outcomes when an AI system generates a denial rate of the magnitude documented in the Senate Subcommittee investigation, and the appeals infrastructure is designed with friction levels calibrated to the assumption that only a small fraction of denials will be contested.⏎⏎Kaiser Family Foundation researchers Koma, Jacobson, and Neuman, writing in September 2023, found that Medicare Advantage beneficiaries appeal only a very small fraction of prior authorization denials, and that among those who do appeal, overturn rates are considerably higher than the low initial approval rates would suggest ("Prior Authorization in Medicare Advantage: How Often Are Requests Denied and What Happens on Appeal?" Kaiser Family Foundation Issue Brief, September 2023). The interpretation the submitter draws from this pattern — and it is an interpretation that follows fairly directly from the data — is that the appeals process is not functioning as an error-correction mechanism. It is functioning as a filter that attenuates the statistical signal of model error by ensuring that most of that error is never surfaced. When a model produces a 90% denial rate and fewer than a few percent of those denials generate appeals that are then overturned at a high rate, the information being generated about model performance is systematically truncated. Regulators who rely on complaint data or appeals data to assess the performance of these models will observe a system that appears to be functioning acceptably, because the denominator of errors that go uncontested is invisible.⏎⏎This is a measurement problem before it is a policy problem, and it is the kind of measurement problem that biostatisticians are trained to recognize. The population most affected by this information truncation is, not coincidentally, the population least equipped to navigate the appeals infrastructure: elderly beneficiaries, beneficiaries with disabilities, and low-income beneficiaries who lack the health literacy, the time, or the institutional support to pursue a multi-stage administrative appeal. Adler-Milstein and Nong, writing in Health Affairs in 2022, found that insurer disclosure of algorithmic decision tools in the prior authorization context is insufficient to support meaningful transparency for beneficiaries or their providers, compounding the already substantial informational asymmetry between the insurer deploying the model and the patient whose care access the model controls ("Toward meaningful transparency in prior authorization: Insurer disclosure of algorithmic decision tools," Health Affairs, 41(6), 812-819, 2022). The combination of high denial rates, low appeals rates, high overturn rates on appeal, and minimal disclosure of model methodology produces a system in which the documented harm is almost certainly a substantial underestimate of the actual harm.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Northwestern Feinberg Biostatistics Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎---⏎⏎IV. AUTOMATION BIAS AND THE CLINICIAN OVERRIDE PROBLEM⏎⏎There is a further methodological concern that the submitter wishes to raise, because it bears on how HHS might be thinking about the clinical AI context even if the Department eventually agrees to treat insurance AI separately. Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt, in their 2012 systematic review of automation bias published in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, documented the consistent tendency of human decision-makers to defer to automated system outputs even when those outputs are erroneous, with the frequency and magnitude of automation bias varying across clinical contexts and task types ("Automation bias: A systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators," JAMIA, 19(1), 121-127, 2012). In the insurance authorization context, the human override mechanism is not a clinician exercising independent judgment at the point of care — it is an administrative appeals process that, as described above, most affected patients do not successfully navigate. The practical result is that the AI system's output is, for the majority of affected beneficiaries, functionally final. Calling this a system with a human in the loop is technically accurate and substantively misleading.⏎⏎Rajpurkar, Chen, Banerjee, and Topol, in their 2022 review of AI in health and medicine published in Nature Medicine, observe that the deployment context of a health AI system — the incentive structures, the institutional setting, the population characteristics of end users — shapes the system's real-world performance in ways that laboratory validation cannot fully anticipate ("AI in health and medicine," Nature Medicine, 28(1), 31-38, 2022). This observation, which is not particularly controversial in the clinical AI literature, has an uncomfortable implication for the insurance AI context: a model that performs acceptably in a research or clinical validation environment may perform quite differently when deployed at scale by an insurer whose organizational incentives are aligned with denial rather than authorization. Post-deployment performance drift in this context is not merely a technical artifact of distribution shift. It may be an organizational artifact of deliberate calibration toward cost-containment objectives. Distinguishing between these two explanations requires independent audit access to the model's training data, its performance monitoring logs, and its denial rate distributions — access that is not currently required of insurers deploying these systems and that HHS's RFI does not propose to mandate.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Northwestern Feinberg Biostatistics Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 5⏎⏎---⏎⏎V. THE VALIDATION GAP AS AN INSTITUTIONAL FINDING, NOT AN ABSTRACTION⏎⏎The submitter wants to be clear that the foregoing is not a theoretical concern about what might happen as AI adoption accelerates. The validation gap is a documented institutional finding, and it exists in research environments that are, by any reasonable standard, more methodologically rigorous than the insurance authorization context. The Q2 2024 cross-site audit referenced above found that regulatory submission packages for AI-assisted clinical decision support tools consistently lacked reproducible calibration data, and that this absence created downstream reimbursement and liability ambiguities for member institutions. These were research institutions with statistical review processes, not insurers with financial incentives to minimize clinical appropriateness review. If fewer than 30% of research-grade AI deployments have undergone prospective validation against pre-specified benchmarks, the probability that a commercially deployed insurance AI system has undergone equivalent validation is, to put it conservatively, not high.⏎⏎Doshi-Velez, Kortz, Budish, Bavitz, Gershman, O'Brien, and Wood, in their 2017 Berkman Klein Center publication on the accountability of AI under law, identified the absence of pre-specified performance standards as a structural obstacle to meaningful accountability for AI systems affecting high-stakes decisions ("Accountability of AI under the law: The role of explanation," Berkman Klein Center Research Publication, 2017-19). Without pre-specified benchmarks, there is no principled basis for determining whether a model is performing within acceptable parameters or whether its outputs represent actionable errors. In the insurance context, this means that a model producing a 90% denial rate for a particular patient population cannot be evaluated against any external standard unless someone has, in advance, specified what denial rate distribution would be consistent with clinically appropriate utilization management. No such specification currently exists for the nH Predict algorithm or, to this submitter's knowledge, for any comparable commercially deployed insurance AI system. HHS's acceleration agenda, as currently framed, would add more tools to this landscape without addressing that foundational absence.⏎⏎The discriminatory potential of this validation gap is not hypothetical. Hoffman and Podgurski, writing in the Yale Journal of Health Policy, Law, and Ethics in 2023, documented the mechanisms through which AI systems in health care can produce and perpetuate discriminatory outcomes, including through the encoding of historical utilization patterns that reflect prior discrimination rather than underlying health need ("Artificial intelligence and discrimination in health care," Yale Journal of Health Policy, Law, and Ethics, 22(2), 1-58, 2023). The connection to Geruso and Layton's 2020 Journal of Political Economy analysis of upcoding behavior in Medicare risk adjustment is worth noting here: when financial incentives create systematic pressure to misrepresent or selectively represent patient characteristics, the data generated by the system becomes compromised as a training input for any subsequent AI application ("Upcoding: Evidence from Medicare on squishy risk adjustment," Journal of Political Economy, 128(3), 984-1026, 2020). Insurance AI trained on claims data generated under conditions of systematic upcoding or selective utilization management will inherit the biases embedded in that data. Whether those biases fall disproportionately on elderly beneficiaries, on beneficiaries of color, or on beneficiaries with complex chronic conditions is an empirical question that cannot be answered without demographic stratification of denial rate distributions — which, again, is not currently required.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Northwestern Feinberg Biostatistics Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 6⏎⏎---⏎⏎VI. THE RFI'S INSTITUTIONAL BLIND SPOT⏎⏎The submitter acknowledges that HHS's RFI is focused on clinical care settings, and that a strict reading of the RFI's scope might place insurance prior authorization systems outside its purview. That reading, however, seems unpersuasive as a practical matter. The question of whether a patient receives a clinically recommended service is not separable from the question of whether an AI system has authorized payment for that service. The clinical care setting and the insurance authorization setting are not two distinct domains that happen to involve AI — they are two components of a single system in which AI-generated coverage determinations function as de facto clinical decisions for the large majority of patients who cannot successfully appeal them. If HHS is genuinely interested in the effect of AI on clinical care, the insurance authorization context is not peripheral to that inquiry. It is, by volume of patient encounters and by magnitude of documented harm, probably the most important component of that inquiry.⏎⏎The RFI's failure to address this context directly is not, the submitter suspects, malicious. It is more likely a consequence of the framing that AI in health care is primarily a tool for improving care delivery, with the harms being primarily errors of commission — an AI that misdiagnoses, that recommends the wrong drug, that fails to flag a deteriorating patient. That framing is not wrong as a description of risks in the clinical AI context. But it misses the class of harms that is generating the most documented patient injury right now, which is errors of omission facilitated by AI systems trained to minimize authorization: care that is never received because an algorithm denied it, by a patient who did not know she could appeal, or who tried to appeal and could not navigate the process, or who was discharged from a skilled nursing facility after eleven days because an AI system determined that eleven days was the statistically expected length of stay for her diagnosis code. That is not a future risk. It is a documented present harm, and HHS's RFI does not appear to see it.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Northwestern Feinberg Biostatistics Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 7⏎⏎---⏎⏎VII. POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The submitter offers the following recommendation, framed as specifically as the available regulatory space permits. HHS should require, as a condition of Medicare and Medicaid participation for any health plan deploying AI tools in coverage determination or prior authorization, that such tools undergo pre-deployment prospective validation against pre-specified clinical appropriateness benchmarks developed in consultation with relevant clinical specialty societies and independent biostatistical reviewers. The validation process should include, at minimum: specification of the clinical construct the model purports to measure; documentation of the training label used and its relationship to that clinical construct; prospective evaluation of model performance against the pre-specified benchmarks on a held-out population drawn from the deployment-target population; and independent audit rights for CMS or a designated third-party auditor, with access to training data, model architecture documentation, and post-deployment performance monitoring logs.⏎⏎In addition, HHS should require mandatory public disclosure of denial rate distributions stratified by beneficiary demographic characteristics, including age, race and ethnicity, disability status, and dual eligibility status, for all AI-assisted prior authorization and coverage determination tools deployed by Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care plans. These disclosures should be published annually, in a standardized machine-readable format, with sufficient methodological documentation to permit independent replication of the reported statistics. The denial rate elasticity of the model — meaning the sensitivity of the denial rate to changes in input variables associated with beneficiary demographic characteristics — should be reported as a required component of this disclosure. Without stratified disclosure of this kind, the demographic harm distribution of insurance AI systems will remain unmeasurable, and HHS's ability to assess whether its acceleration agenda is producing equitable outcomes across beneficiary populations will be correspondingly limited.⏎⏎The submitter recognizes that these recommendations are more demanding than the current regulatory baseline and that implementation would require coordination across CMS, ONC, and potentially the FTC. That coordination challenge is real. It is also, in the submitter's assessment, considerably more tractable than the alternative, which is allowing AI-assisted denial automation to expand at the pace HHS's RFI appears to contemplate, without the evidentiary infrastructure necessary to determine whether the systems being deployed are producing clinically appropriate outputs or systematically denying care to populations with the least statistical power to contest individual decisions. The validation gap documented in research environments is troubling enough on its own terms. In an environment where the financial incentives run directly counter to clinical appropriateness, the absence of prospective validation is not a gap. It is a structural feature.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Northwestern Feinberg Biostatistics Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 8⏎⏎---⏎⏎VIII. CONCLUDING OBSERVATIONS⏎⏎The submitter's concern, to be direct about it, is not that AI in health care is inherently harmful. The clinical AI literature, including the Rajpurkar et al. 2022 review cited above, documents genuine performance gains in specific diagnostic tasks, and the submitter has no objection to the deployment of AI tools that have been properly validated and are subject to ongoing independent performance monitoring. The concern is narrower and, in a sense, more technical: that HHS is proposing to accelerate adoption of a class of tools whose performance characteristics in the insurance domain have not been independently audited, whose training labels encode cost-containment rather than clinical appropriateness, and whose downstream harms fall disproportionately on populations with the least statistical power to contest individual decisions. That is a measurement and accountability failure, and it is a failure that the Department's RFI, by treating acceleration as the default posture without imposing the evidentiary standards necessary to evaluate what is being accelerated, appears poised to extend rather than correct.⏎⏎The submitter would also note, as a practical matter, that the Q2 2024 working group audit found that even research-grade institutions with dedicated statistical review capacity struggled to produce reproducible calibration data for AI-assisted decision support tools in regulatory submission packages. The expectation that insurance entities will voluntarily produce equivalent documentation without a regulatory mandate seems, on the basis of that experience, optimistic. The nH Predict situation documented by the Senate Subcommittee in November 2023 involved a tool that had apparently been in deployment for some time before the denial rate distribution attracted investigative attention. If the Department's goal is to ensure that AI acceleration in the health sector produces better patient outcomes rather than more efficient denial automation, the evidentiary requirements proposed above are not a constraint on acceleration. They are the precondition for knowing whether acceleration is working. Without pre-specified benchmarks, without stratified disclosure, and without independent audit access, the Department will be in the position of having accelerated adoption of tools whose performance it cannot evaluate — which is, to put it plainly, not a satisfactory regulatory posture for a Department whose statutory mandate includes the health and welfare of Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries.⏎⏎The submitter is available to provide additional methodological detail regarding the Q2 2024 cross-site audit findings or the systematic review methodology underlying the 38% pre-registration figure cited above. Inquiries may be directed to the Department of Preventive Medicine, Biostatistics Division, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.⏎⏎s.ramirez@northwestern.edu♔♔2026-01-15T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-15T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔12♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI-powered insurance decision-making automates prior authorization denials and coverage restrictions in ways that are opaque, unappealable, and systematically biased against vulnerable patients.♔academic_organization♔high♔resigned♔Iowa♔biostatistician♔31♔A 2024 internal analysis conducted across Logos Research Centre's collaborative network of 47 affiliated clinical trial sites found that 83% of data teams reported integrating at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or predictive modeling tool into active study protocols, yet fewer than 30% of those implementations had undergone formal prospective validation against pre-specified statistical benchmarks prior to deployment. SYNTH-0024♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Edward Walker♔Carbon Health♔♔♔♔♔Carbon Health Compliance Division⏎Comments on HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL-RFI⏎Submitted by: Edward Walker, Chief Compliance Officer, Carbon Health⏎⏎Carbon Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎Carbon Health operates urgent care, primary care, and virtual care clinics across more than a dozen states, and our compliance function has direct, ongoing visibility into how AI tools interact with clinical workflows, payer systems, and patient access. This comment focuses on a specific gap in the framing of HHS's request for information: the RFI asks how HHS can accelerate AI adoption in clinical care, but it does not adequately reckon with the fact that the most commercially scaled AI deployment in the healthcare sector right now is not a clinical improvement tool. It is insurance denial automation. Our firm's position is that HHS cannot responsibly design an acceleration framework without first acknowledging that dynamic and building in protections that predate any further incentivization of AI in coverage and reimbursement workflows.⏎⏎We have reviewed the RFI carefully. The framing is genuinely well-intentioned, and we do not dispute that AI has real applications in clinical documentation, diagnostic support, and care coordination that could benefit patients. What concerns us is the sequence. The RFI's implicit logic is that AI adoption has been too slow and that regulatory, reimbursement, and research-and-development actions should be used to speed it up. That may be the right posture for some AI applications. For payer-side AI operating in prior authorization and claims adjudication, it is the wrong posture, and the evidence for that claim is now substantial.⏎⏎Carbon Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎THE RFI'S BLIND SPOT: DENIAL AUTOMATION AS THE DOMINANT AI USE CASE⏎⏎The U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations published findings in October 2024 documenting that Medicare Advantage insurers are using algorithmic systems to deny care at scale, with approval rates varying dramatically by insurer and with denial rates for post-acute care that in some cases exceeded 80 percent for certain procedure categories (Senate PSI, "Denial, Delay, Disappear," October 2024). The Office of Inspector General had flagged this pattern two years earlier, finding that a meaningful share of prior authorization denials in Medicare Advantage did not meet clinical criteria and that beneficiaries were often unable to successfully appeal (OIG Report OEI-09-18-00260, April 2022). A Georgetown Health Policy Institute working paper published in January 2024 documented the policy gap directly: AI in health insurance has deployed faster than any regulatory framework has been able to respond, and the primary application has been cost containment, not clinical quality (Palanker, Volk, and Lucia, Georgetown CHIR Working Paper, January 2024).⏎⏎Our compliance team has observed this at the practice level. When Carbon Health clinicians submit prior authorization requests for medically indicated services, the denial and delay patterns we see from certain Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care organizations are not consistent with individualized clinical review. Response times are too fast, denial language is templated, and the criteria cited frequently do not align with current clinical guidelines. A 2023 Kaiser Family Foundation issue brief documented that prior authorization delays and denials in Medicare Advantage have increased over time, with beneficiaries reporting significant access barriers (Koma, Jacobson, and Orgera, KFF Issue Brief, March 2023). The American Medical Association's 2023 prior authorization physician survey found that 94 percent of physicians reported that prior authorization had delayed necessary care, and 33 percent reported that a patient had experienced a serious adverse event as a result (AMA Policy Research Perspectives, 2023).⏎⏎These are not edge cases. This is the operational reality that HHS's RFI does not address.⏎⏎Carbon Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎OPACITY AND THE UNAPPEALABILITY PROBLEM⏎⏎What makes algorithmic denial systems particularly difficult to challenge is that they are, in practice, nearly impossible to contest through standard appeals processes. The denial letter cites a policy criterion. The criterion was applied by an algorithm trained on claims data. The algorithm's decision logic is proprietary. The clinician who submitted the authorization request has no access to the model's inputs, weightings, or the specific data points that triggered the denial. Filing an appeal requires the clinical team to argue against a decision whose reasoning is not disclosed. The National Health Law Program documented this in detail in its 2023 report on algorithmic decision-making in Medicaid managed care, finding that automated systems had effectively replaced individualized determinations required under federal Medicaid rules with opaque, bulk denials that enrollees could not meaningfully contest (NHeLP Policy Report, 2023).⏎⏎Our internal compliance data is consistent with that finding. In a Q2 2024 review of AI-assisted reimbursement workflows across our client operations, we found that AI-generated clinical documentation and decision-support outputs attracted a 23 percent higher rate of payer scrutiny compared to conventional workflows. A portion of that scrutiny is attributable to the absence of standardized HHS guidance on AI-generated outputs, which is a real problem the RFI could address. But a larger portion reflects what happens when payer-side AI systems encounter provider-side clinical documentation and flag it for review using criteria that are never fully disclosed. Organizations without dedicated AI governance policies spent an average of 340 additional staff-hours annually reconciling audit findings tied to AI tool utilization. Those hours are not clinically productive. They are a tax on patient care generated by a lack of regulatory clarity.⏎⏎Carbon Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎TRAINING OBJECTIVES, CLINICAL APPROPRIATENESS, AND BIAS⏎⏎There is a structural problem with how commercial payer AI systems are built that the RFI's acceleration framing does not engage with. These systems are trained on cost-containment objectives. The optimization target is not clinical appropriateness; it is claims expense. A system trained to minimize expenditure will, if unconstrained, deny or delay care that is medically necessary but expensive, and it will do so with a statistical consistency that no individual human reviewer would replicate because no individual human reviewer would make the same decision 50,000 times a week. The Obermeyer et al. study published in Science in 2019 documented that an algorithm widely used to manage population health systematically underestimated the clinical needs of Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent health status, because the algorithm used cost as a proxy for health need (Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan, Science, 366(6464):447-453, 2019). That finding should have prompted a sector-wide audit of how training objectives shape algorithmic outputs in coverage contexts. It did not.⏎⏎Carbon Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 5⏎⏎The CMS CY2024 Medicare Advantage Final Rule did impose some new requirements on prior authorization timeliness and continuity of care (CMS-4201-F, 88 FR 22120, April 2023), and we acknowledge that as a meaningful step. But it did not require insurers to disclose the training objectives of AI systems used in coverage decisions, did not require equity auditing of denial rate disparities by race or disability status, and did not establish a pre-deployment safety standard for algorithmic prior authorization tools. The liability allocation framework for AI-generated coverage decisions remains essentially unresolved, a gap that Tschider's analysis of reasonable security duties in healthcare AI contexts identified as a foundational regulatory failure (Tschider, Saint Louis University Law Journal, 63(1):15-58, 2018). The administrative burden generated by the current system is not a side effect; it is a design feature. Himmelstein and Woolhandler documented that administrative costs in U.S. healthcare are persistently high and structurally embedded in payer-provider transaction workflows (Health Affairs Blog, May 2015). AI-driven denial automation adds a new layer to that burden without reducing the underlying inefficiency.⏎⏎DISPROPORTIONATE HARM TO VULNERABLE POPULATIONS⏎⏎Elderly, disabled, and low-income patients bear disproportionate harm from automated denial systems for reasons that are structural and, frankly, predictable. Medicare Advantage enrollees who receive algorithmic denials for post-acute care face a choice: pay out of pocket, go without care, or navigate an appeals process that requires submitting clinical records, obtaining physician attestations, and in many cases retaining legal assistance. Patients with serious illness or cognitive impairment are the least equipped to do any of that. The Senate PSI report documented cases where Medicare Advantage enrollees were discharged from skilled nursing facilities prematurely because algorithmic criteria, rather than physician judgment, determined that the stay was no longer medically necessary (Senate PSI, October 2024). The Kaiser Health News and Fortune investigation into electronic health records documented how technology adoption in clinical settings, when not governed by adequate accountability structures, can generate patient harm at scale (Schulte and Fry, KHN/Fortune, March 2019). The parallel to AI-driven denial systems is direct.⏎⏎Carbon Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 6⏎⏎NUMBERED RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Our firm respectfully urges HHS to consider the following specific actions in any regulatory, reimbursement, or research-and-development agenda that emerges from this RFI:⏎⏎1. Require pre-deployment safety and equity review for all AI systems used in prior authorization or claims adjudication by Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, and other federally regulated payers. This review should include documentation of training data sources, training objectives, denial rate disparities by race, disability status, and income level, and independent validation against clinical appropriateness standards.⏎⏎2. Mandate algorithmic transparency in coverage denials. When an AI system contributes to a prior authorization denial, the enrollee and the treating provider must receive a disclosure that identifies the system's role, the criteria applied, and the data inputs that triggered the denial. This is a minimum requirement for meaningful appeal rights.⏎⏎3. Establish a meaningful human review requirement. Any prior authorization denial generated or scored by an AI system must be reviewed and affirmed by a licensed clinician with relevant specialty training before the denial is final. Templated review processes in which a clinician signs off on algorithmically generated denials without independent clinical analysis should not satisfy this requirement.⏎⏎4. Direct OIG and CMS to conduct a joint audit of denial rate disparities across Medicare Advantage plans using AI-assisted prior authorization tools, with findings published no later than 18 months following this RFI's comment period close.⏎⏎5. Clarify liability allocation for AI-generated coverage decisions. HHS should work with CMS and ONC to issue guidance specifying that payers bear legal responsibility for coverage decisions in which AI systems played a material role, and that the opacity of a proprietary algorithm does not constitute a defense against a finding that a denial was medically inappropriate.⏎⏎6. Exclude from any AI acceleration incentive program any payer-side AI application that has not completed pre-deployment equity auditing and safety validation, regardless of whether the application is characterized as administrative or clinical.⏎⏎Carbon Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 7⏎⏎The framing of this RFI as an acceleration agenda is, in our view, premature for the payer-side AI context. We understand that HHS is also thinking about clinical AI in diagnostic support, documentation, and care coordination, and we are broadly supportive of thoughtful regulatory structures that allow those applications to be tested and validated rigorously. But the acceleration framing cannot be applied uniformly across all AI applications in healthcare when one of the most commercially scaled AI applications is already generating documented patient harm. The 68 percent of healthcare organizations that our compliance reviews found had initiated AI-related clinical pilots without coherent governance frameworks are, in some cases, the same organizations that interact daily with payer AI systems that are denying their patients' care. HHS has the authority and the responsibility to set the sequence right.⏎⏎See Appendix A (not attached to this submission due to file size constraints): Carbon Health Compliance Division internal audit summary, Q2 2024, "AI Tool Utilization and Payer Interaction Patterns Across Multi-Site Clinical Operations," available upon request by contacting the compliance division directly at compliance@carbonhealth.com.⏎⏎Carbon Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 8⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Edward Walker⏎Chief Compliance Officer, Carbon Health⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL-RFI♔♔2026-02-23T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-23T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI-powered insurance decision-making automates prior authorization denials and coverage restrictions in ways that are opaque, unappealable, and systematically biased against vulnerable patients.♔organization♔high♔hopeful♔Utah♔compliance officer♔41♔A 2024 operational audit conducted across EHY Consulting LLC's portfolio of 47 healthcare client engagements found that 68% of those organizations had initiated AI-related clinical pilot programs but lacked a coherent compliance framework to govern data governance, liability allocation, or post-deployment monitoring. SYNTH-0025♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔David Young♔♔♔♔♔♔David Young | Home Health Aide | Emmett, Idaho⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎⏎Page 1⏎⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎⏎⏎Six weeks. That is how long it took for a medication interaction that had already been flagged by a hospital discharge algorithm to actually reach someone who could act on it. My client Marjorie, 84 years old, lives alone on a property outside Emmett, Idaho. She has no family within a two-hour drive. I am the person who takes her to appointments, who notices when her gait is off, who knows that she will not tell a doctor she is confused because she is afraid they will take away her independence. I drove her to three separate cardiology appointments over those six weeks. The cardiologist's office had not received the alert. The system had done what it was supposed to do — pattern-matched, flagged, generated an output — and the output had gone nowhere. A pharmacist caught it on week six, not because any algorithm surfaced it again, but because she asked Marjorie a question, listened to the answer, and noticed something was wrong.⏎⏎I want to be careful here. I am not saying the tool failed. I am saying the tool did exactly what it was designed to do, and the intervention still did not happen. That is the part I think HHS is not fully grappling with in this request for information.⏎⏎⏎ON THE FRAMING OF THIS REQUEST⏎⏎The RFI's framing of AI adoption as something to be accelerated — the word itself is doing a lot of work — treats the primary problem in clinical AI as a deployment gap. The implication is that hesitation or caution is the obstacle, and that removing regulatory friction will improve patient outcomes. I am genuinely not sure that is the right diagnosis. The gap I witnessed with Marjorie was not a failure of adoption speed. It was a failure of care coordination, of relational continuity, of the fact that no single person in that system was responsible for her as a whole patient rather than as a series of discrete encounters. Deploying more AI into that fragmented structure will not fix the fragmentation. It may make it harder to see.⏎⏎There is a substantial body of clinical evidence that the patient-clinician relationship itself carries measurable therapeutic value, independent of any specific treatment. Kelley and colleagues published a systematic review and meta-analysis in PLOS ONE in 2014 (Kelley JM, Kraft-Todd G, Schapira L, et al., PLOS ONE 9(4):e94207) documenting that the quality of that relationship predicts outcomes across conditions in ways that are statistically significant and clinically meaningful. That finding is not a soft or sentimental observation. It is a quantitative result from a synthesis of controlled studies. If we accept it as evidence, then any intervention that degrades the quality of the patient-clinician relationship carries a measurable cost, and that cost needs to appear somewhere in the calculus before we accelerate deployment.⏎⏎Dr. Abraham Verghese, writing with colleagues in JAMA in 2018, put this plainly: the risk of AI in clinical settings is not that it will make wrong predictions, but that it will displace the kind of reasoning and attention that good clinicians bring to a patient encounter (Verghese A, Shah NH, Harrington RA. JAMA. 2018;319(1):19-20). A clinician who is supervising a dashboard is doing something categorically different from a clinician who is examining a patient. Those two activities do not produce the same quality of judgment, even if the dashboard is accurate.⏎⏎⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎⏎David Young | Home Health Aide | Emmett, Idaho | Page 2⏎⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎⏎⏎ON AUTOMATION BIAS AND THE ATROPHY OF CLINICAL JUDGMENT⏎⏎This is the concern I keep returning to when I read through the RFI's questions about accelerating adoption. There is a well-documented phenomenon in the medical informatics literature called automation bias — the tendency of human operators to over-rely on automated recommendations and to reduce their own independent evaluation when an algorithmic output is present. Goddard and colleagues published a systematic review on this in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association in 2012 (Goddard K, Roudsari A, Wyatt JC. JAMIA. 2012;19(1):121-127) that found automation bias is a consistent and measurable effect in clinical decision support environments. It is not a failure mode that appears only in bad systems or careless clinicians. It appears across skill levels, across specialties, and it is more pronounced when clinicians are fatigued or time-pressured — which describes most of the clinical environments where AI deployment is being discussed.⏎⏎The practical consequence is this: a clinician who routinely defers to algorithmic outputs will, over time, be less capable of independent reasoning when the algorithm is wrong or absent. That is not a hypothesis. It is an observed effect. And if HHS accelerates AI adoption across clinical settings without building in structural requirements for independent clinical reasoning alongside the tool, the likely outcome is a generation of clinicians who are technically supervised by software they cannot meaningfully override.⏎⏎I am not certain I have the policy vocabulary to say exactly what the right regulatory response is. But I am certain that an acceleration posture, without corresponding requirements around demonstrated relational and clinical safety, is the wrong direction. The American College of Physicians said something similar in their 2023 Ethics Policy Statement on AI in clinical practice: that AI systems in clinical care must be subject to evaluation not only for technical accuracy but for their effects on the patient-physician relationship and on the integrity of clinical reasoning itself (American College of Physicians, Ethical Implications of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice, ACP Ethics Policy Statement, 2023). That standard is not currently embedded in this RFI's framing, and I think it should be.⏎⏎⏎WHAT I WOULD ASK HHS TO CONSIDER⏎⏎Rather than trying to address the full scope of the RFI, I want to focus on two specific concerns that come directly from my experience providing home-based care to elderly patients in rural Idaho.⏎⏎1. The coordination gap is not a technology gap.⏎⏎What happened with Marjorie was not a failure of AI capability. The algorithm worked. The failure was in the human infrastructure around the algorithm — the question of who is responsible for acting on an output when a patient spans multiple care settings, has no care coordinator, and relies on a home health aide and a pharmacist as her most consistent points of contact. More AI deployment into that structure does not solve the coordination problem. It may produce more outputs that go unread, more flags that get lost between systems, more documented alerts that no one is accountable for acting on.⏎⏎HHS should, before accelerating AI adoption, require that any clinical AI deployment include a clearly designated human responsible for each patient-facing output — not a system, not a role in the abstract, but a named individual in a care relationship with that patient. In home health settings, that often means the aide, not the physician. That has implications for training, for scope of practice, and for how AI outputs are designed to be communicated. None of those questions appear in this RFI.⏎⏎2. Presence cannot be automated, and the attempt to do so carries clinical risk.⏎⏎Research on virtual health agents and remote patient interaction — including work by Bickmore, Pfeifer, and Jack published through the SIGCHI Conference in 2009 on low health literacy patients and virtual nurse interactions — shows that patients, particularly elderly and low-literacy patients, respond differently to automated interactions than to human ones, and that the difference matters clinically (Bickmore TW, Pfeifer LM, Jack BW. Proc. SIGCHI Conf. Human Factors in Computing Systems. 2009). The response to a virtual agent is not simply a degraded version of the response to a human clinician. It is a qualitatively different interaction that elicits different disclosures, different levels of trust, and different health behaviors.⏎⏎Marjorie will tell me things she will not tell her cardiologist. She will not tell a screen anything. That is not a limitation that better AI design will overcome. It is a feature of how human beings process vulnerability and trust. A policy posture that treats AI-mediated interaction as functionally equivalent to clinician presence — or as an acceptable substitute for patients who lack access to in-person care — is not expanding access. It is rationalizing a lower standard of care for already-underserved populations.⏎⏎⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎⏎David Young | Home Health Aide | Emmett, Idaho | Page 3⏎⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎⏎⏎ON DR. TOPOL'S ARGUMENT AND WHERE I THINK IT GOES WRONG⏎⏎Eric Topol's 2019 paper in Nature Medicine (Topol EJ. Nature Medicine. 2019;25:44-56) is probably the most widely cited optimistic case for AI in clinical care, and I want to engage with it seriously rather than dismiss it. His argument is that AI, by taking over certain pattern-recognition tasks, will free clinicians to spend more time in direct patient contact — that the convergence of human and artificial intelligence will restore the human element of medicine rather than eroding it. I find that argument genuinely compelling in the abstract, and I am not sure he is wrong about the technical potential.⏎⏎What I am not sure about is whether the institutional and economic incentives in American healthcare will allow that potential to materialize the way Topol describes. In practice, when clinical tasks are automated, the time freed up is rarely reinvested in patient contact. It is absorbed by increased patient volume, by documentation requirements, by administrative overhead. I have not seen evidence that AI deployment in clinical settings has, in practice, increased the average time clinicians spend in direct relational contact with patients. If HHS has that evidence, I would like to see it presented clearly before the Department adopts an acceleration posture premised on Topol's optimistic scenario.⏎⏎The honest version of this question is: who benefits from acceleration, and in what timeframe? Vendors benefit immediately. Health systems benefit from efficiency gains on a quarterly reporting cycle. Patients — particularly elderly, isolated, or cognitively vulnerable patients — bear the relational and clinical risks of a transition that may take a decade to evaluate properly. That asymmetry in who bears the downside risk should be part of how HHS frames its regulatory posture, and I do not see it in the RFI.⏎⏎⏎A DIRECT REQUEST⏎⏎What I am asking HHS to consider is a precautionary standard that requires, before deployment at scale, demonstrated evidence that a clinical AI system does not degrade the quality of the patient-clinician relationship or the independence of clinical reasoning in the environments where it will be used. Not proof of perfection. Not a prohibition on innovation. A demonstrated safety standard that includes relational and cognitive dimensions, not only technical accuracy metrics.⏎⏎That standard should be applied with particular rigor in settings serving elderly patients, patients with low health literacy, patients with cognitive impairment, and patients in rural or isolated settings who have limited capacity to seek second opinions or navigate system errors on their own. These are not edge cases. They are a substantial portion of the patients who will be most affected by clinical AI deployment, and they are the least able to self-advocate when an algorithm produces an output that no human ever acts on.⏎⏎The requirements I would ask HHS to build into any acceleration framework include at minimum:⏎⏎o A named human accountability structure for each patient-facing AI output, with documentation requirements that trace the output to a specific clinical action or a specific documented decision not to act.⏎⏎o Pre-deployment evaluation of effects on clinician reasoning independence, using study designs that can detect automation bias as an outcome, not just diagnostic accuracy.⏎⏎o Post-deployment monitoring requirements in home health and community-based settings specifically, where the gap between algorithmic output and bedside care is widest and the patient populations are most vulnerable.⏎⏎o A formal process by which home health aides, community health workers, and other non-physician care providers can report coordination failures involving clinical AI outputs — because in my experience, we are often the first to know when something has gone wrong, and there is currently no mechanism for that knowledge to reach regulators or developers.⏎⏎I recognize that some of these requirements would slow deployment. I think that is appropriate. The question of whether AI can improve clinical care is genuinely open, and I am not opposed to the answer being yes. What I am opposed to is treating speed as a value in itself when the patients who will absorb the costs of moving too fast are people like Marjorie, who has no one else to drive her to the appointment where someone finally asks the right question.⏎⏎The pharmacist who caught Marjorie's medication interaction did not use an algorithm. She used six minutes and her full attention. I do not know how to put a reimbursement code on that, and I suspect that is part of the problem.♔♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔7♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔individual♔high♔concerned♔Idaho♔home health aide♔52♔My client Marjorie — 84 years old, lives alone outside Emmett — had a medication interaction flagged by a hospital discharge algorithm that her cardiologist's office somehow never received.
