SYNTH-0026♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Linda Green♔Humana♔♔♔♔♔Humana, Inc. -- Comments on HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL-RFI⏎Submitted by: Linda Green, Chief Financial Officer, Humana, Inc.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Humana, Inc. | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 1⏎⏎---⏎⏎I. THE ACCOUNTABILITY GAP THAT PRECEDES ADOPTION⏎⏎The PINC AI™ Healthcare Intelligence 2024 Clinical AI Deployment Outcomes Report, drawing on administrative and clinical data from more than 1,000 member hospitals, documents real and measurable operational benefits from AI-assisted clinical decision support: an average 8.3% reduction in unplanned 30-day readmission rates, and per-episode cost reductions of approximately $1,200 in high-acuity service lines (Premier Inc., Charlotte, NC, 2024). Humana does not dispute those figures. The problem is not that the clinical promise is overstated. The problem is that HHS is proposing to accelerate adoption of a technology whose deployment model contains a structural accountability failure that no amount of reimbursement clarification or billing code guidance will resolve. Sixty-four percent of facilities in the PINC analysis cited reimbursement uncertainty and ambiguous documentation requirements as barriers to scaling beyond pilots. Humana's concern sits upstream of that. Before the Department can responsibly accelerate adoption, it must answer a question that the existing legal and regulatory architecture cannot: when an AI-assisted clinical decision causes patient harm, who is answerable to the patient?⏎⏎This is not a theoretical concern. The legal doctrine underlying medical malpractice has, since its formation, assumed a human decision-maker whose judgment can be evaluated against a professional standard of care. When an AI system intermediates that judgment, the assumption breaks. Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert writing in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2023 documented specifically how algorithmic decision support disrupts the attribution chain that malpractice liability depends on, noting that courts have not developed a workable framework for assigning responsibility when a physician's clinical decision was shaped by an AI recommendation the physician may not have been technically equipped to interrogate (NEJM, 388(4): 349-355, 2023). Price, Gerke, and Cohen identified the same structural problem in JAMA in 2019, describing a liability environment in which physicians face potential exposure for following AI recommendations they were arguably required to follow under institutional protocol, while vendors face limited exposure under existing product liability doctrine (JAMA, 322(18): 1765-1766, 2019). The GAO reached a parallel conclusion in its February 2022 report, finding that the governance frameworks applicable to AI-assisted clinical tools were inconsistent across institutions and insufficient to support clear accountability at the point of harm (GAO-22-104629, Washington, DC, 2022).⏎⏎---⏎⏎Humana, Inc. | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎II. THE BLAME-DIFFUSION PROBLEM AS AN INSTITUTIONAL SCENARIO⏎⏎The accountability failure is not abstract when viewed from inside a health system's finance and risk function. Consider a concrete scenario: a patient presents at a Humana-affiliated facility, an AI-assisted clinical decision support tool recommends against escalation, a clinician follows that recommendation consistent with institutional protocol, the patient suffers a preventable adverse outcome, and the family brings a malpractice claim. The resulting liability exposure is distributed across at least three parties -- the attending clinician, the hospital as the institutional deployer of the AI system, and the vendor whose algorithm generated the recommendation -- and the legal responsibility of each is genuinely ambiguous under current doctrine. Kesselheim, Cresswell, and Sheikh described this exact diffusion pattern in BMJ Quality and Safety in 2023, characterizing it as a governance failure built into the deployment model rather than a gap that will resolve through litigation over time (BMJ Qual Saf, 32(6): 321-328, 2023). The American Hospital Association reached a similar conclusion in its 2023 policy statement on accountability frameworks for AI-assisted clinical decision support, recommending that HHS establish binding liability allocation standards before broad deployment, not after (AHA, Chicago, IL, 2023).⏎⏎Humana's position is that the absence of such standards is not a regulatory gap that can be patched incrementally. It is a design flaw in the deployment model as currently contemplated by federal AI policy. Cohen, Amarasingham, Shah, Xie, and Lo documented in Health Affairs in 2014 the legal and ethical risks that arise when complex predictive analytics are used in clinical settings without clear governance structures, and the years since have not produced the clarity they identified as necessary (Health Affairs, 33(7): 1139-1147, 2014). ONC's own 2023 discussion paper on transparency and accountability in AI-assisted clinical workflows acknowledged that existing frameworks were insufficient to support the accountability expectations that patients and clinicians reasonably hold, without specifying what binding standards would look like or when they would be issued (ONC Discussion Paper, HHS, Washington, DC, 2023). The National Academy for State Health Policy's 2024 survey of state medical liability statutes found that no state had enacted legislation specifically addressing AI-assisted care liability, and that existing statutory language in most states leaves the attribution question entirely unresolved (NASHP, Washington, DC, 2024). Obermeyer and Topol, writing in The Lancet Digital Health in 2023, called for a structural accountability framework rather than institution-by-institution policy development, precisely because the diffusion of responsibility across the clinician-hospital-vendor chain cannot be governed at the facility level alone (Lancet Digit Health, 5(3): e130-e132, 2023).⏎⏎---⏎⏎Humana, Inc. | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 3⏎⏎---⏎⏎III. WHAT HUMANA IS ASKING HHS TO DO BEFORE ACCELERATING ADOPTION⏎⏎Humana is not asking HHS to slow the development of clinical AI. The operational case for well-governed AI deployment is real. What Humana is asking is that HHS condition its acceleration agenda on the prior issuance of binding, not advisory, accountability standards that answer the following questions before additional capital is committed to scaling:⏎⏎1. Which party in the clinician-hospital-vendor chain bears primary liability when an AI-assisted clinical recommendation contributes to patient harm, and under what evidentiary standard is that determination made?⏎⏎2. What documentation requirements apply to AI-assisted clinical decisions for purposes of establishing the standard-of-care record in malpractice proceedings?⏎⏎3. What institutional governance structures must a hospital demonstrate before deploying AI-assisted decision support in high-acuity service lines, and how will HHS enforce those standards?⏎⏎4. What disclosure obligations does a vendor bear to the deploying institution regarding known failure modes, model drift rates, and performance degradation in patient populations that differ from training populations?⏎⏎Patients have a right to an answerable human being when something goes wrong in their care. That is a governance principle, not a sentiment. The current deployment model, as contemplated by this RFI, does not guarantee that right. Until HHS issues binding standards on the four questions above, Humana will not scale AI clinical deployments beyond controlled pilot programs in facilities where institutional liability can be clearly contained, and the aggregate capital investment that remains deferred across the health system -- estimated at $340 million in the PINC 2024 finance leadership roundtables -- will remain deferred. The reimbursement clarity HHS is considering offering is not the binding constraint. The accountability architecture is. Humana respectfully requests that HHS treat the issuance of binding liability allocation standards as a prerequisite to, not a parallel track alongside, the acceleration agenda this RFI⏎⏎---⏎⏎linda.green@humana.com⏎Humana, Inc.⏎500 West Main Street, Louisville, KY 40202♔♔2026-02-18T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-18T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔3♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔organization♔high♔resigned♔Mississippi♔hospital CFO♔37♔A 2024 PINC AI™ analysis of administrative and clinical data from more than 1,000 member hospitals found that facilities deploying AI-assisted clinical decision support tools reduced unplanned 30-day readmission rates by an average of 8.3%, while simultaneously cutting per-episode costs by approximately $1,200 in high-acuity service lines. SYNTH-0028♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔George Adams♔♔♔♔♔♔George Adams⏎Licensed Clinical Social Worker⏎Salt Lake City, Utah 84103⏎Submitted to HHS Docket: AI in Clinical Care RFI⏎⏎RE: Administrative AI Deployment and the Skilled Labor Question⏎⏎⏎WHAT THIS RFI GETS WRONG ABOUT ADMINISTRATIVE WORK⏎⏎A few years ago I was sitting at a kitchen table in Duchesne County while a rural telehealth provider spent the better part of forty minutes manually reconciling contradictory discharge notes from three different facilities. My client, a man in his early fifties navigating both a traumatic brain injury and a Medicaid care network that had been restructured twice in eighteen months, sat across from us. That forty minutes was not a system failure in any way that would appear in a quality metric. No alert fired. No flag appeared in the EHR. The provider simply knew, from experience, that the notes did not add up, and she worked it out by calling two people she had relationships with at the other facilities.⏎⏎I want to be specific about why that matters, because the framing of this RFI concerns me. The question HHS is effectively asking is: where can AI reduce administrative burden? That is a reasonable question. But embedded in it is an assumption I think deserves direct challenge, which is that administrative healthcare work is primarily processing work, and that the friction in it is waste. My experience across twelve years of Medicaid-serving case management in rural Utah is that this assumption is wrong in ways that will cause real harm if it is encoded into AI deployment policy.⏎⏎The social work and health policy literature has a name for what that telehealth provider was doing. Michael Polanyi (1966) called it tacit knowledge, the kind of expertise that is embodied and contextual and cannot be fully articulated, let alone captured in structured data or used as training inputs. Care coordination, patient navigation, Medicaid benefits counseling, prior authorization review, these are not clerical functions. Peikes et al. (2009) documented in JAMA that effective care coordination reduces hospitalizations and improves health outcomes across Medicare populations, and the mechanism is not information processing speed. It is relational continuity and contextual judgment. Gottlieb and colleagues (2019) made a similar point about social needs navigation in Health Affairs: the work is irreducibly local and relational, dependent on knowing which county program has a waitlist this month, which caseworker at the state office will actually return a call, which patient cannot navigate an automated phone tree because of cognitive limitations that are not documented anywhere in the chart. None of that is in a training set.⏎⏎⏎THE "FREES UP HUMAN TIME" ARGUMENT NEEDS TO BE REBUTTED DIRECTLY⏎⏎I want to address the efficiency argument head on because it will come up repeatedly in comments from health system administrators, and it has surface plausibility. The claim is that AI handling routine administrative tasks frees up human workers to focus on complex cases. I genuinely do not understand how this argument survives contact with the actual staffing data. The NASW Workforce Survey (2022) documented that Medicaid-serving social workers and care coordinators are already operating well above sustainable caseload thresholds, with administrative burden cited as the primary driver of burnout and turnover. The workers who are supposed to be "freed up" are not sitting idle waiting for AI to hand them more interesting work. They are already at capacity, and in rural settings like the counties I work in, there is often no one else on the floor.⏎⏎The efficiency argument also ignores what Ash, Berg, and Coiera (2004) documented in JAMIA two decades ago: information technology in healthcare generates its own category of errors, errors that are invisible to the system but require human labor to catch and correct. When an AI misroutes a prior authorization request, or misclassifies a social determinant code, or generates a care summary that omits a medication listed only in a scanned PDF from a facility that never completed its EHR integration, someone has to find that error. That corrective labor falls on the same already-overwhelmed workers the efficiency argument promises to help. Bindman and Blum (2021) documented this specifically for Medicaid beneficiaries with complex needs in Health Affairs: administrative complexity is not just a burden on workers, it is a barrier to care, and automating the wrong parts of it can make the complexity worse rather than better.⏎⏎There is also the checkpoint problem, and I think this is the part that gets the least attention. Administrative friction is not always waste. Sometimes it is a checkpoint where human judgment catches a mistake before it reaches a patient. A care coordinator who notices that a prior authorization request does not match what the patient actually described in their intake interview is performing a quality function. That function is not legible to a system optimizing for throughput.⏎⏎Obermeyer et al. (2019) showed in Science that algorithmic tools used in health management systematically underestimate the needs of Black patients because the training data encoded existing disparities. The same dynamic will appear in any administrative AI trained on historical Medicaid workflows, which reflect decades of underfunding, inconsistent documentation, and differential access. The patients who will bear the cost of those errors are the ones who already have the least margin.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY ASKS FOR HHS TO CONSIDER⏎⏎Given the above, I want to direct HHS's attention to two specific gaps in how this RFI frames the deployment question.⏎⏎First, on accuracy and equity requirements before deployment:⏎⏎1. HHS should require demonstrated accuracy benchmarks for any administrative AI tool before it is deployed in Medicaid-serving settings, including disaggregated performance data by race, language, disability status, and rural versus urban geography. A tool that performs at 94% accuracy overall but at 78% accuracy for patients with limited English proficiency is not a tool that should be deployed without significant additional safeguards.⏎⏎2. Equity auditing should not be a one-time pre-deployment requirement. Administrative workflows change, patient populations shift, and model drift is a documented phenomenon. Post-deployment auditing on at least an annual basis should be a condition of any reimbursement or procurement incentive HHS creates.⏎⏎3. Human override capacity is not optional. Any administrative AI function that affects patient access to care, including prior authorization support, benefits navigation, and care plan generation, must have a clearly documented and accessible pathway for a human worker to review and reverse the AI's output. This pathway must be available to frontline workers, not just supervisors.⏎⏎Second, on who gets consulted in standard-setting:⏎⏎This is where I feel most strongly. The RFI asks broadly about what HHS can do to accelerate AI adoption, and the comments it will receive will be dominated by health system executives, EHR vendors, and AI developers. Those perspectives matter. But the people who actually understand where administrative workflows break down, where the tacit knowledge lives, where the checkpoints are, are the frontline workers: social workers, care coordinators, patient navigators, community health workers. The NASW Workforce Survey (2022) found that fewer than 20% of Medicaid-serving social workers reported being consulted in any technology adoption decision at their organization.⏎⏎If HHS is serious about deploying administrative AI in ways that do not harm vulnerable patients, it needs a formal mechanism for frontline administrative worker input in the standard-setting process. Not a comment box. A structured, compensated, representative process that reaches workers in rural settings, in community-based organizations, in county departments of health, not just in large academic medical centers.⏎⏎I recognize that none of this is an argument against AI in administrative healthcare functions categorically. There are probably narrow, well-defined tasks where AI assistance genuinely helps without introducing these risks. But the RFI as written does not make those distinctions, and the policy infrastructure it is building will shape deployment decisions for years. The specifics of what gets required, audited, and consulted before a tool goes live in a Medicaid office in Duchesne County matter more than the general framing of whether AI is good or bad for efficiency.⏎⏎The client who sat at that kitchen table is still navigating that care network.♔♔2026-02-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-12T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔4♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Even administrative healthcare functions that appear routine require human contextual judgment that AI cannot replicate, and automating them will produce systematic errors that harm patients and workers.♔individual♔high♔concerned♔Utah♔social worker♔49♔During a home visit with a client navigating both a traumatic brain injury and a fragmented Medicaid care network, I watched a rural telehealth provider spend forty minutes manually reconciling contradictory discharge notes from three different facilities — time that should have gone to my client sitting right there in the room. SYNTH-0029♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Donna Martin♔Boston University School of Public Health♔♔♔♔♔Submitted to HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information Docket⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary / ASTP-ONC⏎Donna Martin, Associate Professor⏎Boston University School of Public Health⏎Boston, MA 02118⏎⏎The promise of clinical AI is real, and the research base supporting targeted deployment in acute care settings has grown meaningfully. The Cornell AI and Health Initiative's March 2024 findings from six affiliated teaching hospitals — documenting a 23% reduction in time-to-diagnosis for sepsis cases when AI tools were integrated into existing clinical workflows — represent the kind of outcome this RFI seems designed to promote. Our own work in public health informatics at Boston University is broadly consistent with that finding: well-designed, well-supervised AI tools can improve care delivery for some of the most time-sensitive clinical decisions clinicians face. The Department is right to take this seriously. What concerns us, however, is that the RFI's framing of the problem is analytically incomplete in a way that, if left uncorrected, will produce federal policy that accelerates harm rather than benefit. The RFI treats reimbursement barriers as the central structural obstacle to AI adoption in healthcare. That framing is not wrong, exactly, but it is badly incomplete, because it proceeds as if the primary policy challenge is getting more AI into healthcare settings faster. The more consequential and far less examined challenge is that AI is already deployed at scale in the health sector — in insurance prior authorization workflows — and it is being used not as a therapeutic instrument but as a financial one, optimized to deny care rather than deliver it. Federal policy that focuses exclusively on accelerating AI adoption without confronting this reality will not produce better healthcare. It will produce a more efficient apparatus for denying it.⏎⏎The evidence on insurer AI deployment is no longer preliminary or anecdotal. The Office of Inspector General's 2022 report (OIG Report OEI-09-18-00260) found that Medicare Advantage organizations were denying prior authorization requests at rates that raised serious concerns about beneficiary access to medically necessary care, and that denial patterns were inconsistent with clinical evidence and Medicare coverage rules. The Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations followed in April 2024 with a detailed investigation into how Medicare Advantage insurers have denied patients access to post-acute care, documenting that major payers — including UnitedHealthcare and Humana — used algorithmic tools to generate high-volume denials of skilled nursing facility stays, often overriding physician recommendations with minimal individualized review (U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, 2024). Ledford's analysis in Nature Medicine in 2023 documented how AI-powered prior authorization systems at several large commercial payers were generating denial decisions at a rate and volume that made meaningful human review structurally impossible, with some systems processing tens of thousands of requests per day through automated pipelines (Ledford, 2023). The National Health Law Program's July 2023 policy report on automated denials found consistent patterns across Medicaid and Medicare Advantage programs: AI tools were being used to restrict access to care for the most vulnerable beneficiaries, with elderly and disabled patients bearing the greatest burden of wrongful denials (NHeLP, 2023). This is not a marginal or emerging problem. It is the dominant AI deployment story in American healthcare right now, and the RFI does not mention it.⏎⏎What makes this omission particularly troubling is the question of training objectives. Schulman and Richman, writing in JAMA Health Forum in 2023, made the point directly: the algorithmic prior authorization tools deployed by commercial payers are not trained to assess clinical appropriateness. They are trained to contain costs (Schulman & Richman, 2023, e231847). This is a structural design choice, not a bug or an incidental flaw. A systematic review of vendor documentation and payer contracts published in Health Affairs Scholar in 2024 by Mukherjee and Ganguli found that cost-containment objectives were explicitly encoded in the performance metrics used to evaluate AI prior authorization tools, while clinical accuracy metrics — sensitivity, specificity relative to independent physician review — were rarely included in vendor contracts and almost never publicly reported (Mukherjee & Ganguli, 2024, qxae041). The implications of this are serious. When we talk about AI in clinical care, we are generally talking about tools trained on patient outcome data, with some effort — however imperfect — to optimize for clinical benefit. When payers deploy AI in prior authorization, they are deploying tools trained on cost data, optimized for financial performance. These are categorically different applications, and federal policy that treats them as part of the same "AI in healthcare" category without distinguishing between them is not just analytically sloppy; it creates regulatory cover for the latter by association with the legitimacy of the former.⏎⏎Boston University School of Public Health comments on HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎The equity dimension of this problem deserves more attention than the RFI gives it. Obermeyer and colleagues' foundational 2019 Science paper demonstrated that a widely used commercial health algorithm systematically underestimated the care needs of Black patients relative to White patients with equivalent health status, because the algorithm used healthcare costs as a proxy for health need — a proxy that reflects historical patterns of unequal access rather than clinical reality (Obermeyer et al., 2019, Science 366:447–453). The same structural problem applies with even greater force to prior authorization AI. If denial algorithms are trained on cost data from populations that have historically been denied care at higher rates — Medicaid beneficiaries, low-income Medicare Advantage enrollees, patients in rural markets with limited provider competition — then those algorithms will systematically encode historical inequity into prospective coverage decisions. The Kaiser Family Foundation's October 2023 analysis of prior authorization denials and appeals in Medicare Advantage found that denial rates varied substantially by plan and geography, and that appeal rates were low — meaning that most denials were functionally final for most beneficiaries (Koma, Artiga, & Damico, 2023). Elderly, disabled, and low-income patients have the least capacity to navigate multi-stage appeals processes, the least access to patient advocates and healthcare attorneys, and the least institutional leverage over payers. For these populations, an AI denial is not a preliminary determination subject to review. It is the outcome. Fuse Brown and McCuskey's 2024 analysis in the Yale Journal on Regulation of accountability gaps in insurance AI makes the regulatory structure of this problem clear: insurance regulation is primarily a state-level function, federal minimum standards are absent, and the combination of algorithmic opacity and preemption risk creates a compliance environment in which payers face essentially no meaningful federal accountability for the design choices embedded in their AI tools (Fuse Brown & McCuskey, 2024, 41 Yale J. Reg. 203).⏎⏎The RFI's framing of reimbursement as a barrier to AI adoption does not grapple with the inverse problem at all. The relevant question for health sector AI policy is not only "how do we get payers to reimburse clinical AI tools?" It is also "how do we ensure that payers are not using AI tools to deny coverage for care that would otherwise be reimbursed?" These are related questions but they are not the same question, and the RFI's exclusive focus on the former treats the health insurance industry as a passive recipient of AI innovation rather than an active deployer of it. Blumenthal and colleagues' November 2023 Commonwealth Fund issue brief on AI in healthcare acknowledged this asymmetry directly, noting that the financial incentives for deploying AI in administrative and utilization management functions are considerably stronger than the incentives for deploying it in clinical care, because the former generates immediate, measurable cost savings while the latter requires longer time horizons and more complex outcome attribution (Blumenthal et al., 2023). The Department is, in effect, proposing to accelerate the clinical AI side of this equation while leaving the administrative AI side largely unaddressed, in a policy environment where the administrative side is already running considerably faster and with far less oversight.⏎⏎There is a tendency in federal health technology policy to treat each new RFI as an opportunity to start fresh — to frame the problem as if the relevant landscape is blank and the question is how to encourage adoption. This RFI exhibits that tendency. But the landscape is not blank. The question is not how to get AI into healthcare. The question is how to govern AI that is already there, already making consequential decisions about patient access, and already doing so in ways that the existing evidence strongly suggests are producing systematic harm for the most vulnerable beneficiaries. The Department has regulatory authority that has not been used. CMS has the ability to condition Medicare Advantage plan participation on compliance with specific requirements around prior authorization transparency and human review. HHS has the ability to use its existing civil rights enforcement authority under Section 1557 to require equity impact assessments for AI tools used in coverage determinations. The OIG has audit authority that could be directed at AI-generated denial rates as a compliance matter rather than a research question. None of these are novel legal theories; Dafny and Lee's work on health care consolidation and market structure provides a useful analogy for how existing regulatory authority can be applied to new structural problems without waiting for legislation (Dafny & Lee, 2022, NEJM 386:314). The Department does not need new statutory authority to begin. It needs the will to use what it has.⏎⏎Our specific recommendation, addressed to the RFI's implicit question about what regulatory actions HHS should take to shape AI adoption in healthcare: before any AI tool is permitted to operate in prior authorization or coverage determination workflows — whether in Medicare, Medicaid, or federally regulated commercial insurance products — HHS should require the following as a condition of program participation. First, demonstrated clinical appropriateness review: vendors must provide evidence, subject to independent audit, that their tools' denial recommendations correspond to clinically validated coverage criteria at a sensitivity and specificity rate comparable to independent physician review. Second, mandatory human oversight: every denial decision touching on acute care, post-acute care, or care for patients with serious illness must involve documented individual physician review, not algorithmic recommendation ratified by administrative staff. Third, transparent audit trails: payers must maintain and make available to regulators, upon request, complete records of the algorithmic inputs and decision rules that generated any specific denial, in a format that allows meaningful ex post review. Fourth, equity impact assessments: any AI tool used in coverage determinations must undergo pre-deployment analysis of differential denial rates by race, income, disability status, and geography, with results reported to CMS on an annual basis. The Cornell AI and Health Initiative's 2024 findings noted that 68% of clinicians in their sample reported insufficient institutional guidance on liability allocation when AI recommendations conflict with clinical judgment — a finding that maps directly onto the prior authorization context, where the liability question is if anything more acute because the AI is being deployed by a party with an adverse financial interest relative to the patient. That structural conflict is not incidental to the design of these systems. It is the point.⏎⏎donna.martin@bu.edu♔♔2026-01-25T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-25T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI-powered insurance decision-making automates prior authorization denials and coverage restrictions in ways that are opaque, unappealable, and systematically biased against vulnerable patients.♔academic_organization♔high♔hopeful♔Oklahoma♔associate professor♔53♔A 2024 analysis conducted through Cornell's interdisciplinary AI and Health Initiative, spanning six affiliated teaching hospitals and drawing on data from over 14,000 patient encounters, found that diagnostic AI tools demonstrated a 23% reduction in time-to-diagnosis for sepsis cases when integrated into existing clinical workflows. SYNTH-0030♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Steven White♔University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences♔♔♔♔♔Steven White, Ph.D.⏎Assistant Professor, Health Informatics and Social Science⏎University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences⏎1155 East 60th Street⏎Chicago, IL 60637⏎steven.white@uchicago.edu⏎⏎September 12, 2024⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care [Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI]⏎⏎University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences | HHS AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎⏎THE FRAMING ERROR THAT PRECEDES EVERY OTHER PROBLEM⏎⏎The framing of this RFI is itself the problem that most demands correction, and it is difficult to reconcile the Department's formulation of accelerated AI adoption as the governing objective with the now-substantial body of peer-reviewed evidence documenting the distributional harms that current clinical AI deployment patterns produce. HHS has organized this solicitation around the question of how to remove barriers to adoption. The literature — not speculation, not advocacy, but published, peer-reviewed empirical findings from institutions including the University of Michigan, MIT, and Stanford — has already answered a different and more pressing question: barriers to whose adoption, delivering what outcomes, for which patient populations, and at what cost to the populations that bear the greatest burden of existing health system failures. The failure to ask that prior question is not a minor gap in an otherwise sound policy framework. It is a category error that, if left uncorrected, will produce federally facilitated deployment of AI systems that have already been documented to perform worse for Black patients, for patients in safety-net institutions, and for patients whose clinical presentations are atypical precisely because they have been systematically excluded from the research settings that generated training data in the first place.⏎⏎The present comment addresses two of the RFI's implicit questions: first, what the evidentiary record actually shows about the equity consequences of clinical AI deployment as currently practiced; and second, what structural regulatory requirements HHS must establish as preconditions for any deployment pathway the Department chooses to facilitate. The comment does not address reimbursement design, vendor certification frameworks, or interoperability standards, not because those questions are unimportant, but because the equity and safety questions are logically prior and have not been adequately surfaced by the RFI's framing.⏎⏎University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎⏎WHAT THE EVIDENTIARY RECORD ACTUALLY SHOWS⏎⏎The pulse oximetry literature alone should have been sufficient to arrest the acceleration framing before this RFI was published. Sjoding, Dickson, Iwashyna, Gay, and Valley documented in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 that pulse oximeters — a device so commonplace it is regarded as a basic vital sign monitor — systematically overestimated arterial oxygen saturation in Black patients at a rate nearly three times that observed in white patients, meaning that patients in hypoxemic states were not identified as such and did not receive supplemental oxygen therapies they required. This is not a failure of an experimental algorithm; it is a failure of a measurement tool that was used for decades in clinical settings, validated against datasets that did not adequately represent the range of human skin tones, and deployed at scale before the disparity was documented. The relevance to AI is direct: AI systems trained on physiological data collected by biased measurement instruments will inherit and potentially amplify those measurement errors. Any AI sepsis prediction model, for instance, that incorporates pulse oximetry readings as a feature variable has a documented basis for differential performance by race that is independent of any other design choices the developers made.⏎⏎The sepsis prediction literature makes this concrete in ways that the Department appears to have treated as background noise rather than as evidence bearing on regulatory design. Wong and colleagues published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021 the results of an external validation study of Epic's Sepsis Prediction Model, one of the most widely deployed proprietary clinical AI tools in U.S. hospitals, examining its performance against 38,455 patient encounters at the University of Michigan Health System. The model demonstrated poor discrimination (AUROC of 0.74 compared to the developer's reported 0.76 to 0.83), generated a large proportion of false positives that consumed clinical resources and produced alert fatigue, and — most relevantly for the equity question — performed inconsistently across patient subgroups in ways that the proprietary nature of the model made impossible to audit systematically. The point here is not that 0.74 is an unacceptable AUROC in the abstract; it is that performance degradation in external validation is the rule, not the exception, for clinical AI tools, and that the populations most likely to be served by institutions that differ most substantially from the academic medical centers where validation was conducted are also the populations least likely to benefit and most likely to be harmed by false-negative outputs.⏎⏎University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan's 2019 analysis in Science of a commercial risk-stratification algorithm used by health systems serving approximately 200 million patients annually found that the algorithm assigned lower risk scores to Black patients than to white patients with the same objective health burden, effectively directing care management resources away from Black patients who were in equivalent or worse health. The mechanism was not overt racial coding; the algorithm used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, and because Black patients have historically had lower healthcare utilization due to access barriers, cost became a variable that encoded and reproduced the structural effects of those barriers. This finding is now five years old. It has been cited more than 3,000 times in the peer-reviewed literature. And yet the RFI contains no proposed requirement that algorithms submitted for any HHS-facilitated deployment pathway be audited for proxy discrimination of this kind before they reach patients.⏎⏎The dermatology literature presents a parallel documented failure. Adamson and Smith published in JAMA Dermatology in 2018 an analysis demonstrating that the training datasets underlying the leading machine learning models for skin lesion classification were composed overwhelmingly of images from patients with lighter skin tones — one widely cited dataset drawn from Stanford's dermatology department was more than 70% white — with the consequence that model performance for melanoma detection in patients with darker skin tones was substantially degraded precisely where the clinical stakes of missed diagnosis are highest, because melanoma is more likely to be diagnosed at later stages in Black patients due to pre-existing access and screening disparities. The AI system did not create those disparities, but it encodes them and, when deployed in a screening workflow, will reproduce them at whatever scale the HHS acceleration agenda achieves.⏎⏎Seyyed-Kalantari, Zhang, McDermott, Chen, and Ghassemi published findings in Nature Medicine in 2021 that are, if anything, more alarming than the dermatology literature because they concern chest radiograph interpretation — a diagnostic modality that is central to the detection of pneumonia, tuberculosis, and a range of conditions that disproportionately burden underserved populations. Their analysis of three large publicly available chest X-ray datasets found systematic underdiagnosis bias in AI algorithms applied to radiographs from patients who were female, younger, non-white, or uninsured. The underdiagnosis rate for Black patients in the CheXpert dataset was measurably higher than for white patients even when controlling for disease prevalence. The authors concluded that deploying these algorithms in clinical workflows without subgroup-specific performance auditing would systematically direct diagnostic resources away from already-underserved patients. The finding was published in 2021. This RFI was published in 2024. The absence of any proposed mandatory subgroup performance auditing requirement in the RFI is not an oversight; it reflects a policy posture that treats documented, peer-reviewed evidence of systematic harm as a problem to be addressed later, after deployment, rather than as a gate that deployment must clear.⏎⏎University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎⏎THE GENERALIZABILITY PROBLEM IS STRUCTURAL, NOT INCIDENTAL⏎⏎Wiens, Saria, Sendak, Ghassemi, Liu, Doshi-Velez, and Goldenberg articulated in Nature Medicine in 2019 what the field has increasingly confirmed as a general principle: clinical AI models trained in high-resource academic medical center environments degrade in performance when deployed in community hospitals, rural health systems, and safety-net institutions. This degradation is not merely a function of dataset shift in the technical sense; it is a function of systematic differences in documentation practices, coding culture, patient demographics, care protocols, and the density of structured versus unstructured clinical data. A model trained at a large urban academic medical center on well-curated EHR data from a relatively affluent and insured patient population will encounter, at a rural critical access hospital in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, a data environment that differs in nearly every dimension that affects model performance. Gianfrancesco, Tamang, Yazdany, and Schmajuk documented in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2018 the specific mechanisms by which EHR data introduces biases: missing data patterns are non-random and correlate with socioeconomic status and insurance coverage; coding completeness varies by institution type; and patients with less frequent healthcare contact — often the poorest and most marginalized patients — have records that are structurally less informative to algorithms trained on data from patients with richer interaction histories. These are not hypothetical bias vectors; they are documented characteristics of the data environments in which clinical AI will be deployed if HHS achieves the acceleration it is soliciting comment on.⏎⏎The practical implication is that a tool that demonstrates 88% sensitivity in a prospective validation study at a tertiary care academic medical center may demonstrate 71% sensitivity when deployed at a federally qualified health center in rural Mississippi, and the patients who receive false-negative outputs at that second institution are already the patients with the least access to follow-up care, the fewest redundant safety mechanisms in their care pathways, and the greatest vulnerability to the downstream consequences of missed diagnosis. Rajpurkar, Chen, Banerjee, and Topol summarized the state of AI in health and medicine in Nature Medicine in 2022 and were explicit that the gap between research performance and real-world deployment performance remains one of the field's most serious unresolved problems. The Department appears to have read the optimistic sections of that literature and not the cautionary ones.⏎⏎University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences | HHS AI RFI | Page 5⏎⏎Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 a systematic analysis of race correction in clinical algorithms — the practice of adjusting algorithm outputs based on patient race under the assumption that race is a proxy for biological difference — and found that this practice, embedded in algorithms for kidney function estimation, lung function assessment, vaginal birth after cesarean risk scoring, and other clinical decision tools, systematically withheld interventions from Black patients by making their clinical profiles appear less severe than those of white patients with equivalent objective findings. The eGFR race correction, for instance, assigned Black patients higher estimated kidney function scores, delaying referral to nephrology and transplant evaluation. The authors documented that this practice had no valid biological justification and that it encoded social constructs as if they were biological facts, with the result that the algorithms produced systematically worse outcomes for Black patients as a class. Several of the algorithms discussed by Vyas and colleagues were implemented in EHR systems that are now being used as training data for new AI tools. The bias is being inherited, not corrected.⏎⏎University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences | HHS AI RFI | Page 6⏎⏎⏎THE AUTOMATION BIAS PROBLEM MAKES EVERYTHING WORSE⏎⏎Cabitza, Rasoini, and Gensini published an analysis in JAMA in 2017 — seven years ago, predating the current wave of large language model deployment in clinical settings — identifying automation bias as one of the primary mechanisms by which AI-assisted clinical decision support produces unintended consequences. Automation bias is the well-documented tendency of human decision-makers to reduce their own independent evaluation of a situation when an algorithmic recommendation is present, and to accept that recommendation with less scrutiny than they would apply to an equivalent recommendation from a human colleague. The clinical implications are significant: a clinician who would normally question a risk stratification score that conflicts with their gestalt assessment of a patient may be less likely to question an AI-generated score, particularly under time pressure, because the AI output carries an aura of computational authority that human judgment does not. Char, Shah, and Magnus addressed this dynamic in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018, noting that the implementation of machine learning in clinical workflows raises ethical challenges that are distinct from the technical performance questions, specifically because the opacity of many model architectures makes it difficult for clinicians to know when to trust the output and when to override it.⏎⏎The interaction between automation bias and the generalizability failures described above is where the distributional harm concentrates most acutely. A clinician at a community hospital deploying an AI sepsis prediction tool that was validated at a large academic medical center is, unknowingly, operating a tool whose performance characteristics do not match the environment. When the tool generates a low-risk score for a patient who is actually deteriorating, the clinician who might otherwise have pursued further evaluation is less likely to do so because the algorithmic output has anchored their assessment. The patient who is harmed is the patient at the community hospital, who is statistically more likely to be a patient of color, a Medicaid beneficiary, or a patient in a rural or economically distressed community. The AI system that fails them was validated somewhere else, on someone else's data, and the failure is invisible in aggregate performance metrics that do not disaggregate by deployment site or patient subgroup.⏎⏎University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences | HHS AI RFI | Page 7⏎⏎Parikh, Teeple, and Navathe addressed the bias problem in JAMA in 2019 and proposed a framework for bias identification that included prospective subgroup analysis, external validation in demographically diverse settings, and post-deployment monitoring with predefined equity metrics. The framework they proposed five years ago contains every element that HHS has failed to include as a mandatory requirement in the current RFI. The Department is not being asked to invent new regulatory infrastructure from scratch; it is being asked to operationalize recommendations that have been present in the peer-reviewed literature since before the current wave of AI deployment began.⏎⏎University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences | HHS AI RFI | Page 8⏎⏎⏎WHAT MANDATORY REQUIREMENTS MUST LOOK LIKE⏎⏎The following specifications are submitted as minimum necessary conditions for any HHS-facilitated deployment pathway, whether through regulatory guidance, reimbursement design, or research and development funding. They are not offered as a complete framework; they are offered as the floor below which no deployment pathway should be permitted to descend.⏎⏎1. Pre-deployment equity auditing. Any clinical AI tool seeking access to an HHS-facilitated deployment pathway must demonstrate, prior to deployment, subgroup-specific performance on the following dimensions at minimum: race and ethnicity (using OMB categories as a floor, not a ceiling), sex assigned at birth and gender identity where data are available, insurance status, geographic classification (urban/suburban/rural/frontier), and primary language. Performance metrics must be reported separately for each subgroup, not only in aggregate. Tools that demonstrate statistically significant performance differentials across subgroups must be accompanied by a documented plan for addressing those differentials before deployment, not after.⏎⏎2. External validation in non-academic settings. Validation studies conducted exclusively in academic medical centers with well-curated, homogeneous data must not be accepted as sufficient evidence for deployment in community hospitals, rural health systems, or safety-net institutions. HHS should require that any tool seeking deployment in settings that serve predominantly Medicaid or uninsured populations demonstrate validation performance in at least one institution of comparable type and patient composition. This requirement is not novel; it is a direct implementation of the recommendation made by Wiens and colleagues in 2019.⏎⏎3. Post-deployment bias surveillance. Deployment approval must be conditioned on the implementing institution's commitment to ongoing monitoring of model performance disaggregated by the subgroup dimensions specified above. Monitoring must occur at intervals no greater than six months for the first two years of deployment, with results reported to a designated HHS registry. Institutions that identify performance differentials during post-deployment monitoring must be required to notify HHS and to implement a remediation plan within a specified timeframe. The absence of this requirement in the current RFI is the single most significant regulatory gap identified in this comment.⏎⏎4. Proxy variable auditing. All clinical AI tools submitted for HHS-facilitated deployment must disclose the feature variables used in model training and must demonstrate that no feature variable functions as a proxy for race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, or insurance status in ways that would produce the kind of differential risk scoring documented by Obermeyer and colleagues in 2019. This requirement applies regardless of whether the tool's developers intended the proxy relationship; the Obermeyer finding is precisely that proxy discrimination can emerge from design choices that appear facially neutral.⏎⏎5. Transparency requirements for proprietary models. The proprietary nature of a model's architecture does not exempt it from equity auditing requirements. HHS should establish a mechanism by which proprietary models can be audited by a designated third-party evaluator under appropriate confidentiality protections, with findings made available to the institutions considering deployment. The situation documented by Wong and colleagues — in which a widely deployed proprietary sepsis model could not be systematically audited because of its closed architecture — must not be replicated at scale under a federally facilitated deployment framework.⏎⏎University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences | HHS AI RFI | Page 9⏎⏎⏎THE SPECIFIC QUESTION OF WHAT "ACCELERATION" MEANS FOR SAFETY-NET INSTITUTIONS⏎⏎The RFI's acceleration framing is particularly problematic when read against the actual distribution of AI adoption across institution types. The tools that HHS proposes to accelerate are, in practice, being adopted first by large, well-resourced academic medical centers and integrated health systems that have the technical infrastructure, data governance capacity, and clinical informatics expertise to implement them. Community health centers, critical access hospitals, rural health clinics, and federally qualified health centers are not the leading edge of AI adoption; they are, for the most part, watching from a distance while the technology is validated and refined in environments that bear little resemblance to their own. When acceleration reaches these institutions — and the RFI's logic implies that it should — the tools arriving will have been designed, trained, and validated somewhere else. The performance degradation documented in the generalizability literature will arrive with them, invisible to the institutions and the patients experiencing it because post-deployment monitoring requirements do not currently exist.⏎⏎This is not a speculative scenario. It is the pattern that has already been documented for earlier generations of clinical decision support tools. The acceleration of AI deployment to safety-net institutions without the structural requirements described above does not democratize access to beneficial technology; it democratizes exposure to tools whose performance has not been characterized in the environments where they will operate, for the patient populations they will serve. That is a distinct and more serious harm than the harm of delayed access, and the RFI's framing does not appear to have weighed the two against each other.⏎⏎University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences | HHS AI RFI | Page 10⏎⏎It is also worth noting, though this comment does not develop the point at length, that the acceleration framing creates asymmetric incentives for developers. A regulatory environment that prioritizes speed of deployment and minimizes pre-deployment requirements rewards developers who move quickly with tools that have not been rigorously characterized across the demographic and institutional dimensions most relevant to equity. A regulatory environment that conditions access to HHS-facilitated pathways on demonstrated equity performance rewards developers who invest in that characterization. The current RFI's framing creates the former incentive structure, not the latter. This is correctable, but only if HHS treats equity auditing as a precondition for deployment access rather than as a voluntary best practice or a post-deployment accountability mechanism.⏎⏎University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences | HHS AI RFI | Page 11⏎⏎⏎ON THE QUESTION OF WHAT THE DEPARTMENT OWES THE RECORD⏎⏎The peer-reviewed literature on algorithmic bias in clinical AI is not a fringe concern; it is the mainstream of health informatics scholarship. The findings summarized in this comment — Obermeyer et al. 2019, Sjoding et al. 2020, Wong et al. 2021, Seyyed-Kalantari et al. 2021, Adamson and Smith 2018, Gianfrancesco et al. 2018, Vyas et al. 2020, Wiens et al. 2019, Char et al. 2018, Cabitza et al. 2017, Parikh et al. 2019, Rajpurkar et al. 2022 — are not outliers or preliminary findings awaiting replication. They are a convergent body of evidence from multiple research groups, multiple clinical domains, multiple data environments, and multiple methodological approaches, all pointing toward the same structural conclusion: clinical AI systems trained on historically biased data, validated in non-representative settings, and deployed without subgroup-specific performance monitoring will reproduce and potentially amplify existing health disparities. The evidentiary record on this point is not ambiguous.⏎⏎What HHS owes the administrative record, and what the populations most vulnerable to the harms described in that literature deserve, is a regulatory framework that takes this evidence seriously as a design constraint rather than as a caveat to be acknowledged in the preamble and then set aside in favor of the acceleration agenda. The framing of this RFI as primarily a question of removing barriers to adoption is analytically indefensible given the state of the literature. The barriers that exist are not all the same kind of barrier. Some are bureaucratic friction that imposes costs without producing safety benefits. Others are the functional equivalent of requiring that a pharmaceutical undergo clinical trials before it is administered to patients. The RFI does not distinguish between these categories, and the consequence of that failure to distinguish is that the regulatory framework being solicited comment on has no mechanism for identifying which barriers are serving a protective function for which populations.⏎⏎University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences | HHS AI RFI | Page 12⏎⏎The University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences respectfully but directly requests that HHS publish a supplemental RFI or issue interim guidance that specifically addresses the equity auditing and post-deployment bias surveillance questions that this RFI has not adequately surfaced. The acceleration of AI adoption in clinical care is not inherently harmful, but it is harmful in the specific form that the current RFI proposes to facilitate — without mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing, without external validation requirements in non-academic settings, without post-deployment monitoring conditioned on deployment approval, and without proxy variable disclosure requirements. The literature cited throughout this comment was available to the Department when this RFI was drafted. The decision to frame the RFI as an acceleration problem rather than a safety and equity problem was a choice, and the populations who will bear the consequences of that choice are the same populations that have borne the consequences of every prior iteration of health system design that optimized for aggregate performance while treating distributional outcomes as secondary.⏎⏎The specific requirement for a post-deployment bias surveillance registry — modeled on the adverse event reporting infrastructure that already exists for medical devices under FDA's MedWatch program — deserves particular attention from the Department. The absence of any equivalent infrastructure for clinical AI means that harms occurring in community hospitals in rural Michigan or in safety-net institutions in Chicago's South Side will not be systematically detectable at the federal level until they have accumulated to a scale that produces visible population-level signals. By that point, the patients harmed will have been harmed, the tools will have been embedded in clinical workflows that are difficult to disrupt, and the institutional momentum behind deployed systems will make correction politically and operationally difficult. The time to establish the monitoring infrastructure is before the deployment it is designed to monitor, not after.⏎⏎Steven White, Ph.D.⏎Assistant Professor, Health Informatics and Social Science⏎University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences⏎steven.white@uchicago.edu⏎(773) 834-XXXX♔♔2026-02-23T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-23T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔13♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔academic_organization♔high♔frustrated♔Michigan♔assistant professor♔39♔Pictor Labs' internal analysis of 47 federally funded clinical AI pilots conducted between 2021 and 2024 found that 68% encountered regulatory ambiguity as the primary barrier to deployment, specifically around FDA software-as-a-medical-device classification thresholds and CMS reimbursement eligibility for AI-assisted diagnostic workflows. SYNTH-0031♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Mark Perez♔American Association of Physician Assistants♔♔♔♔♔American Association of Physician Assistants⏎2318 Mill Road, Suite 1300⏎Alexandria, VA 22314⏎government.affairs@aapa.org⏎⏎March 14, 2025⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Attention: Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎AAPA Comments on HHS Health Sector AI RFI: Workforce Consultation, Procurement Governance, and the Labor Conditions of AI Deployment in Clinical Settings⏎⏎The American Association of Physician Assistants (AAPA) submits these comments in response to the Department's solicitation on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care. AAPA represents more than 175,000 certified physician assistants practicing across every clinical specialty and care setting in the United States. Our government affairs team has engaged directly with the workforce dimensions of AI adoption through our own policy research and through the findings of affiliated clinical networks whose institutional data we draw upon here. Specifically, a 2024 needs assessment conducted across a network of 47 hepatology centers of excellence found that 68% of participating institutions reported diagnostic delays of six months or more for nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma. The clinicians surveyed identified the absence of validated AI-assisted imaging interpretation tools — and, critically, the absence of reimbursement frameworks to sustain their use — as the primary structural barriers. AAPA does not dispute that finding. AI's diagnostic promise in settings like hepatology is real and documented (Government Accountability Office, 2023, GAO-23-105980). What these comments address is a different and, in our assessment, underweighted dimension of the RFI: the conditions under which AI is actually being deployed on frontline clinical workers, and whether those conditions are consistent with the Department's stated goal of improving care quality.⏎⏎THE STRUCTURAL INCENTIVE PROBLEM⏎⏎The Department's RFI frames AI adoption primarily as a question of accelerating uptake — removing regulatory friction, clarifying reimbursement pathways, and supporting research and development. AAPA does not object to any of those goals in the abstract. What the RFI does not adequately account for is the incentive environment into which AI tools are being deployed. Health systems operating under sustained financial pressure — and most are, particularly in rural states like Arkansas where AAPA members practice in facilities with thin margins — will evaluate AI procurement decisions through a cost-reduction lens before a care-quality lens. This is not a criticism of hospital administrators; it is a structural observation about how capital allocation decisions get made. National Nurses United documented in 2023 that AI tools marketed as burnout-reduction and efficiency solutions were being operationalized primarily to justify reduced staffing ratios and increased caseload assignments (NNU, 2023, "Staffing by Algorithm"). Freedman et al. (2022) found analogous labor displacement effects following electronic health record adoption, with measurable reductions in certain administrative and clinical support roles that required contextual human judgment (Journal of Health Economics, 82, 102598). The Department should not assume that accelerating AI adoption will produce workforce benefits simply because the technology is capable of generating them. The benefits accrue only under governance conditions that do not currently exist at most institutions.⏎⏎AAPA Comments | HHS AI RFI | March 2025 | Page 2⏎⏎This concern is not speculative. Kellogg, Valentine, and Christin (2020) documented in their systematic analysis of algorithmic management in professional workplaces that AI-driven productivity monitoring systematically shifts authority from frontline workers to administrators and vendors, creating what they describe as a new "contested terrain of control" over professional labor (Academy of Management Annals, 14(1), 366-410). Physician assistants and other advanced practice clinicians are already experiencing this dynamic. ONC's own 2023 annual report to Congress on health IT and clinician burden found that EHR-related administrative obligations remain a primary driver of clinician dissatisfaction, contributing directly to the burnout rates documented by Shanafelt et al. (2022), who found that more than half of U.S. physicians reported at least one symptom of burnout as of 2020 (Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 97(3), 491-506). If AI systems are layered onto already-burdened clinical workflows without changing the underlying governance structures that produced that burden, the result will be more monitoring, not less.⏎⏎THE SURVEILLANCE AND PROFESSIONAL AUTONOMY PROBLEM⏎⏎AAPA wants to be precise about what is meant here by "surveillance," because the term can obscure more than it clarifies. The concern is not with AI tools that assist clinical decision-making — AAPA supports the responsible development of clinical decision support systems (CDSS), and the diagnostic applications documented in the hepatology needs assessment represent exactly the kind of deployment that merits federal support. The concern is with AI systems deployed to monitor, measure, and generate productivity scores for clinical workers, and with the use of those scores as inputs to staffing, scheduling, and performance evaluation decisions. SEIU Healthcare's 2023 policy brief on AI in the hospital documented worker accounts of real-time productivity dashboards that flagged clinicians for "inefficiency" based on metrics that did not account for patient complexity, communication time, or the kind of contextual judgment that cannot be reduced to throughput (SEIU Healthcare, 2023, "AI in the Hospital"). Dyrbye et al. (2023) found in a systematic review that EHR burden — which is increasingly algorithmically mediated — is directly correlated with clinician burnout, and that burnout is itself a patient safety variable, not merely an HR concern (Journal of General Internal Medicine, 38(4), 1041-1052).⏎⏎The American Medical Association's 2023 policy document on augmented intelligence in health care explicitly calls for AI systems to preserve rather than supplant clinician judgment, and for deployment frameworks to include mechanisms for clinician override and ongoing feedback (AMA Policy H-480.940). AAPA endorses that position and urges HHS to treat it as a floor, not a ceiling. Topol (2023) made a related argument in the New England Journal of Medicine, drawing on early deployment failures to contend that clinician involvement in AI governance is not a procedural nicety but a substantive determinant of whether AI systems perform safely in real-world conditions (NEJM, 389(12), 1143-1147). The Department's RFI asks how HHS can accelerate adoption; AAPA's answer is that adoption without governance frameworks protecting professional autonomy will produce AI-augmented workflows that are less safe, not more, because the clinicians who must catch the errors will have been systematically demoralized and de-skilled. Obermeyer et al. (2019) demonstrated that algorithmic bias can propagate at scale when clinician judgment is not preserved as a corrective mechanism (Science, 366(6464), 447-453). That finding should inform how HHS designs any federal support for AI deployment.⏎⏎AAPA Comments | HHS AI RFI | March 2025 | Page 3⏎⏎THE PROCUREMENT EXCLUSION PROBLEM AND AAPA'S SPECIFIC REQUESTS⏎⏎The most direct and correctable failure in current AI deployment practice is the systematic exclusion of frontline clinical workers from procurement governance. The tools being deployed to monitor, optimize, and in some cases replace clinical labor are being selected by administrators and vendors whose incentive structures are not aligned with clinical quality or professional autonomy. This is not an accusation — it is a structural observation confirmed by the stakeholder roundtables referenced in the 2024 hepatology needs assessment, where near-unanimous agreement emerged that current institutional AI governance processes do not include meaningful frontline clinician input. AAPA urges HHS to address this through enforceable participation requirements as a precondition for any federally supported AI deployment in clinical settings.⏎⏎Specifically, AAPA requests that HHS pursue the following actions:⏎⏎1. Mandatory frontline worker consultation in AI procurement. Any AI system deployed in a clinical setting that receives federal support — whether through Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement, ONC certification, or HHS research funding — should be subject to a documented consultation process that includes frontline clinical staff, not only physician leadership or administrative representatives. This requirement should specify that consultation occurs before contract execution, not after.⏎⏎2. Prohibition on using AI-generated productivity data as the primary basis for staffing decisions. HHS should establish, through guidance and as a condition of federal support, that AI-generated productivity metrics may not serve as the sole or primary determinant of staffing ratio decisions, scheduling algorithms, or performance evaluations for clinical staff. Bates et al. (2021) documented how poorly governed AI outputs generate downstream harms when clinical judgment is not preserved as a check (JAMIA Open, 4(1), ooab002). The same principle applies to workforce AI.⏎⏎3. Transparency requirements for any AI system used to monitor or evaluate clinical staff. Health systems that receive federal support and deploy AI systems to generate performance data about clinical workers should be required to disclose to affected workers: the nature of the data being collected, the algorithmic logic used to generate scores or flags, the decisions those outputs inform, and the process for contesting outputs that the worker believes are inaccurate or contextually misleading.⏎⏎4. Explicit exclusion of AI-generated staffing optimization as a qualifying use case for any new CMS reimbursement pathway created in response to this RFI. The Department should not inadvertently create financial incentives for deploying AI against the workforce rather than for patients.⏎⏎AAPA acknowledges that these requests go somewhat beyond the framing of the RFI, which is oriented primarily toward clinical care applications rather than workforce governance. But the distinction between those two categories is not as clean as the RFI implies. The clinician who is being monitored in real time for throughput efficiency is the same clinician interpreting the AI-assisted imaging result. The governance conditions affecting one directly affect the other. HHS has not yet adequately grappled with that connection, and AAPA hopes these comments are useful in framing the gap.⏎⏎AAPA's government affairs team is available to discuss these recommendations in further detail and can be reached at the contact information above. We would also note that AAPA submitted related comments to ONC's 2023 health IT burden report process and can provide that record upon request.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Mark Perez⏎Director of Government Affairs⏎American Association of Physician Assistants⏎Alexandria, Virginia♔♔2026-01-05T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-05T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare will be used by employers and insurers as a mechanism for workforce surveillance, productivity extraction, staffing cuts, and the devaluation of clinical expertise rather than genuine care improvement.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔concerned♔Arkansas♔director of government affairs♔52♔A 2024 needs assessment conducted across GLI's network of 47 hepatology centers of excellence found that 68% of participating institutions reported diagnostic delays of six months or more for nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) and early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma, conditions where timely identification is directly correlated with survival outcomes.
