SYNTH-0032♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Dorothy Taylor♔Patient Advocate Foundation♔♔♔♔♔Patient Advocate Foundation⏎700 Thimble Shoals Blvd., Suite 200⏎Newport News, VA 23606⏎⏎October 14, 2024⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Re: Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket: HHS-ONC-2024-AI-RFI (89 FR [docket number])⏎⏎Dear Deputy Secretary and ONC Leadership:⏎⏎Patient Advocate Foundation submits these comments in response to the Department's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. The Foundation has worked for more than two decades alongside patients navigating the most disorienting moments of their lives — the cancer diagnosis delivered on a Tuesday afternoon, the chronic pain that resists every name a provider tries to give it, the family sitting in a waiting room whose body language tells a clinician something the chart never could. It is from that particular vantage point, grounded in the irreducibly human texture of medical encounters, that we offer the following observations. We address here two of the RFI's core areas: the Department's framing of AI as a productivity instrument, and the question of what preconditions must be satisfied before clinical AI deployment can be considered responsible.⏎⏎⏎THE CATEGORY ERROR AT THE CENTER OF HHS'S FRAMING⏎⏎Patient Advocate Foundation | HHS-ONC-2024-AI-RFI | Page 2⏎⏎The Department's RFI consistently positions AI adoption as a mechanism for accelerating care delivery and reducing clinician burden. We do not dispute that administrative waste is real, or that documentation overhead contributes to the burnout documented so carefully by Hartzband and Groopman in the New England Journal of Medicine (382(26), 2485-2487, 2020). But the framing of AI as primarily a productivity-enhancement instrument rests on a premise this Foundation considers empirically and philosophically mistaken: that the time a clinician spends in effortful, attentive engagement with a patient is a form of inefficiency.⏎⏎It is not. A substantial body of evidence — including the systematic review and meta-analysis by Kelley and colleagues published in PLOS ONE (9(4), e94207, 2014) — demonstrates that the quality of the clinician-patient relationship is itself a determinant of health outcomes, independent of the technical accuracy of any diagnosis or the pharmacological appropriateness of any treatment plan. Zulman and colleagues, writing in JAMA in 2020 (323(1), 70-81), identified specific practices through which physicians foster presence and connection during clinical encounters, and found that those practices had measurable effects on patient experience and adherence. Emanuel and Dubler, writing a quarter-century earlier about managed care's threat to the physician-patient relationship (JAMA, 273(4), 323-329, 1995), identified the same structural dynamic the Foundation sees in the current RFI: a policy environment that treats relational medicine as a cost to be reduced rather than a resource to be protected.⏎⏎The Foundation is not arguing that AI has no place in clinical settings. Topol's 2019 synthesis in Nature Medicine (25(1), 44-56) makes a persuasive case that AI, deployed thoughtfully, could free clinicians to do precisely the relational work that machines cannot replicate. That is a very different argument from the one the Department appears to be making. HHS's framing is not "AI can protect the clinician-patient relationship by absorbing administrative load." The framing is "AI can accelerate care delivery." Those are not the same thing, and the difference matters enormously for how deployment decisions get made at the point of care.⏎⏎Verghese, Shah, and Harrington put the concern precisely in their 2018 JAMA piece (319(1), 19-20): what clinical AI systems need, above all, is a physician who remains capable of independent judgment. The risk is not simply that an AI system will produce an incorrect recommendation. The risk is that, over time, clinicians will lose the practiced capacity to recognize when it has.⏎⏎⏎Patient Advocate Foundation | HHS-ONC-2024-AI-RFI | Page 3⏎⏎THE AUTOMATION-BIAS PROBLEM AND SKILL ATROPHY⏎⏎This is the concern the Foundation wants to press with some care, because it tends to get lost in discussions that focus on AI accuracy rates and algorithmic fairness. The literature on automation bias — the tendency for human operators to defer to automated recommendations even when those recommendations are wrong — is by now substantial. Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt's systematic review in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association (19(1), 121-127, 2012) identified automation bias as a consistent phenomenon across clinical decision-support contexts, and found that its frequency increased with system reliability: the more accurate a system appeared, the more operators trusted it uncritically. Parasuraman and Manzey (Human Factors, 52(3), 381-410, 2010) documented the attentional mechanism: when humans delegate judgment to automated systems, they reallocate cognitive resources away from the task, and those resources do not simply return on demand when the automation fails.⏎⏎What this means for clinical medicine is not a hypothetical. It means that a hospitalist who has relied on an AI-assisted diagnostic tool for three years may, when that tool produces a confident but erroneous recommendation, lack the practiced pattern-recognition to catch the error. The Tversky and Kahneman framework for judgment under uncertainty (Science, 185(4157), 1124-1131, 1974) helps explain why: clinicians, like all humans, are susceptible to anchoring on the first confident estimate they receive, and an AI recommendation is a very confident estimate indeed.⏎⏎The Foundation wants to be specific about what it is asking the Department to take seriously here. The concern is not that AI will replace clinicians. The concern is subtler and, we think, more dangerous: that AI intermediation will gradually hollow out the diagnostic and relational competencies that make clinicians capable of independent judgment, while leaving the formal structure of physician oversight intact. Human oversight of machine outputs is not the same thing as meaningful human judgment. A physician who reviews an AI recommendation without the cognitive resources to genuinely evaluate it is not exercising oversight in any clinically meaningful sense. The Department's RFI does not appear to have grappled with this distinction.⏎⏎Consider what this means practically for the patients this Foundation serves. A woman with a complex, undifferentiated pain syndrome — the kind of patient whose chart reads as unremarkable until a clinician notices that she has stopped making eye contact, that her affect has changed, that something in the room is different from the last visit — is precisely the patient most likely to be failed by a pattern-matching system. Bickmore and Picard's foundational work on long-term human-computer relationships (ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction, 12(2), 293-327, 2005) demonstrated that even the most sophisticated conversational systems cannot establish the kind of trust that allows a patient to disclose what she is actually afraid of. The clinician who has that trust, and who has the practiced perceptual skills to use it diagnostically, is a clinical instrument. AI intermediation, deployed without precaution, risks degrading that instrument without anyone noticing until the harm has accumulated.⏎⏎⏎Patient Advocate Foundation | HHS-ONC-2024-AI-RFI | Page 4⏎⏎WHAT THE DEPARTMENT SHOULD DO INSTEAD⏎⏎Patient Advocate Foundation urges HHS to replace its accelerationist posture with a precautionary, human-centered framework that conditions clinical AI deployment on demonstrated relational and clinical safety. Specifically, the Foundation recommends:⏎⏎1. Require prospective demonstration of relational safety before deployment. Any clinical AI system intended to interact with patients, or to mediate the clinician-patient encounter, should be required to demonstrate — through prospective study, not retrospective analysis — that its deployment does not degrade the quality of the therapeutic relationship as measured by validated instruments. The Foundation acknowledges that this is a harder standard to satisfy than technical accuracy metrics, and that is precisely the point.⏎⏎2. Establish a meaningful human judgment standard, distinct from human oversight. The Department should articulate, in regulatory guidance, a definition of "meaningful human judgment" that goes beyond nominal physician review of AI outputs. This definition should account for the automation-bias literature and should require that clinicians retain — through training, practice, and system design — the cognitive capacity to independently evaluate AI recommendations. Oversight without that capacity is not oversight.⏎⏎3. Fund longitudinal research on skill atrophy in AI-assisted clinical environments. The Foundation is not aware of a robust research agenda within HHS or NIH focused specifically on the question of whether, and at what rate, clinical AI adoption affects the independent diagnostic and relational competencies of practicing clinicians. That gap should be addressed before deployment is accelerated, not after.⏎⏎4. Require equity-centered relational assessment for any AI system deployed in safety-net settings. Haque's 2021 analysis in Psychiatric Services (72(12), 1371-1374) documented the ways in which digital health transformation can reproduce and amplify existing disparities in care quality. The Foundation's concern is not only that AI systems may perform less accurately for historically marginalized populations — that concern is real but is addressed elsewhere — but that the relational dimensions of care may be most at risk precisely in the settings where patients have fewest alternatives.⏎⏎5. Commission an independent review of the Department's productivity framing. HHS should ask an independent body — not an AI industry stakeholder — to evaluate whether the RFI's core framing accurately characterizes the problem that clinical AI is being asked to solve, and whether that framing is consistent with the evidence base on what determines health outcomes.⏎⏎⏎Patient Advocate Foundation | HHS-ONC-2024-AI-RFI | Page 5⏎⏎The Foundation wants to close not with a summary but with a practical observation that has come up repeatedly in our direct work with patients in Maine, Texas, and across the country over the past several years. When patients describe what went wrong in a clinical encounter that failed them, they almost never describe a diagnostic error in isolation. They describe feeling unheard. They describe a clinician who seemed distracted, or who appeared to be reading from a screen rather than listening. They describe the moment when the encounter stopped feeling like a conversation and started feeling like a transaction. Those descriptions are not incidental. They point to the relational substrate of medicine that the evidence consistently shows is therapeutic in its own right, and whose degradation carries clinical consequences that do not show up cleanly in outcome metrics.⏎⏎The Department has an opportunity here to set a standard for responsible AI integration that the rest of the health sector will follow. That standard should begin with the question: what are we trying to protect? The answer, this Foundation believes, is not productivity. It is the capacity of a clinician to be genuinely present with a patient who is frightened, and the capacity of that patient to trust that the person in the room with them is actually attending to them — not to a screen, not to a recommendation generated elsewhere, but to them specifically, in that room, on that day.⏎⏎The Foundation's executive director, Dorothy Taylor, is available to discuss these comments and can be reached at the address above or at⏎⏎dtaylor@patientadvocate.org⏎⏎Sincerely,⏎⏎Dorothy Taylor⏎Executive Director⏎Patient Advocate Foundation⏎Newport News, Virginia♔♔2026-01-07T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-07T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔supportive♔Maine♔executive director♔39♔A 2024 TMA survey of 4,200 practicing Texas physicians found that 58% had used at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or clinical decision-support tool in the prior 12 months, yet 74% of those respondents reported uncertainty about liability exposure when acting on AI-generated recommendations. SYNTH-0033♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Daniel Wright♔Association of Black Cardiologists♔♔♔♔♔Association of Black Cardiologists⏎5600 Fishers Lane, Suite 300⏎Rockville, MD 20857⏎⏎Daniel Wright, J.D., M.P.H.⏎Director of Policy and Government Affairs⏎⏎June 3, 2025⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Attention: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care, 89 FR [docket pending] — Formal Comment Submission on Behalf of the Association of Black Cardiologists⏎⏎---⏎⏎Association of Black Cardiologists | HHS AI RFI Comments | June 2025 | Page 1⏎⏎---⏎⏎PRELIMINARY STATEMENT⏎⏎The Association of Black Cardiologists submits these comments on behalf of our membership and the patient communities we serve, with particular attention to two dimensions of the HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information (Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, 2024) that we believe have received insufficient public scrutiny: the democratic legitimacy of an acceleration agenda pursued through regulatory action, and the structural irreversibility of AI embedding in clinical healthcare infrastructure once that embedding has proceeded past a threshold the Department has not attempted to define, measure, or limit. We note at the outset that our comments do not address algorithmic bias in clinical prediction specifically, as our organization has submitted a separate technical comment on that question drawing on the foundational work of Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan (2019), whose dissection of racial bias in a widely deployed population health algorithm documented disparities that should still be generating institutional alarm five years later. These comments address something prior to that question, something that sits upstream of any technical evaluation framework: whether HHS has the legitimate authority to treat AI acceleration as a departmental objective at all, and whether the American public has ever been asked.⏎⏎THE EMPIRICAL FOUNDATION: WHAT OUR SURVEY DATA ACTUALLY SHOWS⏎⏎In 2024, the Association conducted a membership survey across 1,200 clinical laboratory and pathology constituents. Sixty-eight percent of those facilities had piloted or deployed at least one AI-assisted diagnostic tool within the preceding 24 months. That number, taken in isolation, is the kind of statistic that proponents of the HHS acceleration agenda would cite as evidence of momentum, as confirmation that the market is moving and that regulatory uncertainty is the only thing standing between the present and a transformed healthcare system. We submit that this reading is precisely backwards, and that our survey data tells a more troubling story than adoption percentages alone can convey.⏎⏎Fewer than 30% of facilities that had deployed AI-augmented interpretive tools reported receiving adequate reimbursement for those services under existing CPT coding structures. Our Q3 2024 policy working group, which convened six roundtable sessions between July and October of that year with laboratory directors, pathologists, and health system administrators across Michigan, Ohio, and Tennessee, consistently identified two barriers as primary: reimbursement misalignment and ambiguous liability frameworks. What the roundtables also revealed, and what we believe the Department has not adequately processed, is a third dynamic that participants described with a consistency that we found striking. Clinical and administrative workflows were being reorganized around vendor-supplied AI systems at a pace that was outrunning institutional capacity to evaluate, challenge, or reverse those reorganizations. Laboratory directors at safety-net hospitals in particular — institutions already operating on margins that leave no room for redundant capacity — described a situation in which the question of whether to adopt a given AI system had already been effectively answered before any formal evaluation process could be convened. The system was there. The workflow had been built around it. The staff who might have performed the function manually had been reassigned or not replaced. As Friedman, Wong, and Blumenthal (2010) documented in the context of health information technology infrastructure more broadly, dependency trajectories in clinical settings are not linear and reversible; they are path-dependent in ways that foreclose options on a timeline measured in months, not years.⏎⏎Association of Black Cardiologists | HHS AI RFI Comments | June 2025 | Page 2⏎⏎THE IRREVERSIBILITY PROBLEM⏎⏎This is the first place where we believe the Department's framing requires direct challenge. The HHS RFI treats AI adoption as a process that can be accelerated, evaluated, and — if necessary — corrected. This assumption of correctability is foundational to the entire regulatory posture the Department has adopted, and it is, we submit, empirically unfounded. The embedding of AI systems in healthcare infrastructure is not a reversible policy experiment. It is an institutional transformation that, once past a certain threshold of workflow dependency, staffing reorganization, and knowledge atrophy, becomes practically irreversible even when documented harms demand reversal.⏎⏎Coiera, Ash, and Berg (2016) documented the unintended consequences of health information technology deployment in terms that apply with equal force to AI systems: once clinical workflows are reorganized around a technological infrastructure, the capacity to function without that infrastructure atrophies within years. The knowledge, the staffing models, the institutional memory — all of it degrades. Dafny and Lee (2016), writing about institutional lock-in dynamics in healthcare markets, described how market consolidations that appear reversible at the moment of execution become structurally irreversible within a regulatory cycle or two, because the competitive alternatives have been absorbed or have exited. The same dynamic applies here. Once a health system has reorganized its cardiology imaging workflow around a vendor-supplied AI interpretation system, the radiologists and cardiologists who might interpret those images without AI assistance have either left, retired, or lost the practiced fluency that made their judgment reliable. Irreversibility is not a theoretical concern. It is an observable institutional dynamic that our roundtable participants described from direct operational experience.⏎⏎The Department's RFI does not use the word "irreversible" once. It does not contain any framework for assessing the degree of dependency that AI adoption creates, no threshold beyond which the Department would consider a deployment to have foreclosed future democratic choices, no mechanism for preserving the optionality that democratic governance requires. This is not an oversight. It reflects a foundational assumption that acceleration is, in itself, a legitimate departmental objective — that the question of whether healthcare should be transformed by AI has been answered, and that the only remaining questions are technical and administrative. We reject that assumption.⏎⏎Association of Black Cardiologists | HHS AI RFI Comments | June 2025 | Page 3⏎⏎THE "REDUCE UNCERTAINTY" TELL⏎⏎The RFI states, in language we want to treat with the precision it deserves, that HHS is seeking to "reduce uncertainty that impedes AI innovation." This phrase is a tell. It reveals the Department's actual posture: not neutral facilitation, not balanced evaluation, but active promotion of a technological trajectory that has not been authorized by any democratic process. The word "impedes" is doing a great deal of work in that sentence. Regulatory scrutiny does not impede innovation; it shapes it, constrains it, and ensures that its benefits are distributed equitably and its risks are borne by those with the capacity to absorb them. When HHS frames scrutiny as impediment, it is not describing a regulatory philosophy — it is announcing a political commitment to a particular outcome.⏎⏎This matters for a reason that goes beyond the specific question of AI in healthcare. Democratic societies retain the legitimate sovereign right to determine which domains of human activity should be governed by market efficiency and which should remain stubbornly resistant to that logic. Michael Sandel (2012) has articulated this argument with a clarity that the policy community has largely declined to engage: the question of whether medicine should be organized around efficiency maximization or around some other set of values — professional judgment, human relationship, institutional accountability — is not a technical question. It is a moral and political question, and democratic societies answer such questions through deliberation, not through regulatory acceleration. When HHS acts to "reduce uncertainty that impedes AI innovation," it is not resolving a technical ambiguity. It is preempting a democratic judgment that has not yet been made.⏎⏎Virginia Eubanks (2018), in her study of algorithmic governance in public institutions, documented how automated systems consistently transfer decision-making power away from frontline workers and local institutions toward distant corporate entities that have no accountability to the communities affected by their decisions. Shoshana Zuboff (2019) described this dynamic in systemic terms: the transfer of institutional knowledge and decision-making capacity from human actors to proprietary algorithmic systems is a transfer of power, and it is largely irreversible because the knowledge that would be required to reclaim that power degrades in proportion to the degree of dependency. Frank Pasquale (2015) located the democratic problem precisely: when the systems that govern consequential decisions are proprietary and opaque, democratic oversight becomes structurally impossible, because there is no mechanism by which affected communities, frontline clinicians, or elected representatives can examine, challenge, or correct the logic of those systems. Andrew Selbst and Solon Barocas (2018) extended this analysis to show that the intuitive appeal of "explainable" AI systems masks a deeper opacity: even systems that produce explanations do not thereby become transparent in any democratically meaningful sense, because the explanation is itself a product of the system's design choices, which remain proprietary and unexaminable.⏎⏎Association of Black Cardiologists | HHS AI RFI Comments | June 2025 | Page 4⏎⏎THE EQUITY DIMENSION WE CANNOT SEPARATE FROM THIS ARGUMENT⏎⏎We want to be precise about why the Association of Black Cardiologists is raising what might appear to be a philosophical argument about democratic theory in a regulatory comment about healthcare AI. The reason is that our members' patients are disproportionately likely to be governed by AI systems they cannot see, cannot challenge, and cannot hold accountable — and that the communities in which those patients live are disproportionately likely to lack the political and institutional resources to push back when those systems produce harmful outcomes. The analysis of our member-submitted operational data found that laboratories serving rural or safety-net populations faced implementation costs that were disproportionate relative to reimbursement recovery. But the deeper problem is not economic. It is structural. Safety-net institutions adopting AI systems under financial pressure are not making free choices about technology adoption. They are making constrained choices under conditions that Eubanks (2018) would recognize: institutions with the fewest resources are the most likely to adopt systems that transfer power to vendors, and the communities they serve are the most likely to bear the costs of that transfer without any mechanism for accountability or redress.⏎⏎Eric Topol (2019) has argued, and we do not dismiss this argument, that the convergence of human and artificial intelligence in clinical medicine holds genuine promise for improving diagnostic accuracy and extending access to specialist expertise in underserved communities. We acknowledge this argument. We acknowledge that AI-assisted cardiac imaging interpretation, deployed thoughtfully and with appropriate human oversight, could extend the reach of cardiological expertise to communities that currently lack access to board-certified cardiologists. We are not making a categorical argument against AI in medicine. We are making an argument about process, about power, and about the conditions under which democratic choices can be made and unmade. The acceleration agenda HHS is pursuing treats the deployment of AI in healthcare as a destination rather than as a choice that communities should be empowered to make and, if necessary, to reverse. Doshi-Velez and Kim (2017) have argued that interpretability in machine learning systems is not merely a technical preference but a prerequisite for meaningful human oversight — a prerequisite that, in the clinical context, extends to the democratic oversight that communities must be able to exercise over the institutions that govern their health.⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING THE RFI'S FRAMING⏎⏎The Association wishes to identify, with specificity, the dimensions of the RFI's framing that we find most problematic from a democratic governance standpoint:⏎⏎1. The RFI solicits comment on how to "accelerate" AI adoption, not on whether to accelerate it, what conditions must be met before acceleration is appropriate, or what mechanisms would allow communities to slow or reverse adoption trajectories that produce documented harms. The framing assumes the destination and asks only about the route.⏎⏎2. The RFI does not contain any framework for assessing irreversibility. There is no proposed threshold of workflow dependency, staffing reorganization, or institutional knowledge atrophy beyond which HHS would consider an AI deployment to have foreclosed future choices in ways that require heightened scrutiny or mandatory reversibility planning.⏎⏎3. The RFI's treatment of "uncertainty" as an obstacle to be reduced rather than as information about the limits of our current knowledge reflects a regulatory philosophy that is incompatible with the precautionary principles that have historically governed the introduction of novel technologies into clinical medicine.⏎⏎4. The RFI's stakeholder engagement model, as described, is weighted heavily toward technology developers, health system administrators, and payers — the entities with the greatest financial stake in acceleration. It is not structured to elicit the perspectives of frontline clinicians, community health workers, patient advocates from underserved communities, or the democratic publics who will ultimately bear the consequences of the choices being made.⏎⏎5. The proprietary opacity of the AI systems under discussion — documented systematically by Pasquale (2015) and Selbst and Barocas (2018) — means that any reimbursement or regulatory framework HHS develops will be governing systems whose logic is inaccessible to the regulators, the clinicians, and the communities it purports to protect.⏎⏎Association of Black Cardiologists | HHS AI RFI Comments | June 2025 | Page 5⏎⏎THE DEMOCRATIC LEGITIMACY QUESTION HHS HAS NOT ANSWERED⏎⏎We want to be direct about what we are arguing, because we believe the Department deserves a clear statement of our position rather than a set of technical recommendations that paper over a fundamental disagreement. HHS has authority to regulate healthcare. It has authority to establish reimbursement frameworks, to set certification standards, to require transparency and accountability from technology developers. What HHS does not have is the authority to preempt the democratic deliberation that should precede any decision to reorganize American healthcare around a technological infrastructure that is proprietary, potentially irreversible, and concentrated in the hands of a small number of corporate entities with no accountability to the communities they will serve.⏎⏎The question of whether medicine should remain, in some meaningful sense, a human practice — whether the relationship between a cardiologist and a patient should be mediated by an algorithm whose logic neither party can examine or challenge — is not a technical question that HHS can resolve by reducing regulatory uncertainty. It is the kind of question that Sandel (2012) identifies as requiring democratic deliberation precisely because it involves a choice about the kind of society we want to be, not merely a choice about how to optimize an existing system. Democratic societies have the right to decide that certain domains should resist efficiency logics, should preserve human judgment even at some cost to throughput, should maintain the institutional capacity for reversal even when the economics of reversal are unfavorable. HHS, by treating AI acceleration as a departmental objective, is foreclosing that deliberation before it has occurred. The irreversibility dynamic we have documented in our member survey and roundtable findings is not merely a policy risk. It is evidence that the window for democratic choice is closing faster than the deliberative processes of a democratic society can operate.⏎⏎This is the core of our submission. The Department is moving faster than democracy can follow, and the consequence of that speed — as Zuboff (2019) documented in a broader context and as our own roundtable participants described from direct operational experience — is that the power to make choices about the organization of healthcare will have transferred to corporate entities before the public has had any meaningful opportunity to participate in that transfer. Irreversibility, in this context, is not a feature of successful technology deployment. It is a catastrophic policy risk that the Department has not acknowledged and has not built any mechanism to manage.⏎⏎Association of Black Cardiologists | HHS AI RFI Comments | June 2025 | Page 6⏎⏎SPECIFIC DEMAND: DEMOCRATIC DELIBERATION BEFORE ACCELERATION⏎⏎The Association of Black Cardiologists makes one specific, actionable demand in response to this RFI. Before any acceleration agenda proceeds — before HHS reduces regulatory uncertainty, expands reimbursement coverage for AI-augmented services, or establishes certification frameworks that presuppose AI adoption as a baseline — the Department must commission an independent democratic deliberation process on the question of whether, and under what conditions, the American public consents to the reorganization of clinical healthcare around proprietary AI infrastructure.⏎⏎This deliberation process must be structured in a way that is meaningfully distinct from existing stakeholder engagement processes, which are dominated by entities with financial stakes in acceleration. It must include:⏎⏎o Randomly selected citizen panels, modeled on deliberative democracy frameworks used in Ireland, France, and Canada, with demographic representation weighted toward communities that have historically borne disproportionate costs from healthcare technology deployments.⏎⏎o Structured input from frontline clinicians — not health system administrators — including nurses, community health workers, and primary care physicians in safety-net settings who interact daily with the patients most affected by AI governance decisions.⏎⏎o Independent academic input from scholars in bioethics, democratic theory, and the sociology of technology, with explicit exclusion of researchers with financial relationships to AI developers or health system vendors.⏎⏎o A formal finding, published in the Federal Register, on whether the deliberation process has identified conditions under which AI adoption in clinical care is democratically legitimate, what those conditions are, and what mechanisms are required to preserve the public's capacity to reverse adoption decisions that produce documented harms.⏎⏎We are aware that this demand will be characterized by some as impractical, as a delay tactic, or as an expression of technological skepticism that is inconsistent with the Department's mission to improve health outcomes. We reject each of those characterizations. Democratic legitimacy is not a delay tactic. It is the precondition for durable policy. An acceleration agenda that proceeds without it will be fragile in the ways that matter most: vulnerable to political reversal, resistant to course correction, and incapable of generating the public trust that any transformative healthcare policy requires to sustain itself over time.⏎⏎The Association further requests that HHS publish, within 90 days of the close of this comment period, a formal response to the irreversibility question — specifically, a description of the mechanisms the Department proposes to maintain public and institutional capacity to reverse AI adoption decisions, and the threshold of workflow dependency or institutional lock-in beyond which HHS would consider heightened regulatory scrutiny to be warranted. The Department's silence on this question in the RFI is itself a policy choice, and it is one that our members, and the patients they serve, have a right to have explained.⏎⏎We note, finally, that the six roundtable sessions our policy working group convened in 2024 included a session held in Detroit in September of that year, at which a laboratory director from a Wayne County safety-net hospital described a situation in which the hospital's AI-assisted electrocardiogram interpretation system had been in continuous operation for 14 months before anyone on staff had read the vendor contract closely enough to discover that the hospital had no right to export its own patient data from the system without paying a fee that the hospital's operating budget could not absorb. That is not an anecdote about vendor economics. It is an illustration of what power transfer looks like in practice, at the level of a single institution, before the acceleration agenda has fully run its course. We ask the Department to sit with that example before it proceeds.⏎⏎dwright@abcardio.org⏎www.abcardio.org/policy⏎⏎Sincerely,⏎⏎Daniel Wright, J.D., M.P.H.⏎Director of Policy and Government Affairs⏎Association of Black Cardiologists♔♔2026-02-18T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-18T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔10♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Once AI systems are embedded in healthcare infrastructure, they become practically irreversible and resistant to democratic oversight, creating a permanent transfer of power from clinicians, patients, and regulators to technology vendors.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔angry♔Michigan♔policy director♔33♔A 2024 membership survey conducted across our 1,200 clinical laboratory and pathology constituents found that 68% had piloted or deployed at least one AI-assisted diagnostic tool within the preceding 24 months, yet fewer than 30% of those facilities reported receiving adequate reimbursement for AI-augmented interpretive services under existing CPT coding structures. SYNTH-0038♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Thomas Green♔American Thoracic Society♔♔♔♔♔American Thoracic Society⏎25 Broadway, 18th Floor⏎New York, NY 10004⏎⏎June 12, 2025⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Attn: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎RE: American Thoracic Society Comments on HHS RFI — Health Sector Artificial Intelligence: Accelerating Adoption in Clinical Care Settings⏎⏎⏎THE DEMOCRATIC STAKES OF THIS RFI⏎⏎The American Thoracic Society submits these comments with both institutional urgency and considerable frustration — frustration that is not directed at the goal of improving diagnostic care through technology, but at the framing of this Request for Information, which treats the question of how AI is deployed in clinical settings as a technical optimization problem rather than a question of democratic self-governance. Before addressing specific elements of the RFI, the Society wishes to establish its standing in this proceeding and the evidentiary basis for its concerns, because what follows is not opposition to AI in healthcare broadly construed. The Society's organizational partners at the Global Liver Institute (GLI) have documented, through a national patient registry encompassing data from more than 47,000 individuals living with chronic liver disease, that 68% of those patients experienced diagnostic delays of six months or longer — delays attributable in substantial part to the absence of AI-assisted diagnostic tools at community and safety-net facilities. A parallel survey of 312 hepatology care sites, conducted in partnership with the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases, identified inadequate reimbursement pathways and unclear FDA/CMS alignment on AI-enabled clinical decision support as the two most frequently cited barriers to adoption. The Society takes those findings seriously. The 68% figure is not an abstraction; it represents patients who waited through disease progression that might have been arrested, families who received news months too late, clinicians who lacked the tools their patients needed. The Society wants AI to work for those patients. What the Society cannot accept is the proposition that urgency, however real, dissolves the obligation to govern this technology with democratic accountability.⏎⏎⏎THE PROBLEM WITH "REDUCING UNCERTAINTY THAT IMPEDES AI INNOVATION"⏎⏎The RFI explicitly frames one of its core objectives as "reducing uncertainty that impedes AI innovation" — and the Society wants to be precise about what is troubling in that phrase. Regulatory scrutiny is not uncertainty in the pejorative sense. It is, structurally and historically, the mechanism through which democratic societies exercise collective judgment about which technologies enter their most sensitive institutions and on what terms. When HHS characterizes that scrutiny as an impediment, the Department is not making a neutral technical observation; it is making a normative claim — that the pace of commercial AI deployment should not be slowed by the processes through which the public retains meaningful oversight. Frank Pasquale documented this dynamic with considerable precision in The Black Box Society (Harvard University Press, 2015), observing that the opacity of proprietary algorithmic systems is not incidental but structural: it is baked into the architecture of commercial AI in ways that make external audit practically impossible even when regulators nominally possess that authority. The Society believes HHS must confront this directly rather than elide it in the language of innovation acceleration. Selbst and Barocas (2018), writing in the Fordham Law Review, made the further point that the intuitive appeal of "explainability" as a regulatory solution frequently obscures the deeper problem — that the proxies and training data embedded in clinical AI systems encode value choices that no post-hoc explanation layer can adequately surface for democratic deliberation. ONC's own HTI-1 Final Rule (88 Fed. Reg. 23746, 2023) took a meaningful step toward algorithm transparency requirements, and the Society is genuinely concerned that the acceleration framing of this RFI creates institutional pressure to treat those requirements as friction rather than floor.⏎⏎⏎ATS Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎hhs-ai-rfi@hhs.gov⏎⏎⏎PATH DEPENDENCY AND THE IRREVERSIBILITY PROBLEM⏎⏎Paul Pierson's foundational work on increasing returns and path dependence in political institutions (American Political Science Review, 94(2), 2000) provides the theoretical vocabulary for what the Society regards as the most consequential and least discussed risk in HHS's acceleration agenda: the practical irreversibility of embedded AI infrastructure. Pierson's argument, developed in the context of political and economic institutions, holds that once a technology or institutional arrangement reaches sufficient scale, the costs of reversal escalate nonlinearly — not because the arrangement is necessarily optimal, but because the surrounding infrastructure, workforce competencies, and economic relationships have reorganized themselves around it. Healthcare is not immune to this dynamic; in some respects it is especially vulnerable to it. Dafny and Lee (2016), analyzing consolidation patterns in the New England Journal of Medicine, observed that institutional path dependencies in healthcare markets tend to calcify quickly and prove remarkably resistant to correction even when the original rationale for a structural choice has been thoroughly discredited. The analogy to AI adoption is not perfect, but it is instructive. If HHS succeeds in accelerating the embedding of proprietary AI systems into clinical decision workflows at the pace this RFI contemplates, the Society submits that within a decade — probably less — the question of whether those systems should have been deployed differently will be largely academic, because the institutional knowledge, clinical workflows, and vendor contracts organized around them will have made meaningful reversal practically impossible regardless of what subsequent evidence shows.⏎⏎Atul Gawande's 2018 New Yorker essay "Why Doctors Hate Their Computers" documented this dynamic with unusual clarity in the context of electronic health record adoption. Gawande described how EHR systems, adopted rapidly under meaningful federal financial incentives, became so thoroughly embedded in clinical workflows that physicians found themselves unable to function without them even when those systems were actively degrading the quality of clinical encounters. The point is not that EHRs were a mistake — it is that the speed of adoption foreclosed the kind of iterative, evidence-based refinement that would have produced better systems, because by the time the problems were well-documented, the institutional capacity to function without the technology had atrophied. Shortliffe and Sepúlveda (2018), writing in JAMA, made a related observation about clinical decision support systems specifically: that the gap between a system's demonstrated performance in controlled research settings and its behavior in real-world clinical environments is frequently large, and that this gap tends to be discovered after deployment rather than before, precisely because pre-deployment evaluation frameworks have not kept pace with the complexity of the systems being deployed. The Society is asking HHS to take that history seriously as a governance lesson, not merely as a technical footnote.⏎⏎⏎ATS Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE OPACITY PROBLEM IS NOT SOLVABLE THROUGH REIMBURSEMENT ALIGNMENT⏎⏎A significant portion of the RFI is organized around the premise that the primary barriers to AI adoption are reimbursement misalignment and regulatory uncertainty — and the GLI data cited above does confirm that clinicians and health systems identify those barriers as significant. The Society does not dispute that reimbursement reform could meaningfully accelerate adoption at community and safety-net facilities, where the 68% diagnostic delay finding is most acute. But the Society is concerned that the RFI's framing conflates two distinct problems: the problem of access (how do we get functional AI tools to under-resourced facilities that need them?) and the problem of governance (how do we ensure that the AI tools being deployed are safe, unbiased, auditable, and subject to meaningful democratic oversight?). These are not the same problem, and solving the first without adequately addressing the second would be, in the Society's assessment, worse than the status quo.⏎⏎Obermeyer and colleagues (Science, 366(6464), 2019) demonstrated with considerable methodological rigor that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to manage care for millions of patients encoded racial bias at a scale that systematically disadvantaged Black patients — not through any intentional design choice, but through the use of healthcare cost as a proxy for healthcare need, a substitution whose discriminatory effect was invisible until external researchers conducted an independent audit that the algorithm's developer had not performed. The Society wants to be precise about what that finding means for this RFI: it means that a system that was generating revenue, that had passed whatever internal validation the vendor had performed, and that was embedded in the clinical workflows of major health systems, was actively harming a population of patients in ways that were architecturally invisible to the regulators, clinicians, and patients it affected. Coiera (2019), writing in the Journal of Medical Internet Research, called this the "last mile" problem — the gap between a system's performance on benchmark datasets and its behavior in the messy, heterogeneous reality of actual clinical practice. The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) addressed this class of problem through a precautionary, risk-tiered framework that requires demonstrated conformity assessment, transparency obligations, and human oversight mechanisms before high-risk AI systems — including those used in health and safety contexts — can be deployed at scale. The Society is not suggesting that the EU framework is directly transplantable to the U.S. regulatory context, but it is worth asking why HHS's framing of this RFI is organized around acceleration rather than around the precautionary logic that the European Parliament, after extensive democratic deliberation, concluded was appropriate for exactly this category of technology.⏎⏎⏎ATS Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎hhs-ai-rfi@hhs.gov⏎⏎⏎THE DEMOCRATIC MANDATE QUESTION⏎⏎This is the point the Society most wants HHS to engage with directly, because it has received the least attention in the academic and policy literature on health AI and the Society believes it is the most consequential. HHS is a Cabinet-level department operating under delegated statutory authority. Its mandate extends to protecting and promoting the health of the American public — a mandate that is both broad and, in democratic terms, bounded. The question of whether the United States, as a democratic society, should embed proprietary AI systems into the life-and-death decision infrastructure of its healthcare system on an accelerated timeline, with governance frameworks to be determined later, is not a question that falls within HHS's unilateral authority to answer on behalf of the American public. That is not a procedural objection. It is a substantive one. Eric Topol's influential work in Nature Medicine (2019) made a compelling case for the efficiency gains available through human-AI convergence in clinical settings, and the Society does not dismiss those gains. But Topol's framework, which the RFI's efficiency-first framing broadly reflects, assumes that the relevant question is how to realize those gains as quickly as possible — not whether the American public has been asked whether efficiency optimization is the value it most wants to govern the transformation of its healthcare system. A democratic society retains the legitimate and sovereign right to decide that certain domains — medicine chief among them — should remain stubbornly, deliberately human even at the cost of measurable efficiency gains. HHS lacks the mandate to preempt that collective judgment through an acceleration agenda dressed in the language of patient benefit, however sincere that language may be.⏎⏎Mittelstadt, Russell, and Wachter (FAT* Conference Proceedings, 2019) observed that the literature on AI explainability frequently conflates two distinct goals: producing explanations that satisfy technical audit requirements, and producing explanations that enable meaningful human deliberation about whether a system should be used at all. The Society believes that distinction is directly relevant here. HHS can create reimbursement pathways, reduce regulatory uncertainty in the narrow sense, and publish guidance on algorithm transparency — and none of those actions would constitute a democratic mandate for the wholesale embedding of AI into clinical care. The institutional question — who decides, on what basis, and with what mechanisms for reversal if the decision proves wrong — remains entirely unaddressed by the RFI's current framing, and the Society regards that omission as the most significant deficiency in the document.⏎⏎⏎ATS Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 5⏎⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD DO INSTEAD⏎⏎The Society's recommendations are directed specifically at the RFI's questions concerning regulatory frameworks and research and development priorities, which are the areas where the democratic governance concerns are most acute. On regulatory frameworks, the Society urges HHS to reject the framing of regulatory scrutiny as an impediment to innovation and to instead articulate, clearly and publicly, that demonstrated safety, auditability, and freedom from discriminatory bias are preconditions for federal reimbursement support — not aspirational goals to be pursued after deployment. This means that any reimbursement pathway developed in response to this RFI should require, as a condition of payment, that the AI system in question has undergone independent third-party audit of its training data, its validation methodology, and its performance across demographic subgroups. The Obermeyer et al. (2019) findings are now six years old. The field has not self-corrected. The argument that industry will voluntarily address bias and opacity without regulatory requirement has been tested and has failed. ONC's HTI-1 transparency requirements represent a meaningful starting point, but they apply to a narrower category of systems than the AI tools this RFI contemplates, and the Society urges HHS to treat them as a floor that this rulemaking should expand rather than a ceiling that subsequent guidance should accommodate.⏎⏎On research and development priorities, the Society urges HHS to fund, through the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality and through NIH mechanisms, independent research on the governance of AI in clinical settings — not merely on the clinical performance of AI systems, but on the institutional and democratic conditions under which AI adoption either preserves or erodes meaningful human oversight. The liver disease diagnostic delay problem documented in GLI's registry is real, and the Society believes that well-governed AI tools, deployed with appropriate transparency and accountability requirements, could meaningfully reduce that 68% figure. But the path to that outcome runs through governance, not around it. The Society is also concerned that the RFI's current framing will produce a public comment record dominated by technology vendors and health systems with strong financial incentives to accelerate deployment, while the patient communities most likely to be harmed by poorly governed AI — communities of color, patients in safety-net settings, patients with limited health literacy — are least represented in formal regulatory proceedings. HHS should take affirmative steps to solicit input from those communities before finalizing any regulatory or reimbursement framework, and should treat the absence of such input as a deficiency in the democratic legitimacy of whatever framework results.⏎⏎⏎ATS Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 6⏎hhs-ai-rfi@hhs.gov⏎⏎⏎THE SOCIETY'S DIRECT REQUEST TO HHS⏎⏎The American Thoracic Society respectfully but directly demands that HHS reframe this RFI around precautionary governance rather than acceleration. That reframing requires, at minimum, three things: first, that the Department explicitly acknowledge, in any final guidance or rulemaking that follows from this proceeding, that democratic societies have the right to choose human-centered care over efficient algorithmic care, and that HHS's role is to facilitate that choice rather than to preempt it; second, that demonstrated safety, auditability, and demographic equity be established as preconditions for federal reimbursement support rather than post-deployment compliance expectations; and third, that the Department commission, through existing research infrastructure, an independent assessment of the governance frameworks — including the EU AI Act's risk-tiered approach — that would be necessary to ensure that the embedding of AI in clinical settings does not foreclose the ability of future administrations, legislatures, or patient communities to reverse or substantially modify those choices if the evidence warrants. The Society is aware that these demands are in tension with the timeline pressures that motivated this RFI, and the Society does not dismiss those pressures. The 47,000-patient registry, the 68% delay figure, the 312-site survey — these are not abstractions to the Society's membership or to the patient communities it represents. But the answer to institutional urgency is not to bypass the governance processes through which democratic accountability is maintained. The answer is to build governance frameworks that are fast enough to be real and rigorous enough to be meaningful.⏎⏎The Society also wants to note, because it has not seen this acknowledged anywhere in the RFI or in the supporting documentation, that the question of vendor lock-in and contract terms for AI systems in clinical settings has received essentially no regulatory attention in this proceeding. Health systems that adopt proprietary AI tools for clinical decision support are entering contractual relationships whose terms — regarding data access, model updates, audit rights, and termination — are largely invisible to regulators and to the patients whose data those systems consume. The Society does not have a fully developed regulatory proposal for addressing this problem in this comment, but it regards it as directly connected to the irreversibility concern that Pierson's framework identifies: once a health system's clinical workflows are organized around a proprietary AI system and the vendor holds the contractual leverage that typically attaches to that position, the practical ability of that health system to exit the relationship — even in response to documented patient harm — is substantially constrained. That is a governance problem that no amount of reimbursement alignment will solve, and the Society urges HHS to treat it as such in any subsequent rulemaking.⏎⏎Sincerely,⏎⏎Thomas Green⏎Senior Policy Analyst, Health Policy Division⏎American Thoracic Society⏎25 Broadway, 18th Floor⏎New York, NY 10004⏎tgreen@thoracic.org♔♔2026-01-06T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-06T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔9♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Once AI systems are embedded in healthcare infrastructure, they become practically irreversible and resistant to democratic oversight, creating a permanent transfer of power from clinicians, patients, and regulators to technology vendors.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔angry♔Georgia♔senior policy analyst♔43♔A 2024 analysis of GLI's national patient registry, encompassing data from more than 47,000 individuals living with chronic liver disease, found that 68% experienced delays of six months or longer in receiving a definitive diagnosis—delays attributable in substantial part to the absence of AI-assisted diagnostic tools at community and safety-net facilities. SYNTH-0041♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Patricia Baker♔♔♔♔♔♔My mother died in August 2019 at 67. Three separate EKGs over fourteen months, all read as unremarkable. She had an arrhythmia the whole time. When my cardiologist at UCHealth mentioned during my October stress test that their team was piloting an AI tool to flag irregular readings before a second human review, I didn't feel afraid of the technology. I felt something closer to grief that it hadn't existed five years earlier, and then almost immediately I started wondering whether it would have actually worked for someone like her, a Mexican-American woman with atypical symptom presentation and a primary care record that had gaps in it because she'd gone years at a time without insurance. That question is what I want HHS to sit with seriously, because I don't think the RFI is asking it with enough urgency.⏎⏎I want to be clear that I am not opposed to AI in clinical care. I've spent five years reading the research on diagnostic error in cardiac care for women over sixty, which means I've also spent five years reading the literature on what algorithmic tools can and can't do. What I've found is that the documented risks of premature or inequitably validated deployment are serious and specific, and the RFI frames the problem almost entirely as one of insufficient adoption, which gets the risk calculus wrong in ways that matter most for patients who are already underserved. Obermeyer and colleagues published a paper in Science in 2019 showing that a widely used commercial algorithm for managing high-risk patient populations systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients because it used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, and Black patients with identical health burdens had historically generated lower costs due to structural barriers to access. The algorithm wasn't broken in any obvious technical sense. It was doing exactly what it had been trained to do. The bias was baked into the training data, and it took years of deployment and a careful external audit to surface it. Obermeyer et al., Science 366(6464), 2019.⏎⏎That same year, Sjoding and colleagues published findings in the New England Journal of Medicine showing that pulse oximeters, which are not AI tools but which are increasingly being integrated into automated monitoring systems, had occult hypoxemia rates nearly three times higher in Black patients than in white patients because the devices had been calibrated on populations that didn't reflect the full range of human skin tones. Sjoding et al., NEJM 383(25), 2020. Wong and colleagues published an external validation of the Epic sepsis prediction model in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021 and found that the model's performance degraded substantially when applied outside the academic medical center where it was developed, with a positive predictive value low enough that it was generating a significant burden of false alerts in community hospital settings. Wong et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 181(8), 2021. Gianfrancesco and colleagues had already laid out in 2018 exactly why this was predictable: EHR data reflects patterns of care-seeking that are themselves shaped by access, socioeconomic status, and prior documentation quality, so any model trained on that data will encode those structural inequities unless developers take active steps to identify and correct for them. Gianfrancesco et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 178(11), 2018. Char, Shah, and Magnus made the same point in the New England Journal of Medicine that same year, noting that the ethical challenges of implementing machine learning in health care are not primarily philosophical, they are technical and operational, and they require institutional structures to address. Char et al., NEJM 378(11), 2018.⏎⏎What concerns me about the RFI is that it does not treat post-deployment surveillance as a regulatory requirement with teeth. It asks open-ended questions about how to accelerate adoption and what reimbursement structures might support it, but the question of how HHS will ensure that tools validated in one setting actually perform equitably in another setting, specifically in community health centers and safety-net hospitals and rural critical access hospitals where patients are most likely to have incomplete records and atypical presentations, that question is present only as a vague gesture toward "responsible AI." I want to be specific about what responsible actually means in practice, because I think the research supports a set of concrete requirements rather than aspirational principles. Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones wrote in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 about the way race corrections embedded in clinical algorithms, whether explicit or implicit, can perpetuate harm even when the algorithms appear to be performing well on aggregate metrics. Vyas et al., NEJM 383(9), 2020. Adamson and Smith had made a related point about dermatology AI in JAMA Dermatology in 2018, where training datasets that skewed heavily toward lighter skin tones produced models with measurably lower accuracy for patients with darker skin, which is the kind of finding that only surfaces if you actually stratify your performance data by demographic subgroup. Adamson and Smith, JAMA Dermatology 154(11), 2018. The pattern across all of these papers is consistent. Performance gaps exist. They are measurable. They are not inevitable. They require active monitoring to detect and correct, and that monitoring does not happen by default.⏎⏎So what I am actually asking HHS to do is this. First, require that any AI tool seeking Medicare or Medicaid reimbursement undergo mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing with performance metrics stratified by race, ethnicity, sex, age, insurance status, and care setting, not just aggregate accuracy statistics. Second, require post-deployment surveillance as an ongoing condition of reimbursement, with reporting intervals short enough to catch performance degradation before it causes systematic harm, and with explicit requirements that surveillance data be analyzed across the same demographic subgroups as the pre-deployment audit. Third, establish performance standards that apply specifically to community and safety-net settings, because a tool that performs adequately at an academic medical center with dense, longitudinal EHR records may perform very differently at a federally qualified health center where patients may have years of care gaps or records that arrived from multiple disconnected systems. These are not radical demands. They are the minimum that the published literature says is necessary to avoid replicating the documented failures of the last decade at much larger scale.⏎⏎There is also something I want to say about automation bias that I don't see addressed anywhere in the RFI framing. When a system presents a recommendation with apparent algorithmic authority, clinicians are documented to defer to that recommendation even when they would otherwise question it on clinical grounds. This isn't a character flaw in clinicians. It is a predictable cognitive response to a system that presents with apparent precision and confidence, and it means that an AI tool with embedded bias can actually amplify the harm it causes because it suppresses the clinical skepticism that might otherwise catch the error. If my mother's third EKG had been read by a cardiologist assisted by an AI tool that returned a "low probability of arrhythmia" recommendation, I genuinely don't know whether that clinician would have pushed back. I hope so. But the literature on automation bias suggests that the institutional structures matter enormously, including whether clinicians are trained to interrogate algorithmic recommendations, whether they have time to do so, and whether they work in settings where questioning a tool's output is culturally supported rather than treated as inefficiency. HHS has the ability to make those structures a condition of reimbursement rather than a nice-to-have, and I think that is where the regulatory energy should be concentrated.⏎⏎The distance between what AI can apparently do now and what actually reaches patients equitably in exam rooms is real and it is not going to close on its own. I believe the technology can help. What I am not willing to accept is the argument that we have to move fast and sort out the equity problems later, because the patients most likely to be harmed by an inadequately validated tool are the same patients who have the least recourse when something goes wrong, and they are the ones for whom the promise of better diagnostics is most urgent.
