SYNTH-0042♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Joseph Lewis♔National Council of Asian Pacific Islander Physicians♔♔♔♔♔NATIONAL COUNCIL OF ASIAN PACIFIC ISLANDER PHYSICIANS⏎Comments in Response to HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket: HHS-ONC-2024-AI-RFI⏎Submitted by: Joseph Lewis, Research Director⏎National Council of Asian Pacific Islander Physicians (NCAPIP)⏎⏎ncapip.research@ncapip.org⏎⏎---⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎The National Council of Asian Pacific Islander Physicians submits these comments with considerable urgency, and with a degree of institutional frustration that the record should reflect. HHS is soliciting input on how to accelerate AI adoption in clinical settings at precisely the moment when our own survey data — and the broader research literature — make plain that health systems have already deployed AI tools far faster than they have built any meaningful capacity to govern them. The Health AI Institute's 2024 survey of 312 health system members found that 67% had deployed at least one clinical AI tool within the prior 18 months, yet only 29% reported having a formal governance framework in place to evaluate algorithmic performance or manage model drift over time. NCAPIP regards that 38-percentage-point gap not as a temporary lag to be corrected by further acceleration, but as direct evidence that HHS is being asked to pour more water into a vessel that is already cracked. These comments address two of the RFI's areas of inquiry: workforce impacts of AI deployment and the appropriate preconditions for any federal reimbursement pathway for AI-assisted clinical services.⏎⏎---⏎⏎NCAPIP Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎SECTION I: THE PROCUREMENT LOGIC DRIVING AI ADOPTION IS NOT WHAT HHS THINKS IT IS⏎⏎The framing embedded in this RFI — that AI adoption in health care is primarily a story about care quality, diagnostic accuracy, and clinician burnout relief — does not match what NCAPIP has observed in its research and member engagement over the past several years. The dominant driver of AI procurement decisions in health systems is not care quality. It is financial pressure, and specifically the pressure to demonstrate productivity gains that justify staffing decisions already made or anticipated. This distinction is not semantic. It determines everything about how AI tools are actually configured, what they measure, and whose interests they serve once deployed.⏎⏎Consider the specific case of prior authorization review, which has become one of the most aggressively automated clinical-adjacent functions in health systems over the past three years. Prior authorization is not a clerical function, despite the frequency with which health system administrators describe it that way to justify automation. Experienced prior authorization specialists — many of whom are nurses or clinically trained social workers — apply contextual judgment about patient history, insurer behavior patterns, and documentation strategy that directly determines whether a patient receives a medically necessary service in a clinically relevant timeframe. When that function is handed to an AI tool trained on historical approval rates, the system optimizes for throughput, not for the individual patient whose situation may not resemble the training distribution. Obermeyer et al. (2019) demonstrated in Science that a widely deployed population health algorithm systematically underestimated the clinical need of Black patients precisely because it was trained on cost as a proxy for health need — a methodological choice made for efficiency, not for accuracy. The prior authorization context carries analogous risks: automation trained on historical approval patterns will reproduce and entrench whatever biases existed in those patterns, and frontline workers who would otherwise catch those errors are no longer in the loop.⏎⏎Patient navigation is a second function undergoing rapid automation that NCAPIP regards as a category error. Patient navigators — a role that NCAPIP member organizations have helped develop and staff specifically to serve Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander communities with significant language and cultural barriers to care — perform work that is irreducibly relational. They build trust over multiple interactions. They understand why a patient did not show up for a follow-up appointment in a way that no algorithm trained on scheduling data can replicate. The Government Accountability Office noted in its 2023 report on AI in health care (GAO-23-105491) that the evidence base for AI tools in care coordination remains limited and that implementation context substantially mediates outcomes. Health systems deploying AI-driven patient outreach and navigation tools are, in NCAPIP's assessment, substituting a cheaper automated interaction for a more expensive human one and calling it innovation.⏎⏎---⏎⏎SECTION II: 'BURNOUT REDUCTION' AS RHETORICAL COVER FOR STAFFING EXTRACTION⏎⏎NCAPIP wants to be precise about this, because the burnout framing is genuinely seductive and HHS should not be misled by it. Physician and nurse burnout is real, documented, and severe. Shanafelt et al. (2022), writing in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, found that burnout rates among physicians had worsened between 2011 and 2020 even as satisfaction with work-life integration declined across the same period. Dyrbye et al. (2017) identified the administrative burden of electronic health records as among the most consistently cited contributors to that burnout. Melnick et al. (2020) found a statistically significant association between perceived EHR usability problems and professional burnout among U.S. physicians, with poor usability functioning as a stressor compounding the underlying moral injury of feeling unable to deliver adequate care. These findings are real. NCAPIP does not dispute them.⏎⏎What NCAPIP disputes is the claim — made implicitly throughout AI vendor marketing and, regrettably, echoed in the framing of this RFI — that deploying AI tools to automate documentation, flag deteriorating patients, or streamline scheduling constitutes a meaningful response to the conditions producing burnout. Wachter and Goldsmith argued in the Harvard Business Review in 2018 that fixing burnout requires fixing the structural conditions that produce it, not adding technological layers onto dysfunctional systems. That argument has not become less true in the intervening years. What has happened instead is that health systems have used the burnout narrative as procurement justification — "this tool will reduce your physicians' administrative burden" — while simultaneously using the efficiency gains those tools produce to reduce headcount, increase panel sizes, and extract more productivity from remaining staff. The National Nurses United research report published in 2023, "Staffing by Algorithm," documented specific instances in which health systems used AI-generated acuity scoring data to justify nurse-to-patient ratios that NNU's own nursing staff members regarded as unsafe. This is not a marginal phenomenon. It is the predictable consequence of deploying productivity tools inside organizations whose financial incentives reward staffing reduction.⏎⏎Petersen et al. (2022), in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, examined workforce implications of AI-assisted clinical documentation across a multi-site EHR implementation and found that while documentation time did decrease for some clinician categories, the time savings were largely absorbed into expanded caseloads rather than recovered as professional time. The efficiency gain went to the institution. The clinician experienced no net relief. This is the pattern NCAPIP has observed repeatedly in member engagement, and it is the pattern HHS will entrench if it builds reimbursement pathways for AI-assisted services without first requiring evidence that those services produce workforce benefit rather than merely institutional cost savings.⏎⏎---⏎⏎NCAPIP Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎SECTION III: AI-DRIVEN WORKPLACE SURVEILLANCE AND THE DEGRADATION OF CLINICAL JUDGMENT⏎⏎The RFI does not ask directly about workplace surveillance, but NCAPIP regards this as an omission that the record should correct. A significant and growing category of health system AI deployment is not directed at patients at all — it is directed at workers. Productivity monitoring tools that track physician documentation speed, flag nurses for deviation from protocol-recommended actions, score care coordinators on call handling efficiency, and generate real-time performance dashboards visible to supervisors constitute a form of algorithmic workplace control that the academic literature has examined with some care. Kellogg, Valentine, and Christin (2020), writing in the Academy of Management Annals, described algorithmic management systems as creating a "new contested terrain of control" in which workers are subject to continuous performance evaluation by systems they cannot interrogate, contest, or appeal. The health care context makes this dynamic particularly damaging because clinical judgment is not a deviation from protocol — it is the professional core of clinical work. A nurse who slows down to spend additional time with a distressed patient is not underperforming. An algorithm that flags her for low throughput does not know the difference.⏎⏎The American Medical Association's 2023 policy document on responsible AI deployment in clinical settings specifically cautioned against AI applications that function as performance surveillance tools without clinician input into their design, metrics, or governance. The AMA's position is that AI tools should augment clinical judgment, not evaluate it. NCAPIP endorses that principle and would extend it: AI tools that generate worker performance data must not be permitted to feed into staffing ratio decisions, performance reviews, or employment actions without explicit regulatory prohibition. The current absence of such prohibition is not a minor gap. It means that health systems can deploy AI surveillance tools today, under the cover of patient safety or quality improvement framing, and use the resulting data to discipline or eliminate workers who exercise the kind of contextual clinical judgment that Topol (2019) identified in Nature Medicine as the irreplaceable human contribution to high-performance medicine. Topol's vision of human-AI collaboration assumed that the human remained empowered and present. Health system AI deployment as currently practiced is systematically removing that condition.⏎⏎---⏎⏎SECTION IV: WORKFORCE HARM IS PATIENT HARM — AND THE EVIDENCE IS SUFFICIENT TO ACT⏎⏎NCAPIP anticipates that some commenters will argue that workforce concerns, however valid, are separable from patient safety concerns and should be addressed through labor regulation rather than health care AI governance. This argument is wrong, and NCAPIP wants to be direct about why. The clinical literature on burnout and patient outcomes does not support a clean separation between how clinicians are treated and how patients fare. Bates et al. (2021), reviewing evidence on AI's potential to reduce diagnostic errors in BMJ Quality & Safety, noted that human factors — including clinician fatigue, cognitive overload, and disengagement — are among the primary contributors to diagnostic error, and that AI tools deployed into high-burnout environments may not produce the error-reduction benefits observed in controlled research settings. A demoralized, surveilled, and overloaded physician is not the human partner that AI-assisted diagnostics was designed to work with. The governance vacuum documented in the Health AI Institute's 2024 survey is not just an administrative problem. It is a patient safety problem.⏎⏎NCAPIP also notes that the workforce being most rapidly displaced or subjected to algorithmic oversight is disproportionately composed of nurses, medical assistants, care coordinators, and patient navigators — roles that are themselves disproportionately filled by workers of color, including the Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander communities NCAPIP serves. When HHS designs AI adoption policy without mandatory workforce impact assessments, it is not making a neutral technical decision. It is making a distributional decision about whose labor is expendable and whose concerns do not require regulatory attention before acceleration proceeds.⏎⏎---⏎⏎NUMBERED RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎NCAPIP submits the following specific regulatory demands. These are not suggestions for further study. The research base is sufficient to act.⏎⏎1. HHS must require mandatory frontline worker consultation as a precondition for any AI procurement decision in health systems receiving federal reimbursement. "Consultation" must be defined to require meaningful input prior to vendor selection, not post-hoc notification. The 2024 Health AI Institute survey found that frontline workers were systematically excluded from procurement decisions at the overwhelming majority of deploying health systems. This exclusion is not accidental — it reflects the financial logic driving procurement — and it will not be corrected without explicit federal requirement.⏎⏎2. HHS must prohibit the use of AI-generated productivity or performance data in staffing ratio decisions, nurse-to-patient ratio calculations, or employment actions, absent an independent clinical review process with worker representation. This prohibition must be a condition of participation in any CMS reimbursement pathway for AI-assisted services, not a voluntary best practice.⏎⏎3. Any federal reimbursement pathway for AI-assisted clinical services must be conditioned on demonstrated workforce impact assessment, conducted by an independent entity, prior to deployment at scale. The Health AI Institute analysis referenced in this RFI found that sites operating under explicit CMS coverage pathways demonstrated three times the sustained deployment rate of those using ad hoc billing practices. HHS should use that leverage. Reimbursement certainty is a powerful tool, and conditioning it on workforce protection is not a radical ask — it is basic stewardship of the clinical labor infrastructure on which patient care depends.⏎⏎4. HHS must require that AI governance frameworks — specifically including those governing model drift, algorithmic bias, and performance monitoring — be in place before deployment, not developed concurrently or post-deployment. The 29% governance framework adoption rate documented in the 2024 survey is the current baseline. HHS acceleration policy must not treat that number as acceptable.⏎⏎5. HHS should commission a targeted study, with NCAPIP and analogous physician and nursing organizations as named consultants, examining AI deployment impacts specifically within health systems serving Asian American, Native Hawaiian, Pacific Islander, and other underrepresented minority patient populations. The racial bias findings of Obermeyer et al. (2019) established a methodological precedent for this kind of targeted audit. That precedent has not been systematically applied to the AI tools currently in deployment across health systems serving NCAPIP's member communities.⏎⏎---⏎⏎NCAPIP Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎APPENDIX NOTE⏎⏎NCAPIP is preparing a supplementary appendix documenting specific AI procurement practices observed across seven health systems in Arizona, California, and Hawai'i, including three instances in which AI acuity scoring tools were deployed in facilities with significant NHPI patient populations without any cultural competency review of the underlying training data. That appendix is not attached to this submission due to timing constraints but will be submitted to the docket under separate cover no later than 30 days following the close of the comment period. NCAPIP requests that HHS hold the record open for supplementary submissions from named organizational commenters for a period of 45 days following the formal close of the comment period, consistent with the complexity of the issues raised.⏎⏎---⏎⏎CLOSING NOTE ON PROCESS⏎⏎NCAPIP recognizes that HHS is operating under genuine pressure to demonstrate that federal AI policy is keeping pace with private sector deployment. That pressure is understandable. What it cannot justify is designing acceleration policy around the assumption that governance, workforce protection, and equity review can follow adoption rather than precede it. The 2023 GAO report on AI in health care concluded that the evidence base for many deployed clinical AI tools remains insufficient to support confident efficacy claims — a finding that received considerably less attention in AI vendor communications than it deserved. NCAPIP's member physicians, many of whom are themselves being subjected to AI-driven performance monitoring in their own clinical environments, are not opposed to AI as a category. They are opposed to being governed by systems they had no role in designing, evaluated by metrics they cannot contest, and told that the resulting efficiency gains represent progress in care delivery. The reimbursement pathway question that sits at the center of this RFI is, at its core, a question about who captures the value that AI generates in health systems. SYNTH-0043♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Ashley Hall♔American College of Emergency Physicians♔♔♔♔♔American College of Emergency Physicians⏎4950 W. Royal Lane⏎Irving, TX 75063⏎⏎Ashley Hall, MS, PhD⏎Research Director, Health Policy and Clinical Informatics⏎American College of Emergency Physicians⏎⏎February 14, 2025⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎---⏎⏎ACEP COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI | February 2025 | Page 1⏎⏎---⏎⏎The American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP) submits these comments in response to the Department's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. ACEP represents more than 40,000 emergency physicians practicing across every care environment in the country, including the community hospitals, rural critical access facilities, and safety-net emergency departments where the equity consequences of poorly validated AI will be felt most acutely. Our comments are focused specifically on two areas where the RFI's current framing is, in our assessment, dangerously incomplete: the absence of mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing requirements, and the absence of any proposed post-deployment bias surveillance infrastructure. The Department has framed this proceeding as an exercise in removing barriers to adoption. ACEP does not object to removing barriers that are genuinely obstructive. What concerns us is that HHS appears prepared to remove barriers while leaving the underlying validation gap entirely unaddressed — and the populations that will pay for that choice are already documented in the peer-reviewed literature.⏎⏎THE VALIDATION PROBLEM IS STRUCTURAL, NOT INCIDENTAL⏎⏎A 2024 policy survey conducted across ACEP's 1,200 member laboratories and affiliated clinical sites found that 68% have either piloted or actively deployed at least one AI-assisted diagnostic tool. Seventy-four percent of those respondents cited the absence of standardized clinical validation frameworks as the primary barrier to broader institutional adoption. This is not a funding problem or a workflow problem. It is a structural problem: the AI development pipeline generates tools that are validated primarily on data from large academic medical centers, and those tools are then deployed into community hospitals and safety-net emergency departments that bear no meaningful resemblance to the environments where the validation work was done. The consequences are predictable and have been documented repeatedly. Wong et al., in their 2021 external validation study published in JAMA Internal Medicine, examined a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model and found that its performance degraded substantially when applied outside the academic medical center where it was developed, with particularly poor sensitivity in precisely the patient subpopulations where early sepsis identification matters most (Wong A, Otles E, Donnelly JP, et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2021;181(8):1065-1070). That is not a cautionary hypothetical. That is a deployed, commercially available tool that failed in the field in ways that its internal validation data did not predict.⏎⏎The sepsis example is not isolated. Seyyed-Kalantari and colleagues published findings in Nature Medicine in 2021 demonstrating that AI algorithms applied to chest radiographs systematically underdiagnosed pathology in underserved patient populations, with the underdiagnosis bias correlating directly with demographic characteristics including race and insurance status (Seyyed-Kalantari L, Zhang H, McDermott MBA, Chen IY, Ghassemi M. Nat Med. 2021;27(12):2176-2182). Adamson and Smith, writing in JAMA Dermatology in 2018, documented that dermatology AI trained predominantly on lighter-skinned patient images performed materially worse on darker skin tones, a finding that is particularly consequential given that melanoma misclassification carries direct mortality implications (Adamson AS, Smith A. JAMA Dermatol. 2018;154(11):1247-1248). Gianfrancesco and colleagues identified in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2018 that electronic health record data used to train machine learning models contains systematic biases reflecting historical patterns of differential documentation, differential access, and differential treatment — biases that the models then reproduce and, in some cases, amplify (Gianfrancesco MA, Tamang S, Yazdany J, Schmajuk G. JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(11):1544-1547).⏎⏎---⏎⏎ACEP COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI | February 2025 | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎These are not edge cases. They are representative findings from a literature that has been accumulating for at least seven years. Obermeyer and colleagues published in Science in 2019 a systematic dissection of a commercial algorithm used to manage population health that was found to assign lower risk scores to Black patients than to comparably sick white patients, effectively reducing Black patients' access to care management programs (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. Science. 2019;366(6464):447-453). Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones wrote in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 about race correction embedded in clinical algorithms — adjustments that appear technical and neutral but encode assumptions that have no validated biological basis and that systematically disadvantage Black patients in renal function estimation, spirometry interpretation, and other domains (Vyas DA, Eisenstein LG, Jones DS. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(9):874-882). The pulse oximetry literature is perhaps the most viscerally clear example: Sjoding and colleagues published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 that pulse oximeters — a device, not an algorithm, but one whose performance data informed oxygen therapy decision-making throughout the COVID-19 pandemic — systematically overestimated oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin pigmentation, meaning that Black patients were treated as less hypoxic than they actually were at a moment when that error was potentially lethal (Sjoding MW, Dickson RP, Iwashyna TJ, Gay SE, Valley TS. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(25):2477-2478).⏎⏎The Department has access to all of this literature. ACEP is not presenting novel findings. What ACEP is saying is that HHS's RFI, which is organized around the question of how to accelerate adoption, proceeds as though this body of evidence does not exist or does not constrain the policy response. That framing is a choice with consequences.⏎⏎AUTOMATION BIAS AS A STRUCTURAL AMPLIFIER OF INEQUITY⏎⏎The equity problem is compounded by what the human factors literature identifies as automation bias: the well-documented tendency of clinicians to over-rely on automated decision support outputs, particularly when those outputs are presented with the authoritative visual design and numerical precision that characterize most commercial AI tools. Sendak and colleagues, writing in the Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability and Transparency in 2020, documented that clinicians frequently treat deep learning outputs as more reliable than their own clinical judgment, even in circumstances where the model's inputs and limitations are poorly understood (Sendak MP, Elish MC, Gao M, et al. Proc ACM Conf Fairness Accountability Transparency. 2020:99-109). Char, Shah, and Magnus identified in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018 that the integration of machine learning into clinical workflows creates accountability diffusion — no single clinician owns the error when the algorithm fails, which means errors are less likely to be identified, escalated, or corrected (Char DS, Shah NH, Magnus D. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(11):981-983).⏎⏎In a well-resourced academic medical center with robust quality infrastructure, automation bias and accountability diffusion are serious problems. In a community hospital emergency department operating with three physicians covering 60,000 annual visits, those problems are catastrophic. The AI doesn't simply fail — it fails in an environment where the failure is least likely to be caught, in a population whose clinical presentations are already underrepresented in the training data, and in a workflow where the time pressure is highest. Pierson and colleagues published in Nature Medicine in 2021 an analysis demonstrating that algorithmic approaches to pain management systematically underestimated pain severity in underserved populations, a finding that maps directly onto the emergency department context where pain assessment and treatment decisions are made rapidly and often with AI-assisted clinical decision support (Pierson E, Cutler DM, Leskovec J, Mullainathan S, Obermeyer Z. Nat Med. 2021;27(1):136-140). Wiens and colleagues articulated in Nature Medicine in 2019 a responsible machine learning framework that explicitly requires prospective validation in deployment-representative populations before clinical implementation — a standard that is conspicuously absent from anything HHS has proposed in this proceeding (Wiens J, Saria S, Sendak M, et al. Nat Med. 2019;25(9):1337-1340).⏎⏎---⏎⏎ACEP COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI | February 2025 | Page 3⏎⏎---⏎⏎HHS'S OMISSION OF EQUITY AUDITING IS A POLICY CHOICE, NOT AN OVERSIGHT⏎⏎The regulatory infrastructure to require algorithmic transparency already exists. The Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability: Certification Program Updates, Algorithm Transparency, and Information Sharing Final Rule — HTI-1 — published at 45 CFR Parts 170 and 171, 89 Fed. Reg. 1192 (January 9, 2024), established transparency requirements for clinical decision support tools as a condition of certification. HTI-1 represents a meaningful step, but it does not require pre-deployment equity auditing across demographic subgroups, and it does not require post-deployment bias surveillance with public reporting. HHS knows this. The Department chose to certify transparency without mandating equity performance. That choice can be revisited, and ACEP is formally requesting that it be revisited in the context of this proceeding.⏎⏎What mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing would require, at minimum:⏎⏎1. Stratified performance reporting across race, ethnicity, sex, age, insurance status, and primary language for any AI tool seeking deployment authorization in a clinical care setting.⏎⏎2. External validation in patient populations that are demographically representative of the intended deployment environment — meaning that a tool intended for use in a Federally Qualified Health Center cannot be validated exclusively on data from a quaternary academic medical center.⏎⏎3. Documentation of training data composition, including the demographic characteristics of the source population and the dates of data collection, with particular attention to whether historical periods of documented discriminatory treatment are represented in the training set in ways that would perpetuate those patterns.⏎⏎4. Pre-specified performance thresholds that trigger deployment suspension if the tool fails to meet equity criteria across subgroups — not just aggregate accuracy metrics, which can mask severe subgroup failures behind acceptable overall performance.⏎⏎Post-deployment surveillance requirements should include mandatory adverse event reporting when AI-assisted clinical decisions are associated with patient harm, demographic disaggregation of performance monitoring data submitted to a central registry, and public reporting of that data at intervals sufficient to identify emerging bias patterns before they become entrenched in clinical practice. Fewer than 12% of AI-augmented laboratory tests currently qualify for distinct CPT coding, which means health systems are absorbing integration costs without reimbursement recognition — a financial structure that creates strong incentives to deploy tools quickly and weak incentives to invest in the monitoring infrastructure that would catch failures. HHS's reimbursement policy and its safety policy are not separable questions.⏎⏎ACEP acknowledges that mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing will slow some deployments. That is not an argument against requiring it. The relevant comparison is not between fast deployment and slow deployment. It is between deployment that predictably harms marginalized patients in ways that are difficult to detect and deployment that is required to demonstrate it will not do so before it reaches clinical practice. The literature reviewed above — Obermeyer et al., Sjoding et al., Seyyed-Kalantari et al., Wong et al., Pierson et al. — describes harms that were observable after deployment precisely because no one required they be evaluated before deployment. ACEP's position is that HHS should not replicate that error at scale under the banner of acceleration.⏎⏎The Department should not issue deployment authorizations for AI tools in clinical care settings without requiring: (a) mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing with stratified performance reporting across all relevant demographic subgroups, and (b) mandatory post-deployment bias surveillance with public reporting requirements and pre-specified performance thresholds that trigger review. ACEP requests that HHS publish, for public comment, a proposed framework for both requirements before finalizing any policy guidance that would expand AI deployment in clinical care settings. The absence of such a framework from the current RFI — given the volume and consistency of the evidence base described above — is something ACEP intends to continue raising in every available regulatory forum.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Ashley Hall, MS, PhD⏎Research Director, Health Policy and Clinical Informatics⏎American College of Emergency Physicians⏎⏎acep.healthpolicy@acep.org⏎https://www.acep.org/federal-advocacy/♔♔2026-02-13T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-13T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔angry♔Washington♔research director♔35♔A 2024 policy survey conducted across our 1,200 member laboratories found that 68% have either piloted or actively deployed at least one AI-assisted diagnostic tool, yet 74% of those respondents cited the absence of standardized clinical validation frameworks as the primary barrier to broader institutional adoption. SYNTH-0044♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Lisa Perez♔American Geriatrics Society♔♔♔♔♔American Geriatrics Society — Public Comment Submission⏎HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Lisa Perez, Community Organizer, American Geriatrics Society, New Hampshire Chapter⏎Docket Reference: HHS-2024-AI-Clinical-RFI⏎⏎⏎THE GOVERNANCE VACUUM ALREADY EXISTS⏎⏎The American Geriatrics Society submits these comments in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care settings, and does so with a specific concern that the RFI, as structured, does not adequately grapple with: there is no accountability infrastructure currently governing how AI-assisted clinical decisions are made, reviewed, or contested when something goes wrong. This is not a theoretical concern awaiting future evidence. A 2024 member survey conducted by the Association for Diagnostics & Laboratory Medicine (ADLM) found that 62% of the 9,800 member laboratorians and pathologists surveyed reported direct exposure to at least one AI-assisted diagnostic tool in their clinical workflow, yet fewer than one in four described having formal institutional protocols governing how AI outputs are reviewed, validated, or escalated for human oversight (ADLM Quality Practices Committee Member Survey on AI Governance in Clinical Laboratories, 2024). The same survey, drawing on case reports from more than 400 laboratory settings spanning academic medical centers, community hospitals, and reference laboratories, identified recurring concerns about opaque model versioning and silent software updates that altered test interpretation thresholds without notifying the clinicians relying on those outputs. The governance vacuum the RFI proposes to accelerate is not a gap waiting to be filled — it is already operational, and patients in New Hampshire and across the country are already inside it.⏎⏎What the ADLM findings describe is not primarily a technical problem. The AI tools themselves may function within their stated parameters. The problem is structural: who is responsible when the tool's output shapes a clinical decision that harms a patient, and that output was generated by a model version nobody in the clinical setting knew had been updated? The Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology identified similar governance concerns in its 2021 landscape review of AI and health IT, noting the absence of clear accountability mechanisms for AI-assisted decision support in clinical environments (ONC, 2021). The U.S. Government Accountability Office reached comparable conclusions in its 2022 report on AI in health care, which found that existing regulatory frameworks were not designed to address the iterative, self-updating characteristics of deployed AI systems and that the absence of clear lines of responsibility for AI-assisted harm represented a structural risk to patient safety (GAO-22-104629, 2022). These are not fringe observations. They are the findings of the federal oversight apparatus itself. The question the American Geriatrics Society is placing before HHS is whether the Department has read its own literature before proposing to accelerate adoption.⏎⏎⏎THE LIABILITY VACUUM IS A DESIGN FEATURE, NOT AN OVERSIGHT⏎⏎American Geriatrics Society Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 2⏎⏎The liability vacuum that currently surrounds AI-assisted clinical harm is not an accident of regulatory lag. It is, in a meaningful structural sense, a design feature of how AI tools are deployed in clinical settings. Medical malpractice doctrine, as it has developed over more than a century of common law, presupposes an identifiable human decision-maker whose professional judgment can be evaluated against a standard of care (Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, & Studdert, 2020). That assumption is not merely a procedural convenience — it is the moral foundation of the entire liability system, because it answers the question that patients have the most urgent right to ask: who was responsible for my care? AI intermediation severs that assumption at the root. When a laboratorian relies on an AI-assisted diagnostic output that turns out to have been generated by a silently updated model version, the clinician can plausibly argue that they were not informed of the change; the hospital can argue that it deployed the vendor's tool within its specified parameters; and the vendor can argue that its documentation warned against uncritical reliance on model outputs, or that the harm resulted from user misapplication rather than product defect. The patient is left at the center of a three-way contractual indemnification arrangement between institutional actors, none of whom has accepted clear, non-delegable responsibility for the outcome. Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen (2020) describe this distributed accountability structure as one of the defining ethical and legal challenges of AI-driven health care, precisely because it does not merely complicate liability — it dissolves the conditions under which liability can be assigned at all.⏎⏎Frank Pasquale's analysis in New Laws of Robotics (2020) frames this dynamic in terms that are directly relevant to HHS's RFI: when AI systems are embedded in professional workflows, they do not simply augment human judgment — they restructure the institutional conditions under which human judgment is exercised, often in ways that make it progressively more difficult for human professionals to identify, contest, or override the system's outputs. This matters for accountability because once an AI tool is embedded in a clinical workflow, institutional dependency creates a practical barrier to the kind of critical review that malpractice doctrine assumes is occurring. Clinicians facing alert fatigue from high-volume AI-assisted decision support tools are less likely to scrutinize individual outputs with the rigor the system nominally requires (Kesselheim, Cresswell, Phansalkar, Bates, & Sheikh, 2011). What begins as augmentation becomes, over time, delegation — and delegation without accountability is not a clinical tool, it is a liability transfer mechanism that moves risk from well-resourced institutional actors onto patients who have no contractual standing in the arrangements that produced their harm.⏎⏎⏎WHAT THE RFI DOES NOT ASK⏎⏎The RFI poses a range of useful questions about reimbursement pathways, research priorities, and interoperability standards. The American Geriatrics Society does not dispute that these are legitimate policy questions. What the RFI does not ask — and this omission is the organizing concern of this comment — is what accountability framework must be in place before adoption incentives are extended. The RFI treats the governance question as either downstream of adoption or as a parallel workstream that can be developed concurrently with scaling. That framing is incorrect, and the consequences of accepting it will fall disproportionately on the populations this organization represents: older adults, patients with complex chronic conditions, and individuals in community health settings that lack the legal and technical resources to contest AI-assisted clinical errors after the fact. Char, Shah, and Magnus (2018) argued in the New England Journal of Medicine that the ethical deployment of machine learning in clinical settings requires, as a precondition, clarity about who bears responsibility for algorithmic recommendations — not as an aspirational goal, but as a threshold condition for deployment. That argument was made in 2018. The governance gap it identified has not closed; by the ADLM survey's account, it has widened.⏎⏎The concern is compounded by what Price and Cohen (2019) identified as the opacity problem in medical AI: the systems generating clinical recommendations are often trained on data that is not accessible to the clinicians using them, updated through processes that are not visible to the institutions deploying them, and evaluated against performance benchmarks that do not necessarily correspond to the clinical outcomes that matter to patients. Doshi-Velez and colleagues (2017) framed the accountability challenge precisely: when an AI system cannot explain its outputs in terms that allow meaningful human review, the accountability mechanisms that law and professional ethics assume are present simply cannot function. An AI tool that altered diagnostic thresholds through a silent software update — the pattern the ADLM survey documented across more than 400 laboratory settings — is not a tool that supports accountable clinical judgment. It is a tool that substitutes for it, invisibly, and then distributes the consequences of that substitution across a liability structure designed to ensure that no single party absorbs them. Cohen, Evgeniou, Gerke, and Minssen (2020) noted in The Lancet Digital Health that even the European AI strategy, which is considerably more prescriptive than current U.S. regulatory approaches, has struggled to establish enforceable accountability norms for AI in clinical settings. HHS should not interpret the absence of a completed international model as license to proceed without one.⏎⏎⏎American Geriatrics Society Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE MORAL DIMENSION HHS HAS NOT ADDRESSED⏎⏎There is a dimension of this issue that tends to get lost in policy discussions focused on reimbursement codes and interoperability frameworks, and the American Geriatrics Society wants to name it directly. Patients have a right to know that a specific human being is answerable for their care. That right is not satisfied by a chain of contractual arrangements between a hospital, a vendor, and a platform operator. It is not satisfied by a consent form that discloses the general use of AI-assisted tools. It is not satisfied by a vendor's terms of service that allocate risk to the deploying institution while insulating the developer from liability for outputs the developer's own model generated. Obermeyer and Emanuel (2016) observed that the integration of machine learning into clinical medicine raises not only technical questions but questions about the nature of clinical responsibility itself — who is the decision-maker, and what does it mean to be accountable for a decision that was materially shaped by a system the decision-maker did not design, cannot fully audit, and may not have known was running a different version than it was running the week before. That question has not been answered. HHS's RFI does not propose to answer it. The RFI proposes, instead, to extend financial incentives for adoption into a governance environment where the question remains open — and where the practical effect of scaling adoption before the answer is established will be to entrench institutional dependency on AI systems in ways that make the question progressively harder to revisit.⏎⏎The American Geriatrics Society's specific policy position, in response to the RFI questions concerning reimbursement and adoption incentives, is this: HHS must not advance any reimbursement pathway or adoption incentive for AI-assisted clinical decision support until the Department has established a mandatory accountability framework that assigns clear, non-delegable legal and regulatory responsibility for AI-assisted patient harm to an identifiable human or institutional party. That framework must address, at minimum, the following structural conditions: it must require that clinicians be notified of any material change to an AI tool's model version or decision thresholds before the updated tool is used in clinical care; it must establish that silent software updates affecting clinical outputs are a form of material modification that triggers regulatory review obligations; it must specify which party — clinician, hospital, or vendor — bears primary liability for AI-assisted harm in defined circumstances, and that specification must be enforceable, not merely advisory; and it must create a mechanism through which patients who have been harmed by AI-assisted clinical errors can identify the responsible party without first having to litigate the threshold question of who the responsible party is. The ADLM survey documented that fewer than one in four laboratory settings had formal protocols for reviewing or escalating AI outputs as of 2024. If HHS extends reimbursement incentives before those protocols are required, the incentive structure will reward adoption without governance, and the institutions that move fastest will be the ones that have externalized the most risk.⏎⏎The American Geriatrics Society recognizes that these are not simple demands to operationalize. The technical and legal questions involved in assigning non-delegable liability for AI-assisted harm in multi-vendor clinical environments are genuinely difficult, and the Department will need to work across CMS, ONC, FDA, and potentially the Federal Trade Commission to develop a framework that is both enforceable and workable. What the American Geriatrics Society is insisting on is the sequencing: the framework must precede the incentives, not follow them. Once AI systems are embedded in clinical workflows at scale — once hospitals have restructured staffing, documentation requirements, and reimbursement submissions around AI-assisted outputs — the institutional cost of imposing accountability requirements retroactively will be used as an argument against imposing them at all. That is not a hypothetical concern. It is the pattern that played out with electronic health record adoption following the HITECH Act, where interoperability and data governance requirements that should have been threshold conditions for incentive eligibility were instead deferred and are still being negotiated more than a decade later. The American Geriatrics Society does not want to be submitting a comment like this one in 2035 about the governance gaps that HHS chose not to address in 2024 because the adoption incentives had already gone out.⏎⏎A point of contact for follow-up questions regarding this submission:⏎lperez@americangeriatrics-nh.org♔♔2026-02-28T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-28T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔concerned♔New Hampshire♔community organizer♔40♔A 2024 survey of ADLM's 9,800 member laboratorians and pathologists found that 62% reported direct exposure to at least one AI-assisted diagnostic tool in their clinical workflow, yet fewer than one in four described having formal institutional protocols governing how AI outputs are reviewed, validated, or escalated for human oversight. SYNTH-0047♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Deborah Rodriguez♔National Women's Health Network♔♔♔♔♔NATIONAL WOMEN'S HEALTH NETWORK⏎SUBMISSION TO THE HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI REQUEST FOR INFORMATION⏎Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL-RFI⏎Submitted by: Deborah Rodriguez, Policy Director⏎1875 Connecticut Avenue NW, Suite 650, Washington, DC 20009⏎drodriguez@nwhn.org⏎⏎NWHN Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎The National Women's Health Network (NWHN) submits these comments in response to HHS's request for information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. The NWHN has represented women's health interests in federal policy since 1975 and draws its policy positions directly from member research, claims data analysis, and ongoing engagement with clinical care centers across the country. We write today neither as reflexive opponents of health AI nor as uncritical advocates. Our position is grounded in documented evidence on both sides of this technology's real-world record.⏎⏎A 2024 analysis of a member needs assessment survey — completed by more than 6,800 individuals living with multiple sclerosis across 47 states — found that 68% reported experiencing delays of three months or more in receiving a confirmed MS diagnosis, and 54% identified specialist access as their primary barrier to timely disease-modifying therapy initiation. Our policy team's review of claims data submitted by participating neurology centers identified that AI-assisted lesion quantification tools, where deployed, reduced radiological read-to-report turnaround by an average of 11 days per patient encounter. These findings align with outcomes reported at a 2024 Clinical Research Roundtable, where 14 MS care centers presented evidence that AI-integrated diagnostic workflows meaningfully narrowed care gaps for patients in rural and underserved communities. That data is real. That promise is real.⏎⏎And yet the NWHN is compelled to state directly: HHS's RFI as framed treats "AI in healthcare" as a category of intervention that is net-positive by default, requiring only acceleration and reimbursement alignment to realize its benefits. This framing is incomplete in a way that is not merely analytically insufficient — it is dangerous. The most consequential AI application currently operating at scale in the United States health system is not diagnostic imaging support or clinical decision assistance. It is automated prior authorization denial. These systems are already deployed. They are already generating harm. And HHS's RFI, which asks how to "foster competition among clinical care AI tool builders" and expand reimbursement pathways, does not once grapple with the documented reality that insurer AI investment is concentrated not in care delivery but in coverage denial.⏎⏎The NWHN urges HHS to address this asymmetry before any further acceleration of health AI adoption. We focus our comments on two of the RFI's question areas: reimbursement and coverage policy mechanisms, and research and development priorities. We do not address clinical AI bias, workforce impacts, or vendor market concentration, which we understand are being addressed in separate organizational submissions.⏎⏎NWHN Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎THE DOCUMENTED REALITY OF ALGORITHMIC DENIAL⏎⏎The U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations published a report in October 2023 — "Denial, Delay, Deny: How Medicare Advantage Plans Use AI to Override Physician Judgment," S. Prt. 118-22 — that documented, in granular detail, how major Medicare Advantage insurers deployed AI-driven utilization management tools that generated prior authorization denials at rates far exceeding what physician reviewers had historically produced. The Subcommittee found that at least one major insurer's algorithm denied claims at a rate 22 times higher than the insurer's own human reviewers had previously denied similar requests. Twenty-two times. That number deserves to sit on the page without embellishment.⏎⏎The Office of Inspector General's April 2022 report, OIG Report OEI-09-18-00660, reached a similar conclusion through independent analysis: some Medicare Advantage organizations denied prior authorization requests that met Medicare coverage criteria and would, under fee-for-service Medicare, have been approved. The OIG found that a meaningful share of these denials were reversed on appeal — but only when beneficiaries or their providers actually filed appeals, which most do not. The structural asymmetry here is not incidental. It is the mechanism. Denial systems generate revenue when patients do not appeal, and the populations most likely not to appeal are elderly beneficiaries, individuals with disabilities, and low-income patients who lack the administrative support, health literacy infrastructure, or physical capacity to navigate multi-step appeals processes. A Kaiser Family Foundation issue brief published in March 2024 (Koma, Cubanski, and Neuman, "Prior Authorization in Medicare Advantage: Trends and Beneficiary Experiences") found that Medicare Advantage beneficiaries faced prior authorization requirements for services that traditional Medicare covers without restriction, and that denial rates varied dramatically across plans — a variation that correlates poorly with any clinical rationale and closely with insurer cost-containment objectives.⏎⏎The American Medical Association's 2023 Prior Authorization Physician Survey documented that 94% of physicians reported that prior authorization had delayed necessary care for their patients, and 33% reported that prior authorization had led to a serious adverse event for a patient in their care. These are not edge cases. These are the operating conditions of the current system, into which AI denial tools have been introduced not as neutral efficiency improvements but as deliberate cost-containment instruments. Hempstead, Cantor, and Monheit, writing in Health Affairs in 2023 ("Automated Utilization Management and Prior Authorization Denial Rates in Commercial Insurance: A Multi-Payer Analysis," 42(9):1214–1223), found that commercial insurers using automated utilization management systems exhibited denial rate increases of between 14% and 29% compared to pre-automation baseline periods, with no corresponding evidence of improved clinical appropriateness in the denied claims.⏎⏎NWHN Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎The NWHN wants to be precise about the mechanism because precision matters for policy design. These denial systems are not failing to achieve their design objectives. They are succeeding. They are trained on cost-containment outcomes, not clinical appropriateness criteria. The training data reflects insurer financial optimization behavior — a phenomenon documented in other contexts by Geruso and Layton in their 2020 Journal of Political Economy analysis of upcoding and risk adjustment gaming in Medicare programs (128(3):984–1026), which established that insurer behavior in public insurance markets is systematically oriented toward financial optimization in ways that diverge from patient welfare. When the optimization objective is denial volume and cost reduction, an AI system trained on historical denial data will produce more denials. This is not a technical failure. It is a design specification.⏎⏎What makes this particularly difficult to address after the fact is the opacity problem. Schulte and Fry's 2019 investigation in Kaiser Health News and Fortune ("Death by a Thousand Clicks") documented the broader problem of algorithmic decision-making opacity in health administration — the pattern by which automated systems produce consequential decisions without generating legible reasoning that patients, providers, or regulators can interrogate. Prior authorization denial letters generated by AI systems frequently cite general policy language rather than patient-specific clinical reasoning. Physicians cannot effectively appeal what they cannot read. Patients cannot effectively contest what they cannot understand. The Center for Medicare Advocacy's September 2023 policy brief on AI-driven prior authorization documented specific cases in which denial letters provided no clinical rationale beyond boilerplate coverage language, making meaningful appeal practically impossible for beneficiaries without legal or clinical representation.⏎⏎HHS's RFI asks how the Department can "foster competition among clinical care AI tool builders" as part of its reimbursement policy agenda. The NWHN's concern is not with competition per se — Dafny, Gruber, and Ody's 2015 American Journal of Health Economics analysis (1(1):53–81) established the basic relationship between insurer market structure and premium dynamics, and competitive markets can in principle reward quality. The concern is that "clinical care AI" is not where insurer AI investment is concentrated. Insurers are not primarily investing in AI to improve care delivery. They are investing in AI to optimize coverage denial, and the RFI's framing does not acknowledge this. Acceleration of health AI adoption without mandatory guardrails on the utilization management application will not produce a more competitive clinical AI market. It will produce a more efficient denial apparatus.⏎⏎NWHN Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎WHAT THE RFI SHOULD ADDRESS BUT DOES NOT⏎⏎The NWHN recognizes that HHS's authority over insurer utilization management practices is shared with CMS, state insurance commissioners, and Congress, and that an RFI on clinical care AI is not the natural home for a comprehensive prior authorization reform agenda. We raise this not to expand the RFI's scope arbitrarily but because the reimbursement and coverage questions the RFI does ask cannot be answered coherently without addressing insurer AI. Any reimbursement pathway HHS creates for AI-assisted clinical tools will interact with insurer prior authorization systems. If a clinician uses an AI-assisted diagnostic tool to identify an MS lesion pattern and recommend a specific disease-modifying therapy, the clinical benefit of that AI tool is immediately contingent on whether an AI denial system on the insurer side approves the resulting treatment request. The two AI applications are not separate policy domains. They are the same patient's journey through the same system.⏎⏎The research priority questions in the RFI are similarly incomplete. HHS asks how to accelerate research and development of clinical AI tools. The NWHN supports this goal. The 11-day reduction in radiological read-to-report turnaround documented in our claims data analysis represents a genuine patient benefit that merits policy support. Ziad Obermeyer and colleagues' 2023 review in NPJ Digital Medicine ("Algorithmic Fairness in Health and Medicine: A Review," 6:114) documents the state of the science on health AI fairness, including both the genuine clinical promise and the equity risks that arise when training data reflects historical disparities. But the RFI's research priority framing does not include a single question about AI applications in coverage and utilization management. HHS is proposing to fund and accelerate the clinical AI side of the equation while leaving the denial AI side unexamined by federal research investment. This is not a neutral research priority decision.⏎⏎The populations the NWHN represents — women, particularly women of color, low-income women, women in rural states like Montana where specialist access is structurally constrained — are precisely the populations who face the highest burden from algorithmic denial and the least administrative capacity to contest it. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan's foundational 2019 Science paper ("Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations," 366(6464):447–453) established that commercially deployed health algorithms can encode racial bias at scale even when race is not an explicit input variable. The same structural dynamic applies to denial AI: when training data reflects historical patterns of differential access and differential denial, automated systems trained on that data will reproduce and amplify those patterns. HHS cannot accelerate clinical AI adoption in a way that benefits underserved communities without simultaneously constraining the algorithmic denial systems that will intercept the resulting treatment recommendations.⏎⏎NWHN Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 5⏎⏎NUMBERED POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The NWHN offers the following specific recommendations directed at the reimbursement and research priority questions in the RFI. These are not aspirational principles. They are concrete regulatory and administrative actions HHS can take under existing authority or pursue through legislative recommendation.⏎⏎1. Mandatory Pre-Deployment Equity and Safety Audits for AI Used in Coverage or Utilization Management Decisions.⏎⏎HHS should require, as a condition of participation in federal health programs, that any AI or algorithmic system used by a participating insurer or managed care organization to make, support, or recommend prior authorization, utilization management, or coverage determination decisions be subject to independent pre-deployment audit. The audit must assess: (a) the training data composition and the outcome variable used to train the model; (b) denial rate differentials across demographic subgroups, including race, disability status, age, and rural/urban residence; (c) the degree to which denial outputs reflect clinical appropriateness criteria as distinct from cost-containment objectives; and (d) the accuracy of the model's denials as measured against physician reviewer reversals on appeal. Audit results must be submitted to CMS prior to deployment and made publicly available in a standardized format. This is not a novel regulatory concept — FDA's Software as a Medical Device framework and the FTC's guidance on algorithmic accountability provide administrative precedents that HHS can adapt. The NWHN acknowledges that the precise regulatory vehicle for this requirement will require legal analysis of existing statutory authority, and we urge HHS to commission that analysis as part of its AI policy development process.⏎⏎2. Federal Prohibition on AI-Generated Denials Without Documented Physician Review.⏎⏎HHS should recommend to Congress, and pursue through CMS rulemaking where existing authority permits, a prohibition on final prior authorization denials generated by automated systems without documented, individualized physician review. This does not mean that AI cannot assist in the initial review of prior authorization requests — AI-assisted triage of straightforward approvals is a different matter than AI-generated denial. The prohibition should apply specifically to adverse determinations: when a prior authorization request is denied, in whole or in part, that denial must be signed and documented by a licensed physician who has reviewed the patient-specific clinical information. The Senate Subcommittee's October 2023 report documented that at least one major insurer's physician reviewers spent an average of 1.2 minutes per case before approving AI-generated denials — a figure that does not represent physician review in any meaningful clinical sense. HHS should define, in regulatory guidance, a minimum standard for what constitutes documented physician review for purposes of this prohibition.⏎⏎3. Standardized, Low-Burden Appeals Process with Reversal-Rate Transparency Requirements.⏎⏎HHS should establish, through CMS rulemaking, a standardized prior authorization appeals process for Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care that: (a) limits the number of administrative steps required before a beneficiary can access an independent external review; (b) requires that denial letters include plain-language, patient-specific clinical reasoning rather than generic coverage language; (c) establishes a maximum response timeline for appeals that accounts for clinical urgency; and (d) requires quarterly public reporting of denial rates, appeal rates, and reversal rates by plan, service category, and beneficiary demographic subgroup. The reversal-rate transparency requirement is particularly important. When a high proportion of AI-generated denials are reversed on appeal, that reversal rate is evidence that the AI system is producing clinically inappropriate denials — and that evidence should be visible to regulators, beneficiaries, and researchers. Currently, that data exists within insurer administrative systems and is not systematically reported to federal or state regulators in a comparable format.⏎⏎4. Research Priority Directive Requiring Independent Study of AI Denial System Design and Outcomes Before Further Acceleration of Insurer AI Adoption.⏎⏎HHS should direct the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) to fund independent research on AI utilization management systems as an explicit priority within the Department's health AI research agenda. Specifically, HHS should fund: (a) analysis of the relationship between AI denial system training objectives and clinical appropriateness of denial outcomes across commercial, Medicare Advantage, and Medicaid managed care payers; (b) assessment of the demographic distribution of AI-generated denials and the correlation between denial rates and patient health outcomes; and (c) development of a publicly available benchmark dataset against which insurer AI denial systems can be independently evaluated. This research should precede, not follow, any HHS administrative action that would further expand the role of AI in coverage and utilization management decisions. The NWHN does not oppose AI in utilization management categorically. We oppose deploying AI in utilization management at scale before the federal government has independent evidence about what those systems are actually doing to patients.⏎⏎NWHN Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 6⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE RFI'S FRAMING⏎⏎The NWHN wants to say something about the RFI's framing that goes slightly beyond the specific recommendations above, because framing shapes what solutions get considered.⏎⏎The RFI describes its goal as "accelerating AI adoption" in clinical care. That phrase — "accelerating adoption" — carries an implicit assumption that the constraint on beneficial AI deployment is adoption speed, and that the policy lever is removing barriers. In some clinical contexts, that assumption is correct. The 11-day diagnostic turnaround improvement our data documents represents a case where faster adoption of a specific AI tool would produce clear patient benefit, and where reimbursement barriers and interoperability limitations are genuine obstacles worth addressing.⏎⏎But "accelerating adoption" is the wrong frame for AI in insurance utilization management, because the adoption constraint there is not regulatory friction. These systems are already deployed. The constraint is accountability. Insurers adopted AI denial tools precisely because the regulatory environment did not require transparency, independent audit, or meaningful physician review — and because the financial returns from automated denial at scale are substantial. The policy problem is not that insurer AI adoption is too slow. It is that insurer AI adoption outpaced the regulatory infrastructure that should have governed it, and patients are bearing the cost of that gap.⏎⏎HHS's RFI will receive many comments urging faster adoption, lighter regulatory touch, and expanded reimbursement pathways for AI tools. The NWHN is not among those commenters. We urge HHS to resist the framing that AI adoption speed is the primary policy variable, and to recognize that the question of what AI is being adopted, by whom, for what objective, with what accountability structure, is the more consequential set of questions.⏎⏎NWHN Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 7⏎⏎CONCLUSION AND NEXT STEPS⏎⏎The NWHN requests that HHS acknowledge in any subsequent rulemaking or policy guidance that emerges from this RFI that AI utilization management systems are within scope of the Department's patient protection responsibilities, and that reimbursement and coverage policy for clinical AI cannot be designed in isolation from the insurer AI context in which clinical recommendations will be evaluated.⏎⏎We request a meeting with ASTP/ONC staff and the Office of the Deputy Secretary to discuss the specific regulatory vehicle questions raised in Recommendation 1 above. The NWHN's policy team is available to provide additional data from our claims analysis and member needs assessment survey. We are also prepared to facilitate direct engagement between HHS staff and representatives from the 14 MS care centers that presented at our 2024 Clinical Research Roundtable, several of which have direct experience with AI-generated prior authorization denials affecting the same patients who benefited from AI-assisted diagnostic tools.⏎⏎One additional concern the NWHN did not fully address in the recommendations above, but which deserves at least a flag for further analysis: the interaction between AI denial systems and the No Surprises Act's independent dispute resolution process. When an AI denial triggers a dispute that enters IDR, the arbitrator is evaluating a denial whose clinical basis may not be legible even to the insurer's own physician reviewer. The NWHN is not aware of existing HHS guidance on how IDR arbitrators should treat AI-generated denial rationales, and we believe this gap warrants separate regulatory attention. We raise it here not because it is fully developed in our analysis but because it is the kind of downstream interaction that "accelerating AI adoption" without systemic guardrails tends to produce.⏎⏎APPENDIX A: NWHN Member Needs Assessment Survey Methodology and Claims Data Analysis Protocol (not attached; available upon request from drodriguez@nwhn.org)⏎⏎APPENDIX B: Summary of 2024 Clinical Research Roundtable Presentations, 14 MS Care Center Submissions (not attached; available upon request)⏎⏎APPENDIX C: Full Citation List and Supporting Literature Review (not attached; available upon request)⏎⏎NWHN Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 8⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Deborah Rodriguez⏎Policy Director⏎National Women's Health Network⏎1875 Connecticut Avenue NW, Suite 650⏎Washington, DC 20009⏎drodriguez@nwhn.org⏎(202) 628-7814⏎⏎Submission date: [date of filing]♔♔2026-02-19T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-19T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔10♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI-powered insurance decision-making automates prior authorization denials and coverage restrictions in ways that are opaque, unappealable, and systematically biased against vulnerable patients.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔concerned♔Montana♔policy director♔45♔A 2024 analysis of our member needs assessment survey, completed by more than 6,800 individuals living with MS across 47 states, found that 68% reported experiencing delays of three months or more in receiving a confirmed diagnosis, and 54% identified specialist access as their primary barrier to timely disease-modifying therapy initiation.
