SYNTH-0048♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Kimberly Hall♔Google Health♔♔♔♔♔Google Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎RE: Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Google Health, Office of Government Relations⏎Contact: Kimberly Hall, Director of Government Relations⏎Date: October 15, 2024⏎⏎kimberly.hall@google.com⏎1600 Amphitheatre Parkway, Mountain View, CA 94043⏎⏎---⏎⏎PRELIMINARY STATEMENT⏎⏎Google Health submits these comments in response to HHS's request for information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care settings (89 Fed. Reg., Health Sector AI Request for Information, 2024). Google Health operates at the intersection of large-scale data infrastructure and clinical application development, and the questions posed in this RFI bear directly on the operational and governance architecture that will determine whether AI tools actually reach patients in a durable, accountable way. These comments focus primarily on two areas where Google Health has both technical depth and genuine concern: the governance preconditions for responsible deployment, and the question of whether the RFI's own framing adequately accounts for the democratic legitimacy questions that clinical AI raises.⏎⏎Google Health acknowledges that HHS has a legitimate interest in removing unnecessary friction from the adoption pathway. That said, Google Health wants to be direct about something that the RFI's framing choices seem to elide: reducing uncertainty for innovators and vendors is not the same thing as building the accountability architecture that patients and clinicians actually need. The RFI's language around "accelerating adoption" and "reducing uncertainty" (Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, 89 Fed. Reg., 2024) positions speed as the organizing value, with governance considerations as secondary constraints to be rationalized rather than as structural prerequisites. Google Health respectfully disagrees with that ordering, and the remainder of these comments explain why.⏎⏎Google Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE GOVERNANCE FRAMING PROBLEM⏎⏎The phrase "accelerating AI adoption" appears repeatedly in the RFI as though the primary obstacle to better patient outcomes is the pace of technology deployment. Google Health has direct experience building and deploying AI tools at scale in clinical environments, and the more consistent finding from that work is that speed of deployment is rarely the binding constraint on patient benefit. What actually limits benefit is the absence of the institutional scaffolding that makes deployed tools auditable, correctable, and trustworthy over time. Coiera, Ash, and Berg documented this dynamic carefully in their 2016 analysis of unintended consequences in health information technology: once a tool embeds itself into clinical workflow, the practical costs of removal or modification escalate sharply, and institutions become structurally committed to systems regardless of whether subsequent performance data would have justified that commitment (Coiera, Ash, & Berg, 2016, Yearbook of Medical Informatics, 25(1), 163-169). That is the irreversibility problem, and it is not primarily a technical problem. It is a governance problem.⏎⏎Dafny and Lee's analysis of institutional lock-in dynamics in healthcare markets is instructive here, even though their focus was on hospital mergers rather than AI deployment (Dafny & Lee, 2016, New England Journal of Medicine, 374(19), 1804-1806). The structural mechanism is similar: once a vendor relationship or a clinical decision support dependency is established at the enterprise level, the switching costs become high enough that continued use persists even when alternatives would be preferable. Google Health raises this not to argue against AI adoption, but to argue that the governance architecture needs to be built before widespread deployment, because building it afterward is substantially harder. The RFI's framing, which positions governance requirements as potential barriers to acceleration, gets this causality backwards.⏎⏎The democratic legitimacy dimension of this argument is not merely rhetorical. Certain domains of human activity have historically been reserved for human judgment as a matter of democratic preference, not because machines cannot perform the relevant computations, but because the community has decided that accountability, explainability, and the possibility of appeal are values worth preserving even at some cost to efficiency. Dworkin's foundational analysis of rights and democratic legitimacy is relevant here: legitimate authority requires not just that decisions produce good outcomes in the aggregate, but that the decision-making process is one that the affected community can recognize as theirs (Dworkin, 1977, Taking Rights Seriously, Harvard University Press). Medicine has historically been one of those domains. Criminal justice has been another. The question of whether AI systems should be authorized to make or substantially determine clinical judgments is a question about democratic preference, and it deserves a democratic answer, not a determination made implicitly through reimbursement policy and regulatory classification.⏎⏎Google Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎---⏎⏎ON THE LIMITS OF TRANSPARENCY AS A SAFEGUARD⏎⏎The RFI gestures toward transparency and explainability requirements as mechanisms for ensuring accountability. Google Health supports transparency requirements as a floor, but wants to be precise about what they can and cannot accomplish. Selbst and Barocas have documented the limits of transparency requirements as democratic safeguards with some care: the intuitive appeal of explainable machines rests on an assumption that explanation produces genuine understanding, but for complex systems operating at clinical scale, the explanations available to end users are often post-hoc rationalizations of model behavior rather than actual accounts of how the system reached its output (Selbst & Barocas, 2018, Fordham Law Review, 87(3), 1085-1139). This matters for HHS's purposes because if the governance architecture for clinical AI is built primarily around disclosure and explanation requirements, it may produce the appearance of accountability without the substance.⏎⏎Rudin's argument in this space is sharper still. The structural impossibility of meaningfully auditing black-box systems in high-stakes decision contexts is not a problem that can be solved by requiring vendors to produce better explanations (Rudin, 2019, Nature Machine Intelligence, 1(5), 206-215). It requires a different design approach at the model architecture level, and it requires that interpretability be a procurement criterion rather than a post-deployment aspiration. Google Health has a direct interest in this question, and Google Health's position is that interpretable model design is both technically feasible and commercially viable for the majority of clinical decision support applications. The argument that interpretability requirements would chill innovation is, in Google Health's assessment, overstated.⏎⏎Pasquale's broader analysis of algorithmic accountability is also worth engaging here, even though his focus extends beyond the health sector. The core argument in The Black Box Society is that opacity in consequential decision systems is not a technical inevitability but a structural choice, and that the accountability deficit it creates is a democratic problem as much as a technical one (Pasquale, 2015, The Black Box Society, Harvard University Press). HHS has the authority to make interpretability a condition of reimbursement eligibility, and Google Health believes it should. Not because this is a costless requirement, but because the alternative is a deployment pathway that systematically forecloses the kind of human oversight that democratic accountability in medicine requires.⏎⏎Google Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎---⏎⏎REGULATORY FRAGMENTATION AND THE CLASSIFICATION GAP⏎⏎The GAO documented in its 2022 report on AI in health care that regulatory classification gaps create substantial uncertainty about which AI tools require FDA clearance, which fall under ONC certification requirements, and which operate in an effectively unregulated space (GAO, 2022, GAO-22-104629). Google Health has navigated this classification uncertainty directly in deploying tools across different clinical settings, and the operational reality is that the same underlying model can be classified differently depending on how its clinical indication is framed in marketing materials. That is not a stable governance architecture.⏎⏎The National Academy for State Health Policy documented in 2023 that state-level approaches to regulating clinical AI are fragmented to a degree that creates genuine compliance complexity for tools deployed across state lines (NASHP, 2023, State Approaches to Regulating Artificial Intelligence in Health Care). As of that survey, fewer than a dozen states had enacted any specific regulatory framework for clinical AI, and the frameworks that existed were inconsistent in their scope and requirements. Google Health operates in all fifty states and encounters this fragmentation in practice. The practical effect is not that innovation is accelerated by the absence of uniform standards. The practical effect is that compliance resources are consumed by jurisdictional uncertainty rather than by substantive safety and performance work.⏎⏎HHS has the authority, through ONC's certification programs and through CMS reimbursement conditions, to establish a federal floor that would reduce this fragmentation without preempting states that want to go further. Google Health supports that approach. The specific mechanism matters, though. A certification pathway that is structured primarily around vendor self-attestation will not produce the accountability architecture that clinical AI requires. Google Health's recommendation is that any federal certification pathway for clinical AI include:⏎⏎1. Prospective performance benchmarking against specified clinical comparators, with results publicly available before deployment authorization.⏎⏎2. Mandatory post-market surveillance requirements with defined reporting intervals and performance thresholds that trigger review.⏎⏎3. Interpretability standards that are specified at the model architecture level, not satisfied by post-hoc explanation interfaces.⏎⏎4. Demonstrated reversibility as a precondition for deployment authorization, meaning that institutions must be able to document a viable pathway for removing or modifying a tool without clinical workflow disruption.⏎⏎The fourth item on that list is the one Google Health most wants HHS to take seriously. The reversibility requirement is not about making tools easy to discard; it is about ensuring that the structural irreversibility dynamic documented by Coiera and colleagues does not foreclose future choice for institutions or for the patients they serve.⏎⏎Google Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 5⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE RACIAL BIAS PROBLEM AND WHAT IT MEANS FOR GOVERNANCE DESIGN⏎⏎Obermeyer and colleagues' 2019 analysis of racial bias in a widely deployed population health management algorithm is by now well known in the policy community, but its implications for governance design are worth stating explicitly here (Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, & Mullainathan, 2019, Science, 366(6464), 447-453). The algorithm in question was built by a reputable vendor, deployed by sophisticated health systems, and used at scale for years before the bias was documented. The bias was not detectable from the vendor's disclosed performance metrics because those metrics did not stratify by race. The lesson is not that the vendor was uniquely negligent. The lesson is that the governance architecture for clinical AI cannot rely on vendor disclosure alone, and that performance metrics must be specified externally and must include stratification requirements as a condition of deployment authorization.⏎⏎Google Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 6⏎⏎This is directly relevant to HHS's questions about what regulatory actions would accelerate beneficial adoption. Google Health's answer is that the actions most likely to produce durable benefit are not those that reduce the regulatory burden on vendors but those that establish the external performance monitoring infrastructure that vendors cannot credibly provide for themselves. Topol's optimistic account of human-AI convergence in medicine is worth citing here, but in a specific way: Topol's analysis presupposes the existence of an oversight infrastructure that does not yet exist at the federal level (Topol, 2019, Nature Medicine, 25(1), 44-56). The clinical performance gains he documents are real, but they were achieved in controlled research settings with robust monitoring. The question of whether those gains replicate at deployment scale, without that monitoring infrastructure, is genuinely open.⏎⏎---⏎⏎REIMBURSEMENT POLICY AND THE INCENTIVE ARCHITECTURE⏎⏎Google Health wants to address the reimbursement question directly, because the RFI treats it primarily as a barrier-reduction problem and Google Health thinks that framing misses something important. The question is not only whether CMS reimbursement pathways cover AI-assisted clinical services; it is what behaviors those pathways incentivize. A reimbursement structure that rewards volume of AI-assisted encounters without conditioning payment on performance monitoring creates incentives for deployment that may not align with patient benefit.⏎⏎Google Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 7⏎⏎CMS has used coverage with evidence development as a mechanism for conditioning reimbursement on ongoing data collection in other technology contexts, and that model is directly applicable here. Google Health recommends that HHS consider a clinical AI reimbursement framework that ties continued coverage to participation in a federal post-market surveillance registry, with data contributed on a standardized basis and available for independent analysis. This is not a novel idea; the structure is analogous to what CMS has done for certain medical devices and procedures. The distinction is that for clinical AI, the performance characteristics can change over time as model drift occurs, which means that the evidence development requirement needs to be continuous rather than episodic.⏎⏎The 14-month average delay between AI tool procurement and billable clinical deployment that has been documented in multi-state provider surveys is a real problem, and Google Health does not dismiss it. But the cause of that delay is not primarily regulatory overhead. It is the absence of clear, federally-specified performance standards that would allow institutions to make deployment decisions with confidence. The delay is a symptom of governance ambiguity, not of governance excess. Building a faster pathway without resolving the underlying ambiguity would accelerate deployment without improving the quality of deployment decisions.⏎⏎---⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE RFI'S FRAMING OF DEMOCRATIC OVERSIGHT⏎⏎Google Health wants to close by returning to the framing critique raised at the outset, because it is the comment that Google Health most wants HHS to take away from this submission. The RFI is framed as a question about how to accelerate adoption, with the implicit assumption that faster adoption is better adoption. Google Health's experience building and deploying clinical AI tools at scale does not support that assumption. The tools that have produced durable clinical benefit are the ones deployed into environments with strong governance infrastructure, clear performance accountability, and genuine clinical ownership of the deployment decision. The tools that have produced the most significant problems are the ones deployed quickly into environments where the accountability architecture was built, if at all, after the fact.⏎⏎Google Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 8⏎⏎HHS has an opportunity with this RFI to reframe the federal role in clinical AI governance. Rather than asking how to reduce uncertainty for innovators, the Department might ask how to build the accountability infrastructure that would make clinical AI trustworthy enough to justify broad adoption. Those are related questions but they are not the same question, and the answer to one is not necessarily the answer to the other. Google Health's specific request is that HHS reframe the purpose of any resulting policy framework from acceleration to governance-first, and that demonstrated reversibility and auditable transparency be treated as preconditions for any deployment authorization pathway, not as aspirational goals to be achieved post-deployment.⏎⏎The distinction matters because, as the NASHP survey documented, the states that have moved furthest on clinical AI governance have generally done so by specifying preconditions rather than post-hoc accountability mechanisms (NASHP, 2023). The federal framework should learn from that pattern rather than defaulting to a disclosure-and-monitor approach that the academic literature consistently finds insufficient for high-stakes decision systems.⏎⏎Google Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 9⏎⏎There is one additional question that Google Health has not seen addressed directly in any of the comment solicitations related to clinical AI governance, and it is worth raising here even if it falls slightly outside the RFI's stated scope. Several of our policy staff have heard questions from provider organizations about whether AI-assisted clinical decision support reimbursed through federal programs would be covered for beneficiaries enrolled in TRICARE. The TRICARE coverage determination process operates under a separate statutory and regulatory framework from Medicare and Medicaid, and it is genuinely unclear to many providers whether clinical AI tools that receive CMS coverage determinations would automatically apply to TRICARE beneficiaries, or whether the Defense Health Agency would need to make independent coverage determinations. This is not a question Google Health can answer from its current regulatory analysis, and it is not clearly addressed in the RFI or in any of the associated guidance documents Google Health has reviewed. HHS and DoD have overlapping jurisdictions in this space that are not well mapped, and providers serving military families are likely to encounter this ambiguity in practice as clinical AI tools move toward broader deployment. Google Health raises this not because it has a specific policy recommendation on TRICARE coverage determinations, but because the gap in federal guidance is real and the provider community will need clarity before the 14-month procurement-to-deployment delay documented in multi-state surveys can realistically be reduced for institutions that serve mixed Medicare and TRICARE populations.⏎⏎Google Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 10⏎⏎---⏎⏎SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Google Health's comments have ranged across several interconnected questions, and it may be useful to collect the specific policy asks in one place for HHS's review.⏎⏎On governance architecture: Google Health recommends that HHS reframe the purpose of the clinical AI policy framework from acceleration to governance-first, with demonstrated reversibility and auditable transparency as preconditions for deployment authorization rather than aspirational post-deployment goals.⏎⏎On certification standards: Google Health recommends that any ONC certification pathway for clinical AI require prospective performance benchmarking with publicly available results, mandatory post-market surveillance with defined reporting intervals, and interpretability standards specified at the model architecture level.⏎⏎On reimbursement design: Google Health recommends that CMS consider a coverage-with-evidence-development structure for clinical AI reimbursement that conditions continued coverage on participation in a federal post-market surveillance registry, with standardized data contribution requirements.⏎⏎On racial and demographic stratification: Google Health recommends that performance metric specifications for clinical AI certification include mandatory stratification by race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic indicators, as a condition of deployment authorization rather than a voluntary reporting element.⏎⏎On regulatory classification: Google Health recommends that HHS and FDA coordinate to establish a clear, publicly accessible classification framework that specifies which clinical AI functions require FDA clearance, which require ONC certification, and which require both.⏎⏎Google Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 11⏎⏎On TRICARE and DoD coordination: Google Health recommends that HHS initiate a formal coordination process with the Defense Health Agency to clarify whether CMS clinical AI coverage determinations apply automatically to TRICARE beneficiaries or require independent DHA action, and to publish guidance that providers can use to make deployment decisions for mixed-population patient panels.⏎⏎The last recommendation is the most operationally specific, and it may seem out of place in a comment focused primarily on governance theory. Google Health includes it because the abstract governance architecture questions and the concrete coverage determination questions are connected in practice. Providers making deployment decisions need clarity at both levels, and the absence of clear TRICARE guidance will be a real operational obstacle for health systems serving military beneficiaries in states like Iowa, Texas, Virginia, and the other states with large active-duty and veteran populations. The Defense Health Agency's clinical AI coverage policies as of the date of this submission are not publicly documented in a way that allows providers to make clear deployment decisions, and that gap will compound the regulatory fragmentation that the NASHP survey documented at the state level.⏎⏎Google Health thanks HHS and ASTP/ONC for the opportunity to comment and looks forward to continued engagement as the Department develops its clinical AI policy framework.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Kimberly Hall⏎Director of Government Relations⏎Google Health⏎⏎kimberly.hall@google.com⏎1600 Amphitheatre Parkway | Mountain View, CA 94043⏎⏎Google Health Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 12♔♔2026-01-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-31T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔10♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Once AI systems are embedded in healthcare infrastructure, they become practically irreversible and resistant to democratic oversight, creating a permanent transfer of power from clinicians, patients, and regulators to technology vendors.♔organization♔high♔concerned♔Iowa♔director of government relations♔57♔A 2024 survey of Michigan Healthcare Freedom's 214 member organizations — spanning independent physician practices, rural critical access hospitals, and Federally Qualified Health Centers — found that 68% had explored at least one AI-assisted clinical decision support tool within the prior 24 months, yet only 23% had successfully integrated such tools into active patient care workflows. SYNTH-0049♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Barbara Smith♔American Society of Nephrology♔♔♔♔♔American Society of Nephrology⏎1510 H Street NW, Suite 800⏎Washington, DC 20005⏎policy@asn-online.org⏎⏎June 17, 2025⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Attention: AI in Clinical Care Request for Information⏎200 Independence Avenue SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎The American Society of Nephrology (ASN) submits these comments in response to HHS's request for information on regulatory, reimbursement, and research and development actions the Department might take to accelerate artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. ASN represents more than 21,000 kidney health professionals, and our policy work over the past several years has brought us into direct, granular contact with what AI tools actually do inside the clinical encounter — not in controlled pilot environments, but in the dialysis units, transplant clinics, and chronic kidney disease management practices where our members spend their working lives. We have watched with genuine interest as these tools have improved in their technical performance. We have also watched, with considerably more unease, as the federal policy conversation has drifted toward a framing that we believe mischaracterizes the clinical encounter at a fundamental level — and we want to be direct about that concern here, because we think it has consequences that are not adequately reflected in the questions HHS has posed.⏎⏎ASN Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 2⏎⏎The RFI opens by describing AI as a mechanism to improve "productivity" in clinical care, and we want to name that word as a problem before we get into anything else. Productivity is a manufacturing concept. It describes the rate at which inputs are converted into outputs, and it is a perfectly appropriate metric for evaluating supply chain optimization, billing throughput, or scheduling efficiency. But when applied to the clinical encounter itself — to the fifteen minutes a nephrologist spends with a patient who is frightened about starting dialysis — it imports a transactional logic that is not merely inadequate to describe what is happening in that room, but actively hostile to it. The clinical encounter is not a production process. Diagnosis and healing depend on a clinician's capacity to tolerate ambiguity, to attend to what is not being said, to hold a patient's fear without resolving it prematurely into a data field. The research literature on this is not new or contested. Kelley and colleagues, in a 2014 systematic review and meta-analysis published in PLOS ONE, found that the quality of the patient-clinician relationship independently predicted healthcare outcomes across randomized controlled trials — not as a confounding variable, but as a causal mechanism. Hojat and colleagues, writing in Academic Medicine in 2011, demonstrated that physician empathy scores predicted glycemic control in diabetic patients with statistical significance that should give any serious health policymaker pause. These findings are not soft or qualitative. They are quantified, replicated, and in some cases more predictive of clinical outcomes than the technical accuracy of the diagnostic tool being used. When HHS uses the word "productivity" to frame AI adoption, it is not merely being imprecise. It is signaling a model of care in which these relational effects are not counted, and that omission will shape every downstream policy choice the Department makes.⏎⏎ASN Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 3⏎⏎To make this concrete: one of ASN's member nephrologists, practicing at an academic medical center in Durham, North Carolina, described an encounter from his transplant clinic in the fall of 2024. His patient was a 71-year-old man with early-stage cognitive decline, accompanied by his adult daughter, who had driven four hours to be at the appointment. The AI-assisted clinical decision support tool the clinic was piloting flagged the patient's creatinine trajectory and generated a recommendation that was technically accurate — the algorithm correctly identified that the patient's graft function had declined at a rate inconsistent with his medication adherence profile. What the algorithm could not see was that the patient was nodding along to questions he did not fully understand, that his daughter was gripping her own hands in her lap and had not yet said what she had come to say, which was that she no longer believed her father could manage his immunosuppression regimen independently. The nephrologist saw all of this. He spent the next twenty minutes not talking about the creatinine, but creating the conditions in which the daughter could say what she needed to say. That conversation changed the clinical plan entirely — not because the algorithm was wrong about the creatinine, but because the algorithm had no access to the information that actually mattered most at that moment. This is not an edge case. This is medicine. The question HHS needs to answer before accelerating AI intermediation in these encounters is not whether the algorithm's technical outputs are accurate, but whether the deployment context preserves the conditions under which a clinician can still see the daughter's hands.⏎⏎ASN Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 4⏎⏎A second vignette, because the first one involves a relatively clear failure mode and we want to illustrate something subtler. Another ASN member, a general nephrologist in a rural practice in eastern North Carolina, described a patient she had been managing for six years for hypertensive nephropathy. The patient, a 58-year-old man, presented for a routine visit with labs that were unremarkable — the AI dashboard showed green across every indicator. But she noticed, as she walked into the room, that he was sitting differently than he usually sat. Not dramatically. Just slightly forward, with his arms crossed in a way that was not his posture. She asked him, not about his medications and not about his blood pressure, but about how things were at home. What followed was a disclosure that he had stopped taking one of his antihypertensives three weeks earlier because he could not afford the copay and had been too embarrassed to say so. His labs had not yet reflected this. The AI system had not flagged anything. The nephrologist's six years of accumulated knowledge about how this specific patient occupied space in a chair — knowledge that is not codeable, not transmissible to an algorithm, not reproducible by pattern-matching on population-level data — was the diagnostic instrument. Verghese, Shah, and Harrington wrote in JAMA in 2018 that "the patient's body is the text" and that what computers need, in clinical settings, is a physician who can read that text. We agree with that framing, and we would add that the reading of that text is not a supplement to AI-assisted care. It is the thing that AI-assisted care is at risk of displacing.⏎⏎ASN Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 5⏎⏎The human factors literature on automation bias is relevant here and is, in our view, substantially underweighted in HHS's framing. Parasuraman and Manzey, writing in Human Factors in 2010, documented that human operators working alongside automated systems demonstrate measurable decreases in independent vigilance over time — not because they become lazy, but because the cognitive architecture of human attention is genuinely altered by sustained interaction with reliable automated outputs. Skitka, Mosier, and Burdick, in a 1999 study in the International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, showed that automation bias leads operators to miss errors that they would have caught without the automated system present. In clinical medicine, the analog is what we might call diagnostic skill degradation: a nephrologist who has spent five years deferring to an AI-assisted interpretation of a renal ultrasound will, over time, lose the perceptual granularity that made her an independent reader of that image. Choudhry, Fletcher, and Soumerai, in a 2005 systematic review in the Annals of Internal Medicine, found that clinical experience and independent judgment accumulate in ways that are specific, contextual, and not easily recovered once the conditions that generate them are removed. The pipeline of clinical expertise is not robust to the removal of its training conditions. If HHS accelerates AI deployment without requiring that clinical training pathways preserve independent skill development, the Department will be engineering a generation of clinicians who are competent machine overseers and increasingly dependent on the machines they oversee. This is not a hypothetical risk. It is a predictable consequence of the deployment trajectory HHS is currently encouraging, and it deserves a direct policy response.⏎⏎ASN Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 6⏎⏎We also want to address the concept of therapeutic alliance, because we think it is being systematically undervalued in the HHS framework and in much of the clinical AI literature that the Department appears to be drawing on. Therapeutic alliance, as the term is used in the clinical psychology literature and increasingly in medicine more broadly, refers to the collaborative, affective bond between clinician and patient that mediates treatment engagement, self-disclosure, and adherence. It is not reducible to patient satisfaction scores. It is a functional relationship property that has been shown to predict outcomes independently of treatment modality. Zulman and colleagues, in a 2020 JAMA paper on physician presence and connection, identified specific, learnable practices — attending to the patient's emotional state, making explicit space for uncertainty, acknowledging the patient as a person with a life outside the clinic — that generate therapeutic alliance in ways that are time-efficient but deeply dependent on the clinician's undivided attentional presence. The AI deployment models currently being piloted in nephrology and other specialties frequently interrupt that attentional presence. Clinicians report spending a meaningful portion of the encounter managing the AI interface — reviewing flags, reconciling alerts, documenting in real time to satisfy algorithmic prompts — in ways that fragment the very attentional quality that therapeutic alliance requires. Torous and Roberts, writing in JAMA Psychiatry in 2017, raised analogous concerns about digital health tools in mental health settings, noting that transparency about what these tools displace, not just what they add, is a basic requirement of responsible deployment. HHS has not asked that question systematically, and we think it should.⏎⏎ASN Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 7⏎⏎We want to be clear that ASN is not categorically opposed to AI in nephrology. Topol, writing in Nature Medicine in 2019, made a case for AI augmentation in medicine that we find largely persuasive — the argument that AI can absorb the computational burden of pattern recognition and thereby free clinicians to do what only clinicians can do. We agree with that aspiration. What we do not agree with is the assumption, embedded in HHS's current framing, that the aspiration is self-executing — that deploying AI tools will automatically free clinicians to be more present, more relational, more diagnostically attentive. The evidence from our members' practices does not support that assumption. What we see, consistently, is that AI deployment in clinical settings tends to reorganize clinical attention around the interface, not away from it. Hartzband and Groopman, in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020, described how electronic health record burdens have already substantially eroded the conditions for meaningful clinical presence, and they were writing before the current wave of AI-assisted tools layered additional interface demands on top of existing documentation requirements. The ONC's 2024 Federal Health IT Strategic Plan acknowledges the need to reduce clinician burden, but the mechanisms proposed are largely technical — interoperability improvements, data standardization — and do not address the attentional and relational costs of AI intermediation in the encounter itself. That gap in the policy framework is, in our view, the most consequential thing HHS could address in the near term, and it is not addressed by accelerating deployment.⏎⏎ASN Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 8⏎⏎There is also a research and development question embedded in all of this that we want to flag, even though it sits slightly outside the scope of the specific RFI questions. The validation frameworks currently used to evaluate clinical AI tools measure technical performance — sensitivity, specificity, area under the curve, calibration against reference standards. These are appropriate and necessary metrics. They are not sufficient. A tool that achieves 94% sensitivity on a held-out test set and simultaneously fragments the therapeutic alliance in 40% of the encounters in which it is deployed may produce net negative clinical outcomes, and the current regulatory and research infrastructure has no mechanism for detecting that. Bickmore and Picard, writing in ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction in 2005, observed that human-computer relationships have structural properties that are distinct from human-human relationships and that the substitution of one for the other carries costs that are not visible in performance metrics. That observation was made twenty years ago in a largely theoretical context. It is now a practical problem that HHS's deployment acceleration is making more urgent. We are asking the Department to fund research that measures relational outcomes — not patient satisfaction, which is a proxy with well-documented limitations, but therapeutic alliance, clinician attentional presence, and the long-term trajectory of independent clinical judgment in AI-assisted practice environments. Without that evidence base, HHS is accelerating a deployment whose full effects it cannot measure.⏎⏎ASN Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 9⏎⏎ASN's direct policy ask to HHS is this: before any AI system intended for use in direct clinical care is approved for deployment, reimbursed under federal programs, or recommended in federal guidance, the Department must require demonstrated preservation of the therapeutic relationship as a precondition — not as a post-deployment evaluation criterion, not as a voluntary reporting element, but as a prospective requirement with defined measurement standards and a threshold below which deployment is not authorized. We recognize this is a harder regulatory problem than measuring algorithm accuracy. We recognize there is not yet consensus on the right measurement instruments, though the literature on therapeutic alliance assessment offers several candidates that could be adapted for this purpose. We recognize that requiring this will slow the deployment timeline that HHS appears to have in mind. We think that is the right outcome. The encounters described earlier in these comments — the transplant patient in Durham whose daughter had not yet spoken, the hypertensive patient in eastern North Carolina who was sitting slightly forward in his chair — are not outliers that an efficient regulatory framework can afford to treat as acceptable losses. They are the thing medicine is for. The Department's accelerationist posture assumes that getting AI tools into clinical settings faster is straightforwardly good, and that assumption has not been subjected to the kind of scrutiny that a policy with this scope and this set of consequences deserves. We would ask HHS to sit with that before the next deployment guidance is issued — and specifically, to consider whether the reimbursement incentives currently being contemplated for AI-assisted encounters have been modeled for their effects on encounter duration, clinician attentional allocation, and the⏎⏎ASN Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 10⏎⏎conditions under which a clinician can notice that a patient is holding his arms differently than he did six months ago.⏎⏎Sincerely,⏎⏎Barbara Smith⏎Policy Director⏎American Society of Nephrology⏎1510 H Street NW, Suite 800⏎Washington, DC 20005⏎policy@asn-online.org♔♔2026-02-16T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-16T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔8♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔frustrated♔North Carolina♔policy director♔50♔A 2024 survey of 1,847 dental practices affiliated with the Dental Standards Institute found that 68% had evaluated at least one AI-assisted diagnostic tool within the preceding 18 months, yet only 23% had fully integrated such tools into routine clinical workflows—citing inconsistent reimbursement pathways and the absence of recognized performance benchmarks as the primary barriers. SYNTH-0052♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Donna Johnson♔Nuvation Bio♔♔♔♔♔Nuvation Bio Practice Management Division | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 1⏎⏎⏎Submitted to: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Donna Johnson, Practice Manager, Nuvation Bio⏎Date: March 14, 2025⏎⏎⏎PRELIMINARY STATEMENT⏎⏎Nuvation Bio's practice management function oversees administrative and clinical operations across a multi-site care delivery structure and works in direct coordination with a broader network of partner practices. This comment responds specifically to the RFI's questions about regulatory and reimbursement actions HHS can take to accelerate AI adoption in clinical settings. We are not writing to oppose AI integration in health care. We are writing because the framing of this RFI — with its emphasis on acceleration — treats speed as the operative problem when, from where we sit operationally, the actual problem is that the current procurement and deployment architecture for clinical AI systematically bypasses the people who do the work, and HHS is being asked to subsidize that architecture with federal endorsement and reimbursement dollars before any accountability structures are in place.⏎⏎That concern is not abstract. Our participation in Onboard AI's network of 47 partner clinical practices generated operational data showing that 68% of care coordinators in that network spend more than six hours per week on documentation and prior authorization workflows. AI-assisted tools have demonstrated capacity to reduce that burden by 40 to 55 percent in controlled pilots. That is a real number and a real opportunity. But a Q3 2024 survey of 312 practice managers across primary care, specialty, and urgent care settings found that 79% of respondents cited reimbursement uncertainty as a barrier to deployment, and 74% cited liability ambiguity. Neither of those barriers is a workforce protection problem. They are administrative and financial framing problems. And the proposed remedy — federal action to clear reimbursement and regulatory pathways — would remove those barriers while leaving entirely intact the structural conditions under which AI tools are being used to justify reduced staffing ratios and intensified productivity surveillance of frontline clinical and administrative staff.⏎⏎⏎SECTION I: THE DEPLOYMENT PROBLEM HHS IS NOT ADDRESSING⏎⏎A structured review of implementation timelines across 18 practices that attempted AI integration during 2023 and 2024 found that regulatory and billing framework gaps accounted for an average 8.3-month delay between tool validation and clinical deployment. HHS has cited figures like this as evidence that deployment barriers need to be cleared. We read the same figure differently. An 8.3-month delay is, in many cases, a period during which a practice has time to ask whether the tool it is about to deploy actually serves the people who will use it. The delay is not always a problem. Sometimes it is the only window available for the kind of institutional deliberation that the RFI's accelerationist framing would compress or eliminate.⏎⏎The more important question is what is happening during deployment, not before it. The Government Accountability Office's 2023 review of AI in health care (GAO-23-105491) found that clinical AI tools are frequently implemented with inadequate attention to real-world workflow integration, and that the gap between controlled pilot performance and operational performance is often substantial. That finding maps directly onto what our network has observed. When AI tools are deployed primarily because administrators and vendors have agreed on a procurement arrangement, without structured input from the nurses, care coordinators, and prior authorization reviewers who will use them daily, the tools tend to be calibrated around metrics that matter to the people who bought them — throughput, documentation speed, billing capture rates — rather than metrics that matter to the people who operate them.⏎⏎Nuvation Bio Practice Management Division | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 2⏎⏎⏎Freedman et al. (2023), writing in Health Affairs, documented this dynamic directly in a study of algorithmic management implementations across hospital systems. Their findings showed that AI tools introduced into clinical workflows without frontline input were more likely to be used to monitor worker productivity and less likely to produce the care quality improvements vendors had projected (Freedman, S., et al., "Algorithmic Management and Worker Autonomy in Healthcare Settings," Health Affairs, 42(7), 912–921). That is a structural finding, not a vendor-specific one. The incentive misalignment runs through the entire procurement architecture. Vendors design tools that optimize what administrators can measure. Administrators purchase tools that administrators can measure. Frontline workers inherit tools that were never designed around their actual workflow constraints or clinical judgment requirements.⏎⏎The National Nurses United research report from 2023, "Understaffed and Overworked: AI, Surveillance, and the Erosion of Safe Staffing Standards in U.S. Hospitals," documented cases where AI productivity monitoring tools were deployed as a basis for reducing nurse-to-patient ratios, on the argument that AI-assisted documentation and decision support reduced the per-patient cognitive load sufficiently to justify leaner staffing. That argument is being made in procurement conversations right now, in health systems across the country, without any evidentiary standard and without any mechanism for frontline workers to contest it formally before deployment occurs.⏎⏎⏎SECTION II: BURNOUT IS NOT BEING SOLVED — IT IS BEING REPACKAGED⏎⏎The RFI references burnout reduction as one of the primary workforce benefits HHS expects AI adoption to deliver. Shanafelt et al. (2022) documented physician burnout rates and work-life integration satisfaction across a longitudinal study spanning 2011 to 2020, finding that burnout had worsened significantly over that period and that electronic health record burden was among the most consistently cited contributing factors (Shanafelt, T.D., et al., "Changes in Burnout and Satisfaction With Work-Life Integration in Physicians and the General US Working Population Between 2011 and 2020," Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 97(3), 491–506). Bates et al. (2021) argued in npj Digital Medicine that AI holds real potential to reduce documentation burden specifically, and that this reduction could translate into meaningful burnout relief if tools are designed with that goal as primary rather than incidental (Bates, D.W., et al., "The Potential of Artificial Intelligence to Reduce Burnout While Maintaining Quality of Care," npj Digital Medicine, 4(1), 135).⏎⏎We do not dispute that potential. What we dispute is whether the current deployment pattern is realizing it. Kroth et al. (2019) found that EHR design and use factors were directly associated with clinician stress and burnout, and that the relationship was mediated by how much control clinicians had over their own workflows within the system (Kroth, P.J., et al., "Association of Electronic Health Record Design and Use Factors With Clinician Stress and Burnout," JAMA Network Open, 2(8), e199609). Sinsky et al. (2020) extended that line of analysis, finding that efficiency metrics imposed through EHR systems often increased cognitive burden rather than reducing it, because the metrics required documentation behaviors that did not align with how clinicians actually thought through patient care (Sinsky, C.A., et al., "Metrics for Measuring the Impact of Electronic Health Records on Physician Burnout and Efficiency," Journal of General Internal Medicine, 35(5), 1440–1447).⏎⏎The parallel to current AI deployment is direct. When AI tools are introduced to generate productivity metrics that administrators then use to set caseload expectations, the tools do not reduce burnout. They restructure it. The documentation burden may decrease in raw minutes, but the surveillance burden increases. The cognitive autonomy that clinicians rely on to do their work well is replaced by algorithmic prompts and performance flags. Topol (2023) made this point in The Lancet, arguing that physician presence — meaning the kind of contextual, relational clinical judgment that cannot be automated — is not a complement to AI but is actively threatened by deployment models that treat AI outputs as authoritative rather than advisory (Topol, E.J., "The Imperative for Physician Presence in the Age of AI," The Lancet, 401(10375), 408–410). We find that framing accurate and the concern it articulates operationally real.⏎⏎Nuvation Bio Practice Management Division | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 3⏎⏎⏎SECTION III: PROCUREMENT EXCLUSION IS A PATIENT SAFETY ISSUE⏎⏎The American Medical Association's 2023 policy report on augmented intelligence in health care identified frontline clinician involvement in AI procurement as a core governance requirement, noting that tools deployed without clinical input are more likely to generate alert fatigue, workflow disruption, and errors of omission — cases where AI-assisted documentation misses clinically relevant information because the tool was not designed around the actual complexity of the patient interaction (AMA, "Augmented Intelligence in Health Care: Policy Principles and Workforce Implications," 2023). The SEIU Healthcare Policy Brief from 2024, "Automated and Abandoned: How Health System AI Procurement Is Bypassing Frontline Workers," documented that in a majority of surveyed health system AI procurements, frontline workers were not consulted during vendor selection or tool configuration (SEIU, 2024).⏎⏎What this means in practice: tools are being selected by people who will not use them, calibrated around metrics that reflect administrative rather than clinical priorities, and then deployed onto the workflows of nurses, care coordinators, and physicians who had no input into the decision. The workers then bear the adjustment costs — the learning curve, the workflow disruption, the cognitive load of operating a system that does not quite fit how they work — while administrators capture the efficiency metrics and vendors capture the contract revenue.⏎⏎Obermeyer et al. (2019) demonstrated in a now-widely-cited Science paper that a commercial algorithm used to allocate health care resources systematically underestimated the severity of illness in Black patients, because it was trained on health care spending data rather than health outcomes data (Obermeyer, Z., et al., "Dissecting Racial Bias in an Algorithm Used to Manage the Health of Populations," Science, 366(6464), 447–453). That finding is about algorithmic bias, and it has received appropriate attention. But the procurement failure it exposes is broader than bias. It is a failure of the institutional process that allowed a tool with those properties to reach clinical deployment without the input of the clinicians who would have recognized, from direct patient care experience, that spending data and severity data are not the same thing. Frontline workers carry knowledge that vendors and administrators do not have. When they are excluded from procurement, that knowledge is excluded too.⏎⏎⏎SECTION IV: WHAT THE DATA FROM OUR NETWORK SHOWS⏎⏎To be specific about what operational exclusion looks like: in our review of 18 practices that attempted AI integration during the 2023–2024 period, the average time from tool validation to clinical deployment was delayed 8.3 months by regulatory and billing framework gaps. What that figure does not capture is the number of practices where deployment proceeded on the administrative side — meaning the tool was technically live and generating data for administrators — while frontline workers were still in the process of being trained on it, or had not been trained at all. In at least four of those 18 practices, care coordinators reported that they were informed of AI tool deployment through a staff-wide email, with no opportunity for structured feedback on the tool's design or workflow fit before go-live.⏎⏎This is not an unusual pattern. It is the norm. And it has direct operational consequences that show up in ways that are harder to measure than deployment timelines:⏎⏎1. Alert fatigue accumulation, where AI-generated flags are ignored because frontline workers have not been involved in calibrating the sensitivity thresholds and do not trust the outputs.⏎⏎2. Documentation workarounds, where clinicians develop informal practices to route around AI-assisted documentation tools they find inaccurate or disruptive, generating shadow workflows that are invisible to the administrators relying on AI-generated efficiency metrics.⏎⏎3. Increased cognitive load from dual-track documentation, where workers are simultaneously managing AI-assisted inputs and maintaining their own clinical notes because they do not trust the AI record to be complete.⏎⏎4. Attrition among experienced staff who find the surveillance and productivity monitoring dimensions of AI deployment incompatible with their professional self-understanding, particularly among workers with more than ten years of clinical experience who have the most contextual knowledge to lose.⏎⏎Nuvation Bio Practice Management Division | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 4⏎⏎⏎None of these consequences appear in the efficiency metrics that administrators use to evaluate AI deployment success. They are visible only to the people doing the work, and they accumulate silently until they surface as patient care errors, staff turnover spikes, or both. The 2023 GAO report noted that many health systems lack the internal evaluation infrastructure to detect these second-order effects, which means the performance data being used to justify AI adoption is systematically incomplete (GAO-23-105491).⏎⏎⏎SECTION V: WHAT HHS SHOULD REQUIRE⏎⏎This comment does not argue that HHS should slow AI adoption in clinical settings across the board. There are genuine efficiency gains available, and there are specific workflow categories — prior authorization documentation, medical coding, scheduling coordination — where AI assistance could reduce burden without threatening clinical judgment if deployed well. The question is what "deployed well" requires as a precondition, and our position is that the current regulatory and reimbursement framework answers that question inadequately.⏎⏎HHS should condition any federal reimbursement endorsement or regulatory safe harbor for clinical AI tools on documented evidence of the following, at minimum:⏎⏎a. Frontline worker consultation conducted during tool selection, not after vendor contract execution. Consultation means structured engagement with the workers who will use the tool — not a post-hoc training session or a checkbox informational meeting. It means that care coordinators, nurses, prior authorization reviewers, and other directly affected staff had opportunity to evaluate the tool against their actual workflow requirements before procurement was finalized.⏎⏎b. A formal objection and response process, through which frontline workers can raise concerns about a deployed tool's design, performance, or workforce implications, and through which those concerns are documented and addressed by the deploying organization within a defined timeframe. The SEIU's 2024 policy brief proposed a model framework for this kind of process, and HHS should review it.⏎⏎c. Performance benchmarks that include worker wellbeing metrics, not only efficiency and throughput metrics. If a tool reduces documentation time by 30 minutes per shift but increases reported cognitive burden or alert fatigue, that is a relevant performance finding. It should be part of the evaluation record that receives federal reimbursement endorsement.⏎⏎d. Prohibition on using AI-generated productivity data as the primary basis for staffing ratio decisions, without independent clinical review and worker input. This is the most direct mechanism through which AI tools marketed as burnout solutions are being converted into staffing reduction justifications.⏎⏎e. Transparency requirements for vendors, specifying what training data the tool was built on, what performance benchmarks were used during validation, and what known limitations the tool has in the specific workflow categories for which it is being deployed. The Obermeyer et al. (2019) finding is a decade-old warning about what happens when this information is not available at the point of procurement.⏎⏎Nuvation Bio Practice Management Division | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 5⏎⏎⏎These requirements are not novel in concept. The AMA's 2023 policy report called for clinician involvement in AI governance as a foundational principle. The GAO's 2023 review identified evaluation framework gaps as a central implementation risk. What is missing is not the analysis. What is missing is a federal requirement that makes these governance structures a precondition for the reimbursement and regulatory endorsements HHS is now being asked to extend. Without that requirement, the acceleration this RFI proposes will accelerate the adoption of tools through a procurement architecture that is already demonstrating harm to the frontline workforce, and the federal endorsement will make that architecture harder to challenge, not easier.⏎⏎⏎SECTION VI: A NOTE ON THE FRAMING OF THIS RFI⏎⏎We want to say something directly about the framing of this request for information, even though it is slightly tangential to the specific policy recommendations above. The RFI describes the goal as "accelerating AI adoption in clinical care settings." That framing assumes the rate of adoption is the primary variable HHS should be trying to move. Our experience, and the data from our network, suggests the rate of adoption is not the problem. The distribution of who benefits from adoption and who bears the costs is the problem. Practices are adopting AI tools. The adoption is happening. What is not happening is any systematic accountability for whether the adoption is improving care quality or worker wellbeing, or whether it is primarily serving administrative cost-reduction goals that are being labeled as efficiency gains.⏎⏎Bates et al. (2021) were careful to note that AI's potential to reduce burnout is conditional — it depends on how tools are designed and deployed, not on whether AI is present in the workflow at all. Topol (2023) made the same point from a clinical quality direction, arguing that AI deployment models that displace rather than support physician judgment are likely to produce worse outcomes than no AI at all in certain high-complexity care contexts. Neither of those arguments is against AI. Both of them are against the assumption that more AI, deployed faster, is straightforwardly beneficial.⏎⏎The workforce data supports that caution. Shanafelt et al. (2022) found that physician burnout worsened across a decade during which health care organizations were also investing heavily in technology intended to improve efficiency. The EHR experience, documented by Kroth et al. (2019) and Sinsky et al. (2020), is the most direct precedent: a technology that promised substantial workflow improvement was deployed at scale, without adequate frontline input into design and implementation, and produced a burnout crisis that HHS is still working to address. The AI deployment trajectory currently underway has the same structural features. The RFI should acknowledge that history explicitly, because the practices and health systems responding to it deserve a federal framing that takes the EHR lesson seriously rather than repeating the conditions that produced it.⏎⏎Nuvation Bio Practice Management Division | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 6⏎⏎⏎CLOSING RECOMMENDATION⏎⏎HHS should require, as a precondition for any federal reimbursement endorsement or regulatory safe harbor extended to clinical AI tools, documented evidence that frontline workers directly affected by a given tool's deployment were consulted during procurement and had access to a formal process for raising and resolving concerns about the tool's design, performance, and workforce implications. That requirement should apply to tools deployed in any clinical or administrative care coordination workflow, including prior authorization, documentation, scheduling, clinical decision support, and patient communication functions. The requirement should be specific enough to preclude checkbox compliance — meaning HHS should define minimum standards for what a consultation process must include, how it must be documented, and how objections must be resolved, rather than leaving those questions to deploying organizations whose incentive structure has already demonstrated a pattern of exclusion.⏎⏎We recognize that this recommendation will be read by some as an obstacle to the acceleration this RFI is designed to promote. Our view is that a reimbursement and regulatory framework that accelerates adoption of tools through a broken procurement architecture is not actually solving the problem HHS has identified. It is subsidizing the problem. The 8.3-month average delay between tool validation and clinical deployment is not the metric that should be driving federal policy. The metric that should be driving federal policy is whether the tools being deployed are actually improving care quality and worker wellbeing, as measured by people with direct operational and clinical visibility into what is happening on the ground — not by the administrators and vendors whose financial interests are served by a faster deployment pipeline regardless of what the tools actually do once they are live.⏎⏎For questions regarding this submission, contact:⏎Donna Johnson⏎Practice Manager, Nuvation Bio⏎djohnson@nuvationbio-practiceops.org⏎⏎Nuvation Bio Practice Management Division | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 7♔♔2026-02-15T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-15T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔10♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare will be used by employers and insurers as a mechanism for workforce surveillance, productivity extraction, staffing cuts, and the devaluation of clinical expertise rather than genuine care improvement.♔organization♔high♔supportive♔Minnesota♔practice manager♔37♔A 2024 operational analysis conducted across Onboard AI's network of 47 partner clinical practices found that 68% of care coordinators spend more than six hours per week on documentation and prior authorization workflows that AI-assisted tools have demonstrated capacity to reduce by 40–55% in controlled pilots.
