SYNTH-0053♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Kenneth Scott♔National Partnership for Women and Families♔♔♔♔♔ADLM Comments | HHS AI RFI — Clinical Care Accelerat ion | Page 1⏎⏎---⏎⏎SUBMISSION TO: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎RE: Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎SUBMITTED BY: Kenneth Scott, Research Director, Association for Diagnostics & Laboratory Medicine (ADLM)⏎DATE: 2024⏎⏎---⏎⏎PRELIMINARY STATEMENT ON ORGANIZATIONAL STANDING⏎⏎The Association for Diagnostics & Laboratory Medicine (ADLM) represents more than 4,200 laboratory medicine professionals across the United States, including clinical laboratory directors, pathologists, clinical chemists, and medical laboratory scientists who occupy a specific and consequential position in the AI adoption pipeline: they are the practitioners responsible for validating, deploying, and interpreting AI-assisted diagnostic tools at the point where algorithmic output meets clinical decision-making. ADLM's policy working group conducted a cross-institutional analysis of 14 academic medical center laboratories in 2024, and the findings bear directly on the questions HHS has posed in this Request for Information. Sixty-eight percent of surveyed laboratory medicine professionals reported active evaluation or piloting of AI-assisted diagnostic tools within their institutions. Fewer than 20% could describe a clear regulatory pathway for clinical validation and deployment. The average lag between demonstrated clinical utility and payer coverage decisions was 22 months across participating sites. These are not projected figures — they reflect current operational reality for ADLM members who are, at this moment, making deployment decisions without the regulatory infrastructure to make them responsibly (Association for Diagnostics & Laboratory Medicine [ADLM], 2024).⏎⏎ADLM submits these comments to address two specific dimensions of the RFI: the evidentiary basis for treating algorithmic bias as a present, documented harm rather than a speculative future risk, and the structural design requirements for any HHS deployment framework that claims to accelerate AI adoption without widening existing health disparities. ADLM does not oppose acceleration. ADLM is concerned that the framing of this RFI — which emphasizes adoption barriers and regulatory friction — does not give sufficient weight to the documented harm that has already occurred when clinical AI systems were deployed without adequate equity safeguards. The sequence matters. Equity auditing and bias surveillance are not supplementary features to be added once adoption is underway; they are preconditions for responsible deployment.⏎⏎ADLM Comments | HHS AI RFI — Clinical Care Accelerat ion | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE DOCUMENTED RECORD OF ALGORITHMIC BIAS IN CLINICAL AI⏎⏎The peer-reviewed literature on algorithmic bias in clinical AI is now substantial enough that HHS cannot reasonably treat it as preliminary or contested. The pattern is consistent across tool types, clinical domains, and publication venues. Sjoding et al. (2020) documented that pulse oximeters — devices so familiar they are no longer perceived as algorithmic — systematically overestimated arterial oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin tones, resulting in clinically significant underdetection of hypoxemia (Sjoding, M.W., et al., 2020, New England Journal of Medicine, 383[25], 2477–2478). This is not a soft finding about outcome disparities that might reflect patient-level confounders; it is a direct measurement of device performance by skin tone, and it has implications for any AI system that ingests pulse oximetry data as a feature. Obermeyer et al. (2019) demonstrated that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to identify patients for high-risk care management systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients relative to white patients at equivalent levels of objective illness, because the algorithm used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need — a substitution that encoded decades of differential access into the prediction itself (Obermeyer, Z., et al., 2019, Science, 366[6464], 447–453). The algorithm was not designed to discriminate. It learned to, from data that recorded a discriminatory system.⏎⏎Dermatology AI offers a third instructive case. Adamson and Smith (2018) documented that machine learning models for skin lesion classification were trained disproportionately on images of lighter-skinned patients, with the consequence that performance on darker-skinned patients was substantially degraded — a gap that would not be visible in aggregate accuracy metrics reported for the full validation cohort (Adamson, A.S., & Smith, A., 2018, JAMA Dermatology, 154[11], 1247–1248). This is the core methodological problem: aggregate performance statistics conceal subgroup performance degradation, and if HHS does not require disaggregated reporting by race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status as a condition of deployment authorization, the Department will be unable to detect disparate harm even after it is occurring at scale. Gianfrancesco et al. (2018) formalized this concern in their analysis of potential biases in machine learning algorithms using electronic health record data, identifying missing data, misclassification, and selection bias as mechanisms through which EHR-derived training sets systematically misrepresent marginalized populations (Gianfrancesco, M.A., et al., 2018, JAMA Internal Medicine, 178[11], 1544–1547). The structural conditions that produce health disparities — differential access, differential documentation, differential treatment — are precisely the conditions that corrupt training data for any model seeking to learn from historical clinical patterns.⏎⏎ADLM Comments | HHS AI RFI — Clinical Care Accelerat ion | Page 3⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE GENERALIZABILITY GAP AND ITS DISTRIBUTIONAL CONSEQUENCES⏎⏎There is a second layer to this problem that the RFI does not adequately address: the gap between where AI clinical tools are validated and where they are deployed. The overwhelming majority of clinical AI validation studies are conducted at well-resourced academic medical centers with high data quality, large sample sizes, and patient populations that reflect the demographics of those institutions. When those tools are then deployed in community hospitals, rural health systems, and safety-net institutions — which serve higher proportions of patients of color, patients experiencing poverty, and patients with limited English proficiency — performance degrades in ways that the original validation study was structurally unable to detect. Wong et al. (2021) provided a direct empirical illustration of this problem in their external validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model: performance in the external validation cohort was substantially worse than the developer's published figures, with meaningful variation across patient subgroups (Wong, A., et al., 2021, JAMA Internal Medicine, 181[8], 1065–1070). Sendak et al. (2020) documented analogous challenges in real-world integration of a sepsis deep learning technology at Duke University Health System, finding that the translation from model performance to clinical impact was mediated by implementation context in ways the model's developers had not characterized (Sendak, M.P., et al., 2020, JMIR Medical Informatics, 8[7], e15182).⏎⏎The distributional implication is not subtle. If validation is concentrated in high-resource academic settings and deployment is generalized to all care settings without site-specific performance assessment, then performance degradation will be borne disproportionately by patients in the institutions that already provide care to the most vulnerable populations. Wiens et al. (2019) articulated this risk in their roadmap for responsible machine learning in health care, arguing that deployment decisions must account for the specific populations a tool will serve in practice, not merely the populations on which it was validated (Wiens, J., et al., 2019, Nature Medicine, 25[9], 1337–1340). Pierson et al. (2021) demonstrated that algorithmic approaches to pain management disparities in underserved populations require deliberate design choices — they do not emerge as a byproduct of accuracy optimization (Pierson, E., et al., 2021, Nature Medicine, 27[1], 136–140). HHS should take both of those findings seriously as design constraints for any deployment framework.⏎⏎ADLM Comments | HHS AI RFI — Clinical Care Accelerat ion | Page 4⏎⏎---⏎⏎AUTOMATION BIAS AS A STRUCTURAL MECHANISM OF HARM⏎⏎One mechanism through which these disparities are likely to propagate deserves explicit attention: automation bias. When clinical AI systems present outputs with numerical precision and the implicit authority of computational processing, clinicians are less likely to apply the critical scrutiny they would apply to a colleague's informal opinion. The authoritative appearance of an AI output — a sepsis risk score of 0.87, a flagged laboratory value with a predicted diagnosis — suppresses the metacognitive skepticism that would otherwise function as a check on algorithmic error. Char, Shah, and Magnus (2018) addressed this dynamic in their analysis of ethical challenges in implementing machine learning in health care, noting that the design of AI interfaces can either support or undermine appropriate clinician skepticism, and that interface design choices are rarely scrutinized as carefully as model architecture choices (Char, D.S., Shah, N.H., & Magnus, D., 2018, New England Journal of Medicine, 378[11], 981–983). This is particularly relevant in laboratory medicine, where ADLM members observe that AI-assisted diagnostic outputs are increasingly integrated into reporting workflows in ways that make them visually indistinguishable from validated reference ranges.⏎⏎The automation bias mechanism interacts with the generalizability gap in a specific way: the clinicians most likely to encounter patients for whom an AI tool performs poorly are the clinicians in community and safety-net settings who are also, on average, working with fewer resources, higher patient volumes, and less institutional infrastructure for performance monitoring. Those clinicians are least positioned to catch algorithmic errors precisely when the probability of those errors is highest. Parikh, Teeple, and Navathe (2019) described this as a structural amplification problem — the populations most harmed by biased AI are those least equipped to detect and correct that bias in deployment (Parikh, R.B., Teeple, S., & Navathe, A.S., 2019, JAMA, 322[24], 2377–2378). HHS's deployment framework must address this explicitly. Requiring post-market performance monitoring only at the deploying institution assumes that deploying institutions have the capacity for that monitoring — an assumption that is empirically unjustified for a large portion of the care delivery landscape.⏎⏎A related concern that ADLM wishes to flag, though it is somewhat tangential to the core equity argument: the use of race as a variable in clinical algorithms has its own complex history that interacts with AI bias in ways that are not always intuitive. Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones (2020) documented how race correction in clinical algorithms — ostensibly a form of demographic adjustment — can in practice perpetuate disparities by treating race as a biological variable rather than a social one (Vyas, D.A., Eisenstein, L.G., & Jones, D.S., 2020, New England Journal of Medicine, 383[9], 874–882). Any HHS guidance on equity auditing will need to grapple with this distinction carefully.⏎⏎ADLM Comments | HHS AI RFI — Clinical Care Accelerat ion | Page 5⏎⏎---⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Based on the foregoing analysis, ADLM urges HHS to incorporate the following requirements into any AI deployment framework developed in response to this RFI. These are offered as non-negotiable preconditions for deployment authorization, not as optional best practices or aspirational standards.⏎⏎1. Mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing. Before any clinical AI tool is authorized for deployment in federally funded care settings, the developer must demonstrate disaggregated performance metrics across race, ethnicity, sex, age, insurance status, and geographic setting. Aggregate accuracy statistics are insufficient. The audit methodology must be specified in advance, conducted by an entity independent of the developer, and reported in a standardized format accessible to HHS and to deploying institutions.⏎⏎2. Site-specific performance assessment requirements. Deployment authorization at academic medical centers should not confer deployment authorization at community hospitals, rural health systems, or safety-net institutions. HHS should require that developers conduct site-specific validation studies, or alternatively that deploying institutions conduct prospective performance monitoring against pre-specified equity benchmarks before full clinical integration. The 22-month average lag between demonstrated clinical utility and payer coverage decisions documented in ADLM's 2024 survey (ADLM, 2024) suggests that reimbursement timelines are already a significant barrier; HHS should design equity auditing requirements in a way that does not further extend that lag, but the answer to that design challenge is not to waive equity requirements.⏎⏎3. Mandatory post-deployment bias surveillance. Performance monitoring must be ongoing, not a one-time pre-deployment exercise. HHS should require deploying institutions to report disaggregated performance data to a central registry on a defined schedule — ADLM suggests quarterly reporting for the first two years of deployment, with annual reporting thereafter unless performance flags trigger more frequent review. The registry should be publicly accessible in a machine-readable format.⏎⏎o Surveillance protocols should include pre-specified triggers for deployment suspension or modification — specific thresholds of subgroup performance degradation that automatically require developer response.⏎⏎o HHS should fund surveillance infrastructure at safety-net institutions that lack the data infrastructure to conduct this monitoring independently. The burden of post-market surveillance should not fall disproportionately on the institutions least equipped to bear it.⏎⏎4. Transparency requirements for training data provenance. Developers must disclose the demographic composition of training data, the institutions from which training data were sourced, and the time period covered. Historical clinical data encodes patterns of differential treatment, and a tool trained predominantly on data from a single academic medical center in a demographically homogenous region is not generalizable without that disclosure.⏎⏎ADLM Comments | HHS AI RFI — Clinical Care Accelerat ion | Page 6⏎⏎---⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE ADLM SURVEY FINDINGS AND THEIR POLICY IMPLICATIONS⏎⏎ADLM wants to be direct about what the 2024 survey data mean for this RFI. The finding that fewer than 20% of laboratory medicine professionals can describe a clear regulatory pathway for clinical AI validation is not primarily an argument for faster regulatory clearance — it is an argument for clearer regulatory requirements, including equity requirements, that give deploying institutions a defined standard against which to evaluate candidate tools. The absence of standardized HHS guidance on AI algorithm transparency and post-deployment performance monitoring, which laboratory directors flagged consistently at ADLM's 2024 Annual Scientific Conference, creates a vacuum that is currently being filled by developer-supplied validation data, institutional inertia, and reimbursement signals that have nothing to do with equity performance. That is the actual acceleration problem. The tools are moving faster than the governance infrastructure, and the populations who will bear the cost of that gap are predictable from the existing literature.⏎⏎ADLM Comments | HHS AI RFI — Clinical Care Accelerat ion | Page 7⏎⏎---⏎⏎CONCLUSION⏎⏎HHS has framed this RFI primarily around removing barriers to AI adoption, and ADLM does not dispute that reimbursement uncertainty and regulatory ambiguity are real barriers that deserve serious policy attention. But the framing risks treating equity safeguards as friction in the adoption pipeline rather than as load-bearing infrastructure for a deployment ecosystem that will serve all Americans. The documented cases — pulse oximetry bias (Sjoding et al., 2020), health management algorithm bias (Obermeyer et al., 2019), sepsis prediction disparities (Wong et al., 2021), dermatology AI training set skew (Adamson & Smith, 2018) — are not outliers from an otherwise clean record. They are the record, at least as it currently exists. A deployment framework that treats mandatory equity auditing as a supplement rather than a precondition will replicate these harms at the scale of the tools HHS is seeking to accelerate.⏎⏎ADLM respectfully requests that HHS convene a formal technical working group on clinical AI equity standards, with representation from laboratory medicine professionals, community health centers, and health equity researchers, before finalizing any deployment framework guidance. The specific composition and timeline for that working group is something ADLM would welcome the opportunity to discuss with ASTP/ONC staff directly.⏎⏎Kenneth Scott⏎Research Director, Association for Diagnostics & Laboratory Medicine (ADLM)⏎Delaware⏎⏎adlm-policy@adlm.org⏎www.adlm.org/policy⏎⏎---⏎⏎REFERENCES (partial — full bibliography available upon request)⏎⏎ADLM. SYNTH-0054♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Ashley Smith♔American Medical Association♔♔♔♔♔AMA Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 1⏎⏎⏎SUBMISSION TO THE U.S. DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary / ASTP-ONC⏎Re: Health Sector Artificial Intelligence Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎PRELIMINARY STATEMENT OF ORGANIZATIONAL STANDING⏎⏎The American Medical Association submits these comments with particular attention to the RFI's framing questions regarding reimbursement structures and regulatory streamlining. Our organization does not address every question posed; the governance concerns raised here are substantial enough to warrant focused treatment rather than a comprehensive survey response. Our policy team's analysis of Medicare Physician Fee Schedule data from 2021 through 2024 identified no discrete payment pathway that reflects ongoing computational infrastructure costs separate from traditional professional or technical component billing, and member feedback collected through our 2024 Annual Meeting policy forums identified reimbursement ambiguity as the single greatest reported barrier to scaling AI deployment beyond initial pilot programs. That operational grounding informs everything that follows.⏎⏎⏎AMA Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE DEMOCRATIC GOVERNANCE PROBLEM THAT THIS RFI DECLINES TO NAME⏎⏎The Department's stated purpose — to "reduce uncertainty that impedes AI innovation" — is a framing choice that deserves direct interrogation, because it presupposes that regulatory scrutiny is an obstacle rather than a democratic safeguard. Our organization reads that phrase not as a neutral description of administrative intent but as evidence of an accelerationist posture: one in which the speed of technology deployment is treated as a value that pre-empts deliberation about whether that deployment, at that speed, is what democratic society has actually chosen. As Dafny and Lee argued in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2023, moving fast in health care AI carries hazards that are not correctable after the fact, precisely because the institutional reorganization that follows deployment is itself irreversible (Dafny & Lee, 2023, NEJM 388:291). The National Academy of Medicine's 2023 special publication on AI in health care reached a similar conclusion about the gap between the promise of these tools and the governance infrastructure required to deploy them responsibly. What the RFI does not acknowledge — and what our organization believes HHS is not authorized to decide unilaterally — is whether AI systems should govern clinical decisions at all, at population scale, before society has had the opportunity to deliberate on that question through legitimate democratic processes.⏎⏎This is not a technical objection. It is a structural one about the limits of administrative authority. When the Department frames regulatory review as an impediment, it is not merely adjusting a procurement timeline; it is transferring governance authority over medicine from clinicians, patients, and elected representatives to technology vendors, a transfer that exceeds HHS's legitimate mandate. Pasquale's analysis of algorithmic opacity in The Black Box Society (2015, Harvard University Press) and Zuboff's account of surveillance capitalism's institutional logic (2019, PublicAffairs) both document how embedded technological systems restructure the practical capacity for future democratic choice — not by formal prohibition but by making reversal operationally unthinkable. Coiera, Ash, and Berg, writing in the Yearbook of Medical Informatics in 2016, documented the unintended consequences of prior health information technology deployments and found that institutional knowledge reorganizes around new systems within two to four years of deployment, after which the practical capacity to reverse course atrophies even when documented harms demand it. Our member practices report exactly this dynamic: once clinical workflows, staffing ratios, and continuing education investments are reorganized around a vendor AI system, the multi-year procurement contracts and the erosion of non-AI-dependent clinical skills make reversal effectively impossible regardless of subsequent evidence. The GAO's 2022 report on AI in health care (GAO-22-104629) acknowledged this dependency risk but stopped well short of recommending a governance framework adequate to address it.⏎⏎⏎AMA Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 3⏎⏎⏎The irreversibility concern is worth making concrete rather than leaving at the level of principle. Our organization's member practices describe the following sequence when AI deployment scales past the pilot phase:⏎⏎1.   Staffing models are adjusted downward in the specialties where AI is deployed, on the assumption that the tool's throughput gains are permanent.⏎2.   Institutional training programs deprioritize the manual interpretive skills the AI is performing, because training time is finite and administrators allocate it toward remaining human-dependent tasks.⏎3.   Procurement contracts for AI infrastructure typically run five to seven years, with data-sharing provisions that create vendor dependencies extending well beyond the contract term.⏎4.   When evidence of harm emerges — and Obermeyer et al.'s 2019 Science paper (366:447) documenting racial bias in a widely deployed population health algorithm is the most cited example — the practical capacity to revert is constrained by all three of the above factors simultaneously.⏎⏎Topol's 2019 Nature Medicine analysis of human-AI convergence (25:44) is often cited in support of accelerated deployment, but Topol's argument was premised on robust human oversight remaining in place — a condition that the staffing and training dynamics described above systematically erode. Selbst and Barocas, writing in the Fordham Law Review in 2018 (87:1085), identified the same erosion dynamic in their analysis of explainability requirements, noting that the intuitive appeal of AI systems tends to reduce human interrogation of outputs over time, regardless of what formal oversight policies require. Cohen and colleagues, writing in The Lancet Digital Health in 2020 (2:e376), observed that the European AI strategy was grappling with precisely this governance gap and concluded that no existing regulatory framework was adequate to the task of preserving meaningful human authority after large-scale deployment. Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert's 2023 Milbank Quarterly analysis (101:629) of AI liability in medicine found that the absence of clear accountability structures is not a gap that accelerated deployment will resolve on its own.⏎⏎Our organization's specific demand is this: HHS should reframe this RFI to acknowledge that the question of whether AI should govern clinical decisions at population scale is a democratic governance question, not a technical optimization problem. The Department should impose a moratorium on non-device AI deployment in clinical decision-making contexts pending the development of a governance framework that has been subject to notice-and-comment rulemaking with adequate deliberation time, and should acknowledge formally that efficiency gains do not constitute sufficient justification for foreclosing future public authority over medicine. SYNTH-0055♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Stephanie Baker♔American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons♔♔♔♔♔AMERICAN ACADEMY OF ORTHOPAEDIC SURGEONS⏎Comments in Response to HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI⏎Submitted by: Stephanie Baker, Senior Policy Analyst⏎American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons⏎⏎⏎I. THE RFI'S FRAMING CONFLATES CATEGORICALLY DISTINCT APPLICATIONS⏎⏎The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) welcomes HHS's commitment to creating sustainable pathways for clinically validated AI tools, and our members have documented firsthand the operational promise of AI-assisted clinical decision support in reducing diagnostic turnaround times and improving care coordination. The Academy is prepared to engage constructively on reimbursement policy, coverage determination frameworks, and research-and-development priorities. However, the RFI as structured treats AI adoption in healthcare as a largely uniform policy problem, and that framing is not only incomplete — it is actively dangerous. It conflates AI deployed in service of patients with AI deployed against patients, and any acceleration agenda that fails to draw that distinction will, in practice, function as a federal subsidy for the most harmful AI applications currently operating at scale in the U.S. health system.⏎⏎The most profitable and most rapidly deployed AI tools in healthcare today are not clinical care tools. They are prior authorization denial engines. They are claims adjudication algorithms trained on cost-containment objectives. They are the systems that a major insurer's subsidiary, nH Predict, deployed in Medicare Advantage contexts to generate coverage denials at scale with documented override rates that bore no meaningful relationship to individual patient clinical profiles — a pattern the U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations examined in detail in its October 2023 report, "Denial, Delay, Deny: How Medicare Advantage Plans Use Algorithms to Override Physician Judgment" (S. Prt. 118-22). That investigation found that one insurer's algorithm predicted patients needed far fewer post-acute care days than their treating physicians determined, and that denials generated by the system were upheld on internal appeal at rates that raised serious questions about whether any genuine clinical review was occurring. The HHS Office of Inspector General reached parallel conclusions in its April 2022 report (OIG Report OEI-09-18-00260), finding that some Medicare Advantage organizations denied prior authorization requests in ways that did not align with Medicare coverage rules and that raised concerns about access to medically necessary care.⏎⏎This is not a peripheral problem. The Kaiser Family Foundation documented in March 2023 that prior authorization requirements in Medicare Advantage had grown substantially, with beneficiaries facing denials at rates that varied dramatically across plans in ways unexplained by clinical criteria (Koma, Cubanski, & Neuman, KFF Issue Brief, March 2023). The American Medical Association's 2023 Prior Authorization Physician Survey found that 94% of physicians reported that prior authorization processes delayed access to medically necessary care, and a growing proportion of those physicians specifically identified AI-assisted denial systems as the mechanism generating the initial adverse determination (AMA Policy Research Perspectives, December 2023). Blumenthal and Fowler, writing in the New England Journal of Medicine, characterized the current prior authorization environment as one in which the transfer of clinical authority to actuarial optimization has eroded the physician-patient relationship in ways that are difficult to reverse (NEJM 388: 1557–1560, April 2023).⏎⏎⏎AAOS Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎⏎II. THE EQUITY DIMENSION CANNOT BE DEFERRED⏎⏎The harms from administrative AI are not distributed evenly. Algorithmic systems trained on historical claims data embed and amplify existing disparities in access and treatment. Obermeyer and colleagues demonstrated this mechanism with precision in a 2019 Science article examining a widely used population health algorithm, finding that the system systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent disease burden (Science 366(6464): 447–453, 2019). The National Health Law Program's January 2024 report documented analogous dynamics in Medicaid managed care, where automated decision-making systems generated denial rates for low-income beneficiaries that were structurally insulated from meaningful appeal (NHeLP Policy Report, January 2024). The Center for Medicare Advocacy's February 2024 technical report on Medicare Advantage denial patterns found that beneficiaries who received AI-generated prior authorization denials faced appeals processes with low reversal rates and procedural burdens designed — whether intentionally or by structural inertia — to exhaust rather than redress (CMA Technical Report, February 2024). These findings are consistent with broader data on racial and income-based health disparities documented by Ndugga and colleagues at KFF (KFF Disparities Report, March 2023).⏎⏎The asymmetry here is worth stating plainly. When an AI system denies a Medicare Advantage beneficiary's post-acute rehabilitation following orthopaedic surgery, that patient faces a multi-step appeals process with strict deadlines, limited navigation support, and no guarantee of clinical review. The insurer deploying that system faces no equivalent accountability mechanism. Mukherjee, Bhatt, and Bhavnani argued in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology: Health Informatics that algorithmic prior authorization systems, as currently deployed, lack the clinical validity standards, transparency requirements, and equity review processes that would be required of any clinical decision support tool subject to FDA oversight (JACC: Health Informatics 4(2): 88–97, 2023). This is the regulatory gap at the center of the problem: clinical AI is subject to increasing scrutiny, while administrative AI operates in a largely unregulated space where the primary accountability mechanism is litigation after harm has occurred. Geruso and Layton's analysis of insurer financial optimization behavior in algorithmic risk adjustment contexts suggests that the incentive structures driving these systems are not incidentally misaligned with patient welfare — they are structurally misaligned (Journal of Political Economy 128(3): 984–1026, 2020).⏎⏎⏎III. SPECIFIC POLICY REQUEST⏎⏎AAOS respectfully urges HHS and ONC to take the following actions in response to this RFI:⏎⏎1. Issue formal guidance distinguishing clinical care AI (tools designed to support diagnosis, treatment planning, and care delivery) from administrative and coverage-determination AI (tools used in prior authorization, claims adjudication, and utilization management), with separate regulatory standards applicable to each category.⏎⏎2. Impose an immediate moratorium on AI-generated prior authorization denials in Medicare and Medicaid programs absent:⏎   o Demonstrated clinical validity review by an independent body;⏎   o A completed equity audit examining differential denial rates by race, income, disability status, and geography;⏎   o Mandatory human clinical override at the point of denial, with documented reviewer credentials and accountability;⏎   o Public disclosure of the algorithmic criteria and training data objectives used in the denial determination.⏎⏎3. Direct CMS to condition Medicare Advantage plan participation on compliance with the above standards within a defined implementation timeline.⏎⏎The Academy recognizes that developing the regulatory infrastructure to implement these requirements will require interagency coordination and, in some instances, additional statutory authority. THE EMPIRICAL PREDICATE⏎⏎Before addressing the substance of HHS's Request for Information, Nabla wishes to establish the factual foundation from which these comments proceed, because the Department's framing of AI adoption as a problem of insufficient acceleration is, in our professional assessment, exactly backward from what the data show. In March 2024, PINC AI published its "AI Governance Readiness in U.S. Health Systems: 2024 Member Survey Report," drawing on responses from member facilities across a network of more than 1,500 affiliated hospitals and health systems. The findings were not ambiguous. Sixty-eight percent of member facilities reported having piloted or deployed at least one AI-enabled clinical decision support tool within the preceding twenty-four months. That number is striking on its own. What is more striking, and what this comment is principally about, is the accompanying figure: fewer than 30% of those deploying facilities had a formal governance framework in place to oversee model validation, bias monitoring, or ongoing performance auditing at the time of that survey. These figures were not compiled to support a policy argument Nabla had already decided to make. They were compiled because member compliance officers, in consistent and escalating terms, were flagging the absence of standardized federal guidance on AI accountability structures as the single greatest barrier to responsible adoption. The data preceded the conclusion.⏎⏎What HHS has now proposed, in soliciting public input on how the Department can further accelerate AI adoption across clinical care settings, is to press harder on the deployment accelerator before anyone has installed the brakes. Nabla does not use that analogy loosely. The 2024 survey data reflect a deployment curve that has already outrun the institutional accountability infrastructure necessary to make that deployment safe. The RFI does not acknowledge this. It treats the governance gap as a parallel workstream, something to be addressed alongside acceleration rather than as a precondition for it. That framing is wrong, and this comment will explain why.⏎⏎Nabla | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎II. THE STRUCTURE OF ACCOUNTABILITY DIFFUSION⏎⏎The central problem Nabla's compliance professionals encounter in advising member institutions is not that AI tools perform poorly, though some do (see Obermeyer and Emanuel, "Predicting the Future -- Big Data, Machine Learning, and Clinical Medicine," New England Journal of Medicine, vol. 375, no. 13, 2016, pp. 1216-1219, for a well-documented account of systematic bias in predictive clinical algorithms). The central problem is that the commercial and contractual architecture surrounding AI deployment in clinical settings has been constructed, whether by design or by the accumulated logic of self-interested negotiation, to ensure that when an AI-assisted decision causes patient harm, no single party is clearly and non-waivably responsible for that harm. We refer to this as three-layer accountability laundering, and it operates as follows.⏎⏎At the first layer, AI vendors draft indemnification provisions that contractually transfer liability exposure to the deploying institution the moment the institution configures, deploys, or uses the tool in any clinical context. These provisions are not aberrations; they are standard. Nabla's legal team reviewed procurement contracts from seventeen member institutions during the second half of 2023, and indemnification language pushing liability to the deploying hospital appeared in every single one. The vendor's position, when pressed, is that it provided a tool; how that tool is integrated into clinical workflow is the institution's responsibility. This position is not without legal logic, but it is also not a complete account of where the causal responsibility for model behavior actually lies.⏎⏎At the second layer, hospitals and health systems write internal AI governance policies, where they write them at all, that assign responsibility for AI-assisted clinical decisions to the individual clinician who reviewed and acted on the tool's output. The clinical decision support tool is framed as advisory. The physician or nurse practitioner who received the recommendation is framed as the learned intermediary who exercised independent professional judgment. This is a plausible legal theory under existing medical malpractice doctrine, and it is also a description of how virtually no AI-assisted clinical workflow actually operates in practice. As Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen observed in their 2020 analysis of AI-driven healthcare legal frameworks (Sara Gerke, Timo Minssen, and I. Glenn Cohen, "Ethical and Legal Challenges of Artificial Intelligence-Driven Healthcare," in Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare, Academic Press, 2020, pp. 295-336), the learned intermediary doctrine was developed to address pharmaceutical manufacturer liability in the context of prescription drugs, where a physician reviews a drug's indications, contraindications, and warnings and makes an independent prescribing decision. Transposing that doctrine onto AI clinical decision support requires assuming that clinicians receiving AI-generated recommendations have the same capacity for independent evaluation of the recommendation's underlying logic that a physician reviewing a drug's pharmacological profile does. They do not. In most deployed AI systems, the model's reasoning is opaque to the clinician receiving its output.⏎⏎At the third layer, individual clinicians face the operational reality that overriding AI recommendations in high-volume clinical environments is cognitively and institutionally difficult. Alert fatigue is well-documented. Workflow integration of AI outputs in EHR systems often places AI recommendations in positions of visual prominence that create implicit pressure toward acceptance. The American Medical Association's policy on augmented intelligence (AMA Policy H-480.940, adopted 2018, updated 2023) acknowledges the physician's role as final decision-maker while simultaneously recognizing that AI tools must be designed to support rather than displace clinical judgment. The policy is admirable in intent. It does not resolve the practical reality that a clinician working a twelve-hour hospitalist shift reviewing AI-generated sepsis risk scores for forty patients is not exercising the same quality of independent judgment the learned intermediary doctrine assumes.⏎⏎The result of these three layers operating in combination is that when an AI-assisted clinical error causes harm, the vendor points to the indemnification clause, the hospital points to its policy designating the clinician as the responsible decision-maker, and the clinician points to the fact that the AI system's output was presented as a validated, institutionally-approved recommendation. The patient, or the patient's family, is left without a clearly answerable party. This is not a gap in an otherwise functional system. It is the system working as its contractual architecture intended.⏎⏎Nabla | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 3⏎⏎---⏎⏎III. WHY EXISTING LEGAL DOCTRINE IS INSUFFICIENT⏎⏎Mello et al., writing in Health Affairs in 2023, identified the foundational challenge with precision: existing medical malpractice doctrine is built around the assumption of an identifiable human decision-maker whose judgment can be evaluated against a professional standard of care (Michelle M. Mello et al., "Accountability for AI in Health Care: Legal and Regulatory Frameworks," Health Affairs, vol. 42, no. 3, 2023, pp. 391-399). AI intermediation complicates this assumption in ways that are not merely technical but structural. When a machine learning model trained on historical patient data generates a risk stratification that a clinician acts on, the question of whose judgment is being evaluated against the standard of care is genuinely unclear. Is it the clinician's judgment in accepting the recommendation? The hospital's judgment in selecting and deploying this particular model? The vendor's judgment in training the model on data that may not be representative of the patient population now being served? The Restatement (Third) of Torts addresses product liability in terms that could, in theory, apply to AI tools, but as Price has noted, the application of product liability doctrine to clinical AI is complicated by the fact that AI tools do not fit cleanly into the category of "products" as that term has been interpreted in the context of manufacturing defect, design defect, or failure-to-warn claims (W. Nicholson Price II, "Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: Applications and Legal Implications," The SciTech Lawyer, vol. 14, no. 1, 2017, pp. 10-13).⏎⏎Cohen et al. raised these concerns in an earlier context, noting that complex predictive analytics in health care create legal and ethical challenges that existing frameworks were not designed to address, particularly with respect to transparency, auditability, and the allocation of responsibility when an algorithm's output contributes to an adverse outcome (I. Glenn Cohen et al., "The Legal and Ethical Concerns That Arise from Using Complex Predictive Analytics in Health Care," Health Affairs, vol. 33, no. 7, 2014, pp. 1139-1147). That paper was published a decade ago. The concerns it identified have not been resolved. They have been scaled.⏎⏎The ONC's HTI-1 Final Rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, Jan. 9, 2024) made meaningful progress on algorithm transparency by establishing requirements for the disclosure of certain predictive decision support interventions within certified health IT. Nabla acknowledges this. But transparency disclosure requirements, while necessary, do not assign legal accountability. Knowing that a model exists and knowing who is legally responsible when that model contributes to a patient's injury are different questions. The HTI-1 rule answers the first question in limited contexts. No federal regulation currently answers the second.⏎⏎The contrast with the European Union's approach is instructive, even for those who would not argue that U.S. health care regulation should mirror EU regulatory architecture. The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Official Journal of the European Union, L 2024/1689, June 12, 2024) classifies AI systems intended to influence clinical decisions as high-risk AI, subject to mandatory conformity assessments, post-market monitoring requirements, and specific obligations on providers regarding human oversight and documentation. The Act does not resolve every accountability question, and Nabla does not suggest it should be adopted wholesale. But the EU's regulatory posture reflects a basic judgment that deployment at scale should follow, not precede, the construction of accountability infrastructure. HHS's RFI reflects the opposite judgment.⏎⏎Nabla | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 4⏎⏎---⏎⏎IV. ON THE RFI'S QUESTIONS REGARDING ACCREDITATION AND CREDENTIALING⏎⏎The RFI asks, among other questions, how HHS might use accreditation, credentialing, and certification mechanisms to support responsible AI adoption. Nabla addresses this question directly because it illustrates, in concentrated form, the conceptual error that runs through the entire RFI.⏎⏎Accreditation and certification mechanisms are performance evaluation tools. They assess whether a system does what it claims to do, under specified conditions, within acceptable performance parameters. The Joint Commission's 2023 Sentinel Event Alert on responsible use of health data in AI (Issue 68, 2023) articulated principles for AI governance that include transparency, oversight, and ongoing monitoring. These principles are sound. Certification frameworks built around such principles can, if designed well, improve the quality of AI tools that reach clinical deployment. Nabla does not dispute this.⏎⏎What certification cannot do is assign legal responsibility when a certified system causes harm. Certification tells you that a system met specified performance criteria at the time of evaluation. It does not tell you who is legally accountable when that system performs differently in a real clinical environment with a patient population that differs from the validation dataset, or when model drift degrades performance after deployment, or when a clinician interacts with the system in a way the certification assessment did not anticipate. These are not hypothetical failure modes. They are the failure modes that Nabla's member compliance officers are already managing, in facilities that deployed AI tools that passed whatever informal or vendor-supplied validation process was applied at the time of procurement.⏎⏎Industry-driven self-certification is even less adequate. The structural conflict of interest in vendor-conducted validation is obvious enough that it requires no extended analysis here. Nabla's concern is not only with the quality of vendor self-certification but with the category error involved in treating certification as a substitute for legal accountability assignment. These are different functions. An AI tool can be fully certified, in good faith, by a rigorous independent body, and still produce an output that contributes to patient harm in a specific clinical context. When that happens, certification does not answer the question of who is responsible for that patient's injury. HHS's RFI, by framing accreditation and credentialing as the primary accountability mechanism, conflates these two functions in a way that will, if acted upon without correction, make the accountability laundering problem worse rather than better.⏎⏎The reason it will make the problem worse is this: if a vendor can point to third-party certification as evidence that its tool met applicable standards, the vendor's contractual indemnification position becomes stronger, not weaker. The hospital's ability to hold the vendor responsible for model behavior narrows. The clinician's position as the responsible learned intermediary is reinforced. The three-layer accountability laundering structure does not collapse under the weight of a certification regime; it is fortified by one, because each layer now has a certified document to point to when the question of responsibility arises.⏎⏎Nabla | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 5⏎⏎---⏎⏎V. WHAT HHS MUST DO BEFORE FURTHER ACCELERATION⏎⏎Nabla's position is specific. The Department should condition any further federal action to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care settings on the prior establishment of three structural requirements, none of which is currently in place and none of which can be substituted by certification, accreditation, or voluntary industry commitments.⏎⏎First: A mandatory federal framework assigning non-waivable legal accountability to a specific institutional party for each AI-assisted clinical decision that materially influences patient care. The framework must be non-waivable, meaning that contractual indemnification provisions purporting to transfer this accountability cannot override the federal assignment. This is not a novel regulatory concept; analogous non-waivable liability structures exist in consumer financial protection law, in certain environmental liability regimes, and in aspects of product liability law. The question of which party should bear primary accountability in a given deployment context is a legitimate policy question on which reasonable people differ. What is not a legitimate policy position is the current arrangement, in which no party clearly bears it. Nabla does not prescribe the precise allocation at this stage; we recognize that the appropriate allocation may differ between, say, a hospital that substantially modified a vendor's base model and one that deployed it without modification. But the Department must establish that some identified party is accountable, that this accountability cannot be contractually disclaimed, and that patients harmed by AI-assisted errors have a clearly identified respondent.⏎⏎Second: Required disclosure to patients when AI tools materially influenced their care. The current standard, such as it is, treats AI-assisted clinical decision support as an internal workflow tool whose use need not be disclosed to the patient whose care it shapes. This position is inconsistent with the informed consent principles that govern other aspects of clinical practice. A patient has a right to know, in terms that are meaningful rather than buried in a general consent form, that a machine learning model assessed their risk of deterioration and that this assessment influenced the clinical decisions made on their behalf. Nabla acknowledges the practical complexity of defining "materially influenced" in a way that is both operationally workable and legally meaningful. That complexity is real. It is also not a reason to avoid the requirement. It is a reason to develop the regulatory definition carefully, with input from clinical, legal, and patient advocacy communities, before scaling deployment further.⏎⏎Third: Enforceable audit rights allowing institutions and regulators to inspect vendor model behavior post-deployment. Post-market surveillance of AI clinical tools is currently voluntary, inconsistent, and structurally dependent on vendor cooperation. When a member institution in Nabla's network suspects that an AI tool is performing differently than it did at deployment, perhaps because of model drift, perhaps because the patient population has shifted, perhaps because EHR update changed the input data structure, the institution's ability to investigate is limited by whatever contractual access rights it negotiated at procurement. In most cases, those rights are limited. Vendors treat their model architecture, training data, and ongoing performance monitoring as proprietary. An institution that wants to audit a deployed AI tool's current performance against its validation-era performance may find itself unable to do so without the vendor's active cooperation, which the vendor has no contractual obligation to provide. This is not a theoretical problem. It is the operational reality compliance officers in Nabla's network navigate on a regular basis.⏎⏎The three requirements above are not a comprehensive AI governance framework. They are the minimum preconditions for responsible scaling. Nabla's member compliance officers have reviewed frameworks proposed by various bodies, including the Joint Commission's Sentinel Event Alert guidance, the AMA's augmented intelligence principles, and various state-level AI governance initiatives, and while many of these documents contain sound recommendations, none of them carries the legal force necessary to alter the contractual accountability architecture that currently governs AI deployment. Voluntary principles do not override indemnification clauses. Federal regulation does.⏎⏎Nabla | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 6⏎⏎---⏎⏎VI. A DIRECT RESPONSE TO THE ACCELERATION FRAMING⏎⏎Nabla's member compliance officers are not opposed to artificial intelligence in clinical care. This point deserves direct statement because the argument this comment makes is sometimes read, by those who prefer not to engage with its substance, as technophobia or institutional conservatism. It is neither. The 68% deployment rate documented in the 2024 PINC AI survey reflects genuine institutional investment in AI tools by organizations that believe, with reasonable evidence, that these tools can improve clinical outcomes when properly governed. The concern is not with AI. The concern is with the Department's apparent determination to accelerate deployment before the legal and institutional architecture necessary to make that deployment accountable has been constructed.⏎⏎There is a specific dimension of the RFI's framing that Nabla finds particularly difficult to accept, which is the implicit premise that deployment barriers are primarily problems of regulatory friction, reimbursement uncertainty, or insufficient federal encouragement. The 2024 survey data do not support this premise. When member compliance officers identified the single greatest barrier to broader AI adoption, they did not say "insufficient federal encouragement." They said "absence of standardized federal guidance on AI accountability structures." Fifty-four percent of facilities citing reimbursement uncertainty and liability exposure as co-equal deterrents to AI implementation are not describing a problem that will be solved by CMS coding updates or ONC certification expansions. They are describing a problem of legal risk that cannot be managed under the current accountability architecture because that architecture does not clearly assign the risk to anyone.⏎⏎The Department's failure to propose any framework for assigning clear responsibility for AI-assisted clinical harm is not a regulatory gap that can be filled by future rulemaking while deployment scales in parallel. It is a structural flaw in the current approach that will become progressively more difficult to correct as more facilities deploy more AI tools under contracts that embed the current accountability laundering structure more deeply into institutional practice. Contracts are hard to renegotiate. Liability exposure that has already materialized cannot be retroactively assigned. The moment to establish a clear accountability framework is before deployment reaches a scale at which the political economy of the AI vendor industry makes mandatory accountability assignment practically impossible to legislate.⏎⏎Nabla | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 7⏎⏎---⏎⏎VII. CLOSING OBSERVATIONS⏎⏎Nabla submits these comments in the recognition that the Department faces genuine competing pressures in this space. The clinical case for AI-assisted decision support in areas like sepsis detection, imaging interpretation, and medication reconciliation is real. The administrative burden on health systems is real. The potential for well-designed AI tools to address workforce shortages and improve care consistency in underserved settings is real. Nabla does not dismiss these considerations. What we cannot accept is the framing that treats accountability infrastructure as a secondary concern, to be developed in parallel with or subsequent to scaled deployment, rather than as the precondition for deployment that basic risk management principles require.⏎⏎The compliance officers who participated in the 2024 PINC AI survey were not expressing abstract regulatory anxiety. They were describing the operational reality of managing institutions that have deployed AI tools under contracts that were designed, at the vendor's insistence, to insulate the vendor from legal consequence when those tools contribute to patient harm. They are the parties who will manage the liability exposure when the three-layer accountability laundering structure produces the adverse outcomes it was designed to obscure. They are asking HHS not to slow AI adoption but to build the accountability framework that would make responsible adoption possible. The Department's RFI does not engage with this request. It is Nabla's position that it must, before any further acceleration of deployment is appropriate.⏎⏎One additional matter that has not received adequate attention in the RFI: the question of how post-deployment model changes, including retraining events, architecture updates, and input data structure modifications that occur after initial deployment, should be governed and disclosed. Several member institutions reported in 2023 that vendor-side model updates had altered AI tool behavior in clinical deployment without any notification to the deploying institution. In at least two documented cases, the performance characteristics that had been evaluated at procurement no longer described the model the institution was actually running. This is not a certification problem. It is a post-market surveillance problem, and it is one that no current federal requirement adequately addresses. The HTI-1 rule's transparency provisions apply to certain decision support functions at the point of initial certification; they do not establish ongoing disclosure obligations for post-deployment model changes. This gap needs to be addressed in any framework HHS develops, and it should be addressed before deployment scales further, not as a follow-on rulemaking after the next generation of contracts has been executed without post-deployment disclosure requirements.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Emily Martin⏎Chief Compliance Officer, Nabla⏎Minnesota⏎⏎nablahealth-regulatory@nabla.com⏎⏎Nabla | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 8♔♔2026-01-05T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-05T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔12♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔organization♔high♔angry♔Minnesota♔compliance officer♔52♔A 2024 internal policy review conducted across PINC's network of over 1,500 affiliated hospitals and health systems found that 68% of member facilities had either piloted or deployed at least one AI-enabled clinical decision support tool within the preceding 24 months, yet fewer than 30% reported having a formal governance framework in place to oversee model validation, bias monitoring, or ongoing performance auditing. SYNTH-0058♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Karen Harris♔♔♔♔♔♔Submitted via regulations.gov⏎⏎My mother had her second stroke in 2019 and was admitted to Tulane Medical Center in New Orleans. The neurologist who saw her spent maybe eight minutes at her bedside before moving on. I don't blame him — his patient load was genuinely impossible and I could see that. What I couldn't stop watching was the nurse who spent a good chunk of that afternoon manually re-entering the same medication history into three separate systems because none of them talked to each other. I've managed medical office operations for twenty-two years. I know what a policy failure looks like from the inside, and I knew I was watching one.⏎⏎I'm submitting this comment because I want AI in clinical care. I want it badly. The gap between what these tools can already do and what our staff are actually permitted or reimbursed to use is real and it costs patients. But what HHS is proposing here — accelerating adoption before the legal accountability infrastructure exists to support it safely — is going to hurt the people it's supposed to help, and I don't think the RFI is being honest about that.⏎⏎⏎THE LIABILITY VACUUM PROBLEM⏎⏎Here is what I keep coming back to when I read through this RFI. When an AI-assisted decision harms a patient, who exactly answers for it? The clinician says the tool gave them bad output. The hospital says the clinician had final authority and should have caught it. The vendor says the clinician misapplied the tool or the hospital's implementation deviated from the product specifications. And the training data — well, nobody owns the training data in any meaningful legal sense. What you end up with is a causation chain that diffuses responsibility so completely that the patient is left holding the harm with no clear accountable party.⏎⏎This isn't a hypothetical problem I'm inventing. W.N. Price II wrote about exactly this in the Harvard Law Review Forum in 2019 — the argument is that algorithmic opacity undermines the causation requirements of negligence doctrine in ways that current malpractice law is not equipped to handle. The whole architecture of medical malpractice assumes an identifiable human decision-maker whose conduct can be evaluated against a standard of care. AI intermediation breaks that foundational assumption. The GAO documented related concerns in its February 2022 report on artificial intelligence in health care (GAO-22-104629), noting that the complexity of AI development and deployment chains creates gaps in accountability that existing oversight structures weren't designed to address.⏎⏎Cohen, Amarasingham, Shah, Xie, and Lo made a related point in Health Affairs back in 2014 (Vol. 33, No. 7) — that predictive analytics in clinical settings raise legal and ethical concerns specifically because the decision-making process becomes opaque to the clinician who is nominally responsible for the outcome. That was 2014. We have not solved this problem. We have made the tools more powerful and the opacity more profound, and now HHS wants to accelerate deployment.⏎⏎What I want HHS to understand is that this isn't a regulatory gap that can be patched after the fact. This is a structural design flaw. When you build an accountability vacuum into the deployment architecture before the legal system has developed doctrine to fill it, you're not creating a problem that regulators can fix later — you're scaling a harm-distribution system that is specifically designed, whether intentionally or not, to make patient harm someone else's problem at every level of the chain.⏎⏎⏎WHAT THE RFI GETS WRONG ABOUT READINESS⏎⏎The RFI asks a number of questions about barriers to adoption and reimbursement structures and research priorities. I want to address the framing of those questions directly, because I think it's misleading.⏎⏎The RFI treats accountability as one item among many — something that can be addressed in parallel with accelerating adoption, or perhaps worked out through existing frameworks like respondeat superior or the learned intermediary doctrine. But those frameworks don't transfer cleanly. Respondeat superior assigns liability to an employer for an employee's conduct. An AI system is not an employee. The learned intermediary doctrine, which limits pharmaceutical manufacturer liability when a prescribing physician is in the chain, might seem analogous, but the analogy breaks down because the physician can read a drug insert and understand what they're prescribing. They cannot, in most cases, audit a black-box clinical decision support tool's reasoning process in real time. Delvecchio Good and Good made this point in the Journal of Medical Ethics in 2022 (Vol. 48) — that AI intermediation in clinical decision-making erodes the physician-patient relationship in ways that also erode the accountability structures that relationship supports.⏎⏎The RFI is also largely silent on the ONC's own 2023 Health IT Patient Safety Action and Surveillance Plan, which explicitly documented persistent gaps in adverse event attribution for software-assisted decisions. If ONC has already acknowledged that we can't reliably attribute harm when health IT is in the decision chain, then the answer is not to accelerate the deployment of more sophisticated health IT before we fix the attribution problem. Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert found in their JAMA review (Vol. 323, No. 4, 2020) that malpractice liability, whatever its flaws, does function as a quality signal — it creates pressure on providers to identify and correct unsafe practices. That signal breaks down when liability is diffuse enough that no single party experiences it as meaningful pressure to change behavior.⏎⏎I want to be fair to HHS here. I understand why the Department is pushing on adoption. The clinical case for AI tools is real, the workforce shortage is real, the documentation burden is crushing providers I work with every day, and the status quo has its own serious patient safety costs. Obermeyer and Topol noted in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021 that diffuse development chains in AI systems can obscure responsibility for harmful outputs even when no single party acted in bad faith — which means the accountability problem isn't just about bad actors, it's structural. I accept that. The point I'm making is that accepting the clinical case for AI doesn't require accepting deployment before accountability frameworks exist.⏎⏎⏎WHAT PRECAUTIONARY STANDARDS WOULD ACTUALLY LOOK LIKE⏎⏎I'm not a lawyer and I'm not going to pretend I can draft model legislation in a public comment. But based on twenty-two years of watching how liability plays out in medical office operations, I think there are some minimum conditions that should exist before HHS accelerates AI adoption in clinical care settings. The RFI should be asking about these, and it isn't.⏎⏎1. Clear statutory or regulatory assignment of primary liability when an AI-assisted decision causes patient harm — not a common law question to be litigated case by case over the next two decades, but an affirmative regulatory determination of where liability sits and under what circumstances it can be transferred.⏎⏎2. Mandatory adverse event reporting requirements specifically for AI-assisted decisions, with attribution standards that can actually identify whether the AI system contributed to the harm. The current adverse event reporting infrastructure was not built for this and doesn't do it.⏎⏎3. A requirement that clinical AI tools be explainable at the point of care — not necessarily that every algorithm be fully transparent in a technical sense, but that the clinician using the tool can access a plain-language account of why the tool produced the output it produced, sufficient to exercise genuine independent judgment rather than rubber-stamping.⏎⏎4. Vendor liability that cannot be entirely contractually disclaimed. Right now, many health IT contracts include liability caps and indemnification clauses that effectively transfer all risk to the hospital and ultimately to the patient. That needs to stop before we scale these tools.⏎⏎5. A mandatory post-market surveillance mechanism with real teeth — not voluntary reporting, not a best-practices framework, but a binding requirement with consequences for non-compliance.⏎⏎I'm not saying HHS can do all of this by itself. Some of this is Congress. Some of it is state insurance commissioners and state medical boards. But HHS can decline to accelerate adoption — through reimbursement changes, through certification requirements, through R&D funding priorities — until these structures are in place. The Department has more leverage here than the RFI acknowledges.⏎⏎⏎ONE THING I WANT HHS TO ACTUALLY HEAR⏎⏎I've been in medical offices long enough to know that when a new technology gets deployed without clear accountability structures, the people who absorb the risk are the ones with the least power in the system. That was true when EHRs were rushed into deployment under meaningful time pressure and generated a wave of documentation errors that nobody had a clean legal mechanism to address. It's going to be true with AI, and the harms are going to be harder to trace and harder to litigate.⏎⏎My mother's neurologist had eight minutes. That's a real problem and I want it fixed. But fixing it by deploying AI tools into a liability vacuum doesn't fix the problem — it just makes the next harm harder to attribute and easier for everyone except the patient to walk away from.⏎⏎The RFI asks what regulatory actions HHS can take to accelerate adoption. What I'm asking is for HHS to first answer a different question: what accountability structures need to exist before acceleration is responsible? Because right now, the answer to that question is missing from this entire document, and I don't think that omission is an oversight.⏎⏎I work in Louisiana, where I have watched patients navigate a health system with limited resources, limited legal literacy, and genuine difficulty accessing the legal system when something goes wrong. The accountability diffusion problem I'm describing is not abstract to those patients. When the harm happens and there is no clear party to hold responsible, they don't get a policy discussion about regulatory frameworks. They just don't get recourse.⏎⏎HHS should require that minimum accountability standards be established — through rulemaking, through conditions of participation, through whatever mechanism the Department has available — before reimbursement changes or certification requirements are used to push AI tools into wider clinical deployment. The specific mechanism matters less to me than the sequencing: accountability infrastructure first, then acceleration. Not simultaneously, and definitely not the other way around.⏎⏎I realize this comment is asking HHS to slow down something the Department clearly wants to speed up. I'm asking anyway because I think the people who will be harmed by getting this sequence wrong are the people who can least afford it, and I don't think the RFI as written is taking that seriously enough.⏎⏎Karen Harris⏎Medical Office Manager⏎Louisiana♔♔2026-01-21T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-21T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔individual♔high♔frustrated♔Louisiana♔office manager♔55♔When my mother was admitted to Tulane Medical Center after her second stroke, the neurologist spent less than eight minutes with her before moving on — not because he didn't care, but because his patient load was genuinely impossible.
