SYNTH-0060♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Melissa Young♔American Society of Anesthesiologists♔♔♔♔♔American Society of Anesthesiologists⏎1061 American Lane⏎Schaumburg, Illinois 60173⏎⏎May 12, 2025⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Attention: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎RE: Comments of the American Society of Anesthesiologists on Workforce Accountability and Safety Preconditions for Clinical AI Deployment⏎⏎⏎ASA Comments | HHS AI RFI — Clinical Care | Page 1⏎⏎⏎The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) respectfully submits these comments in response to the Department's Request for Information on accelerating the adoption and use of artificial intelligence in clinical care settings. The ASA represents more than 57,000 physician anesthesiologists and anesthesiology residents across the United States, and our members work at the intersection of high-acuity clinical judgment, real-time monitoring technology, and institutional pressure to reduce perioperative costs. That position gives us a particular vantage point on the risks that accompany poorly governed AI deployment — risks that this RFI, in the ASA's view, does not adequately address before soliciting recommendations for acceleration.⏎⏎Our government affairs office has spent the past eighteen months analyzing how AI tools are actually being deployed in anesthesiology and adjacent perioperative care settings, and the pattern we have observed is consistent with findings from broader physician workforce research. The 2023 AMA Digital Medicine Practice Snapshot documented that while a majority of physicians express conditional openness to AI tools, the most frequently cited concern is not technical performance but loss of clinical autonomy — the sense that tools are being configured by administrators and vendors to constrain physician judgment rather than support it. That concern is not abstract in anesthesiology. Continuous monitoring platforms marketed as decision-support tools have, in several Michigan acute care settings documented by the Michigan Health and Hospital Association Workforce Task Force in its 2023 policy brief, been repurposed within twelve months of deployment to justify reduced anesthesiology staffing ratios in ambulatory surgical centers, with the AI-generated monitoring log used as post-hoc documentation of adequacy rather than as a real-time clinical aid. The ASA does not raise this to oppose technology. We raise it because the Department's RFI frames AI adoption as an unambiguous acceleration problem, and our members' direct professional experience suggests that the framing itself is a governance failure.⏎⏎⏎ASA Comments | HHS AI RFI — Clinical Care | Page 2⏎⏎⏎WORKFORCE SURVEILLANCE AND THE LABOR DISPLACEMENT PROBLEM⏎⏎The central issue that the RFI's framing obscures is the distinction between AI tools that augment physician judgment and AI tools that are deployed to surveil, measure, and ultimately replace it. These are not the same category of technology, and they do not carry the same implications for patient safety. Kellogg, Valentine, and Christin's 2020 analysis in the Academy of Management Annals identified algorithmic monitoring in clinical and near-clinical workplaces as a contested terrain of labor control — one in which the outputs of surveillance systems are routinely used by institutional managers to discipline and restructure clinical workflows in ways that individual clinicians cannot anticipate at the time a procurement decision is made. The ASA's concern is that HHS, by soliciting recommendations on how to accelerate AI adoption without first establishing mandatory workforce accountability standards, is providing institutional cover for exactly this dynamic. When a hospital system deploys an AI scheduling and productivity platform, the clinicians whose workflows are being measured are almost never at the procurement table. National Nurses United documented this pattern in exhaustive detail in its 2023 research report, Staffing by Algorithm, which found that hospital systems across seventeen states had used AI-generated productivity metrics to justify nurse-to-patient ratios that fell below state-recommended safe staffing thresholds, and that frontline nurses had no formal mechanism to contest the algorithmic outputs driving those decisions. Physician anesthesiologists face an analogous dynamic. Perioperative AI platforms that purport to optimize case scheduling, predict anesthesia duration, and flag documentation gaps are increasingly configured to feed into utilization review processes that treat physician time as a variable to be minimized rather than a clinical resource to be appropriately deployed.⏎⏎The patient safety consequences of this dynamic are not speculative. Shanafelt and colleagues' 2022 longitudinal analysis in Mayo Clinic Proceedings documented a sustained and worsening trajectory of physician burnout between 2011 and 2020, with burnout prevalence among physicians running more than double that of the general working population across the entire study period. Dyrbye and colleagues' 2020 study in JAMA Network Open established a direct statistical relationship between unsafe work unit climates and burnout severity among physicians, and burnout, as the literature has consistently shown, is associated with measurable increases in medical error, reduced adherence to safety protocols, and higher rates of adverse patient events. Wachter and Goldsmith identified the electronic health record as one of the primary drivers of clinical demoralization in their 2018 Harvard Business Review analysis, arguing that poorly designed information technology imposed on physicians without adequate workflow integration produces exactly the kind of cognitive overload that increases error risk. The ASA's position is that AI tools deployed without workforce accountability standards are structurally likely to reproduce and amplify this problem. Bates and colleagues' 2021 study in NPJ Digital Medicine noted that AI has genuine potential to reduce burnout in emergency departments — but only when tools are designed with frontline worker input and implemented with attention to how they change the cognitive and emotional demands of clinical work. That conditionality is absent from the RFI's framing, and the ASA believes it should be a precondition for any HHS deployment incentive.⏎⏎⏎ASA Comments | HHS AI RFI — Clinical Care | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE EQUITY AND VALIDATION PROBLEM IN PERIOPERATIVE AI⏎⏎The ASA also wishes to draw the Department's attention to a related concern that we do not believe the RFI adequately addresses: the systematic bias risks embedded in AI tools trained on clinical data that reflects historical disparities in care delivery. Obermeyer and colleagues' landmark 2019 Science analysis demonstrated that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to manage population health systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients relative to white patients at equivalent levels of illness severity, because the algorithm used cost as a proxy for health need — and Black patients had historically received less care, and therefore generated lower cost data, despite equivalent or greater clinical need. This is not an isolated finding. The Government Accountability Office's 2023 report, GAO-23-105491, on artificial intelligence in health care identified bias in training data as one of the two most significant risks associated with clinical AI deployment, alongside the absence of post-market surveillance mechanisms. In perioperative care specifically, where patient risk stratification tools are used to allocate anesthesia resources, predict complications, and guide post-operative monitoring intensity, a biased algorithm can produce systematically worse outcomes for already-disadvantaged patient populations without any individual clinician being aware that the tool is performing inequitably. The ONC's own 2022 data brief on health IT-related patient safety events, ONC Data Brief No. 58, documented that a significant proportion of reported safety events involved clinical decision support tools that had not been adequately validated for the patient populations in which they were deployed. Topol's 2019 Nature Medicine analysis of high-performance medicine argued that the convergence of human and artificial intelligence in clinical settings can produce genuinely superior outcomes, but only when the AI component has been rigorously validated across the demographic and clinical diversity of the population it will serve. The ASA agrees with that framing entirely, and we are concerned that the RFI's acceleration orientation creates pressure to move past validation requirements in the name of speed.⏎⏎⏎ASA Comments | HHS AI RFI — Clinical Care | Page 4⏎⏎⏎REIMBURSEMENT STRUCTURE AND THE PRODUCTIVITY EXTRACTION PROBLEM⏎⏎Our Association is also aware that reimbursement uncertainty is a genuine barrier to beneficial AI adoption, and we do not dismiss that concern. A 2024 member survey conducted by a major state medical association found that more than seventy percent of physicians who had adopted AI tools in their practices identified reimbursement uncertainty as the primary barrier to deeper integration, and our own informal conversations with ASA members in Michigan and Ohio over the past year reflect a similar pattern. The problem, however, is that the reimbursement question cannot be separated from the workforce displacement question. If HHS creates new reimbursement pathways for AI-augmented clinical encounters without simultaneously establishing standards for how AI tools may and may not affect staffing ratios and scope-of-practice boundaries, the net effect is likely to be a transfer of reimbursement value from physician services to AI platform vendors, with institutional administrators capturing the margin by reducing clinical staffing to the minimum level the AI-generated documentation can justify. This is not a hypothetical concern. It is the pattern our government affairs office has documented in Michigan acute care settings, and it is the pattern that the MHA Workforce Task Force's 2023 policy brief described in systematic terms. The ASA's position is that any new reimbursement pathway for AI-augmented care must be conditioned on institutional attestation that AI deployment has not reduced clinical staffing ratios below pre-deployment baselines except through voluntary attrition, and that the reimbursement benefit accrues to the clinical enterprise rather than being captured entirely by the technology vendor or the administrative layer.⏎⏎⏎ASA Comments | HHS AI RFI — Clinical Care | Page 5⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The ASA urges the Department to condition any AI deployment incentive, reimbursement pathway, or regulatory safe harbor on the following preconditions, which we frame not as optional guardrails but as minimum standards without which acceleration is likely to produce patient harm.⏎⏎First, HHS and ONC should require that any AI tool deployed in a clinical care setting that affects physician or nursing workflow, staffing allocation, or scope-of-practice documentation be subject to mandatory frontline clinical worker review prior to procurement. This requirement should be codified in ONC's Health IT Certification Program under 45 CFR Part 170, and should specify that the review body must include practicing clinicians in the relevant specialty — not merely clinical informatics staff or administrative representatives. The ASA is aware that this recommendation will face resistance from hospital systems and vendors on grounds of implementation burden, but the MHA Workforce Task Force's 2023 data suggests that facilities where frontline workers participated in procurement decisions reported substantially higher rates of sustained AI adoption and lower rates of tool abandonment after eighteen months, which is a practical argument for the requirement independent of its ethical justification.⏎⏎Second, the Department should direct CMS to develop a post-deployment surveillance mechanism for AI tools that affect clinical staffing ratios or productivity metrics, modeled on the adverse event reporting requirements in 21 CFR Part 803, and requiring institutional reporting when AI-generated productivity data is used as a basis for staffing reductions that result in adverse patient events. The GAO-23-105491 report specifically identified the absence of post-market surveillance as a gap in the current regulatory framework, and the ASA believes that closing this gap is a prerequisite for any responsible acceleration of AI adoption in clinical settings.⏎⏎Third, HHS should direct ONC to require that any AI tool seeking certification under the Health IT Certification Program demonstrate equity performance across the demographic subgroups defined in 42 U.S.C. 300kk, with particular attention to racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic stratification of algorithm outputs. The Obermeyer et al. 2019 findings in Science should be treated as a baseline warning about what happens when this requirement is absent, and the ASA recommends that ONC condition certification on independent third-party validation rather than vendor self-attestation.⏎⏎Fourth, and perhaps most directly relevant to the reimbursement questions the RFI is soliciting input on, the Department should establish as a condition of any new AI reimbursement pathway under Medicare or Medicaid that the billing entity attest to physician oversight of the AI-generated clinical output and that the AI tool has not been used to reduce the frequency or duration of direct physician contact with the patient below the standard of care for the relevant clinical context. This is not a novel regulatory concept — it is consistent with the existing supervision requirements for diagnostic radiology and pathology services, and it reflects the ASA's core position that meaningful human professional responsibility must be preserved at every point of care regardless of what AI tools are present in the workflow.⏎⏎The ASA recognizes that these recommendations introduce friction into the acceleration process the RFI envisions, and we want to be direct about that. We are not opposed to AI in clinical settings. Our members use and in many cases actively support monitoring and decision-support technologies in perioperative care. What we are opposed to is the institutional pattern — well-documented in the research literature and in our own members' experience in Michigan and elsewhere — in which tools marketed as support for clinical workers are deployed as instruments of labor displacement and productivity extraction, with the costs borne by clinicians and ultimately by patients. HHS has an obligation to get this right before it gets it fast, and the ASA respectfully but firmly urges the Department to revise the framing of this initiative accordingly.⏎⏎We also want to flag, before closing, that the RFI does not address the question of how AI deployment affects the training pipeline for physician anesthesiologists and other procedural specialists. If AI tools take over the monitoring and documentation functions that currently provide trainees with supervised exposure to the full scope of perioperative management, the long-term effect on residency training quality and board certification readiness is a concern the ASA has not yet seen any federal agency adequately address. We raise it here not because we have a fully developed policy recommendation — we do not, and we want to be honest about that — but because we think it belongs in the scope of this RFI and we are concerned it will be treated as out of scope if not explicitly surfaced by commenters.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Melissa Young⏎Director of Government Affairs⏎American Society of Anesthesiologists⏎1061 American Lane⏎Schaumburg, Illinois 60173⏎myoung@asahq.org⏎⏎ASA Comments | HHS AI RFI — Clinical Care | Page 6♔♔2026-01-21T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-21T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔7♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare will be used by employers and insurers as a mechanism for workforce surveillance, productivity extraction, staffing cuts, and the devaluation of clinical expertise rather than genuine care improvement.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔hopeful♔Michigan♔director of government affairs♔36♔A 2024 TMA member survey of more than 2,800 Texas physicians found that 58% reported using at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or administrative tool in their practice, yet 74% of those users identified reimbursement uncertainty as the primary barrier to deeper integration. SYNTH-0061♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Stephanie Jones♔♔♔♔♔♔COMMENT OF STEPHANIE JONES, LCSW⏎Submitted in Response to the HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket: HHS-ASTP-ONC-2024-AI-RFI⏎⏎⏎I. PRELIMINARY STATEMENT⏎⏎My name is Stephanie Jones. I am a licensed clinical social worker based in Chicago, Illinois, with seventeen years of practice in community health settings, the last eight of them focused on care coordination for patients with chronic disease who face significant barriers to access. I am submitting this comment as an individual, not on behalf of any organization.⏎⏎I want to be clear at the outset that this comment is not written in opposition to artificial intelligence in healthcare. I have seen what these tools can do. One of my clients, Darnell, a 58-year-old man with unmanaged Type 2 diabetes and no reliable transportation, was connected through a community health initiative to a telehealth platform that used an AI triage tool to flag symptom patterns in between scheduled visits. His primary care physician called me directly to discuss how quickly the system had identified a deteriorating trend in his self-reported data. That conversation shifted something in how I think about what technology can do for people in under-resourced communities. I am not writing to dismiss that.⏎⏎What I am writing to say is that the question of whether AI can help people like Darnell is entirely separate from the question of whether HHS has the democratic authority to accelerate AI embedding in clinical infrastructure to the point where that embedding becomes practically irreversible. The RFI conflates those questions. That conflation is a governance failure, and I think HHS should hear that from someone who actually believes the technology has promise.⏎⏎⏎II. THE FRAMING PROBLEM IN THE RFI⏎⏎The HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information (ASTP/ONC, 2024) describes regulatory uncertainty as an impediment to innovation and asks what the Department can do to remove barriers to AI adoption. That framing is not neutral. It presupposes that faster adoption is the appropriate goal and positions democratic oversight mechanisms as friction to be reduced. I understand why agencies do this. The pressure to show that government can support innovation is real. But when the RFI language asks how HHS can "accelerate" adoption and treat existing regulatory scrutiny as an obstacle, it has already answered the normative question before soliciting public input on it.⏎⏎Sheila Jasanoff's work on the democratic governance of technology is relevant here in ways that go beyond academic theory. In "The Ethics of Invention" (Norton, 2016), Jasanoff argues that technological transformation of public institutions requires something more than expert consensus and agency initiative. It requires what she calls "civic epistemology" -- the shared frameworks through which societies decide what kinds of futures they are willing to authorize. An RFI, by definition, is not that process. It is a useful input-gathering mechanism, but it reaches primarily the organized and the credentialed. The question of whether medicine should be restructured around systems whose internal logic cannot be audited by the people subject to them is a question that most of Darnell's neighbors in the Austin neighborhood on Chicago's west side have never been asked and are not likely to answer through this docket.⏎⏎Langdon Winner made a version of this argument about technology and politics in 1980 that I keep returning to. In "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" (Daedalus, 109(1), 1980), he observed that technological systems embed power relationships that persist long after the decisions that created them are forgotten. The people who designed those systems made choices -- about what to optimize for, whose data to use, what counts as a good outcome -- and those choices become invisible once the system is operational. Accelerating adoption means accelerating the point at which those embedded choices become the infrastructure. That is a political act, not just a technical one.⏎⏎⏎III. THE IRREVERSIBILITY PROBLEM⏎⏎The argument I want HHS to take seriously is not that AI tools are dangerous in themselves. It is that the pace of adoption the RFI contemplates, and the institutional dependency that follows from it, forecloses future democratic choices in ways that cannot be undone by subsequent regulation.⏎⏎Enrico Coiera wrote about this directly in a 2019 paper in the Journal of Medical Internet Research ("The last mile: where artificial intelligence meets reality," JMIR, 21(11), 2019). His concern was that once clinical workflows are restructured around AI decision support, the human expertise required to function without those tools begins to atrophy. Clinicians stop developing the observational and inferential skills that the AI has taken over. Institutions stop training for them. The knowledge infrastructure that would allow you to identify when the AI is wrong, or to operate without it during a failure, degrades. This is not a hypothetical. It is a documented pattern in other high-stakes domains, from aviation to nuclear power, where automation dependency has created brittleness rather than resilience. In healthcare, the consequence is not just operational disruption. It is patient harm that is invisible precisely because there is no longer a baseline against which to measure it.⏎⏎The irreversibility concern is compounded when the tools in question are proprietary. Ziad Obermeyer and colleagues published a study in Science in 2019 ("Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations," Science, 366(6464)) that found a widely deployed commercial algorithm was systematically underestimating the health needs of Black patients -- not because of malicious intent, but because the algorithm used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, and Black patients with the same disease burden historically generated lower costs due to differential access to care. The bias was structural, embedded in the training data, and invisible to the clinicians using the tool. The authors were able to document it only through external analysis. The institutions that had deployed the tool could not have identified it from the inside.⏎⏎Andrew Selbst and colleagues made a related point in a 2019 paper at the ACM FAccT conference ("Fairness and Abstraction in Sociotechnical Systems," 2019): that AI systems embedded in institutional workflows resist correction even when bias has been documented, because the workflow has been reorganized around the system's outputs, and the cost of correction is borne by the institution, not by the vendor. This is the mechanism through which documented harm fails to produce remediation. The question is not whether HHS can identify bad actors after the fact. The question is whether, once adoption reaches the level the RFI contemplates, the institutional capacity to change course will exist at all.⏎⏎I want to be honest that I don't have a clean answer to this. I'm not sure anyone does. But the absence of a clean answer is an argument for caution, not for acceleration.⏎⏎⏎IV. WHAT THE RFI GETS WRONG ABOUT OVERSIGHT AND INNOVATION⏎⏎The RFI frames regulatory scrutiny and innovation as being in tension. I think this gets the relationship backwards, and I want to say why.⏎⏎The value of prospective oversight is not that it prevents bad things from happening after the fact. It is that it shapes the design choices that get made before deployment. If developers know that a clinical AI tool will be required to disclose training data demographics, audit results, and performance metrics disaggregated by race, income, and geography before receiving reimbursement, they will build tools that can produce that information. If they know they can deploy first and defend later, they will build tools optimized for the metrics that get measured, which in current practice means aggregate accuracy in majority populations.⏎⏎Britanny Mittelstadt and colleagues made this structural point in a 2016 paper in Big Data & Society ("The ethics of algorithms: Mapping the debate," 3(2), 2016): that the conditions for meaningful democratic oversight of algorithmic systems are largely absent under current frameworks, because the information needed to evaluate the systems is held by vendors, the expertise needed to interpret that information is concentrated among researchers who depend on vendor cooperation, and the regulatory infrastructure for independent audit does not exist in clinical AI the way it exists in, say, pharmaceuticals or medical devices. The RFI's approach of soliciting input on how to reduce regulatory barriers does not address any of these structural conditions. It treats oversight as a matter of reducing paperwork rather than as a matter of building the institutional infrastructure that would make oversight meaningful.⏎⏎I should be specific about what I mean. The following are not the same thing:⏎⏎1. Requiring a vendor to self-certify that their tool was tested for bias before deployment.⏎2. Requiring independent pre-market review of training data composition and performance disaggregation as a condition of reimbursement eligibility.⏎3. Requiring post-deployment surveillance with mandatory reporting of adverse outcomes by demographic subgroup, with data held by a public entity rather than the vendor.⏎4. Requiring that any clinical AI system approved for use in federally funded care settings be technically capable of being removed and replaced without loss of core clinical function -- what you might call a reversibility standard.⏎⏎The RFI does not ask about any of these in terms that suggest HHS is considering them as conditions of accelerated adoption. That is a significant omission.⏎⏎⏎V. THE DEMOCRATIC LEGITIMACY QUESTION⏎⏎I want to be careful here because I am not arguing that HHS lacks the legal authority to take the actions it is contemplating. I am arguing something different: that legal authority and democratic legitimacy are not the same thing, and that the scale of transformation contemplated in the RFI deserves a more deliberate public authorization process than an agency information-gathering exercise.⏎⏎When I sit with Darnell and help him navigate his care, I am operating within a system of professional ethics, regulatory accountability, and institutional oversight that has been built up over decades through legislation, litigation, professional standard-setting, and public deliberation. That system is imperfect. It fails people like Darnell in documented, systematic ways. But it is accountable in principle, and the mechanisms of accountability are publicly legible. You can file a complaint, you can sue, you can organize, you can vote. The system responds, slowly and imperfectly, but it responds.⏎⏎What I am worried about is a healthcare infrastructure in which the consequential decisions -- who gets flagged, who gets resources, whose symptoms get taken seriously -- are made by systems whose internal logic is proprietary, whose training data is not public, whose performance by subgroup is not reported, and whose removal, once institutional dependency has set in, is practically impossible regardless of what any democratic process decides. Jasanoff's framework is relevant again here: the question is not whether the technology is good or bad in the abstract. The question is whether the society authorizing its use has the capacity to understand what it is authorizing, to monitor whether it is working as intended, and to change course if it is not. Under the conditions the RFI describes, I am not confident that capacity will exist once adoption reaches scale.⏎⏎I want to say one more thing about the democratic legitimacy question before moving on. A society has the legitimate right to decide that medicine should remain stubbornly human even at some cost to efficiency. I am not sure that is the right decision. I have seen what happened for Darnell, and I do not take that lightly. But the right to make that decision -- and to make it through a process that reaches the people who will bear the consequences, not just the people who will profit from the technology -- is not something HHS can waive by framing regulatory scrutiny as an obstacle to progress. That framing is a choice. It is a political choice dressed up as a technical observation.⏎⏎⏎VI. SPECIFIC REQUESTS⏎⏎Given the foregoing, I am asking HHS to consider the following in its response to this RFI:⏎⏎First, I am asking HHS to explicitly acknowledge in any subsequent guidance or rulemaking that the pace and reversibility of AI adoption in clinical settings are themselves policy choices with democratic implications, and that they require broader public deliberation than this RFI process has provided. This does not mean paralysis. It means transparency about what is being decided and who is deciding it.⏎⏎Second, I am asking HHS to reframe its approach around what I would call precautionary deployment standards -- not as a barrier to innovation, but as a condition of it. Specifically, I would ask HHS to consider requiring, as a condition of Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement for AI-assisted clinical services:⏎⏎a. Pre-deployment disclosure of training data composition, including demographic representation, and independent review of performance metrics disaggregated by race, income, insurance status, and geography.⏎⏎b. Mandatory post-deployment surveillance with adverse outcome reporting by demographic subgroup, with data reported to a public registry rather than held exclusively by the vendor.⏎⏎c. A reversibility standard: any clinical AI system used in federally funded settings must be designed and implemented in a way that allows the institution to remove or replace the system without losing core clinical function. This standard should be evaluated at the time of procurement, not after dependency has developed.⏎⏎d. A public deliberation requirement: before HHS takes any regulatory action to accelerate adoption at scale, it should conduct a structured public engagement process -- not an RFI, but something more like the public comment processes used for major environmental decisions -- in communities that will be disproportionately affected by both the benefits and the failures of clinical AI, including communities of color and communities with limited access to healthcare infrastructure.⏎⏎Third, and I recognize this is a harder ask, I would like HHS to commission and publish an analysis of what "acceleration" means in terms of the institutional dependency and knowledge atrophy dynamics that Coiera and others have documented. If the goal is durable, equitable improvement in clinical outcomes, the speed of adoption is not obviously the right variable to maximize. There may be a pace of adoption that allows institutions to maintain the human expertise and oversight capacity needed to catch algorithmic errors -- and that pace may be slower than what the RFI contemplates. I do not know the answer to that. I am not sure HHS does either, and I think it should say so.⏎⏎⏎VII. A NOTE ON WHERE I LAND⏎⏎I said at the beginning that I am not anti-technology, and I want to be honest about what that means in practice. When I think about Darnell, and about the dozens of clients I have worked with over seventeen years who have fallen through the gaps of a healthcare system that was too slow, too fragmented, and too indifferent to catch them, I am genuinely not sure that a slower, more cautious approach to AI adoption is the right answer. The status quo is not neutral. It harms people. I hold that alongside everything else I have said.⏎⏎But I keep coming back to the Obermeyer study, and to what it means that a tool systematically underestimating the health needs of Black patients was deployed at scale across health systems before anyone outside the research community identified the problem. Darnell is Black. He is 58. He has unmanaged diabetes and no reliable transportation. He is exactly the person who would be most harmed if an algorithm trained on populations with better access to care was applied to him without anyone checking whether the training data reflected his reality. The AI triage tool that helped him -- I still don't know whose patient population it was trained on. I asked. The answer I got was that the information was proprietary.⏎⏎That is not an acceptable answer for a system making clinical judgments about my clients. And the RFI, as currently framed, does not give me confidence that HHS intends to make it unacceptable.⏎⏎I recognize that HHS is trying to do something genuinely useful here. I am asking the Department to do it in a way that takes democratic governance seriously, builds the oversight infrastructure before dependency sets in, and treats the communities most likely to be harmed by algorithmic failure as participants in the decision, not just recipients of the result.⏎⏎Stephanie Jones, LCSW⏎Chicago, Illinois⏎Submitted via regulations.gov♔♔2026-01-21T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-21T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔8♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Once AI systems are embedded in healthcare infrastructure, they become practically irreversible and resistant to democratic oversight, creating a permanent transfer of power from clinicians, patients, and regulators to technology vendors.♔individual♔high♔supportive♔Illinois♔social worker♔40♔When my client Darnell — a 58-year-old with unmanaged Type 2 diabetes and no reliable transportation — finally got connected to a telehealth platform that used an AI triage tool, the difference in how quickly his care team flagged his worsening symptoms was striking enough that his primary care physician called *me* to talk about it. Abbott operates across diagnostics, cardiovascular devices, neuromodulation, and connected care platforms, and our regulatory affairs function maintains structured visibility into how AI tools are being procured, deployed, and used across the payer-provider interface in multiple state markets. That vantage point is precisely why this RFI, despite its breadth, gives Abbott serious pause. The Department has framed this inquiry as though "AI in healthcare" is primarily a clinical care adoption story — a question of how to get more validated diagnostic and decision-support tools into the hands of clinicians faster. That framing is, at minimum, incomplete, and at worst it will produce policy that accelerates harm while the Department congratulates itself on innovation.⏎⏎The most mature, most widely deployed, and most profitable AI applications in the U.S. health sector today are not operating in clinical care pathways. They are operating in payer prior authorization and claims denial workflows. This is not a contested empirical claim. The U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations documented in October 2024 that Medicare Advantage plans have deployed AI systems to systematically override physician judgments at scale, with denial rates in some plans running at multiples of what manual review would produce ("Denial, Delay, Deny," Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, October 2024). STAT News reported in November 2023 that internal UnitedHealth documents revealed the scope of automated claims rejections being generated by the company's AI system, with denial rates that UnitedHealth's own internal reviewers found difficult to reconcile with clinical appropriateness standards (Mukherjee, STAT News, November 2023). The HHS Office of Inspector General concluded in April 2022 that some Medicare Advantage organization denials of prior authorization requests raised serious concerns about beneficiary access to medically necessary care, with the OIG identifying a pattern of denials that were subsequently reversed on appeal at high rates (OIG Report OEI-09-18-00260, April 2022). Abbott finds it genuinely difficult to understand how the Department can solicit broad public input on "AI in healthcare" without once, in the body of the RFI, directly engaging with this documented pattern of AI-driven denial automation.⏎⏎Abbott Laboratories | HHS AI RFI Comments | January 2025 | Page 2⏎⏎THE REIMBURSEMENT ACCELERATION PROBLEM⏎⏎Abbott's concern sharpens considerably when the RFI turns to reimbursement policy. The Department has suggested that reimbursement architecture can function as a lever to "foster competition among clinical care AI tool builders." Abbott does not dispute that reimbursement ambiguity is a real barrier to clinical AI adoption. Our regulatory affairs team's analysis of procurement cycles in payer-provider markets across multiple states is consistent with broader industry findings: coverage uncertainty materially extends time-to-deployment for FDA-cleared AI tools, and coding inadequacy is a genuine structural problem. The Kaiser Family Foundation documented in March 2023 that prior authorization in Medicare Advantage is used at high frequency, with beneficiaries frequently unable to navigate the appeals process when denials are issued (Koma, Jacobson, Damico & Neuman, KFF Issue Brief, March 2023). The American Medical Association's 2023 Prior Authorization Physician Survey found that 94 percent of physicians reported that prior authorization requirements had delayed patient access to necessary care, with a substantial proportion reporting serious adverse clinical events as a result (AMA Policy Research Perspectives, 2023). These are not abstract regulatory concerns. They describe a system in which AI-assisted denial has become a cost-containment instrument deployed against patients who cannot effectively contest it.⏎⏎What troubles Abbott about the reimbursement framing in this RFI is that any coverage or payment architecture that rewards "AI-assisted care decisions" without specifying what counts as a care decision, and without distinguishing between clinical support tools and payer utilization management tools, will be captured by the side of the market where AI denial automation is already generating measurable harm. The National Health Law Program documented in February 2024 that algorithms are replacing human judgment in Medicaid and Medicare Managed Care denials at a pace that has outrun regulatory oversight, with particularly acute effects on elderly, disabled, and low-income beneficiaries who lack the administrative capacity to pursue appeals (NHeLP Policy Report, February 2024). The proposed rule published at 88 Fed. Reg. 82,510 (November 24, 2023) on prior authorization processes for Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, CHIP, and QHP issuers acknowledged some of these concerns but did not address the specific question of AI-generated denials with the specificity the documented harm warrants. If HHS moves forward with reimbursement policies designed to accelerate AI adoption without conditioning those policies on demonstrated clinical appropriateness rather than cost-containment performance, the predictable outcome is not better care. The predictable outcome is a better-funded denial apparatus.⏎⏎Abbott Laboratories | HHS AI RFI Comments | January 2025 | Page 3⏎⏎Abbott also wants to register a concern about algorithmic bias that the RFI's clinical-benefit framing tends to obscure. Obermeyer and colleagues demonstrated in Science in 2019 that a widely used commercial algorithm for managing population health systematically disadvantaged Black patients by using healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, producing racially biased outputs at scale before the bias was identified (Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli & Mullainathan, Science, 366(6464), 447-453, 2019). That finding has direct relevance to payer AI systems, where cost-containment objectives are built into the design architecture in ways that may produce disparate impacts on minority and low-income populations. The Department's RFI does not grapple with this. It treats AI performance primarily as a question of clinical validation metrics rather than as a question of who bears the cost when those metrics are wrong or when the optimization target is misaligned with patient welfare. Abbott recognizes that raising this concern in a comment nominally about clinical care adoption may seem outside scope. Abbott does not accept that framing. If HHS is going to use this RFI as the basis for a broad AI acceleration agenda, the Department is obligated to account for the full distribution of AI deployments in the health sector, not only the ones that are easiest to frame as beneficial.⏎⏎WHAT HHS MUST DO BEFORE PROCEEDING⏎⏎Abbott urges the Department to take three specific actions before any AI reimbursement or coverage acceleration policy is finalized. First, HHS must require that AI-generated prior authorization denials be subject to mandatory, expedited human review by a qualified clinician, with that requirement operationalized through conditions of participation or Medicare Advantage contract requirements, not left to voluntary compliance. The Senate Subcommittee's October 2024 report documented cases in which AI systems were generating denials faster than any human reviewer could plausibly have evaluated the underlying clinical record. That is not utilization management. That is automated obstruction, and it requires a structural remedy, not a guidance document.⏎⏎Second, HHS must require public reporting of prior authorization denial rates, appeal rates, reversal rates, and time-to-determination, disaggregated by patient demographic characteristics including race, ethnicity, age, disability status, and income proxy. Fuse Brown and McCuskey argued in the Harvard Journal on Legislation in 2023 that accountability for algorithmic insurance decisions requires transparency mechanisms that are currently absent from the regulatory framework governing Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care plans (Fuse Brown & McCuskey, Harvard Journal on Legislation, 60(1), 1-58, 2023). Abbott agrees, and would add that demographic disaggregation is not optional if the Department is serious about health equity. A denial rate that looks acceptable in aggregate may conceal systematic disparate impact on protected populations.⏎⏎Abbott Laboratories | HHS AI RFI Comments | January 2025 | Page 4⏎⏎Third, and most directly relevant to the RFI's reimbursement questions, HHS should condition any new AI-related coverage or payment policy on a demonstrated clinical appropriateness standard that is defined independently of cost-containment outcomes. Abbott is a medical device and diagnostics company with a direct commercial interest in seeing FDA-cleared AI tools reach patients faster, and Abbott is still saying this. The reimbursement acceleration the Department is contemplating will not produce the clinical benefit story the RFI anticipates if the policy architecture does not distinguish between tools that support clinical judgment and tools that are designed to override it. Schulte and Fry documented in Kaiser Health News and Fortune in March 2019 that algorithmic systems in healthcare administration have a consistent pattern of generating harms that were not anticipated at deployment and that are difficult to reverse once the administrative infrastructure has been built around them. The prior authorization denial automation problem is a current, live instance of exactly that pattern. HHS has the authority and the obligation to address it before layering additional acceleration incentives onto a market that is already generating documented harm.⏎⏎Abbott appreciates the Department's attention to this submission and requests that these comments be entered into the docket record in full. SYNTH-0067♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Ashley Baker♔National Consumers League♔♔♔♔♔National Consumers League | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 1⏎⏎The National Consumers League submits these comments in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care settings. NCL represents the interests of consumers across healthcare markets, and the organization's work on health equity gives us particular concern about the framework — or rather, the absence of a framework — that this RFI proposes for ensuring that AI tools deployed in clinical settings do not reproduce and amplify the disparities that already define who survives serious illness in this country. These comments focus primarily on the RFI's treatment of equity auditing requirements and post-deployment surveillance, two areas where the Department's current posture is, in our assessment, not merely incomplete but likely to produce foreseeable harm at scale.⏎⏎The Global Liver Institute's 2024 cross-sectional analysis across 47 affiliated hepatology centers found that 68% of liver disease patients experienced diagnostic delays exceeding 90 days between symptom onset and confirmed diagnosis (Global Liver Institute, "Diagnostic Delay in Liver Disease: A Cross-Sectional Analysis Across 47 Affiliated Hepatology Centers," GLI Network Report, 2024). That number is not an abstraction. It represents patients who arrived at hepatocellular carcinoma diagnoses after the window for curative intervention had closed, patients whose fibrosis had progressed from F2 to F4 while they waited for imaging that was never prioritized, patients in rural Louisiana and the Mississippi Delta and communities across the Gulf South where hepatology capacity is thin and primary care providers are managing liver disease without specialist support. GLI's 2023 State of Liver Health Survey, drawing on responses from more than 12,000 patients and caregivers, identified diagnostic delay as the single most consequential barrier to survival among liver disease patients, and specifically called out the intersection of delay with race, geography, and insurance status as the defining structural pattern in who dies preventably from liver cancer and cirrhosis (Global Liver Institute, "State of Liver Health Survey: Patient and Caregiver Perspectives on Diagnostic Delay and Access to Care," GLI Policy Research Series, 2023). GLI's policy team has tracked at least 14 FDA-cleared AI tools with direct applications to liver disease management — tools for non-invasive fibrosis staging, imaging-based HCC risk stratification, and early detection algorithms — that remain largely inaccessible to the patients who need them most because reimbursement pathways are fragmented and clinical integration frameworks do not exist. NCL is raising these points not to rehearse familiar statistics but to establish that the communities at the center of this comment are not hypothetical beneficiaries of AI innovation. They are real patients, in real places, for whom diagnostic delay is already a life-limiting condition, and they are the same communities that will bear the greatest risk if AI tools are deployed without equity safeguards.⏎⏎National Consumers League | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 2⏎⏎The RFI's treatment of equity is aspirational where it should be structural. HHS frames responsible AI deployment as a goal and invites comment on how to encourage equitable outcomes, but the document proposes no mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing and no post-deployment bias surveillance requirements. This is not an oversight. It is a structural choice, and its consequences are predictable because the evidence base documenting algorithmic bias in clinical AI is now substantial enough that regulators cannot credibly claim ignorance of the failure modes. Ziad Obermeyer and colleagues published what has become the landmark empirical demonstration of this problem in Science in 2019: a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to identify high-risk patients for care management programs systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent illness burden, because the algorithm used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, and historical spending patterns reflected decades of discriminatory access rather than actual clinical severity (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S, "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations," Science, 2019;366(6464):447-453). The algorithm was not designed to be discriminatory. It was trained on data that encoded discrimination, and it reproduced that discrimination at scale across every institution that deployed it. That is the mechanism NCL is asking HHS to take seriously: AI systems trained on historical healthcare data do not merely reflect past disparities, they institutionalize them, and they do so in ways that are harder to detect than equivalent human error because the output carries an aura of computational objectivity that discourages scrutiny.⏎⏎The pulse oximetry literature makes the same point through a different modality. Sjoding and colleagues demonstrated in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 that pulse oximeters — devices that had been in routine clinical use for decades — systematically overestimated oxygen saturation in Black patients compared to white patients, and that this measurement bias translated directly into delayed recognition of occult hypoxemia and, by inference, delayed treatment (Sjoding MW, Dickson RP, Iwashyna TJ, Gay SE, Valley TS, "Racial bias in pulse oximetry measurement," N Engl J Med, 2020;383(25):2477-2478). This device had been FDA-cleared, widely adopted, and treated as a reliable physiological measurement for years before the racial bias in its performance was documented. The parallel to AI-assisted diagnostic tools is direct. FDA clearance establishes that a device performs adequately on a validation population. It does not establish that the device performs equitably across the full demographic range of patients who will encounter it in clinical settings, and it does not require manufacturers to disclose the composition of training data or validation cohorts in ways that would allow deploying institutions to assess differential performance risk before purchase. The dermatology AI literature has documented the same validation-gap problem: Adamson and Smith reported in JAMA Dermatology in 2018 that deep learning models for skin lesion classification were trained predominantly on images of light-skinned patients and performed substantially worse on darker skin tones, a disparity that mapped almost perfectly onto the populations with the highest rates of delayed melanoma diagnosis (Adamson AS, Smith A, "Machine learning and health care disparities in dermatology," JAMA Dermatol, 2018;154(11):1247-1248). These are not isolated failure cases. They are a pattern.⏎⏎National Consumers League | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 3⏎⏎The validation-gap problem is particularly acute for the liver disease patients GLI serves because those patients are disproportionately located in the exact clinical settings where AI tools are most likely to fail silently. AI tools for clinical decision support are predominantly developed and validated at academic medical centers with large, well-curated patient datasets, robust EHR infrastructure, and specialist oversight capacity. When those tools are deployed in community hospitals, rural health systems, federally qualified health centers, and safety-net institutions — the settings where liver disease burden is highest and diagnostic delay is most severe — they encounter patient populations that differ systematically from the training and validation populations in ways that matter for model performance: different comorbidity profiles, different patterns of prior healthcare utilization, different imaging equipment, different documentation practices, different laboratory reference ranges. Wong and colleagues published an external validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021 and found that the model's discriminative performance degraded substantially when evaluated outside the institution where it was developed, with the performance gap widening in patient subgroups that were underrepresented in the original training data (Wong A, Otles E, Donnelly JP, et al., "External validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model in hospitalized patients," JAMA Intern Med, 2021;181(8):1065-1070). The model had been deployed across hundreds of hospitals before this external validation was published. Hospitals that had purchased and integrated the tool had no mechanism for detecting that its performance in their specific patient population differed from the performance the vendor had reported. That is the scenario that will replicate itself across liver disease AI tools if HHS does not require pre-deployment validation in the specific institutional contexts where tools will be used, with stratified performance reporting by race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, insurance status, and geography.⏎⏎Automation bias compounds the validation-gap problem in ways that make disparate harm particularly difficult to detect and correct after the fact. The clinical decision support literature has documented consistently that clinicians tend to defer to algorithmic outputs even when those outputs conflict with their own clinical judgment, and that this deference is strongest in high-volume, high-pressure clinical environments where cognitive load is greatest (Char DS, Shah NH, Magnus D, "Implementing machine learning in health care — addressing ethical challenges," N Engl J Med, 2018;378(11):981-983). Those are precisely the environments — understaffed community EDs, rural primary care practices carrying panels that would be unmanageable even with adequate support — where the liver disease patients GLI serves receive care. A primary care provider in a rural Louisiana parish who is managing 2,500 patients with two support staff and no on-site hepatology consultation is not in a position to critically evaluate the output of an AI-assisted risk-stratification tool that tells her a patient's fibrosis risk is low. She is going to trust it, because she does not have the time or the specialist resources to second-guess it, and because the tool arrived with FDA clearance and institutional procurement approval and the implicit endorsement of a health system that marketed it as a quality improvement initiative. If that tool was trained on data from a tertiary academic center where the patient population was 70% white and commercially insured, and it is now being used on a patient population that is 60% Black and 40% Medicaid-enrolled, its risk scores may be systematically wrong in ways that will not become visible until a pattern of missed diagnoses accumulates over months or years. By that point, patients have been harmed. Nagendran and colleagues conducted a systematic review of deep learning studies in medical imaging published in the BMJ in 2020 and found that the majority of studies did not report performance stratified by patient subgroup, making it effectively impossible to assess differential accuracy across demographic groups from the published literature alone (Nagendran M, Chen Y, Lovejoy CA, et al., "Artificial intelligence versus clinicians: systematic review of design, reporting standards, and claims of deep learning studies in medical imaging," BMJ, 2020;368:m689). The reporting gap in the research literature is mirrored by a surveillance gap in clinical deployment, and together they ensure that disparate harm remains invisible.⏎⏎National Consumers League | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 4⏎⏎The race-encoding problem in medical imaging adds another layer of concern that is directly relevant to liver disease AI tools. Gichoya and colleagues published a modelling study in Lancet Digital Health in 2022 demonstrating that AI models trained on medical imaging data could identify patient race from radiological images with high accuracy, even when the images had been stripped of demographic metadata, and even for imaging modalities where no physiological basis for race encoding was known (Wawira Gichoya J, Banerjee I, Bhimireddy AR, et al., "AI recognition of patient race in medical imaging: a modelling study," Lancet Digit Health, 2022;4(6):e406-e414). The mechanism is not fully understood, but the implication is significant: AI tools for imaging interpretation in liver disease — ultrasound-based fibrosis assessment, CT-based HCC detection, MRI-based lesion characterization — may be encoding race as a latent variable in their predictions in ways that are not disclosed by developers, not detectable by deploying institutions, and not auditable under current regulatory frameworks. If a tool's risk scores are influenced by a latent race signal in the imaging data, and if that signal is correlated with historical underdiagnosis in Black patients, the tool may systematically generate lower risk scores for Black patients with equivalent pathology, reproducing the exact diagnostic delay pattern that is already the leading cause of preventable liver cancer death in the communities GLI serves. Vyas and colleagues published an analysis in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 examining the use of race correction in clinical algorithms more broadly and found that race-based adjustments embedded in widely used clinical tools — the eGFR equation, the VBAC risk calculator, the cardiac risk tools — systematically shifted care recommendations in ways that disadvantaged Black patients, often without any valid physiological basis for the race adjustment (Vyas DA, Eisenstein LEI, Jones DS, "Hidden in plain sight — reconsidering the use of race correction in clinical algorithms," N Engl J Med, 2020;383(9):874-882). The liver disease AI tools currently seeking clinical deployment have not been systematically audited for analogous race-encoding problems, and the RFI does not propose any mechanism for requiring such audits.⏎⏎Parikh and colleagues offered a framework for addressing bias in AI health care tools in JAMA in 2019 that remains relevant to the current regulatory question: they argued that bias mitigation requires attention at three stages — data curation, model development, and clinical deployment — and that post-deployment surveillance is indispensable because bias that is not present in development data can emerge when tools encounter real-world patient populations (Parikh RB, Teeple S, Navathe AS, "Addressing bias in artificial intelligence in health care," JAMA, 2019;322(24):2377-2378). The RFI proposes voluntary best practices at the first two stages and says essentially nothing about the third. Pierson and colleagues published a study in Nature Medicine in 2021 that is worth noting in this context because it demonstrates that algorithmic approaches can actually be used to identify and partially correct for unexplained pain disparities in underserved populations — that is, AI is not inherently a vector for inequity, and NCL is not arguing that it is (Pierson E, Cutler DM, Leskovec J, Mullainathan S, Obermeyer Z, "An algorithmic approach to reducing unexplained pain disparities in underserved populations," Nat Med, 2021;27(1):136-140). The argument is rather that AI tools deployed without mandatory equity auditing and post-deployment surveillance will reproduce disparities by default, and that tools deployed with those safeguards have the potential to detect and correct disparities that human clinical judgment has failed to correct for decades. The RFI's framing treats equity safeguards as constraints on innovation when they are more accurately described as the conditions under which innovation can actually reach the patients who need it most.⏎⏎National Consumers League | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 5⏎⏎NCL is therefore requesting that HHS take the following specific regulatory actions in response to this RFI, and NCL wants to be direct that these are not aspirational suggestions but minimum conditions for a deployment framework that will not predictably harm the patients this RFI is ostensibly designed to serve:⏎⏎1. Mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing. HHS should require, as a condition of Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement for AI-assisted clinical decision support tools, that developers submit stratified performance data demonstrating that tool accuracy does not differ meaningfully across patient subgroups defined by race, ethnicity, primary language, socioeconomic status, insurance status, and geography. This audit must be conducted on a validation dataset that is representative of the patient population in the intended deployment context, not merely the population in the developer's training data. Tools for which stratified performance data cannot be produced should not be eligible for reimbursement until such data are available.⏎⏎2. Mandatory post-deployment bias surveillance. HHS should require deploying institutions to implement ongoing monitoring of AI tool performance stratified by the same demographic and socioeconomic variables listed above, with reporting requirements to a centralized federal registry that can identify emerging disparate harm patterns across institutions before those patterns produce widespread patient injury. This surveillance requirement should apply to all AI tools used in clinical decision support, regardless of whether the tool was developed internally or purchased from a commercial vendor.⏎⏎3. A moratorium on deployment in safety-net settings pending context-specific validation. HHS should establish a temporary moratorium on the deployment of AI clinical decision support tools in federally qualified health centers, critical access hospitals, and safety-net institutions until those tools have been validated in patient populations and institutional contexts that are representative of the settings where they will be used. This is not a permanent prohibition. It is a sequencing requirement that ensures tools are validated where they will actually operate before they are used to make clinical decisions about the most vulnerable patients in the system.⏎⏎o  The moratorium should include an expedited pathway for developers who can demonstrate context-specific validation, so that tools that have done the work are not penalized for the failures of tools that have not.⏎⏎o  HHS should provide technical assistance and funding to safety-net institutions to support the infrastructure needed to participate in post-deployment surveillance reporting, recognizing that requiring surveillance without resourcing it will produce a compliance burden that falls heaviest on the institutions least equipped to bear it.⏎⏎The case for these requirements is not theoretical. The 68% diagnostic delay rate documented in GLI's 47-center network analysis represents a baseline harm that already exists in the absence of AI. The question this RFI is actually asking — though it does not frame it this way — is whether AI deployment will reduce that harm equitably or whether it will reduce it for some patients while deepening it for others. The answer depends entirely on whether the deployment framework includes the safeguards described above. Without mandatory equity auditing, tools trained on academic medical center data will be deployed in community settings where they have not been validated, and their performance degradation will be invisible. Without post-deployment surveillance, the first signal of disparate harm will be a pattern of missed diagnoses that took years to accumulate and cannot be retroactively corrected for the patients who were injured. The RFI's current framework would accelerate deployment and leave the equity question to voluntary guidance, which is to say it would leave the equity question unanswered.⏎⏎National Consumers League | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 6⏎⏎NCL wants to acknowledge that there are genuine tensions in this regulatory space that the comment has not fully resolved. The moratorium proposal in particular will generate objection from developers and health systems that have invested in these tools and are eager to deploy them, and NCL recognizes that delay in deployment also has costs — including, for liver disease patients, continued diagnostic delay during the period when validated tools could be helping. That tension is real and NCL does not dismiss it. But the answer to that tension is not to deploy unvalidated tools in vulnerable settings and hope the disparate harm is not too severe. The answer is to invest in the validation infrastructure that would allow equitable deployment to happen faster — to fund the studies, support the data-sharing agreements, build the surveillance systems, and create the regulatory incentives that would make context-specific validation a routine part of the product development cycle rather than an obstacle that slows deployment after the fact. HHS has the authority and the resources to create those incentives, and the RFI is an opportunity to do exactly that. What the RFI currently proposes instead is an acceleration framework that treats equity as an add-on rather than a precondition, and that is the specific choice NCL is asking the Department to reconsider.⏎⏎One additional concern that NCL wants to place on the record, even though it does not fit neatly into the comment's primary argument, is the question of how deploying institutions will know when an AI tool's performance has drifted from its validated baseline. Model drift — the degradation of tool performance as the patient population or clinical context changes over time — is a documented phenomenon in deployed clinical AI, and it is particularly relevant in settings like rural health systems where patient population composition can shift substantially in response to economic or demographic changes. The current regulatory framework has no mechanism for requiring developers or deploying institutions to monitor for drift, and the RFI does not propose one. An institution that deployed a liver disease risk-stratification tool in 2025 based on a validation study conducted in 2023 on a patient population that no longer represents its current patient mix would have no way of knowing that the tool's risk scores had become unreliable. This is not a hypothetical edge case. It is the expected behavior of machine learning models deployed in dynamic real-world environments, and it is a problem that mandatory post-deployment surveillance would at minimum make visible, even if it could not by itself correct the underlying drift. SYNTH-0068♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Nancy Sanchez♔♔♔♔♔♔Nancy Sanchez⏎4812 Hickory Lane⏎Des Moines, Iowa 50317⏎⏎June 3, 2025⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Attention: Health Sector AI Request for Information⏎200 Independence Avenue SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎Two years ago, a cardiologist at a clinic off I-235 in Des Moines caught an irregular rhythm on my EKG that could have ended my CDL certification and, with it, my livelihood. The clinic had recently updated its diagnostic software, and the detection was faster and more precise than it would have been under the older system. I am not writing this comment to argue against that kind of progress. I have logged over a million miles across Iowa and Nebraska, and I understand, in a very practical way, what it means when a small detection window closes before you get another chance. What I want to say to HHS is something more specific than "go slow" or "be careful." What I want to say is that the thing that actually saved me was not the software by itself. It was the cardiologist who looked at me, not just at the readout, and asked whether I had been sleeping, whether the long winter runs had been harder than usual, whether there was stress at home. The software flagged something. The doctor figured out what it meant for a 57-year-old woman who drives twelve-hour shifts in February through western Nebraska.⏎⏎That distinction matters more than I think HHS's current framing acknowledges. When I read through the request for information, I see language about productivity, about adoption rates, about removing regulatory friction. Those are real concerns and I don't dismiss them. But the frame is almost entirely technical and economic, and it leaves out something that a significant body of clinical research has documented carefully. Kelley and colleagues published a systematic review and meta-analysis in PLOS ONE in 2014 showing that the quality of the patient-clinician relationship is an independent predictor of health outcomes, not just a soft measure of patient satisfaction. Hojat and colleagues found in Academic Medicine in 2011 that physicians' empathy scores were directly associated with better glycemic control in diabetic patients — measurably better, not just perceived as better. These are not fringe findings. The therapeutic relationship itself has clinical value that shows up in lab results and readmission rates. When HHS asks how to accelerate AI adoption in clinical settings without first asking what happens to that relationship when AI is inserted into the diagnostic encounter, it is skipping a foundational question.⏎⏎I want to be precise about what I mean, because I think the concern is sometimes caricatured as technophobia. Eric Topol wrote in Nature Medicine in 2019 that the real promise of AI in medicine is to give clinicians more time for the human work that machines cannot do, not less. I agree with that vision completely. What worries me is that the path HHS seems to be proposing — reducing regulatory friction, accelerating reimbursement, moving fast — may produce the opposite effect in practice. When clinics adopt AI tools primarily because they improve billing efficiency or throughput, the pressure is not toward more human time per patient. It is toward less. The tool becomes a substitute for the encounter rather than a support for it. Abraham Verghese has written and spoken at length about what is lost when the physical and relational dimensions of the clinical encounter are treated as optional — his 2011 piece in the Annals of Internal Medicine with colleagues on the bedside evaluation as both ritual and clinical instrument makes the case that the examination itself communicates something to the patient that changes how they receive and act on a diagnosis. I think about that when I imagine a truck driver in a rural DOT clinic getting an AI-generated readout handed to them with minimal clinician explanation. The readout might be accurate. The patient might still leave confused, unheard, and less likely to follow through.⏎⏎There is also a safety dimension that I think belongs in this conversation and that the RFI does not address directly enough. Automation bias is a well-documented phenomenon. Goddard and colleagues published a systematic review in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association in 2012 specifically examining how clinicians over-rely on automated outputs even when those outputs are wrong, and how that bias is harder to counteract than most people assume. Parasuraman and Manzey wrote in Human Factors in 2010 about how complacency in human-automation interaction is an attentional problem, not simply a training problem — meaning that telling clinicians to "stay engaged" is not a sufficient safeguard once automation is embedded in the workflow. For someone in my line of work, this is not abstract. Truck drivers operate in automated environments all the time now. Lane-keeping assist, collision warning systems, automatic braking. And the research on driver automation complacency tracks closely with what Parasuraman and Manzey describe in clinical contexts. The more reliable the system seems, the more the human operator's vigilance degrades. If HHS is going to accelerate deployment of AI diagnostic tools, it needs to require evidence not just that the tool performs accurately in controlled conditions, but that clinician judgment is preserved in real-world use. That is a different question, and it requires different study designs than the ones currently used for AI validation.⏎⏎What I am specifically asking HHS to do — and I want to be concrete here because vague calls for caution don't accomplish anything — is to require, before any clinical AI tool is approved for reimbursement or certified for use, demonstrated evidence that deployment of that tool does not erode the duration, quality, or relational character of the clinical encounter. Not just that the tool's outputs are technically accurate. Not just that clinicians report feeling comfortable with it. Evidence about what happens to the patient's experience of being seen and heard, and about what happens to the clinician's capacity to notice things that don't appear in the data. The ONC Federal Health IT Strategic Plan for 2024 through 2030 mentions patient-centered care as a priority, but the metrics proposed to measure it are almost entirely structural: interoperability, data access, record completeness. Those matter. But a patient can have a perfectly complete, perfectly interoperable digital record and still leave a clinic feeling like no one actually looked at them. HHS should fund research into relational outcomes as a distinct category, not as a subcategory of patient satisfaction scores, which are an imperfect and often misleading proxy.⏎⏎I also want to say something about the rural context specifically, because that is where this question is most consequential for people like me. The DOT physical clinics along I-80 and I-29 where truck drivers stop for certification exams are already operating on thin margins, with limited staff and high patient volume. Those are exactly the settings where AI tools are most likely to be adopted in ways that reduce clinician time per patient rather than improve it. A clinic in a rural corridor does not have the administrative infrastructure to implement AI thoughtfully. It has a medical examiner, a front-desk person, and a waiting room full of drivers who need to get back on the road. If HHS accelerates AI adoption without requiring evidence of relational preservation, the places that will cut corners are the places that can least afford not to. I am not saying AI tools have no place in those clinics. I am saying that the deployment context matters enormously, and the RFI treats deployment context as a secondary consideration when it should be a primary one. A tool validated at a major academic medical center may behave very differently in a one-examiner clinic in Council Bluffs.⏎⏎The thing I keep returning to is what actually happened in that cardiology office in Des Moines. The software flagged the rhythm. But the cardiologist asked me whether the fatigue I'd been feeling was new or whether it had been building. She noticed I seemed a little short of breath when I walked in. She asked about my routes, my sleep schedule, whether I'd had any near-misses on the road that I'd attributed to tiredness. None of that was in any dataset. None of it would have been captured by an AI system, however well-trained. And all of it was relevant to what she recommended and how aggressively she recommended it. I left that office with a clear plan and a follow-up appointment and a genuine sense that someone had understood what was at stake for me specifically. I don't think that is a luxury. I think it is medicine. HHS has an opportunity here to shape how AI enters clinical care in a way that makes more of those encounters possible, especially in the rural and working-class communities that have historically had the least access to them. But that will require asking harder questions about what clinical AI deployment actually does to the human relationship at the center of care, and requiring answers before deployment rather than studying the wreckage afterward. The 2024-2030 strategic plan has the right aspirations. What it needs are requirements with teeth, and research funding directed at measuring what has historically been considered unmeasurable, because the fact that something is hard to quantify does not mean it doesn't matter to the person sitting across the desk from the doctor.⏎⏎Sincerely,⏎⏎Nancy Sanchez⏎Des Moines, Iowa♔♔2026-02-04T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-04T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔individual♔high♔hopeful♔Iowa♔truck driver♔57♔When my cardiologist in Des Moines flagged an irregular rhythm on my EKG two years into my CDL medical certification cycle, the difference between catching it early and missing it entirely came down to whether the clinic had upgraded its software — and that clinic had.
