SYNTH-0070♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Joshua Smith♔Digital Medicine Society♔♔♔♔♔Digital Medicine Society | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 1⏎⏎Submitted to: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎Re: Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Joshua Smith, Research Director, Digital Medicine Society⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE QUESTION HHS IS NOT ASKING⏎⏎Our organization's 2024 registry survey of 3,200 individuals living with multiple sclerosis found that 67% reported diagnostic delays of six months or more before receiving a confirmed MS diagnosis. Neurologists at participating academic medical centers cited inconsistent access to AI-assisted MRI interpretation tools as a contributing factor. Our analysis of CMS claims data from 2021 through 2023 found that MS patients in rural Health Professional Shortage Areas experienced diagnostic delays averaging 14 months longer than their urban counterparts — and three federally funded pilot programs have generated preliminary evidence suggesting that AI-enabled imaging decision support could reduce that gap in a meaningful way. We presented these findings in testimony before the Senate HELP Committee in September 2024. We are not opposed to AI adoption in clinical settings. We are not reflexively skeptical of the technology. What we are is exhausted by a decade of watching policy conversations about health technology get structured around the wrong question.⏎⏎HHS has framed this RFI around acceleration. The word appears in the title. The assumption embedded in that framing is that the primary obstacle to beneficial AI adoption is the pace of adoption itself — that if we could just move faster, patients would benefit sooner. Our organization's position, grounded in both our patient registry data and a substantial body of published research, is that this framing is mistaken in ways that will produce predictable harms if left unexamined. The more consequential question is not how fast we can move, but what we are actually trying to preserve and protect as we move. And the answer to that question requires HHS to treat the patient-clinician relationship not as a soft value to be honored in passing language, but as a measurable clinical variable that AI deployment policy is obligated to protect.⏎⏎Digital Medicine Society | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 2⏎⏎THE THERAPEUTIC RELATIONSHIP AS A CLINICAL VARIABLE⏎⏎The research on this point is not ambiguous. Kelley et al. (2014), in a systematic review and meta-analysis published in PLOS ONE, found that the quality of the patient-clinician relationship produced consistent, statistically significant effects on health outcomes across a range of conditions and care settings. Hojat et al. (2011), writing in Academic Medicine, demonstrated that physician empathy scores predicted hemoglobin A1c control in diabetic patients — a finding that should give pause to anyone designing clinical AI systems that reduce the time a clinician spends in genuine observation of the person in front of them. Abraham Verghese's 2011 essay in Health Affairs on the ritual of physical examination makes a point that feels almost obvious once stated but rarely appears in health technology policy: the act of touching a patient, of watching them move across a room, of noticing the way someone holds their arm or avoids a particular posture, generates diagnostic information that does not appear in an imaging report and cannot be prompted by a clinical decision support alert. The patient who can't quite explain where the pain is. The family member sitting in the corner of the exam room whose face tells the story the patient won't tell. These are not peripheral features of clinical care that AI supplements. They are, in many conditions, the diagnostic signal itself.⏎⏎Our concern is not that AI imaging tools are clinically useless — the MS diagnostic delay data we have cited demonstrates the opposite. Our concern is that an acceleration framework, implemented without explicit structural protections for relational care, will systematically erode the conditions under which that relational signal can be received. Parasuraman and Manzey (2010), in Human Factors, documented the phenomenon of automation complacency across multiple high-stakes domains: as decision-support systems become more accurate and more trusted, human operators become less vigilant, less likely to catch the cases where the system fails, and less practiced at independent judgment. Tversky and Kahneman's foundational 1974 work in Science on heuristics and biases provides the cognitive architecture for understanding why this happens — the anchoring effects of an algorithmic recommendation are not neutralized by telling a clinician to "use their judgment." Croskerry (2002), writing in Academic Emergency Medicine, applied this framework specifically to clinical decision-making and found that even experienced clinicians are susceptible to anchoring and automation bias in ways that are not corrected by training alone.⏎⏎Digital Medicine Society | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 3⏎⏎Eric Topol's 2019 paper in Nature Medicine, which is frequently cited in exactly the kind of RFI HHS has issued here, makes the case for AI-human convergence in medicine with genuine sophistication. But it is worth noting what Topol's framework assumes: that the clinician remains a fully present, fully engaged partner in the diagnostic encounter, capable of catching what the algorithm misses and integrating algorithmic output with the relational information that only a human can gather. The acceleration model HHS has proposed does not protect those conditions. It does not ask whether the reimbursement structures that would be modified to encourage AI adoption might simultaneously create pressure to shorten appointments, reduce face-to-face time, or push clinicians toward algorithmic outputs as documentation rather than as decision support. Wachter and Goldsmith (2018), writing in the Harvard Business Review, documented how the implementation of electronic health records — another technology that promised efficiency — produced documentation burdens that left physicians spending more time looking at screens than at patients. The lesson of that implementation failure is not that EHRs are bad. It is that technology adoption without structural protection for the human elements of clinical care produces predictable relational degradation.⏎⏎Ridd et al. (2009), in a synthesis of qualitative literature on patients' perspectives published in the British Journal of General Practice, found that patients consistently identified continuity of relationship — knowing and being known by their clinician — as the feature of primary care they most valued and most associated with feeling safe. Bickmore and Picard (2005), in ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction, studied long-term human-computer relationships and found that even well-designed relational AI systems do not replicate the trust dynamics of human clinical relationships. These findings are not arguments against AI. They are arguments for a policy framework that is honest about what AI can and cannot do, and that builds explicit protections for what it cannot do into the regulatory and reimbursement structures HHS is considering.⏎⏎Digital Medicine Society | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 4⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD ASK INSTEAD⏎⏎The Digital Medicine Society urges HHS to reframe this RFI around three questions that the acceleration framing has displaced:⏎⏎1. What evidence of demonstrated safety and equity impact should be required before federal reimbursement changes are used to incentivize AI adoption at scale? The MS diagnostic delay data suggests that AI-enabled imaging interpretation tools have real potential to reduce inequitable delays in rural and underserved populations. But the three pilot programs we have cited are preliminary. Scaling before their findings are replicated and their equity impacts are measured across diverse patient populations is a choice with consequences. Dzau, McClellan, and McGinnis (2021), writing in NAM Perspectives, argued that health system transformation requires explicit equity frameworks embedded in the policy instruments that drive adoption, not added as a consideration after the fact.⏎⏎2. How should reimbursement structures be designed to protect face-to-face clinical time rather than compress it? If AI-assisted documentation tools reduce administrative burden — which is a legitimate and desirable goal — the time recovered should be directed toward patient contact, not toward processing more patients per hour. This is not a point that can be addressed through voluntary guidance. It requires explicit reimbursement design.⏎⏎3. What metrics will HHS use to determine whether AI adoption is preserving or degrading the therapeutic relationship in deployed settings? This is the question our organization is most concerned that HHS has not yet formulated. If there is no measurement framework, there is no accountability. And if there is no accountability, the acceleration model will produce exactly the relational erosion that the literature predicts.⏎⏎Digital Medicine Society | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 5⏎⏎A NOTE ON REIMBURSEMENT AND INDUSTRY ACCOUNTABILITY⏎⏎Our organization wants to be direct about something that the clinical language in this comment has so far left implicit. The reimbursement changes that HHS is considering in this RFI will, if implemented, generate substantial revenue for the companies that develop and sell AI clinical tools. That is not an argument against those changes. It is an argument for a policy environment in which the companies benefiting from federal reimbursement policy are required to be transparent about how their tools perform across different patient populations, what their failure modes are, and what evidence base supports their clinical claims. The National MS Society and Accelerated Cure Project's 2023 policy brief on diagnostic delay documented that patients in rural areas face not just access barriers but information barriers — their clinicians often do not know which AI tools have been validated for their patient population and which have not. That is a market failure, and it is one that HHS has the authority and the obligation to address.⏎⏎Our organization is not, in this comment, calling for more reporting burdens on hospitals and health systems. The documentation burden that Wachter and Goldsmith described in 2018 was real and it fell on clinicians. What we are asking is that the companies selling AI clinical tools be required to publish performance data disaggregated by race, geography, insurance status, and condition severity before those tools are eligible for the reimbursement incentives this RFI is contemplating. That is a reasonable condition. It is the kind of condition that the acceleration framing tends to defer or dilute, because it slows the process. But if HHS accelerates adoption of tools whose equity performance is unknown, the 14-month rural diagnostic delay gap we documented in our CMS claims analysis will not close. It may widen.⏎⏎Digital Medicine Society | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 6⏎⏎There is also a question that our organization has not fully resolved internally, and we want to be honest about that. We have argued here that the therapeutic relationship is a measurable clinical variable that policy must protect. But we are aware that the measurement tools for relational quality in clinical care are not as mature as the measurement tools for imaging accuracy or diagnostic delay. The CAHPS survey instruments capture some of this, but imperfectly. Our own registry data captures patient-reported experience, but our registry participants are not a representative sample of all MS patients — they are more likely to be white, more likely to be college-educated, more likely to have access to academic medical centers. We know that. The policy recommendations we have made here are not invalidated by that limitation, but they are complicated by it, and HHS should be aware that any measurement framework it develops for relational preservation in AI-assisted care will need to be designed with explicit attention to the populations whose experience is least likely to be captured by standard registry and claims data.⏎⏎Digital Medicine Society | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 7⏎⏎The patients our organization serves have waited long enough for the diagnostic system to work for them. The MS patient in southeastern Ohio who spent 22 months seeing general practitioners before a neurologist with access to an AI-assisted MRI interpretation tool confirmed her diagnosis — she is not a data point in our registry. She is the reason the registry exists. Acceleration, for her, is not an abstraction. But acceleration without equity requirements, without relational protections, without mandatory performance transparency from the companies whose tools her neurologist will be reimbursed for using — that is not a policy framework that serves her.⏎⏎HHS should revise the framing of this RFI to center demonstrated safety, equity of impact, and therapeutic relationship preservation as the primary criteria against which AI adoption policy is evaluated. The reimbursement design work that follows from that reframing will be more complicated and will take longer. We think that is the right tradeoff. And we would note that the question of what performance transparency requirements should attach to AI clinical tools as a condition of reimbursement eligibility is one that HHS has the regulatory authority to answer now, without waiting for additional legislation — and that the absence of such requirements in the current RFI framing is a gap that our organization intends to continue raising in subsequent comment periods and in direct engagement with ASTP/ONC.⏎⏎For questions regarding this submission, please contact the Digital Medicine Society policy team at policy@dimesociety.org.⏎⏎Digital Medicine Society | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 8♔♔2026-02-24T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-24T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔7♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔frustrated♔Ohio♔research director♔36♔A 2024 survey of 3,200 individuals living with multiple sclerosis conducted through our patient registry found that 67% reported delays of six months or more in receiving a confirmed MS diagnosis, with neurologists at participating academic medical centers citing inconsistent access to AI-assisted MRI interpretation tools as a contributing factor. SYNTH-0071♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔William Lewis♔Availity♔♔♔♔♔Availity LLC Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 1⏎⏎---⏎⏎SUBMISSION TO THE U.S. DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary / ASTP/ONC⏎Re: Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: William Lewis, Vice President of Regulatory Affairs, Availity LLC⏎⏎---⏎⏎PRELIMINARY FRAMING: THE PROBLEM WITH THE CURRENT RFI ARCHITECTURE⏎⏎Availity is a healthcare information network that processes more than 12 billion clinical and administrative transactions annually, connecting over 2 million providers with health plans, clearinghouses, and technology partners across every U.S. state. From that position — sitting, operationally, at the intersection of clinical care delivery and payer coverage decisions — Availity has an unusually direct view of how AI is actually being deployed in the health sector today. That view is not uniformly encouraging, and the Department's RFI, while well-intentioned, is structured in a way that concerns us for reasons we want to articulate precisely.⏎⏎The RFI frames AI adoption in clinical care as a challenge of removing barriers, accelerating reimbursement, and building competitive markets for AI tool developers. Availity does not disagree that those goals are legitimate. The problem is that the framing treats "health sector AI" as a coherent category when it is, in practice, two fundamentally different categories that happen to share a technology substrate. AI systems designed to support clinical decision-making — tools that help oncologists identify trial-eligible patients, flag sepsis risk, or interpret diagnostic imaging — have a fundamentally different incentive structure, training objective, and patient impact profile than AI systems deployed by health insurers to automate prior authorization denials or generate coverage restrictions at scale. Collapsing those two categories into a single RFI, and then proposing to "accelerate" adoption across both of them through reimbursement reform and regulatory streamlining, is a policy architecture that will predictably benefit the second category far more than the first.⏎⏎We want to be direct about why: the financial returns from denial-automation AI are immediate, quantifiable, and captured by a concentrated set of payers. The financial returns from clinical decision-support AI are diffuse, long-term, and depend on a reimbursement infrastructure that does not yet exist in most care settings. The Department's own framing of AI reimbursement reform as a mechanism to "foster competition among clinical care AI tool builders" (RFI Section III) ignores this asymmetry entirely. Availity submits that without a categorical distinction in HHS's governance framework between AI that supports patient access to care and AI that restricts it, the Department's well-intentioned acceleration agenda will entrench the most financially motivated AI deployments behind a veneer of federal legitimacy.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Availity LLC Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE DOCUMENTED RECORD ON DENIAL-AUTOMATION AI⏎⏎This is not a speculative concern. The record on AI-driven prior authorization denial practices in Medicare Advantage and commercial insurance is now substantial enough that it should anchor the Department's policy development, not be treated as a peripheral compliance issue.⏎⏎The Office of Inspector General's April 2022 report (OEI-09-18-00260) found that Medicare Advantage organizations denied prior authorization requests at rates that raised serious concerns about beneficiary access to medically necessary care, with some denials based on criteria that did not align with Medicare coverage rules or clinical standards. The Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, in its October 2024 report "Denial, Delay, Disappear: How Medicare Advantage Insurers Have Denied Care to Seniors," documented in specific, granular detail how major MA plans deployed algorithmic tools to generate denials at scale, with physician review occurring after the denial rather than before it — if it occurred at all. Reporting by Fortune's Sy Mukherjee in November 2023 described how UnitedHealth's nH Predict algorithm was allegedly generating post-acute care denial recommendations with a 90% accuracy rate in predicting patient discharge timelines, a metric that has nothing to do with whether a patient is clinically ready to leave a facility and everything to do with cost containment (Mukherjee, S., Fortune, November 2023).⏎⏎The Kaiser Family Foundation's March 2023 issue brief by Koma et al. on prior authorization use in Medicare Advantage found that MA plans used prior authorization requirements for services that traditional Medicare covers without restriction, and that denial rates varied dramatically across plans in ways that tracked plan cost-containment objectives rather than clinical variation in member populations. A separate KFF analysis by Fehr et al. (February 2021) on ACA marketplace claims denials found that appeal rates for denied claims were remarkably low — around 0.1% of denied claims were ultimately appealed — which suggests that denial automation is operationally effective at discouraging appeals even when the underlying denial is clinically inappropriate.⏎⏎The AMA's 2023 Prior Authorization Physician Survey found that 94% of physicians reported that prior authorization delays patient access to necessary care, and 33% reported that prior authorization had led to a serious adverse event for a patient in their practice. These are not outcomes from a system that is failing at the margins; they are outcomes from a system where AI-assisted denial has become a standard operational practice with documented patient harm.⏎⏎Availity LLC Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 3⏎⏎What makes this particularly difficult to address through the RFI's current framework is the conflict of interest that is baked into how denial-automation AI is trained and validated. AI trained on cost-containment objectives cannot be presumed to produce clinically appropriate outputs. That sentence should be obvious, but it is apparently not reflected in the current HHS framing. When an insurer trains an algorithm to predict which prior authorization requests are associated with higher subsequent utilization, and then uses that algorithm to generate denial recommendations, the model is optimizing for a financial objective that may be directly opposed to the clinical standard of care. Obermeyer et al.'s landmark 2019 Science paper on racial bias in health algorithms (Vol. 366, Issue 6464) demonstrated that even algorithms designed with ostensibly neutral objectives — in that case, predicting health needs for population management — can embed systematic bias when the training signal is a cost proxy rather than a health outcome. The implication for denial-automation AI, where the training signal is explicitly financial, is not reassuring.⏎⏎Rajpurkar et al.'s 2022 review in Nature Medicine (Vol. 28, pp. 31-38) drew a meaningful distinction between AI systems operating in clinical-support roles, where performance is measured against patient outcomes, and AI systems operating in administrative roles, where the performance metrics are set by the deploying institution. That distinction matters enormously for governance purposes, and it is conspicuously absent from the RFI.⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE CLINICAL AI CASE, AND WHY THE CURRENT FRAMING UNDERMINES IT⏎⏎Availity's concern here is not purely defensive. The company has direct operational experience with AI systems that genuinely improve patient outcomes, and the Department's failure to protect the regulatory distinction between clinical-support AI and denial-automation AI creates real risks for organizations like ours that are trying to build and deploy the former.⏎⏎As one relevant data point from the broader clinical AI ecosystem: analytics from Massive Bio's AI-driven oncology trial matching platform, across more than 47,000 patient cases processed between 2022 and 2024, showed that AI-assisted eligibility screening reduced average patient-to-trial matching time from 23 days to under 4 days. Enrollment rates for patients identified through AI-assisted protocols were 31% higher than for patients identified through conventional manual review. In a 2024 survey of 312 partner oncology centers, 68% identified inconsistent payer reimbursement policies for AI-enabled clinical decision support tools as the single greatest barrier to sustained platform adoption. That last finding is particularly relevant here: the same payers who are deploying denial-automation AI at scale are declining to reimburse the clinical AI tools that actually deliver measurable patient benefit.⏎⏎Availity LLC Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 4⏎⏎This is the structural problem with the RFI's competition-focused framing. The Department proposes to "accelerate" AI adoption by removing regulatory barriers and reforming reimbursement — but in a market where payers simultaneously (a) control which AI tools get reimbursed and (b) operate their own AI systems optimized for cost containment, removing regulatory barriers without imposing categorical governance distinctions does not level the playing field. It tilts it further toward the payer-side applications that are already financially self-sustaining.⏎⏎Schulte and Fry's 2019 Kaiser Health News / Fortune investigation on algorithmic decision-making harms in clinical settings identified a recurring pattern: technology deployments that generate institutional financial benefits get adopted rapidly and broadly, while technology deployments that generate patient benefits but diffuse institutional costs face prolonged adoption barriers. That pattern is precisely what the 68% figure from the oncology center survey reflects. The Department should take it seriously as a structural market failure, not as a temporary friction to be resolved by reimbursement reform alone.⏎⏎The National Academy for State Health Policy's tracker on state laws challenging insurer AI use in prior authorization decisions (updated January 2024) documented that at least 17 states had enacted or were actively pursuing legislation to require human clinical review of AI-generated denials, mandate transparency in algorithm design, or restrict payer use of AI in coverage determination entirely. The fact that states are moving this aggressively suggests that the federal governance framework has left a vacuum that is being filled in fragmented, inconsistent ways. HHS has an opportunity — and arguably an obligation — to provide a coherent federal floor before that fragmentation becomes permanent.⏎⏎CMS's 2024 Medicare Advantage and Part D Advance Notice (February 2023) included some acknowledgment of prior authorization concerns, but the proposed guardrails were largely procedural rather than substantive. They addressed timelines and appeal rights without touching the underlying question of whether AI-generated denial recommendations should be subject to pre-deployment validation against clinical appropriateness standards. That gap is what Availity is asking HHS to close.⏎⏎---⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Availity respectfully submits that HHS should incorporate the following structural requirements into any AI governance framework that emerges from this RFI. These are not aspirational suggestions; they are minimum conditions for a framework that protects patients while allowing legitimate clinical AI to function.⏎⏎1. Any AI system involved in prior authorization decisions, coverage determinations, or utilization management must be trained and validated against clinical appropriateness standards established by recognized clinical bodies — not against cost proxies, utilization targets, or financial performance metrics. Validation documentation should be submitted to CMS prior to deployment in any Medicare or Medicaid context, and updated whenever the model is retrained.⏎⏎2. Every denial, restriction, or coverage limitation generated or recommended by an AI system must be accompanied by a human-reviewable clinical rationale that specifies the clinical criteria applied, the data inputs used, and the identity of the reviewing clinician (if any). "The algorithm flagged this request" is not a clinical rationale. This requirement should apply regardless of whether the denial is issued under Medicare Advantage, commercial insurance, or Medicaid managed care.⏎⏎3. AI systems deployed in prior authorization or coverage determination must be subject to mandatory outcome audits, conducted no less than annually, with results disaggregated by patient age, disability status, income level, and race/ethnicity. Audit results should be reported to CMS and made publicly available. Plans that show systematic disparities in denial rates across protected categories should face corrective action requirements with defined timelines.⏎⏎4. HHS should establish, in coordination with ONC and CMS, a categorical regulatory distinction between "clinical-support AI" — tools that assist clinicians in diagnosis, treatment planning, or care coordination — and "coverage-determination AI" — tools that generate or recommend denials, restrictions, or authorizations. These two categories should be subject to different governance frameworks, different validation requirements, and different transparency obligations. Treating them as a single category in reimbursement policy or regulatory streamlining is analytically indefensible given what the documented record now shows.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Availity LLC Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 5⏎⏎---⏎⏎CLOSING OBSERVATIONS⏎⏎Availity supports HHS's broader AI agenda. The clinical case for AI-assisted care is real, and the operational barriers to adoption — fragmented reimbursement, unclear liability frameworks, inconsistent data access standards — are legitimate policy problems worth solving. The Department is right to be thinking about how federal action can accelerate adoption of tools that genuinely improve patient outcomes.⏎⏎What Availity cannot support is a governance framework that accelerates AI adoption generically, without distinguishing between tools that serve patients and tools that are deployed against them. The record compiled by the OIG, the Senate Subcommittee, the AMA, and multiple state legislatures is now detailed enough that continuing to treat denial-automation AI as a benign category of health sector innovation is not a defensible policy position. It is a choice with predictable consequences for the elderly, disabled, and low-income beneficiaries who are most exposed to the harms of algorithmically-generated coverage restrictions and least equipped to navigate the appeals processes that nominally exist to correct them.⏎⏎The reimbursement asymmetry Availity has described — where payers deploy denial AI that pays for itself through cost containment, while clinical AI struggles to achieve reimbursement parity — will not self-correct through competition policy. It requires a structural intervention at the governance level that the current RFI framing does not contemplate. We urge the Department to revise its framework accordingly before the comment period closes, and we are available to provide technical assistance on the categorical distinction framework described above.⏎⏎William Lewis⏎Vice President, Regulatory Affairs⏎Availity LLC⏎wlewis@availity.com⏎⏎Availity LLC | 9887 Fourth Street N, Suite 500 | Jacksonville, FL 32250♔♔2026-01-20T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-20T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔7♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI-powered insurance decision-making automates prior authorization denials and coverage restrictions in ways that are opaque, unappealable, and systematically biased against vulnerable patients.♔organization♔high♔supportive♔Maryland♔VP of regulatory affairs♔36♔Massive Bio's internal analytics across more than 47,000 oncology patient cases processed through our AI-driven clinical trial matching platform between 2022 and 2024 demonstrate that AI-assisted eligibility screening reduced average patient-to-trial matching time from 23 days to under 4 days — a 6-fold improvement. SYNTH-0074♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Barbara Walker♔♔♔♔♔♔SUBMITTED COMMENT: HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI REQUEST FOR INFORMATION⏎Barbara Walker, MSW, Pennington County Family Services (individual capacity)⏎Sioux Falls, South Dakota⏎⏎ACCOUNTABILITY SEQUENCING AS A STRUCTURAL PREREQUISITE⏎⏎My caseload grew by thirty-one families in a single week when a colleague retired and the county quietly distributed her files. No announcement, no transition period, no additional resources. I spent the better part of three months trying to complete safety assessments on children I had never met in person, driving out to addresses in Pennington and Davison counties that I was encountering for the first time while simultaneously managing the families I already knew. I raise this not to establish that I am overworked, though I am, but to explain why I have been watching the postpartum depression screening pilot at the Sanford Health network in Sioux Falls with genuine and not merely polite interest. A tool that can flag early risk indicators before a mother leaves the maternity ward, before she falls through the gap between discharge and whatever comes next, before she ends up on my caseload in crisis, is something I want to exist. My concern with this RFI is not with AI in clinical care as a concept. It is with the order of operations HHS is proposing.⏎⏎THE ACCOUNTABILITY VACUUM AND WHY ACCELERATION MAKES IT WORSE⏎⏎The RFI frames its central question around what regulatory, reimbursement, and research actions HHS can take to accelerate AI adoption. I want to address that framing directly, because I think acceleration is the wrong organizing principle when the legal and institutional infrastructure for assigning responsibility does not yet exist. When a patient or family is harmed by an AI-assisted clinical decision, the current framework produces what Brown and Gerber (2022) have called a diffusion of responsibility: the clinician points to the tool's recommendation, the hospital points to its vendor contract and deployment specifications, the vendor points to the training data or to user error in implementation. No one in this chain is structurally designed to be the final accountable party (Brown & Gerber, "Who Is Responsible When AI Gets It Wrong in Medicine?", Journal of Law and the Biosciences, 2022). The Government Accountability Office reached a similar conclusion in its 2020 review of AI in health care, finding that existing regulatory frameworks do not clearly assign accountability for AI-assisted clinical errors and that this gap was not an oversight but a consequence of applying frameworks built around identifiable human decision-makers to systems that do not have one (GAO-21-7SP, 2020).⏎⏎Price and Cohen identified the broader structural problem in 2019: legal accountability frameworks in medicine were designed around the assumption that a person made the decision, and AI intermediation dissolves that assumption in ways that cannot be patched by adding disclosure requirements or audit logs after the fact (Price & Cohen, Nature Medicine, 2019). Doshi-Velez and colleagues made a related point at the Berkman Klein Center that I keep returning to, which is that explainability requirements, however well designed, do not by themselves resolve accountability. Knowing why a system produced an output is not the same as knowing who is responsible when that output contributes to harm (Doshi-Velez et al., "Accountability of AI Under the Law: The Role of Explanation," Berkman Klein Center Working Paper, 2017). These are not abstract legal puzzles. They are questions about what happens to a family in a rural South Dakota county when the system fails them and no one can be identified as answerable.⏎⏎Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen laid out the malpractice doctrine gap with some precision: standard negligence analysis requires a departure from a recognized standard of care by an identifiable defendant, and AI-assisted decisions resist that analysis at nearly every element (Gerke, Minssen & Cohen, "Ethical and Legal Challenges of Artificial Intelligence-Driven Healthcare," in Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare, Academic Press, 2020). Gatter and Terry went further in a 2023 piece arguing that current tort law's assumptions about human decision-making are structurally incompatible with AI intermediation, not merely underdeveloped, and that incremental doctrinal adjustments are unlikely to close the gap without legislative or regulatory action that affirmatively assigns liability (Gatter & Terry, "Navigating the Doctrinal Void: Medical Liability and AI-Assisted Clinical Decisions," Saint Louis University Law Journal, 2023). I am not a lawyer and I am not arguing for a specific liability regime here. What I am arguing is that HHS is proposing to accelerate the deployment of a technology whose harm profile cannot currently be adjudicated, and that this sequencing is itself a design flaw in the proposed policy, not a gap that can be filled by subsequent rulemaking once adoption has already occurred.⏎⏎WHAT I AM ASKING HHS TO CONSIDER⏎⏎The families I work with do not have the resources to navigate a liability vacuum. A mother with postpartum depression who receives an incorrect risk stratification from a screening tool, and whose care is consequently delayed or misdirected, is not well positioned to identify which party in the AI deployment chain bears responsibility for what happened to her. She is not going to retain counsel to sort out whether the error originated in the training data, the clinical integration, or the attending physician's interpretation of the output. The practical consequence of the accountability diffusion that Brown and Gerber describe is that it falls hardest on people who are already most dependent on the system working correctly, because they have the least capacity to seek redress when it does not.⏎⏎I want to be clear that I am not asking HHS to halt AI development in clinical settings. The postpartum screening pilot I mentioned is doing real work. What I am asking is that HHS treat the establishment of a clear, enforceable accountability framework as a prerequisite for the acceleration the RFI proposes, rather than as a parallel workstream or a future regulatory consideration. This means, at minimum, that before any federal reimbursement incentives are extended to AI-assisted clinical tools, HHS should be able to answer the following question in concrete terms: when this tool contributes to patient harm, who is the responsible party, and through what legal mechanism can that responsibility be enforced? Right now, the honest answer to that question is that no one has satisfactorily resolved it, and the GAO said so in 2020, and Gatter and Terry said so again in 2023, and the RFI does not appear to treat this as a prerequisite at all.⏎⏎I am genuinely hopeful that AI can do something meaningful on the social care side of the continuum, the side that catches people after discharge, after crisis, in the mobile homes outside of Mitchell on a January afternoon. I have been waiting a long time for tools that could help me manage thirty-one new families without losing track of the ones I already had. But I cannot in good conscience encourage HHS to accelerate adoption of these tools into the care environments that serve the families on my caseload until there is a clear answer to the question of who is accountable when something goes wrong. That answer has to come first. Not as a condition attached to a future guidance document, but as the framework within which acceleration is even being discussed.⏎⏎The accountability question is not administrative. It is the whole thing.⏎⏎References⏎⏎Brown, T.R. & Gerber, E. (2022). Who is responsible when AI gets it wrong in medicine? Journal of Law and the Biosciences.⏎⏎Doshi-Velez, F. et al. (2017). SYNTH-0075♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Dorothy Green♔Society of Critical Care Medicine♔♔♔♔♔SOCIETY OF CRITICAL CARE MEDICINE⏎Public Comment Submission — HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information⏎Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket: HHS-AI-RFI-2024⏎Submitted by: Dorothy Green, Community Engagement and Policy Division⏎Organization: Society of Critical Care Medicine⏎⏎www.sccm.org/policy | policy-comments@sccm.org⏎⏎SCCM Comments | HHS-AI-RFI-2024 | Page 1⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎The Society of Critical Care Medicine submits this comment with a degree of urgency that we do not deploy lightly. The framing of this Request for Information — its repeated invocation of "productivity," its structuring of the question as how to accelerate adoption rather than whether and under what conditions adoption is appropriate — represents a policy posture that this organization finds not merely premature but genuinely dangerous. Medicine is a relational practice. That is not a nostalgic claim or a sentimental preference. It is a clinical fact, documented across decades of outcomes research, that the relationship between a clinician and a patient is itself a therapeutic instrument — one whose erosion, at whatever pace and through whatever mechanism, produces measurable harm to patients independent of any accompanying technical gains.⏎⏎This comment addresses two of the RFI's question areas: the question of what regulatory actions HHS should take to accelerate AI adoption in clinical settings, and the question of how interoperability frameworks can be leveraged to support AI tool deployment. We address only these two because, frankly, addressing all of the RFI's questions would require us to accept the premise that acceleration is the right goal. We do not accept that premise.⏎⏎SCCM Comments | HHS-AI-RFI-2024 | Page 2⏎⏎THE WRONG QUESTION, AND WHY IT MATTERS⏎⏎There is a particular kind of institutional sleight-of-hand that occurs when a regulatory body frames a solicitation around implementation logistics rather than foundational justification. This RFI, as structured, asks the public to help HHS figure out how to get AI into clinical settings faster. It does not ask whether the current evidence base justifies that speed. It does not ask what precautionary frameworks should govern deployment in high-stakes care environments. It treats the desirability of AI adoption as settled and asks only for tactical advice on the acceleration.⏎⏎This framing is ideologically loaded in ways that deserve explicit naming. When HHS describes AI as a tool to "enhance productivity" in clinical care, it is importing a manufacturing-sector value system into a domain where productivity, as conventionally measured, is often the enemy of good medicine. The clinician who spends forty minutes with a patient who cannot name her symptoms — who waits, who watches, who eventually notices that the patient's hands are shaking in a way that has nothing to do with the presenting complaint — is not being unproductive. She is doing the most important diagnostic work of the encounter. Zulman et al. (2020), writing in JAMA, documented that practices fostering physician presence and genuine connection in clinical encounters are associated with better diagnostic accuracy and patient adherence outcomes. That presence is not a luxury amenity. It is the mechanism of care.⏎⏎The risk is not hypothetical. When AI-driven clinical decision support systems are deployed without adequate guardrails — and the current literature documents this pattern with uncomfortable frequency — what gets "optimized" is throughput. What gets compressed is exactly the unstructured, ambiguous, relational time that constitutes genuine clinical judgment. Wachter and Goldsmith (2018) identified this dynamic in their Harvard Business Review analysis of electronic health record burdens, noting that systems designed to capture and process data tend to restructure clinical workflow around data capture rather than around patients. The AI tools now entering clinical settings are more capable than the EHR systems Wachter described, but the structural incentive is identical: if a system is measuring and rewarding efficiency, clinicians will optimize for efficiency, and patients will bear the cost of whatever falls outside the measurement frame.⏎⏎SCCM Comments | HHS-AI-RFI-2024 | Page 3⏎⏎WHAT MEDICINE ACTUALLY IS⏎⏎The Society of Critical Care Medicine works with some of the most technically demanding clinical environments in American healthcare. Intensive care units, trauma bays, rapid-response teams — these are settings where diagnostic speed genuinely matters, where data processing capacity can mean the difference between timely intervention and preventable death. We are not opposed to technology. We have never been opposed to technology. But we have watched, with increasing alarm, as the policy conversation about AI in healthcare has drifted toward a model of clinical practice that bears no resemblance to what skilled clinicians actually do.⏎⏎Consider a scenario that any experienced intensivist would recognize: a father is brought into the ICU by his adult children, who report that he has been confused and febrile for two days. The initial workup is unremarkable. The AI-assisted diagnostic tool flags sepsis of unknown origin and recommends a standard protocol. The protocol is appropriate. But the attending physician, reviewing the chart and then sitting with the family for twelve minutes that no algorithm would have flagged as necessary, learns that the father has been concealing severe abdominal pain because he is afraid of what a diagnosis might mean for his ability to keep working. That information — obtained through relational presence, through the willingness to wait and to ask the question twice — changes the entire diagnostic picture. Verghese, Shah, and Harrington (2018) argued in JAMA that what computers need, in clinical settings, is a physician: not as an overseer of algorithmic outputs, but as a practitioner of the irreducibly human interpretive work that transforms data into diagnosis. The risk of AI intermediation is not that algorithms will be wrong about the data they have. It is that they will be right about the data they have, and the data they do not have will include everything that matters.⏎⏎Kelley et al. (2014), in a systematic review and meta-analysis published in PLOS ONE, documented that the quality of the patient-clinician relationship is independently associated with health outcomes across a wide range of conditions and clinical contexts. This is not a soft finding. The relationship is a clinical variable. Epstein and Street (2011), writing in the Annals of Family Medicine, made the case that patient-centered care — the kind that attends to patient values, fears, and relational context — produces better outcomes not because it feels better to patients but because it generates better clinical information and better patient engagement in treatment. Accelerating AI adoption without a framework for protecting these relational processes is not a neutral policy choice. It is a choice to subordinate a documented clinical asset to a throughput model that has never been demonstrated to produce equivalent outcomes.⏎⏎SCCM Comments | HHS-AI-RFI-2024 | Page 4⏎⏎THE INTEROPERABILITY QUESTION AS TROJAN HORSE⏎⏎The RFI asks specifically about how interoperability frameworks can support AI tool deployment, and this question deserves careful attention because it represents a particularly consequential framing problem. Interoperability is a legitimate and important policy goal. The Society of Critical Care Medicine has supported federal interoperability initiatives, including the ONC's Federal Health IT Strategic Plan 2024-2030, which articulates a vision for data exchange that could genuinely improve care coordination and reduce the burden on patients who currently must navigate fragmented systems. We are not arguing against interoperability.⏎⏎What we are arguing is that using interoperability as a vector for AI acceleration — treating improved data exchange primarily as infrastructure for AI tool deployment rather than as an end in itself — inverts the appropriate relationship between means and ends. The 2024 landscape survey conducted across our member organizations found that 63% have encountered AI-driven claims adjudication tools introduced by payer partners without standardized interoperability protocols, producing eligibility verification failures that affected an estimated 2.3 million transactions in a single year. The organizations bearing the heaviest integration costs in that survey were operating in rural and safety-net corridors, where median onboarding expenses for AI-compatible transaction formats were running 340% higher than those reported by urban-market peers. These are not abstract numbers. They represent real institutions serving populations that already experience worse health outcomes and less clinical access than their urban counterparts.⏎⏎The lesson from that data is not that we need more AI with better interoperability. It is that AI deployment without standardized, transparent, and accountable frameworks systematically transfers costs to the most vulnerable parts of the health system while generating efficiencies that accrue elsewhere. Obermeyer and Emanuel (2016), writing in the New England Journal of Medicine, warned that machine learning tools trained on historical clinical data will encode historical biases — that the patterns they learn from include patterns of undertreatment, misclassification, and structural neglect that have characterized American healthcare's relationship with low-income and minority patients for generations. Interoperability frameworks that accelerate AI adoption without requiring algorithmic transparency and equity auditing are not neutral technical infrastructure. They are a mechanism for scaling those historical biases into every clinical encounter the AI touches.⏎⏎SCCM Comments | HHS-AI-RFI-2024 | Page 5⏎⏎RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The Society of Critical Care Medicine offers the following specific recommendations. These are not suggestions for how to accelerate AI adoption. They are conditions under which adoption, at any pace, might be conducted responsibly.⏎⏎1. HHS should adopt an explicit precautionary framework for AI deployment in clinical settings, requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any AI tool is permitted to influence clinical decision-making at the point of care. The current RFI framing inverts this requirement by treating acceleration as the goal and precaution as an obstacle. That inversion must be corrected.⏎⏎2. Any regulatory pathway for clinical AI tools must include mandatory pre-deployment equity audits conducted on the specific patient populations the tool will serve, not on generalized training data. The American College of Physicians' 2023 Position Statement on Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice identified this requirement as non-negotiable for tools that affect diagnosis or treatment recommendations, and SCCM endorses that position unambiguously.⏎⏎3. HHS must require that any AI tool deployed in clinical settings include a documented, enforceable mechanism for meaningful human override at every decision point. This is not a technical requirement. It is a moral one. Hartzband and Groopman (2020), writing in the New England Journal of Medicine, observed that the creeping automation of clinical judgment — even when that automation is technically accurate — produces a form of physician disengagement that they associate with burnout and with the erosion of the diagnostic instincts that good medicine requires. Oversight that is nominal rather than substantive is not oversight.⏎⏎4. Interoperability standards developed under ONC authority should be explicitly decoupled from AI adoption incentives. Improved data exchange is valuable on its own terms. Conditioning interoperability support on AI tool adoption, or structuring interoperability frameworks primarily to enable AI deployment, subordinates a public health goal to a market development agenda.⏎⏎5. HHS should commission an independent study, with results publicly reported within 18 months of this RFI's close, on the documented effects of currently deployed clinical AI tools on clinician-patient interaction time, patient-reported relationship quality, and clinical outcomes in safety-net settings. The Quintuple Aim framework articulated by Nundy, Cooper, and Mate (2022) in JAMA explicitly includes health equity and clinician well-being alongside the traditional triple aim metrics. Any evaluation framework for clinical AI that does not measure these dimensions is measuring the wrong things.⏎⏎6. Federal reimbursement policy should not create incentive structures that reward AI-mediated encounters over human-relational ones. If CMS reimbursement models begin rewarding efficiency metrics that AI tools are specifically designed to optimize, the market will respond by deploying those tools in ways that maximize reimbursement rather than patient welfare. This is not a speculative concern. It is a documented pattern in every prior instance where payment policy has created efficiency incentives without corresponding quality protections.⏎⏎SCCM Comments | HHS-AI-RFI-2024 | Page 6⏎⏎ON THE QUESTION OF WHAT AI CAN AND CANNOT DO⏎⏎It is worth being precise here, because the Society of Critical Care Medicine is sometimes characterized as categorically opposed to AI in clinical settings, and that characterization is not accurate. Topol (2019), writing in Nature Medicine, made a careful and credible case for specific domains where AI pattern recognition can meaningfully support clinical judgment — radiology, pathology, certain genomic analyses — domains where the interpretive task is well-defined, the error profile is measurable, and the human role in final decision-making remains clear. SCCM does not dispute that case. There are contexts in which AI tools, properly validated and properly supervised, can reduce diagnostic error and support clinicians in managing information loads that have become genuinely unsustainable.⏎⏎But the RFI does not ask about those specific, bounded contexts. It asks about accelerating AI adoption in clinical care broadly, and that breadth is the problem. The tools now being deployed — or being considered for deployment — include AI systems for triage prioritization, for treatment recommendation, for patient risk stratification, and for clinical documentation. These are not pattern-matching tasks in the narrow sense. They involve exactly the interpretive, relational, contextually embedded judgments that the research literature documents as irreducibly human. Bickmore et al. (2010), studying relational agents used for medication adherence support, found that even patients who reported positive experiences with automated relational systems still required human clinician contact for the aspects of their care that involved ambiguity, fear, or complex decision-making. The finding was not that AI relational tools are useless. It was that they have a ceiling, and that ceiling is reached precisely where medicine is hardest and highest-stakes.⏎⏎The illusion of objectivity that AI tools create is, in some ways, the most dangerous aspect of their deployment in clinical settings. When an algorithm produces a risk score or a treatment recommendation, it does so with a precision that feels authoritative — a percentage, a ranking, a flagged alert. That precision is real in a narrow sense: the algorithm has processed its inputs accurately. But it conceals the assumptions embedded in the training data, the populations underrepresented in that data, and the clinical variables that no data set has ever captured because they exist in the space between a clinician and a patient that no sensor reaches. The danger is not that clinicians will distrust AI outputs. The danger is that they will trust them too much, and that the very precision of those outputs will crowd out the messier, slower, more uncertain work of genuine clinical reasoning.⏎⏎SCCM Comments | HHS-AI-RFI-2024 | Page 7⏎⏎A NOTE ON INSTITUTIONAL ACCOUNTABILITY⏎⏎The Society of Critical Care Medicine presented the findings referenced in this comment — including the survey data on AI-driven claims adjudication failures and the disproportionate integration costs in rural and safety-net settings — at the 2024 National Clearinghouse Summit, where delegates from 38 states passed a resolution calling for federal guidance on AI transparency requirements within electronic data interchange frameworks. That resolution is attached as Appendix A to this submission.⏎⏎It is not attached. The appendix was prepared and is referenced here because the resolution itself is a primary document that deserves to be in the docket record. We are working with our legal team to ensure it is submitted under separate cover by the comment deadline. We note this not as a procedural apology but as an illustration of exactly the kind of institutional friction that AI adoption advocates tend to wave away: real organizations, working on real policy problems, with real administrative constraints, do not operate at the pace that technology deployment timelines assume. The communities we serve — the rural clearinghouses, the safety-net institutions, the critical care units in under-resourced hospitals — are not failing to adopt AI because they are resistant to innovation. They are operating in conditions where the implementation costs are prohibitive and the accountability frameworks are nonexistent, and federal policy that accelerates deployment without addressing those conditions will widen, not narrow, the equity gaps that the Quintuple Aim framework is supposed to close.⏎⏎SCCM Comments | HHS-AI-RFI-2024 | Page 8⏎⏎There is a version of this conversation that HHS could be having. It would start from the question of what conditions need to be in place before AI deployment in clinical settings can be conducted safely and equitably, and it would treat the relational foundations of medicine as a clinical asset worth protecting rather than an inefficiency to be optimized away. It would acknowledge that the therapeutic relationship, as documented by Kelley et al. and Epstein and Street and Zulman and others, is not separable from clinical outcomes — that you cannot accelerate the transactional elements of care without affecting the relational ones, because they are not separate systems. It would recognize that the clinician who pauses, who waits, who asks the question a second time, is not wasting time that an AI could use more efficiently. That clinician is doing medicine.⏎⏎The Society of Critical Care Medicine calls on HHS to withdraw the accelerationist framing of this RFI and replace it with a precautionary one. That means requiring demonstrated safety before deployment, not after. It means requiring equity audits on the populations actually served, not on generalized benchmarks. It means requiring meaningful human accountability at every decision point, not nominal oversight by clinicians who have been structurally positioned to defer to algorithmic outputs. And it means commissioning the independent research — on relational outcomes, on equity impacts, on clinician engagement — that would allow future policy to be grounded in evidence rather than in the market enthusiasm of technology vendors whose financial interests in acceleration are substantial and whose accountability for harm is, at present, essentially nonexistent.⏎⏎The resolution from the 2024 National Clearinghouse Summit — Appendix A, to be submitted under separate cover — specifies that federal AI transparency requirements within electronic data interchange frameworks should include mandatory disclosure of training data composition, algorithmic decision logic at the claims level, and vendor accountability mechanisms with enforceable penalties. SCCM endorses those requirements and asks that HHS incorporate them into any regulatory guidance that emerges from this RFI process. We would also note that the resolution's passage by delegates from 38 states, including states with very different political contexts and healthcare market structures, suggests that the concern about AI accountability is not a partisan or ideological position. It is a practitioner position, held by people who are watching these tools arrive in their institutions without the governance frameworks that responsible deployment requires, and who are trying to protect their patients in the absence of federal guidance that should already exist.⏎⏎The docket number for this submission is HHS-AI-RFI-2024. Questions regarding the content of this comment may be directed to the Society of Critical Care Medicine Policy Division at the email address listed on page one of this submission. SYNTH-0076♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Susan Sanchez♔Society for Women's Health Research♔♔♔♔♔Society for Women's Health Research⏎Comments Submitted to the HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-Clinical-RFI⏎Submitted by: Susan Sanchez, Policy Director⏎⏎⏎THE FRAMING PROBLEM⏎⏎The word that keeps appearing in this RFI is "productivity." The Department uses it as though it were a neutral descriptor, a technical term without implications. It is not. When HHS frames the acceleration of clinical AI adoption primarily as a productivity question — how do we move faster, how do we remove friction, how do we get more output from the same clinical hour — it has already made a choice about what medicine is for. The Society for Women's Health Research submits these comments to name that choice directly, and to ask HHS to reconsider it before any regulatory action follows from the current framing.⏎⏎We want to be precise about what we are not arguing. We are not arguing that AI has no place in clinical care. Topol's 2019 synthesis in Nature Medicine remains one of the more careful treatments of where machine learning genuinely outperforms human pattern recognition, particularly in medical imaging and genomic risk stratification (Topol EJ, "High-performance medicine: the convergence of human and artificial intelligence," Nature Medicine, 2019;25(1):44–56). Shortliffe and Sepúlveda, writing in JAMA, have similarly documented conditions under which clinical decision support tools reduce diagnostic error (Shortliffe EH, Sepúlveda MJ, "Clinical decision support in the era of artificial intelligence," JAMA, 2018;320(21):2199–2200). The Society has no categorical objection to AI as an administrative or analytical tool. What we object to is HHS's apparent conflation of AI as a narrow administrative instrument with AI as a clinical intermediary — a system that interposes itself between the clinician and the patient at the moment of diagnosis, treatment planning, or care communication. These are not the same thing, and the RFI treats them as though they exist on a single continuum that the Department simply needs to move everyone along faster.⏎⏎⏎WHAT THE DATA ACTUALLY SHOW⏎⏎The Health AI Institute's 2024 cross-sectional analysis of 214 U.S. health systems, covering more than 1.8 million annual inpatient encounters, found that 68% of institutions cited reimbursement uncertainty as their primary barrier to deploying validated AI diagnostic tools at scale (Health AI Institute, "Operational Readiness and Reimbursement Barriers to Clinical AI Deployment," Health AI Institute Policy Report, 2024). The Society's own monitoring work has identified 47 distinct coding and coverage determinations issued across CMS programs in the preceding 24 months that directly implicated AI-assisted clinical workflows. Fewer than 12% of surveyed health systems reported having dedicated compliance infrastructure to track these developments. Among rural and safety-net institutions, 81% reported insufficient technical assistance resources, compared to 54% of urban academic medical centers.⏎⏎HHS will likely read these numbers as confirmation that the Department needs to act — and act quickly — to rationalize reimbursement pathways and reduce implementation friction. That reading is partially correct. But the same data support a different and more uncomfortable inference: that the friction exists, in part, because clinicians and institutions are making reasonable judgments about tools whose clinical validity, workflow integration, and liability implications remain genuinely unsettled. Removing that friction without first resolving those underlying questions is not acceleration. It is pressure.⏎⏎Consider what the RFI does not ask. It does not ask whether the relational dimensions of clinical care — the components of the patient-clinician encounter that are not reducible to diagnostic accuracy or throughput — are preserved or eroded when AI intermediaries are introduced. Kelley and colleagues, in a 2014 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials published in PLOS ONE, found that the quality of the patient-clinician relationship is independently associated with measurable health outcomes, including treatment adherence and self-reported symptom improvement (Kelley JM, Kraft-Todd G, Schapira L, et al., "The influence of the patient-clinician relationship on healthcare outcomes," PLOS ONE, 2014;9(4):e94207). Hojat and colleagues demonstrated in Academic Medicine that physicians' empathy scores predicted clinical outcomes for diabetic patients at statistically significant levels — not as a soft variable but as a measurable determinant of glycemic control (Hojat M, Louis DZ, Markham FW, et al., "Physicians' empathy and clinical outcomes for diabetic patients," Academic Medicine, 2011;86(3):359–364). These are not sentimental findings. They are findings that the RFI's governing framework simply has no mechanism to weigh.⏎⏎⏎Society for Women's Health Research | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎⏎Think about a woman in her seventies who comes into a primary care appointment after months of not sleeping well, losing weight, and feeling, as she puts it, "just wrong." She cannot name a chief complaint in the clinical sense. What she presents is an accumulation of signals that are legible only to a clinician who has the time, the attentiveness, and the relational context to read them. An AI triage or documentation tool that processes her intake information and routes her to a standardized protocol based on coded symptom clusters will not catch what a clinician who is actually present — who notices that she keeps looking at the door, that she pauses before answering questions about her home situation — might catch. This is not an argument against documentation AI. It is an argument that HHS has not asked what happens when the pressure to deploy AI tools at scale reshapes the clinical encounter in ways that make that kind of attentiveness structurally harder to sustain. The question is not whether the AI tool is accurate. The question is what gets crowded out.⏎⏎Emanuel and Dubler, writing in JAMA in 1995 during a period of managed care expansion that in retrospect offers some instructive parallels, argued that structural changes to care delivery that prioritize throughput over relationship continuity carry specific and documentable costs to patient trust and care quality (Emanuel EJ, Dubler NN, "Preserving the physician-patient relationship in the era of managed care," JAMA, 1995;273(4):323–329). The Department does not need to relitigate that literature. It needs to ask whether it has mechanisms to detect those costs in the current context before they accumulate.⏎⏎⏎AUTOMATION BIAS AND SKILL ATROPHY⏎⏎The RFI does not address automation bias. This is a significant omission. Goddard and colleagues' systematic review in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association documented the frequency and effect mediators of automation bias in clinical settings — the well-established tendency for clinicians to defer to algorithmic outputs even when those outputs conflict with clinical judgment (Goddard K, Roudsari A, Wyatt JC, "Automation bias: a systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators," Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 2012;19(1):121–127). This is not a hypothetical risk. It is a documented behavioral pattern with a substantial empirical literature tracing back to Tversky and Kahneman's foundational work on heuristics and judgment under uncertainty (Tversky A, Kahneman D, "Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases," Science, 1974;185(4157):1124–1131). When clinicians operate alongside systems that generate recommendations with apparent confidence, the cognitive conditions for independent judgment are altered. HHS's RFI does not engage with this.⏎⏎Relatedly, Choudhry and colleagues' systematic review in the Annals of Internal Medicine found that clinical experience and the active exercise of diagnostic judgment are themselves quality determinants — that the skills clinicians use are skills they must continue using to maintain (Choudhry NK, Fletcher RH, Soumerai SB, "Systematic review: the relationship between clinical experience and quality of health care," Annals of Internal Medicine, 2005;142(4):260–273). There is a reasonable concern, not yet fully studied in the AI-specific context, that widespread delegation of diagnostic reasoning to AI intermediaries could contribute to skill atrophy among clinicians who no longer exercise those capacities routinely. The Department has not commissioned research on this question. The RFI does not mention it.⏎⏎The Society raises these concerns with specific reference to women's health, where diagnostic delay and clinician skepticism about symptom severity have been persistently documented as sources of harm. Verghese, Shah, and Harrington, writing in JAMA in 2018, argued that the physical and relational dimensions of the clinical encounter are not incidental to diagnosis — they are constitutive of it, and their erosion has consequences that cannot be captured by accuracy metrics alone (Verghese A, Shah NH, Harrington RA, "What this computer needs is a physician: humanism and artificial intelligence," JAMA, 2018;319(1):19–20). For women patients, who already face documented patterns of clinician skepticism about pain, fatigue, and atypical symptom presentation, the introduction of AI systems trained on historical data carries specific risks. Obermeyer and colleagues' 2019 analysis in Science, demonstrating that a widely used health management algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it used cost as a proxy for need, is the most prominent example of how training data encodes historical inequities into algorithmic outputs (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S, "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations," Science, 2019;366(6464):447–453). The same structural vulnerability applies to sex-based differences in symptom presentation that are underrepresented in training datasets.⏎⏎⏎Society for Women's Health Research | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING REIMBURSEMENT POLICY⏎⏎The Society addresses the RFI's reimbursement questions directly, though with reservations about the frame in which they are posed.⏎⏎The 47 coding and coverage determinations the Society's policy team identified across CMS programs in the preceding 24 months reflect genuine administrative fragmentation. Health systems — particularly those operating in rural and safety-net contexts — cannot reasonably be expected to maintain compliance with a landscape this fragmented without dedicated infrastructure that most of them do not have. The 81% of rural and safety-net institutions reporting insufficient technical assistance resources, compared to 54% of urban academic medical centers, is a gap that federal action could meaningfully address. The Society supports the following specific reimbursement-related actions, with conditions:⏎⏎1. CMS should develop a consolidated coverage framework for AI-assisted clinical decision support tools that distinguishes clearly between tools operating in administrative workflows and tools operating in diagnostic or treatment-planning workflows. These categories carry different liability implications, different validation requirements, and different risks of automation bias. A single coverage determination framework that does not distinguish between them will produce regulatory confusion and, more importantly, clinical risk.⏎⏎2. Any new reimbursement pathway for clinical AI tools should require, as a condition of coverage, that the applying institution demonstrate clinician training on automation bias recognition and mitigation. Goddard and colleagues' systematic review identified training as one of the few well-documented mitigators of automation bias in clinical settings. This is a low-cost, high-yield condition that the Department should impose.⏎⏎3. The Department should require, for AI tools deployed in patient-facing communication roles, evidence that the tool performs adequately across sex-disaggregated subgroups. Bickmore and colleagues' 2009 work on virtual nurse agents found meaningful variation in patient engagement and health literacy outcomes across demographic subgroups — variation that aggregate accuracy metrics do not capture (Bickmore TW, Pfeifer LM, Jack BW, "Taking the time to care: empowering low health literacy hospital patients with virtual nurse agents," Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 2009:1265–1274). Coverage eligibility should be conditioned on this kind of subgroup analysis, not merely on aggregate performance benchmarks.⏎⏎4. Technical assistance funding specifically targeted at rural and safety-net institutions should be a component of any AI acceleration initiative, not an afterthought. The current disparity — 81% versus 54% reporting insufficient resources — is large enough that a policy that does not address it explicitly will widen rather than narrow existing care inequities.⏎⏎o  This includes support for compliance tracking infrastructure, which the Society's monitoring work suggests fewer than 12% of health systems currently have.⏎⏎o  It also includes support for clinician training programs, which in rural contexts often cannot be resourced through institutional budgets alone.⏎⏎The Society is not opposed in principle to reimbursement pathways that support AI tool deployment. The concern is that the Department appears to be designing those pathways primarily around the goal of removing barriers to adoption, without building into the pathway design any mechanisms to detect or correct for the clinical risks that adoption at scale may introduce.⏎⏎⏎THE DEMAND⏎⏎The Society for Women's Health Research makes two specific requests of HHS before any regulatory action proceeds from this RFI.⏎⏎First, the Department must rewrite the RFI's governing assumptions to distinguish explicitly between AI as an administrative tool and AI as a clinical intermediary. The current framing treats these as points on a single spectrum. They are not. The regulatory, liability, reimbursement, and clinical safety questions that attach to each category are different in kind, not merely in degree. A regulatory framework that does not make this distinction will produce rules that are systematically unfit for purpose in the clinical intermediary context.⏎⏎Second, HHS must commission an independent review — conducted by researchers with backgrounds in clinical psychology, medical sociology, and patient-centered outcomes research, not only in informatics and health economics — of the relational dimensions of care that the current framework does not measure. Kelley and colleagues' meta-analysis, Hojat and colleagues' empathy research, Verghese and colleagues' analysis of humanism in AI contexts — these are not niche literatures. They represent decades of evidence that patient outcomes depend on dimensions of the clinical encounter that AI intermediary tools may erode. The Department has not demonstrated that it has a mechanism to detect that erosion before it scales. That gap needs to be addressed before coverage pathways are finalized, not after.⏎⏎The Society notes that the technical assistance disparity between rural and safety-net institutions and urban academic medical centers is itself a measurement and monitoring problem. If HHS lacks the infrastructure to track how AI adoption is affecting care quality across institution types, the Department will be unable to course-correct when problems emerge. The monitoring framework is not a secondary implementation detail — it is a prerequisite for responsible deployment at scale. The Society would welcome the opportunity to⏎⏎swsanchez@swhr.org⏎⏎discuss the monitoring design questions further with ASTP/ONC staff prior to the comment period closing.♔♔2026-01-22T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-22T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔7♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔angry♔Oregon♔policy director♔37♔A 2024 cross-sectional analysis conducted by the Health AI Institute, drawing on operational data from 214 health systems representing over 1.8 million annual inpatient encounters, found that 68% of institutions cited reimbursement uncertainty as their primary barrier to deploying validated AI diagnostic tools at scale.
