SYNTH-0077♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Linda Walker♔Association for Molecular Pathology♔♔♔♔♔Association for Molecular Pathology⏎Comments in Response to HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL⏎Submitted by: Linda Walker, Campaign Director⏎⏎AMP EQUITY COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI | PAGE 1⏎⏎PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS: THE GAP BETWEEN ADOPTION AND INTEGRATION⏎⏎Recent data from the Dental Standards Institute's 2024 quality benchmarking network offer a concrete illustration of how AI adoption collapses in under-resourced practice environments: 68% of participating dental practices had evaluated at least one AI-assisted diagnostic tool in the preceding 18 months, yet only 23% had successfully integrated such tools into routine clinical workflows (Dental Standards Institute, 2024). The barriers were not primarily technical. They were structural — inconsistent reimbursement, absent performance standards, unresolved liability. The Association for Molecular Pathology raises this finding not because oral health AI is our primary domain, but because the structural pattern it reveals maps with disturbing precision onto the clinical environments that concern us most: Mississippi's community hospitals, rural critical access facilities, and the Federally Qualified Health Centers serving majority-Black populations across the Delta region. These are precisely the settings where, as the literature now clearly demonstrates, AI performance degrades most sharply — and where the consequences of that degradation fall on patients who have already borne disproportionate costs of medical neglect and experimentation.⏎⏎The RFI poses many questions. The Association addresses two here, because we believe addressing them honestly requires depth rather than breadth.⏎⏎AMP EQUITY COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI | PAGE 2⏎⏎THE EQUITY PROBLEM HHS HAS NOT YET NAMED DIRECTLY⏎⏎The RFI describes acceleration. What it does not describe, with anything approaching the necessary specificity, is the documented pattern of algorithmic harm that will scale alongside any acceleration HHS facilitates. This is not a theoretical concern. Obermeyer et al. (2019) demonstrated in Science that a widely deployed health management algorithm systematically underestimated the severity of illness in Black patients relative to white patients with identical health status, because the algorithm used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need — a proxy that encodes historical patterns of care underutilization driven by structural racism (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S., Science 2019;366(6464):447-453). Sjoding and colleagues established in the New England Journal of Medicine that pulse oximeters — a device so routine it barely registers as "AI-adjacent" — produced materially inaccurate readings for patients with darker skin pigmentation, and that these errors went undetected in clinical settings for years (Sjoding MW, Dickson RP, Iwashyna TJ, Gay SE, Valley TS., N Engl J Med. 2020;383(25):2477-2478). Wong et al. found in JAMA Internal Medicine that a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model failed external validation in hospitalized patients — performing significantly worse in populations and settings that differed from the development cohort (Wong A, Otles E, Donnelly JP, et al., JAMA Intern Med. 2021;181(8):1065-1070). Adamson and Smith documented in JAMA Dermatology that machine learning tools for skin condition classification were trained predominantly on images of lighter skin, producing error rates that were meaningfully higher for patients of color (Adamson AS, Smith A., JAMA Dermatol. 2018;154(11):1247-1248).⏎⏎These are not edge cases. Gianfrancesco et al. (JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(11):1544-1547) catalogued the structural mechanisms by which electronic health record data systematically underrepresents minority and low-income populations, meaning any model trained on EHR data inherits those gaps. Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones (N Engl J Med. 2020;383(9):874-882) demonstrated that race-correction embedded in clinical algorithms can perpetuate rather than correct for structural inequality. Pierson et al. (Nat Med. 2021;27(1):136-140) showed that algorithmic approaches to pain management produced measurably worse outcomes for underserved populations absent deliberate corrective design. Char, Shah, and Magnus identified in the New England Journal of Medicine the ethical architecture required to prevent machine learning from encoding existing disparities into automated decision-making at scale (Char DS, Shah NH, Magnus D., N Engl J Med. 2018;378(11):981-983). And Wiens et al. articulated in Nature Medicine a responsible deployment framework that includes prospective validation across subgroups as a precondition for clinical use, not an afterthought (Wiens J, Saria S, Sendak M, et al., Nat Med. 2019;25(9):1337-1340).⏎⏎AMP EQUITY COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI | PAGE 3⏎⏎The Association is not aware of any provision in the current RFI that would require stratified performance reporting as a condition of reimbursement eligibility. That absence is a policy choice, and HHS should be explicit about the fact that it is making one.⏎⏎Automation bias — the documented tendency of clinicians to defer to algorithmic outputs even when those outputs conflict with clinical judgment — is particularly dangerous in overworked, under-resourced environments (Char et al., 2018). Mississippi's rural critical access hospitals operate with staffing ratios that make extended deliberation over AI-generated flags functionally impossible on many shifts. When an algorithm trained on data from a large urban academic medical center generates a prediction in that environment, the performance gap is not hypothetical. It is already documented in the external validation literature. The Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology has itself acknowledged these concerns in its 2023 guidance on algorithmic bias in federally supported health programs (ONC, 2023). The National Academy for State Health Policy's 2023 report on algorithmic accountability in Medicaid identified the absence of mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing as the single most significant governance gap across state programs (NASHP, 2023). HHS has access to this literature. The question is whether the Department intends to act on it as a precondition for the reimbursement pathways this RFI contemplates.⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS REGARDING REIMBURSEMENT CONDITIONS⏎⏎The Association urges HHS to consider the following as mandatory conditions — not voluntary best practices — for any AI reimbursement pathway:⏎⏎1. Stratified performance reporting, disaggregated by race, ethnicity, insurance status, payer type, and geography, must be submitted as part of any application for reimbursement eligibility. Aggregate accuracy metrics are insufficient and, in the context of the literature summarized above, affirmatively misleading.⏎⏎2. Post-deployment surveillance with defined disparity thresholds must be required. If a deployed tool produces outcome disparities exceeding a pre-specified threshold relative to the development population's performance, deployment in affected settings should trigger mandatory review and, where warranted, suspension pending re-evaluation.⏎⏎3. Third-party auditing, not vendor self-certification, must be the standard. The Association notes that no credible analogy exists in pharmaceutical regulation, device regulation, or clinical laboratory standards under CLIA where the regulated entity is the sole certifier of its own compliance. There is no principled basis for treating AI differently.⏎⏎4. ACA Section 1557 nondiscrimination obligations and 45 CFR Part 92 apply to AI-mediated clinical decisions made by covered entities. HHS should state this explicitly in any final guidance and should specify the enforcement mechanism.⏎⏎AMP EQUITY COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI | PAGE 4⏎⏎The Association for Molecular Pathology supports AI innovation that demonstrably serves all patients across all geographies and income levels. The organization will actively oppose any reimbursement or regulatory pathway that deploys unaudited tools in communities that have already borne the costs of medical experimentation and neglect — and we use the word "oppose" in its full institutional sense, including public advocacy, coalition engagement, and where appropriate, administrative challenge. This is not a posture of obstruction. It is a posture rooted in the recognition that Mississippi's patients cannot afford to be the external validation cohort for tools developed and certified elsewhere.⏎⏎One logistical concern the Association has not seen addressed in the RFI: the timeline for comment response and any subsequent NPRM does not appear to account for the time required to develop the equity audit infrastructure that would actually make stratified reporting feasible for smaller health systems and FQHCs. A reimbursement pathway that goes live before that infrastructure exists will, in practice, be accessible only to large health systems with dedicated compliance resources — which is to say, not the settings this comment is primarily concerned with. That sequencing problem deserves explicit attention in HHS's response, and the Association would welcome the opportunity to⏎⏎References⏎⏎Adamson AS, Smith A. SYNTH-0078♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Brian Rivera♔Walgreens Boots Alliance♔♔♔♔♔Walgreens Boots Alliance Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎Submitted to: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎Re: Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Brian Rivera, Director of Government Relations, Walgreens Boots Alliance⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎HHS has framed this RFI primarily as a question of how to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care settings, and Walgreens Boots Alliance does not dispute that there are genuine clinical applications of AI worth supporting. What this submission argues, with some force, is that the framing itself is doing significant work that HHS appears not to have examined. Specifically, the RFI's stated interest in actions that "foster competition among clinical care AI tool builders" treats AI deployment in healthcare as a uniformly positive phenomenon that needs only to be scaled more quickly. The documented record of AI deployment in insurance administration tells a different story. Prior authorization denial systems powered by AI are currently operating at scale across Medicare Advantage plans, generating coverage refusals at rates that cannot plausibly be explained by clinical appropriateness review, and doing so with the kind of throughput that is only possible precisely because human clinical judgment has been removed from the loop. HHS's acceleration posture, if extended without guardrails to this category of AI use, will expand that harm.⏎⏎Walgreens Boots Alliance operates more than 8,700 retail pharmacy locations across the United States and manages prescription fulfillment, medication therapy management, and specialty pharmacy services for millions of patients, including a substantial proportion of Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries. Our pharmacy operations place us at the direct interface between prior authorization decisions and patient access to care. Our pharmacists routinely see what happens when an automated denial generates a multi-week appeals backlog: patients abandon prescriptions, defer treatment, or attempt to self-manage conditions that require clinical oversight. This is not an abstraction for us.⏎⏎Walgreens Boots Alliance Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎The RFI asks, among other things, what reimbursement and regulatory actions HHS can take to accelerate AI adoption. We are addressing that question specifically, and we want to be direct about what the answer should not include: reimbursement recognition or regulatory endorsement for any AI system used in coverage determination that has not first undergone demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability auditing with public disclosure of results.⏎⏎The Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations published findings in October 2023 establishing that major Medicare Advantage insurers deployed AI-driven prior authorization systems that generated denials at rates materially exceeding what their own internal clinical criteria would have supported (S. Prt. 118-22). The HHS Office of Inspector General, in its April 2022 report (OIG Report OEI-09-18-00260), found that some Medicare Advantage organization denials of prior authorization requests raised substantial concerns about beneficiary access to medically necessary care, with denial rates for certain service categories running at multiples of what traditional Medicare would have produced for the same clinical presentations. ProPublica's March 2023 investigation into Cigna documented a process in which physicians were reviewing and rejecting claims in batches, spending an average of 1.2 seconds per case, a figure that only makes sense in the context of algorithmic pre-screening that had already done the substantive work (ProPublica Investigations, March 2023). The GAO, in GAO-23-105898 published in February 2023, found that prior authorization denials in Medicare Advantage were appealed successfully at rates suggesting systematic initial over-denial. Read together, these findings describe not isolated failures but a system operating as designed: AI deployed to optimize denial throughput, with appeals processes functioning as cost-friction mechanisms rather than genuine corrective channels.⏎⏎Kaye et al., writing in the Journal of Health Politics, Policy and Law (Vol. 49, No. 2, 2024, pp. 211-238), examined the divergence between cost-containment objectives embedded in Medicare Advantage AI training data and clinical appropriateness standards, and found that the two are frequently in direct tension. This is the core problem with HHS's framing. When the RFI talks about "AI tool builders" competing to serve clinical care, it is describing one segment of the AI-in-healthcare market. The segment that is currently generating the most documented patient harm is not clinical care AI at all; it is administrative AI deployed by payers specifically to reduce expenditure. These systems are not being trained on clinical appropriateness guidelines. They are being trained on cost outcomes. The AMA's 2023 Prior Authorization Physician Survey found that 94 percent of physicians reported prior authorization delays associated with adverse patient outcomes, and 33 percent reported that a patient experienced a serious adverse event as a direct consequence of a prior authorization denial or delay (AMA Policy Research Perspectives, January 2024). HHS cannot credibly accelerate "AI in healthcare" while treating payer-side denial automation as outside the scope of this RFI.⏎⏎Walgreens Boots Alliance Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎The populations bearing the greatest burden from automated prior authorization denial are precisely the populations HHS is statutorily charged with protecting. The National Health Law Program's September 2023 policy brief (NHeLP Policy Brief No. 47) documented that AI-driven denials in Medicaid disproportionately affect beneficiaries with disabilities, who are more likely to require non-standard treatment protocols that algorithmic systems flag as outliers from population norms. Elderly Medicare Advantage beneficiaries, many of whom have limited English proficiency, limited digital access, or cognitive conditions that make multi-stage appeals processes genuinely inaccessible, are functionally unable to contest automated denials even when those denials are wrong. The appeals burden is itself a design feature of these systems. CMS's Medicare Advantage Prior Authorization and Utilization Management Final Rule (88 Fed. Reg. 22120, April 12, 2023) attempted to impose some constraints on prior authorization timelines, but it did not address the AI-specific accountability gap: the absence of any requirement that AI systems used in coverage determination be audited for accuracy, equity, or alignment with clinical appropriateness standards before deployment.⏎⏎The accountability vacuum Walgreens Boots Alliance is describing extends to data practices. EPIC's March 2024 policy report on AI in health insurance documented opacity in how insurers are using patient data to train denial-optimization systems, with minimal disclosure to patients or regulators about the secondary commercial uses to which de-identified health information is being put (EPIC Policy Report, March 2024). Our own monitoring of HHS enforcement activity between 2021 and 2023 identified zero penalties issued specifically for AI-related re-identification risks under HIPAA's de-identification safe harbor standards, despite a substantial increase in reported health system AI partnerships during that same period. Obermeyer et al.'s foundational 2019 Science paper (Vol. 366, No. 6464, pp. 447-453) established that health algorithms trained on cost-as-proxy-for-need data embed and amplify racial disparities. There is no reason to believe that payer-side prior authorization AI is exempt from this dynamic, and considerable reason to believe it operates in that direction, given that cost-containment objectives are exactly the kind of proxy that Obermeyer's analysis identified as problematic. HHS has not required any insurer to audit its prior authorization AI for racial or disability-status disparate impact. The RFI does not appear to contemplate doing so.⏎⏎Walgreens Boots Alliance Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎Our specific recommendations, focused on the reimbursement and regulatory questions the RFI poses, are as follows:⏎⏎1. HHS should condition any reimbursement recognition or regulatory endorsement of AI systems used in coverage determination on prior completion of demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability audits, with public disclosure of audit methodology and findings. "Demonstrated safety" should require, at minimum, prospective validation against clinical appropriateness criteria independent of the deploying insurer.⏎⏎2. HHS should extend the CMS prior authorization final rule framework (88 Fed. Reg. 22120) to require that any AI-assisted prior authorization determination be flagged as such in all beneficiary-facing communications, with explicit disclosure of the AI system's denial rate, appeal overturn rate, and any known equity audit findings.⏎⏎3. HHS should direct the OIG to conduct a systematic review of AI-assisted prior authorization denial rates across Medicare Advantage plans, building on the April 2022 OIG report, with particular attention to whether denial rates have increased following AI deployment and whether appeal overturn rates suggest systematic initial over-denial.⏎⏎o Sub-recommendation: This review should include examination of whether de-identified patient data used to train denial-optimization systems was obtained and used in compliance with HIPAA's de-identification standards, and whether any re-identification risks have been assessed.⏎⏎4. HHS should not treat the "foster competition among clinical care AI tool builders" objective as applicable to payer-side denial automation. Competition in denial AI is not a patient benefit. The competitive dynamic in that market runs in the direction of more denials, faster, with less human review.⏎⏎The RFI's framing treats AI adoption as a supply-side problem: there are AI tools, and the question is how to get them adopted more quickly. What the prior authorization record shows is that the adoption problem has already been solved on the payer side, and what resulted was not a clinical improvement but an administrative mechanism for overriding physician judgment at scale. Walgreens Boots Alliance's pharmacy operations put us in direct contact with the downstream consequences of that dynamic every day. Our pharmacists are not equipped to adjudicate coverage disputes, but they are often the last point of contact before a patient abandons a prescription that an AI system has decided, in under two seconds of algorithmic review, is not medically necessary.⏎⏎A reference appendix containing supporting documentation, including our internal analysis of prior authorization delay rates observed across Walgreens pharmacy locations serving Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries in Maryland, Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Illinois during fiscal year 2024, is available upon request and will be submitted as a supplemental filing. SYNTH-0079♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Kevin Ramirez♔♔♔♔♔♔ADMINISTRATIVE AI IN COMMUNITY HOSPITALS: A CAUTION ON TACIT KNOWLEDGE AND CONSEQUENTIAL AUTOMATION⏎⏎The efficiency argument for deploying AI in healthcare administrative workflows rests on a premise that deserves direct examination before HHS builds reimbursement or regulatory policy around it: that the labor currently embedded in care coordination, prior authorization review, benefits counseling, and patient navigation is largely clerical, repetitive, and therefore automatable without significant loss. After twenty-six years of bedside nursing in community hospital settings, including the past several at Palmetto Health in South Carolina, I can say with some confidence that this premise is wrong in ways that will not show up in pilot program metrics. The work of a care coordinator who knows that a particular patient's listed address is a shelter with mail pickup three days a week, or that a specific Medicaid managed care plan in Richland County has a de facto policy of denying DME requests on first submission regardless of documentation quality, is not clerical work. It is what Michael Polanyi described in 1966 as tacit knowledge: the kind of knowing that is embedded in practice and context and cannot be fully articulated, let alone captured in a training dataset. When that knowledge gets replaced by a system that processes structured fields, the errors it produces are invisible to the system itself, which is precisely what Ash, Berg, and Coiera documented in 2004 regarding health IT-generated errors in patient care information systems. The system logs a completed action. The patient doesn't get their equipment.⏎⏎THE EFFICIENCY FRAMING AS CATEGORY ERROR⏎⏎What concerns me about the framing of this RFI is that it positions administrative AI primarily as a burden-reduction mechanism, which is the same framing that gave us EHR documentation architectures designed around billing optimization rather than clinical communication. ONC's own 2023 strategy on reducing administrative burden acknowledged explicitly that the documentation load on clinical staff is a human-labor problem with systemic causes, not a technology deficit waiting to be solved with better software. Himmelstein and colleagues documented in the Annals of Internal Medicine in 2020 that U.S. healthcare administrative costs consumed roughly $812 billion annually, but the relevant point for this comment is not the dollar figure — it's that a substantial portion of that cost represents human judgment about edge cases, eligibility ambiguities, and coordination failures that no amount of structured data exchange resolves cleanly. The National Academy for State Health Policy documented in 2022 that prior authorization workflows in Medicaid are saturated with exactly this kind of judgment-intensive review, where a human navigator's knowledge of local plan behavior and patient circumstance is what gets a decision made correctly rather than merely made quickly. Automating that judgment doesn't eliminate the labor; it shifts the error-correction labor downstream, closer to the patient, and often onto patients themselves, who are the least equipped to absorb it. Obermeyer and colleagues demonstrated in Science in 2019 that algorithmic errors in population health management were systematically invisible to the institutions deploying the algorithms while being concentrated among Black patients — which is precisely the population most dependent on skilled human navigation of a system that doesn't default in their favor. The efficiency gains show up in the dashboard. The harm shows up in the gap between what the system logged and what the patient actually received.⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD REQUIRE⏎⏎There is also a practical point that I think gets lost in discussions about administrative AI: these roles are already critically understaffed in community hospitals, not overstaffed. The assumption that automating administrative tasks will free human capacity for higher-value work assumes there is excess human capacity currently doing lower-value work, and that is not the situation in most non-academic facilities I am aware of. What actually happens when an AI system generates errors in a benefits determination or a care transition summary is that a human has to detect the error, trace it, correct it, and then manage the patient's response to the delay or the wrong outcome. That corrective labor falls on whoever is available, which in a community hospital is usually a nurse. Bates and Gawande noted in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2003 that the safety benefit of health IT is real but depends critically on implementation context, and that poorly implemented systems generate new error types while eliminating old ones. The same principle applies here. My specific ask of HHS is this: any administrative AI deployment seeking reimbursement coverage or regulatory approval should be required to demonstrate safety and equity outcomes in the specific deployment population, not in academic medical center pilots, and should be required to maintain mandatory human review at every consequential decision point, where consequential means any determination that affects patient access to care, services, or benefits. The definition of consequential should not be left to the deploying institution to determine, because the institution's incentives are not aligned with the patient's interests when administrative throughput is the metric being optimized. I would also note that the current absence of any standardized definition of "administrative AI" in federal guidance means that♔♔2026-01-03T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-03T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔2♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Even administrative healthcare functions that appear routine require human contextual judgment that AI cannot replicate, and automating them will produce systematic errors that harm patients and workers.♔individual♔high♔frustrated♔South Carolina♔nurse♔54♔During a twelve-hour overnight shift at Palmetto Health last February, I watched a colleague spend forty-five minutes manually reconciling medication orders that a half-functional EHR kept flagging incorrectly, while the patient in 4B was deteriorating and needed her at the bedside — and that's when it crystallized for me how catastrophically we've miscalibrated what "healthcare technology" is supposed to accomplish. SYNTH-0080♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Richard Campbell♔American Dental Association♔♔♔♔♔American Dental Association | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 1⏎⏎---⏎⏎COMMENTS OF THE AMERICAN DENTAL ASSOCIATION IN RESPONSE TO THE HHS REQUEST FOR INFORMATION ON ACCELERATING AI ADOPTION IN CLINICAL CARE⏎⏎Submitted by: Richard Campbell, Community Engagement and Policy Division⏎Organization: American Dental Association⏎Date: Submitted via regulations.gov⏎⏎---⏎⏎American Dental Association | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE REIMBURSEMENT PROBLEM IS NOT PERIPHERAL — IT IS THE PROBLEM⏎⏎The American Dental Association (ADA) submits these comments with a degree of institutional frustration that, we acknowledge upfront, goes beyond the usual register of regulatory response. The Department has been presented with substantial, practitioner-sourced evidence about what is actually obstructing AI adoption in clinical settings. A 2024 survey conducted across our network of 847 affiliated clinical sites found that 63% of frontline providers cited reimbursement uncertainty as the primary barrier to deploying AI-assisted diagnostic tools. That figure outranked both technical integration challenges and workforce training gaps by a significant margin. Our policy analysis team's review of 34 health system procurement decisions made between 2022 and 2024 identified that fewer than 20% of facilities had received any formal CMS guidance applicable to the AI tools they were evaluating. These findings were formally presented at our annual convening in March 2024, where member representatives from 29 states reached consensus that federal reimbursement frameworks remain the single most consequential lever for accelerating responsible AI adoption in clinical settings. We note, with something approaching disbelief, that the RFI's framing of reimbursement as one consideration among many does not reflect the weight of this evidence.⏎⏎The RFI asks broadly about what regulatory, reimbursement, and research-and-development actions HHS can take. The ADA will not attempt to address every question posed — that exercise, in our view, produces comments that gesture at comprehensiveness while delivering nothing actionable. We address two areas where the Department's current framing is most consequentially incomplete, and where the ADA's evidence base is most directly applicable.⏎⏎---⏎⏎American Dental Association | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 3⏎⏎---⏎⏎STRUCTURAL MISALIGNMENT IN REIMBURSEMENT FRAMEWORKS⏎⏎The core problem is structural. Facilities evaluating AI-assisted diagnostic tools — including caries detection systems, periodontal risk stratification tools, and radiographic analysis software — are making procurement decisions in a reimbursement vacuum. The U.S. Government Accountability Office documented in its 2023 report on artificial intelligence in health care (GAO-23-105980) that CMS reimbursement pathways for AI-enabled clinical tools remain undefined across most care categories. Dental settings are not even addressed in that report, which itself reflects a pattern of omission that the ADA has raised with HHS staff on multiple occasions without receiving a substantive response.⏎⏎What happens in the absence of clear reimbursement guidance is predictable and, at this point, well-documented. Procurement decisions are delayed, deferred, or made on the basis of anticipated future guidance that may or may not materialize. Smaller practices and community health centers, which lack the administrative infrastructure to absorb regulatory ambiguity, are effectively excluded from AI adoption entirely. Bates et al. (2021), writing in npj Digital Medicine, documented the potential for AI tools to meaningfully reduce clinician burnout while maintaining quality of care — but that potential is unreachable for the majority of dental practices operating under fee-for-service reimbursement structures that have no mechanism for capturing the value of AI-assisted workflow. Shanafelt et al. (2022), in the Mayo Clinic Proceedings, have documented the trajectory of burnout and work-life integration failures across clinical professions over a decade; the ADA's own membership surveys track a parallel deterioration in dental practitioner satisfaction that AI adoption, properly reimbursed, could plausibly address.⏎⏎The ADA recognizes that oral health has historically sat at the margins of federal health policy — separated from medical benefits under Medicare in ways that have no coherent clinical rationale. The Affordable Care Act's treatment of adult dental benefits as optional under Medicaid has compounded this marginalization. We raise this not to relitigate coverage policy in this comment, but because the structural separation of dental from medical reimbursement means that CMS guidance on AI tools, when it does eventually materialize, will almost certainly default to frameworks built around physician and hospital settings. Dental AI tools will be left waiting for a second round of guidance that may take years. This is the specific mechanism by which reimbursement uncertainty operates in our sector, and it is different in important ways from the mechanism affecting, say, hospital radiology departments.⏎⏎---⏎⏎American Dental Association | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 4⏎⏎---⏎⏎WORKFORCE AND GOVERNANCE CONCERNS THE RFI UNDERWEIGHTS⏎⏎The second area where the RFI's framing is incomplete concerns the relationship between AI adoption and clinical workforce governance. The ADA is not opposed to AI-assisted clinical tools — our network includes early adopters who report genuine diagnostic value from radiographic AI systems, and we are not in the business of reflexive resistance to technology. But the deployment of AI tools in ways that alter clinical workflows without adequate clinician input creates risks that the RFI's optimistic framing of "acceleration" does not adequately account for.⏎⏎Dillahunt-Aspillaga et al. (2023), publishing in the Journal of Health Politics, Policy and Law, documented patterns of deskilling and professional role erosion in community health centers that deployed EHR-integrated AI tools without structured clinician governance over those deployments. The findings are specific: algorithmic management functions embedded in clinical AI tools shifted decision-making authority in ways that were not transparent to the clinicians nominally responsible for patient care. Gawande (2018), writing in The New Yorker, identified the core governance failure with characteristic precision — the problem is not that computers are bad, but that the humans who deploy them in clinical settings rarely include the clinicians who must use them. The American Medical Association's 2023 policy document on augmented intelligence (H-480.940) articulates principles for ethical deployment and clinician oversight that HHS and ONC should treat as a floor, not a ceiling.⏎⏎The Service Employees International Union (SEIU) published a policy framework in January 2024 calling for healthcare AI governance structures that center frontline worker input in procurement decisions. The ADA shares this concern, though we would frame it differently for a clinical context: the question is not simply labor representation, but clinical accountability. When an AI tool influences a diagnostic recommendation, the clinician who acts on that recommendation must have been involved in evaluating the tool's performance characteristics, its training data, its known failure modes. Obermeyer and Emanuel (2016), writing in the New England Journal of Medicine, made the foundational point that machine learning systems in clinical medicine can encode and amplify the biases present in their training data. That observation is now nearly a decade old. The governance frameworks to address it have not kept pace.⏎⏎National Nurses United documented in their October 2023 policy brief on AI procurement and staffing standards that workforce displacement risk is being systematically understated in health system procurement processes. The Accenture Federal Services / MITRE workforce displacement risk assessment prepared for HHS ASPE under Contract No. HHSP233201600021I reached similar conclusions through a different methodological approach. The ADA raises this not because dental AI tools pose significant displacement risk — the tools currently in deployment in dental settings are genuinely assistive rather than substitutive — but because the governance frameworks being established now will shape how more consequential tools are deployed in the future. Kohn, Corrigan, and Donaldson's foundational work on institutional accountability in health care, To Err Is Human (2000), established the principle that safety systems must be built before failures occur, not reconstructed after them. That principle applies to AI governance as directly as it applied to medication error reduction.⏎⏎---⏎⏎American Dental Association | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 5⏎⏎---⏎⏎SPECIFIC REQUESTS ADDRESSED TO HHS AND ONC⏎⏎The ADA urges HHS and ONC to take the following actions, which we consider the minimum necessary response to the evidence presented in this and prior submissions:⏎⏎1. CMS should issue, within 18 months, specific reimbursement guidance for AI-assisted diagnostic tools in dental care settings, with explicit coverage of caries detection, periodontal risk assessment, and radiographic analysis applications. Guidance that addresses only physician and hospital settings will not reach the dental practices where 63% of our surveyed providers have identified reimbursement uncertainty as their primary barrier.⏎⏎2. ONC should require, as a condition of health IT certification for AI-enabled clinical decision support tools, documented evidence of clinician governance involvement in the tool's clinical validation process. This requirement should be specific enough to be auditable — a general attestation of "stakeholder engagement" is insufficient and, based on our procurement review, is how most current processes are described.⏎⏎3. HHS should commission a sector-specific assessment of AI reimbursement gaps in oral health care, analogous to the GAO-23-105980 report but with dental settings as the primary unit of analysis rather than an afterthought. The ADA is prepared to provide data from our 847-site network to support that assessment.⏎⏎o  Wachter and Goldsmith (2023), writing in Harvard Business Review, argued that fixing the electronic health record is a prerequisite for realizing AI's clinical potential. The ADA would extend that argument: fixing the reimbursement framework is a prerequisite for fixing anything else.⏎⏎o  The ADA also notes, for the record, that our member practitioners have raised a concern that falls somewhat outside the formal scope of this RFI but that we believe the Department should be aware of. Several members have reported that their supplemental coverage premiums increased substantially in the past plan year — one member described a 22% increase — and attributed this in part to administrative costs associated with new technology compliance requirements. The ADA cannot independently verify this attribution, and we recognize it may reflect broader insurance market dynamics rather than anything specific to AI policy. But when frontline practitioners are experiencing cost pressures of this magnitude, the Department's framing of AI adoption as primarily a technical and regulatory challenge misses something real about the financial environment in which these decisions are being made. We flag it because it was raised repeatedly in our member consultation process, and because the Department asked for input on barriers to adoption.⏎⏎---⏎⏎American Dental Association | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 6⏎⏎---⏎⏎The ADA thanks the Department for the opportunity to submit these comments. We note that the March 2024 convening at which these findings were presented included member representatives who traveled from states as distant as Maine and Hawaii specifically because they believed federal action on AI reimbursement was imminent. That belief was based on signals from HHS staff that guidance was being actively developed. We are not aware of any such guidance having been issued or formally proposed as of the date of this submission, and we would welcome clarification from ONC on the current status of that process.⏎⏎The ADA's contact for follow-up on these comments is Richard Campbell, Community Engagement and Policy Division. SYNTH-0081♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Daniel Walker♔Commure♔♔♔♔♔Commure | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 1⏎⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎Submitted electronically via regulations.gov⏎⏎⏎INSTITUTIONAL STANDING AND SCOPE OF COMMENT⏎⏎Commure is a health technology company whose clinical operations infrastructure supports care delivery across a range of settings, including rural and federally qualified health centers in New Mexico that serve predominantly Indigenous, Hispanic, and low-income patient populations. Daniel Walker, MD, Chief Medical Officer, submits this comment on behalf of the organization's clinical leadership. These comments address a narrow but consequential subset of the RFI questions: specifically, what pre-deployment and post-deployment safeguards HHS should require as conditions of any federal endorsement or reimbursement of clinical AI tools. We are not writing to oppose AI adoption. We are writing because the populations our work touches most directly are the populations most likely to be harmed when AI fails quietly.⏎⏎⏎THE BIAS PROBLEM IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL⏎⏎Commure | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 2⏎⏎HHS has framed this RFI around acceleration. That framing concerns our clinical leadership, not because speed is inherently wrong, but because the documented failure modes of clinical AI are already well-established in the peer-reviewed literature and the current proposal contains no mandatory mechanism to catch those failures before they reach patients.⏎⏎The evidence here is not ambiguous. Sjoding et al. (2020) demonstrated in the New England Journal of Medicine that pulse oximeters systematically overestimate arterial oxygen saturation in Black patients, and that AI systems trained on pulse oximetry data have inherited that measurement error as a structural feature of their outputs. This is not a modeling flaw that better engineering will resolve on its own; it is a consequence of building systems on data that encoded discriminatory clinical practices. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan (2019), writing in Science, showed that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to identify patients for high-risk care management systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients because it used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, a substitution that reflected historical patterns of care denial rather than clinical reality. The algorithm was affecting the care of millions of patients before the bias was characterized. Wong, Otles, Donnelly et al. (2021) conducted external validation of a proprietary sepsis prediction model in JAMA Internal Medicine and found that the model's real-world performance degraded substantially compared to internally reported metrics, with false alert rates that created workflow burdens falling disproportionately on already-strained nursing staff at community hospitals. Adamson and Smith (2018) documented in JAMA Dermatology that dermatological AI trained predominantly on images of lighter-skinned patients performed materially worse on darker skin tones, with clinical implications for melanoma detection in populations that already face delays in dermatological access.⏎⏎These are not edge cases from early-stage research. They are findings from peer-reviewed journals describing deployed or near-deployed systems. Seyyed-Kalantari, Zhang, McDermott, Chen, and Ghassemi (2021) published in Nature Medicine a systematic analysis showing that AI algorithms applied to chest radiographs produced underdiagnosis at higher rates in underserved patient populations, including patients on Medicaid, women, and patients over 65. Pierson, Cutler, Leskovec, Mullainathan, and Obermeyer (2021), also in Nature Medicine, found that algorithmic approaches to pain management similarly reflected and reproduced pre-existing disparities in how pain is assessed and treated across racial lines. Gianfrancesco, Tamang, Yazdany, and Schmajuk (2018) identified in JAMA Internal Medicine a range of structural biases introduced when EHR data is used for model training, including selection bias from differential healthcare access, measurement bias from inconsistent documentation practices, and label bias from diagnoses that reflect provider assumptions as much as patient pathology. Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones (2020) argued in the New England Journal of Medicine that race correction embedded in clinical algorithms, even when framed as scientifically grounded, often encodes social categories as biological ones in ways that produce systematically worse care for minority patients.⏎⏎The pattern across these studies is consistent. Historical healthcare data encodes decades of unequal treatment. AI systems trained on that data reproduce those inequalities. The reproduction happens at scale and at speed, and it happens with an appearance of objectivity that makes the errors harder to detect than equivalent errors made by individual clinicians.⏎⏎⏎Commure | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 3⏎⏎THE AUTOMATION BIAS PROBLEM COMPOUNDS THE GENERALIZABILITY PROBLEM⏎⏎There is a second structural issue that the RFI does not appear to grapple with, and it is worth naming directly. Char, Shah, and Magnus (2018) identified in the New England Journal of Medicine that AI outputs carry an epistemic authority that human clinical judgment does not, even when the underlying accuracy is comparable or lower. When a clinician makes an error, other clinicians can recognize it as a clinical judgment call and apply appropriate skepticism. When an algorithm produces an output, the output tends to be treated as a calculation rather than an estimate, and the institutional instinct is to trust it. This is what the cognitive science literature calls automation bias, and it has specific implications for how AI errors propagate through clinical workflows. An algorithmic recommendation that is wrong for a specific patient population will be wrong systematically and repeatedly before anyone notices, precisely because the format of the output discourages the kind of case-by-case scrutiny that would catch a human clinician making the same mistake.⏎⏎Wiens, Saria, Sendak et al. (2019) outlined in Nature Medicine a responsible deployment framework that explicitly addresses this risk, recommending prospective monitoring, clear performance benchmarks, and structured mechanisms for clinician override and feedback. Parikh, Teeple, and Navathe (2019) argued in JAMA that bias mitigation requires not just technical corrections but institutional accountability structures that assign responsibility for monitoring outcomes across demographic subgroups after deployment. Neither of these recommendations is reflected in the current RFI as a mandatory condition.⏎⏎The generalizability problem makes this worse. The validation studies cited in support of most commercially deployed clinical AI tools were conducted at large academic medical centers with well-resourced informatics infrastructure, high data quality, and patient populations that are substantially wealthier and more homogeneous than the populations served by community hospitals, rural facilities, and safety-net institutions. A model validated at a major urban academic center and then deployed at a small hospital in rural New Mexico is operating in a different data environment, with different baseline disease prevalence, different documentation practices, different patient demographics, and different clinical workflows. There is no reason to expect that performance will transfer, and the evidence from Wong et al. (2021) and Seyyed-Kalantari et al. (2021) suggests it often does not.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC REQUESTS TO HHS⏎⏎Our clinical leadership asks HHS to consider the following as conditions of any federal endorsement, certification, or reimbursement of clinical AI tools. These are not aspirational requests. They are minimum structural requirements if the goal is to avoid systematically harming underserved populations.⏎⏎1. Mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing. Before any clinical AI tool is eligible for federal reimbursement or ONC certification, the developer should be required to demonstrate performance equity across demographic subgroups defined at minimum by race, ethnicity, sex, age, insurance status, and rurality. The audit should be conducted using data from settings comparable to the intended deployment environment, not exclusively from academic medical centers. Internal validation is insufficient; external validation in community and safety-net settings should be a condition of market entry for any tool that will affect clinical decision-making.⏎⏎2. Mandatory post-deployment bias surveillance. Deployment should not be treated as the end of the oversight process. HHS should require covered entities deploying AI tools to monitor clinical outcomes disaggregated by demographic subgroup on an ongoing basis, with defined thresholds that trigger review. This does not require new regulatory authority in most cases; it can be structured as a condition of participation in federal reimbursement programs. The monitoring framework should be proportionate to the clinical stakes of the tool, with higher-risk applications subject to more frequent review.⏎⏎3. Transparency requirements for training data provenance. Clinicians and covered entities deploying AI tools should have access to meaningful information about the demographic composition of training datasets, the settings in which validation was conducted, and the known limitations of model performance across subgroups. This is not a novel concept; it is the minimum information a clinician would need to apply appropriate judgment about when to trust an output and when to override it.⏎⏎o A note on format: Commure does not believe a single standardized disclosure template will be adequate across all tool types and clinical contexts. HHS should develop a tiered disclosure framework that scales with clinical risk and requires more detailed provenance information for tools affecting high-stakes decisions like sepsis management, diagnostic imaging interpretation, or triage prioritization.⏎⏎o The disclosure requirements should apply to tools deployed through EHR integrations and third-party clinical decision support platforms, not only to standalone AI products, given that the majority of clinical AI is currently reaching clinicians through EHR-embedded pathways.⏎⏎⏎Commure | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 4⏎⏎Our institution does not oppose the broader goal of expanding access to AI-assisted clinical tools. There are genuine use cases where well-validated AI can reduce burden on clinicians and improve consistency of care, particularly in settings with limited specialist access. The question is not whether to deploy AI but under what conditions. The populations served by our partner facilities in New Mexico, many of whom are members of Pueblo and Navajo communities with documented histories of underrepresentation in medical research and undertreatment in clinical settings, do not have the institutional advocates or legal infrastructure to identify and contest algorithmic harm after the fact. The obligation to prevent that harm before deployment falls to HHS, and it requires structural requirements, not guidance documents or voluntary frameworks.⏎⏎Parikh et al. (2019) made the point clearly: voluntary commitments from developers are not sufficient accountability mechanisms when the populations most likely to be harmed are the populations least likely to have recourse. We agree. The current RFI does not reflect that reality in its framing or its proposed actions, and we urge the Department to revise its approach before clinical AI deployment at scale produces the kind of documented, systematic harm that the peer-reviewed literature has already shown is possible.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Daniel Walker, MD⏎Chief Medical Officer, Commure⏎⏎contact: policy@commure.com♔♔2026-01-06T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-06T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔organization♔high♔supportive♔New Mexico♔chief medical officer♔37♔EPIC's 2024 audit of 47 commercially deployed clinical AI tools found that 89% lacked meaningful data minimization protocols, with patient data routinely retained for model retraining without explicit consent mechanisms or transparent disclosure to covered entities. SYNTH-0083♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Kevin Lopez♔Infectious Diseases Society of America♔♔♔♔♔THE DEMOCRATIC GOVERNANCE OF CLINICAL AI: A COMMENT FROM THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES SOCIETY OF AMERICA⏎⏎Submitted to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Deputy Secretary, and the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy / Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology⏎⏎Docket: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎PRELIMINARY STATEMENT⏎⏎The Infectious Diseases Society of America submits these comments with a specific concern that we believe is not adequately addressed by the framing of this RFI — and, indeed, is actively obscured by it. Our organization has spent the past eighteen months conducting longitudinal analysis of AI-assisted diagnostic deployments across 112 health systems, and what that research has taught us is not primarily about technical performance or clinical integration timelines. What it has taught us is that the embedding of AI systems into clinical infrastructure is, at a certain threshold of institutional dependency, practically irreversible. We document this not as a theoretical concern but as an observed empirical pattern: sites that crossed what our Q4 2024 internal policy report terms the "dependency threshold" — defined as the point at which AI-assisted workflows have displaced the institutional knowledge and staffing structures that previously supported manual or clinician-led alternatives — showed no meaningful pathway back to prior practice configurations, regardless of subsequent regulatory, contractual, or administrative intervention. (Health AI Institute, "Longitudinal Analysis of Clinical AI Deployment Outcomes Across 112 Health Systems, 2022–2024," internal policy report, Q4 2024.) That finding is what grounds everything that follows. HHS is not asking a technical optimization question in this RFI. It is asking, without quite saying so, whether the federal government should use its regulatory and reimbursement authority to push clinical medicine past that dependency threshold at national scale — and it is asking that question without acknowledging that crossing that threshold is, in democratic terms, a one-way door.⏎⏎The Health AI Institute urges HHS and ONC to read these comments as a response to that unacknowledged question, not to the question as formally posed.⏎⏎⏎THE IRREVERSIBILITY PROBLEM AS A DEMOCRATIC PROBLEM⏎⏎Langdon Winner argued in his foundational 1980 essay "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" (Daedalus 109(1):121–136) that technological systems are not neutral instruments deployed in neutral social contexts — they embed political arrangements, redistribute authority, and, once institutionalized, become resistant to democratic revision precisely because the human capacities and social structures that existed before them have atrophied. Winner's canonical example was the highway overpasses of Robert Moses, built too low for public buses, effectively encoding a racial and class geography into infrastructure that outlasted any particular political actor. The analogy to clinical AI is not perfect, but it is closer than the RFI's framing suggests. When AI systems for clinical decision support, diagnostic interpretation, or care coordination are embedded into institutional workflows at the scale HHS is contemplating, they do not merely augment existing human capacities. They gradually displace them. Clinicians stop developing the pattern-recognition skills that the algorithm now performs. Institutions stop hiring the specialists whose judgment the system has replaced. The organizational knowledge that would be required to operate without the vendor's system becomes, over a period of years, simply unavailable — not because it was prohibited, but because it was no longer practiced.⏎⏎Our 18-month longitudinal data documents this trajectory with uncomfortable specificity. At sites that had achieved what we termed "full clinical integration" of AI diagnostic tools — a rate four times higher, incidentally, at sites operating under explicit reimbursement frameworks — the atrophy of alternative institutional capacity was measurable within twelve months of deployment. This is not a peripheral finding. It is the central democratic problem with an acceleration agenda: HHS cannot accelerate clinical AI adoption at scale and simultaneously preserve the conditions under which future administrations, future Congresses, or future communities could meaningfully reverse that adoption. The acceleration and the foreclosure are the same act.⏎⏎Sheila Jasanoff, in "The Ethics of Invention: Technology and the Human Future" (W.W. Norton, 2016), develops the concept of civic epistemology — the shared frameworks through which democratic communities evaluate, contest, and govern transformative technologies. Jasanoff's argument is that different democratic polities have developed different civic epistemologies, and that the legitimacy of technological governance depends on whether those epistemologies are honored in the decision-making process. The United States has a civic epistemology around medicine that is, to put it plainly, stubbornly human. Patients expect a physician's judgment. Clinicians understand their authority as inseparable from their personal accountability. Communities — particularly those with historical reasons to distrust automated systems applied to their health and bodies (see Ruha Benjamin, "Race After Technology: Abolitionist Tools for the New Jim Code," Polity Press, 2019) — have not been asked whether they wish to transfer that judgment to proprietary algorithmic systems. The RFI's framing of acceleration as the obvious goal, and of regulatory scrutiny as an "uncertainty" impeding progress, is precisely the kind of civic epistemology violation Jasanoff warns against. It treats the mechanisms of democratic accountability as friction to be cleared rather than as expressions of legitimate democratic values to be honored.⏎⏎The Health AI Institute is not arguing that clinical AI has no place in American medicine. We are arguing that the question of what place it should have is a democratic question, not a technical one, and that HHS does not have the democratic mandate to answer it unilaterally through an acceleration agenda.⏎⏎⏎STRUCTURAL OPACITY AS A DEMOCRATIC IMPOSSIBILITY, NOT MERELY A TECHNICAL CHALLENGE⏎⏎The RFI solicits comment on regulatory pathways that would accelerate AI adoption in clinical care. Implicit in that solicitation is an assumption that the regulatory apparatus — FDA clearance, CMS coverage determinations, ONC certification requirements — constitutes an adequate framework of democratic oversight for the systems being deployed. The Health AI Institute rejects that assumption, and we do so on structural grounds.⏎⏎Frank Pasquale documented in "The Black Box Society: The Secret Algorithms That Control Money and Information" (Harvard University Press, 2015) that proprietary algorithmic systems are not merely opaque in practice — they are opaque by design, because opacity is itself a competitive asset. Trade secret protections, licensing structures, and the sheer technical complexity of large-scale machine learning systems combine to make meaningful external audit structurally impossible under current legal and regulatory frameworks. Meredith Broussard made a related argument in "Artificial Unintelligence: How Computers Misunderstand the World" (MIT Press, 2018) — that the limits of external audit are not primarily a matter of regulatory will or technical capacity, but of the fundamental architecture of systems that cannot be understood from the outside. More recently, Alondra Nelson and Deirdre Mulligan, in their 2023 Data & Society Research Institute report on algorithmic impact assessments, documented the structural gaps in current audit frameworks for healthcare AI specifically — gaps that persist even where regulatory intent to audit is genuine.⏎⏎What does this mean democratically? It means that the oversight apparatus HHS is relying upon to legitimate the acceleration it is contemplating cannot actually see what it is overseeing. FDA clearance processes for clinical AI systems are based substantially on developer-submitted performance data, evaluated against benchmarks that developers have substantial influence in establishing. CMS coverage determinations do not include independent audit of algorithmic logic. ONC certification requirements, as documented in the agency's own interoperability standards guidance (Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, "Health IT and Health Information Exchange Basics: Interoperability Standards," ONC, 2023), address data exchange architecture but do not reach the internal decision logic of AI systems deployed on top of that architecture. The European Parliament recognized this problem directly in the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Articles 6–17), which establishes mandatory transparency and conformity assessment requirements for high-risk AI systems in healthcare contexts precisely because the alternative — relying on developer self-reporting within a proprietary opacity framework — is not democratically adequate. The United States has no equivalent requirement.⏎⏎A system that cannot be audited cannot be democratically governed. That is not a rhetorical point. It is a structural description of the current regulatory landscape. When HHS frames regulatory scrutiny as "uncertainty" impeding AI adoption, it is, whether intentionally or not, treating the demand for auditable governance as an obstacle rather than as a democratic prerequisite. Shoshana Zuboff's analysis of asymmetric institutional power in data-dependent relationships ("The Age of Surveillance Capitalism," PublicAffairs, 2019) is relevant here: the vendor relationships that clinical AI deployment creates are not symmetric exchanges between parties with comparable information and leverage. Hospitals, particularly those serving Medicaid-majority populations — which our Q3 2024 policy roundtable found to be 2.3 times more likely to abandon AI implementation mid-deployment due to unclear coverage determinations — are not in a position to negotiate meaningful transparency conditions with large AI vendors. The power asymmetry is structural, and acceleration without addressing that asymmetry simply embeds it more deeply.⏎⏎David Vladeck's 2014 analysis in the Washington Law Review ("Machines Without Principals: Liability Rules and Artificial Intelligence," Washington Law Review 89:117) identified the democratic accountability vacuum created when AI systems displace human decision-makers in high-stakes domains — a vacuum that existing liability frameworks were not designed to fill. In clinical care, that vacuum is not abstract. It is the space between the patient who receives a care recommendation and any human being who can be held accountable for the logic that generated it.⏎⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD DO INSTEAD⏎⏎The Health AI Institute acknowledges that this comment does not fit the format the RFI anticipates. We are not offering a list of regulatory actions HHS should take to accelerate clinical AI adoption. We are arguing that acceleration, as a governing frame, is the wrong starting point. With that said, we offer the following specific recommendations:⏎⏎1. HHS should reissue this RFI with an explicitly precautionary framing. The current document presupposes that AI acceleration in clinical care is the goal and solicits comment on how best to achieve it. A democratically adequate RFI would instead ask: under what conditions, with what safeguards, and subject to what community deliberation processes, should clinical AI adoption proceed? The difference is not semantic. It is the difference between a process that honors democratic self-governance and one that forecloses it.⏎⏎2. Before any acceleration agenda is adopted, HHS should convene deliberative community processes — not stakeholder engagement sessions dominated by health system administrators and technology vendors, but genuine deliberative processes that include frontline clinicians, patients, community health workers, and representatives of communities that have historically borne the costs of automated decision-making in public-facing institutional contexts. The Brookings Institution's 2019 analysis of algorithmic bias and democratic accountability (Nicol Turner Lee, Paul Resnick, and Genie Barton, "Algorithmic Bias Detection and Mitigation: Best Practices and Policies to Reduce Consumer Harms," Brookings Institution, 2019) is clear that meaningful accountability requires meaningful community participation in governance design, not merely in complaint processes after deployment.⏎⏎3. HHS should explicitly acknowledge — in regulatory guidance, in coverage determination frameworks, and in ONC certification policy — that communities have the democratic right to decide that medicine should remain, in certain domains and in certain contexts, stubbornly human. The question of whether efficiency gains justify the transfer of clinical judgment to proprietary algorithmic systems is a legitimate democratic judgment. It is not a question that the pace of technology adoption resolves by default.⏎⏎4. Any reimbursement framework for clinical AI should be conditioned on mandatory, independent, third-party audit of algorithmic logic — not performance benchmarks submitted by developers, but actual audit of the internal decision processes of deployed systems. Where such audit is structurally impossible due to proprietary architecture, reimbursement should not be available. This is the minimum condition for democratic governance of systems that are, under current frameworks, ungovernable.⏎⏎5. HHS should conduct and publish a formal irreversibility assessment before adopting any acceleration framework — a structured analysis of the conditions under which clinical AI adoption, at scale, would foreclose future democratic choices about the role of AI in medicine, and what regulatory or contractual mechanisms, if any, could meaningfully preserve those choices.⏎⏎⏎A NOTE ON OUR OWN DATA⏎⏎The Health AI Institute is aware that the empirical findings we cite in support of these recommendations — our 63% reimbursement barrier finding, our 2.3x abandonment rate for Medicaid-majority facilities, our four-times integration rate differential at sites with explicit coverage frameworks — were generated in the context of work oriented toward understanding AI deployment outcomes, not toward the democratic theory argument we are now advancing. We think that context is worth naming, because it would be easy to read our deployment data as simply supporting a case for clearer reimbursement frameworks, which is indeed what most of our network's prior policy work has argued. What eighteen months of watching these deployments unfold has actually taught us is something more uncomfortable: that the sites that integrated most successfully, by the metrics our longitudinal analysis used, are also the sites where institutional dependency formed most rapidly and most completely. Full clinical integration and irreversible vendor lock-in are, in our data, nearly the same phenomenon measured from different angles. We did not expect that finding. We are not entirely sure what to do with it. But we think it belongs in this comment, because it is the honest account of what our research has shown.⏎⏎The acceleration HHS is contemplating is not an optimization of a neutral process. It is a choice about who governs medicine — and once that choice is made at institutional scale, the mechanisms for revisiting it become, as Winner would have predicted, increasingly unavailable. The ONC's own interoperability guidance acknowledges the structural vendor lock-in risks embedded in current health IT architecture; those risks do not diminish when AI systems are layered on top of them. They compound.⏎⏎⏎CLOSING OBSERVATIONS⏎⏎We recognize that these comments do not answer the questions HHS has asked. They contest the frame in which those questions are posed. We do so not as an act of procedural obstruction but because we believe the RFI, as currently framed, is asking the wrong question in a way that makes the right question harder to ask later. The right question is not how to accelerate clinical AI adoption. It is whether, and under what democratically accountable conditions, that acceleration should occur at all — and who has the authority to make that determination.⏎⏎We note, in closing, that our network's 847 clinical AI deployment sites span rural, safety-net, and academic medical center contexts, and that the communities served by those sites have not, to our knowledge, been asked whether they endorse the direction this RFI presupposes. That absence is itself a democratic data point. HHS should treat it as such.⏎⏎The Health AI Institute respectfully requests the opportunity to present these findings in a public meeting before any acceleration framework is finalized. Our contact for follow-up is the Policy and Government Affairs office; we note that the email address on our previous HHS correspondence —⏎⏎policy@healthaiinstitute.org⏎⏎— remains current for this docket.♔♔2026-02-17T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-17T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔8♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Once AI systems are embedded in healthcare infrastructure, they become practically irreversible and resistant to democratic oversight, creating a permanent transfer of power from clinicians, patients, and regulators to technology vendors.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔urgent♔Florida♔community organizer♔40♔A 2024 survey conducted across our network of 847 clinical AI deployment sites found that 63% of respondents identified reimbursement uncertainty as the primary barrier to scaling validated AI tools beyond pilot programs, with an additional 29% citing the absence of standardized FDA-CMS parallel review pathways as a compounding obstacle.
