SYNTH-0084♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Amanda Martinez♔American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases♔♔♔♔♔AASLD Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 1⏎⏎⏎The American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) submits these comments in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. We will address the RFI's reimbursement and workforce questions directly, because those are the domains where our member hepatologists are experiencing the most immediate operational harm. We are not going to pretend that the framing of this RFI is neutral. The word "accelerating" is doing a great deal of work in that title, and we think HHS should be honest about what it signals: the Department has already decided that speed is the goal, and is now asking stakeholders how to get there faster. That is the wrong question, and we intend to say so at some length.⏎⏎Before we do, one institutional note. Our policy team spent considerable time attempting to parse the original Federal Register notice underlying this RFI, and we want to register plainly that the document is nearly incomprehensible to anyone who has not spent years reading administrative law. We recognize that regulatory drafting conventions are longstanding, but when an agency is explicitly soliciting input from frontline clinicians — gastroenterologists, hepatologists, nurses, administrative staff — and then publishes the solicitation in dense legal prose cross-referencing authorities that require a separate law degree to locate and interpret, the agency is structurally excluding the very voices it claims to want. This is not a minor procedural complaint. It is a substantive barrier to democratic participation in rulemaking, and HHS should treat it as such.⏎⏎⏎AASLD Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎ON THE REIMBURSEMENT QUESTION⏎⏎The RFI asks, broadly, what reimbursement structures could accelerate AI adoption in clinical settings. We would reframe this question: before HHS designs payment incentives for AI tools, the Department must first establish what evidence of safety and clinical efficacy is required before those tools are reimbursable at all. The current posture — in which novel AI-assisted clinical decision support systems can be marketed, deployed, and billed without a demonstrated record of performance across racially and socioeconomically diverse patient populations — is not a gap in the reimbursement framework. It is a failure of basic regulatory responsibility.⏎⏎Our members practice in a clinical domain where algorithmic bias has documented, measurable consequences. The foundational work by Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan (2019), published in Science, demonstrated that a widely deployed health management algorithm systematically underestimated the severity of illness in Black patients by using healthcare cost as a proxy for health need — a proxy that reflects historical inequities in access, not actual clinical status (Obermeyer et al., 2019, Science, 366(6464), 447–453). Liver disease is a domain where this kind of bias is not a theoretical concern. Hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance, MELD score interpretation, and transplant waitlist prioritization are all areas where algorithmic error can be directly fatal, and where the patient population most affected by chronic liver disease — including patients with alcohol-associated liver disease, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and viral hepatitis — is disproportionately drawn from communities that are underrepresented in the training data on which most commercial AI tools are built.⏎⏎HHS should therefore condition any new reimbursement pathway for AI-assisted clinical tools on the following minimum requirements:⏎⏎1. Prospective demonstration of performance equity across race, ethnicity, sex, and socioeconomic subgroups, with results reported publicly before CMS reimbursement is extended.⏎⏎2. Mandatory disclosure of training data provenance, including the patient populations represented and the time period covered, with updates required when tools are retrained or significantly modified.⏎⏎3. Binding liability assignment: when an AI tool contributes to a documented adverse patient outcome, the vendor bears co-liability alongside the deploying institution, not solely the individual clinician. The current liability gap is not ambiguous — it is a deliberate design choice that externalizes risk onto the workforce (Kohn et al., 2024, Health Affairs, 43(2), 215–223).⏎⏎4. A prohibition on using AI-generated productivity benchmarks as justification for reducing clinical staffing ratios, a practice that the Service Employees International Union documented in multiple hospital systems in their Q2 2024 policy brief (SEIU, 2024).⏎⏎The Government Accountability Office, in its 2023 report on AI in health care (GAO-23-105491), noted that federal oversight of clinical AI tools remains fragmented across FDA, ONC, and CMS, with no single agency holding clear authority over post-market surveillance of deployed tools. That report was published over a year ago. HHS has not resolved this jurisdictional ambiguity, and the RFI does not appear to treat it as urgent. We do.⏎⏎⏎AASLD Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎ON THE WORKFORCE QUESTION⏎⏎The RFI gestures toward workforce considerations but frames them almost entirely in terms of efficiency gains — how AI can reduce administrative burden, free up clinician time, and so forth. This framing is not wrong exactly, but it is incomplete in a way that produces bad policy. The evidence on clinician burnout and technology burden does not support a simple story in which more AI equals less burden.⏎⏎Dyrbye and colleagues published a systematic review in 2023 in the Journal of General Internal Medicine finding that EHR burden remains one of the strongest predictors of clinician burnout across specialties, and that the addition of clinical decision support tools frequently increases cognitive load rather than reducing it, particularly when those tools generate alerts that clinicians learn to dismiss (Dyrbye et al., 2023, J Gen Intern Med, 38(4), 1012–1024). The ONC's own 2023 data brief on EHR-related patient safety events documented that alert fatigue from poorly calibrated clinical decision support is now a recognized contributor to diagnostic error (ONC Data Brief No. 58, 2023). Wachter and Goldsmith made the same argument in the Harvard Business Review in early 2023: the problem is not that clinicians lack digital tools, it is that the tools they have were designed around billing and documentation workflows rather than clinical reasoning (Wachter & Goldsmith, 2023, Harvard Business Review, March–April 2023).⏎⏎Our members are gastroenterologists and hepatologists who regularly use AI-assisted imaging interpretation tools, FIB-4 calculators embedded in EHR workflows, and — increasingly — vendor-supplied tools that flag patients for advanced fibrosis screening. The clinical promise of these tools is real. We are not Luddites. But the gap between the promise and the actual deployment experience is substantial, and the gap is not primarily technical. It is institutional and economic. Friedberg and colleagues at RAND documented in 2022 that physician professional satisfaction is most strongly predicted not by workload volume per se, but by the degree of autonomy clinicians retain over clinical decisions and care processes (Friedberg et al., 2022, RAND RR-439-AMA). AI procurement processes, as currently structured, systematically exclude frontline clinicians from decisions about which tools are selected, how they are configured, and what thresholds trigger alerts or flags. The Economic Policy Institute's January 2024 working paper on algorithmic management in hospital systems found that in surveyed institutions, fewer than 18% of frontline clinical workers reported having any formal input into AI tool procurement decisions (EPI, 2024).⏎⏎⏎AASLD Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 4⏎⏎⏎This is where we want to be specific about what we are asking HHS to do, not just what we think HHS is getting wrong.⏎⏎The American Medical Association's 2024 policy document on augmented intelligence (AMA Policy H-480.940) calls for meaningful clinician involvement in AI procurement and deployment decisions as a baseline standard. We support that position and urge HHS to make it a regulatory condition, not a recommendation. Specifically, any hospital or health system receiving Medicare or Medicaid reimbursement for AI-assisted clinical services should be required to document a formal frontline worker consultation process prior to deploying any AI tool that affects clinical decision-making, staffing allocation, or patient triage. "Consultation" should mean something: a written record of concerns raised, a response from administration, and a mechanism for clinicians to flag post-deployment performance problems without fear of retaliation.⏎⏎The National Nurses United 2024 policy report documented instances in which nurses who raised concerns about AI-generated care recommendations were subject to disciplinary review under productivity monitoring systems that themselves relied on AI-generated output (NNU, 2024, "Surveilled, Stretched, and Sidelined"). That is a specific and concrete harm, and HHS has the regulatory authority to prohibit it. Shanafelt and colleagues' longitudinal data through 2020 showed that burnout rates among physicians had reached levels with measurable consequences for patient safety and care quality (Shanafelt et al., 2022, Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 97(3), 491–506). Deploying AI tools in ways that increase surveillance, reduce autonomy, and externalize liability onto already-burned-out clinicians will not improve those numbers.⏎⏎We recognize that this comment covers a narrower slice of the RFI than HHS may have hoped. We made that choice deliberately. Our members have specific, documented concerns about liver disease care specifically, and about the hepatology workforce, and we think a focused submission is more useful than a comprehensive one that spreads analysis too thin. We would welcome the opportunity to provide technical assistance to ONC or CMS staff working on implementation guidance for any AI reimbursement framework that emerges from this process.⏎⏎REFERENCES⏎⏎American Medical Association. SYNTH-0085♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Sandra Gonzalez♔Viz.ai♔♔♔♔♔Viz.ai | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 1⏎⏎⏎Sandra Gonzalez⏎Chief Financial Officer, Viz.ai⏎Hospital Finance Advisory Council, Sancian LLC Portfolio⏎Seattle, Washington 98101⏎⏎October 14, 2024⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Attn: Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎To the Office of the Deputy Secretary and ASTP/ONC Staff:⏎⏎Viz.ai and the Sancian LLC hospital portfolio, which spans 14 regional hospital systems across the Pacific Northwest and Mountain West, submit this comment in response to the Department's Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care settings. The organizational perspective offered here is grounded in direct operational experience: a Q2 2024 internal analysis conducted across the Sancian portfolio found that AI-assisted clinical decision support tools reduced average length of stay by 1.3 days in facilities where integration exceeded 60% of eligible workflows, translating to an estimated $4.2 million in annual cost avoidance per facility (Sancian LLC CFO Advisory Council, 2024). Viz.ai has helped deploy the infrastructure behind a meaningful portion of that performance. The data is real, and the financial argument for AI in clinical care is not in dispute here. What is in dispute is whether HHS has thought carefully enough about what happens when those systems are wrong, and who, precisely, answers for that.⏎⏎The Department's RFI is organized around a reasonable set of goals: reduce regulatory friction, clarify reimbursement, expand research capacity. Viz.ai does not object to any of those goals in the abstract. But the RFI proceeds from an assumption that the primary obstacles to AI adoption are financial and regulatory, and that removing those obstacles will produce better patient outcomes. That assumption is incomplete in a way that carries genuine patient safety risk. The deeper obstacle — one the RFI does not address with any specificity — is that AI-assisted clinical decision support creates a structural accountability vacuum. When an AI system intermediates a clinical decision and that decision contributes to patient harm, the question of who is legally and morally responsible becomes genuinely difficult to answer. The clinician can point to the algorithm. The hospital can point to the vendor. The vendor can point to the training data, the integration environment, or the clinician's failure to override. This is not a hypothetical problem. Price, Gerke, and Cohen (2019) identified precisely this dynamic in their JAMA analysis of physician liability in AI-assisted care, noting that standard malpractice doctrine has no settled mechanism for allocating fault when a human decision-maker relies on an opaque algorithmic recommendation. HHS is proposing to scale the deployment of systems with this architecture before the accountability infrastructure exists to support them.⏎⏎⏎Viz.ai | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 2⏎⏎⏎This matters in a specific way that financial executives at regional hospitals understand acutely. The Sancian portfolio systems allocated an average of $6.8 million per system to AI infrastructure investment, with less than 12% of that recoverable through existing CMS billing codes (Sancian LLC CFO Advisory Council, 2024). That funding gap already creates structural disincentives for mid-sized regional hospitals. But the liability exposure problem is, in some ways, a more serious institutional risk than the reimbursement gap, because it is invisible until it materializes. Existing respondeat superior doctrine presupposes an identifiable human agent whose judgment the institution has supervised and for whose decisions the institution can be held vicariously liable. AI-assisted decision support does not fit that model. When a deep learning tool generates a risk score that a clinician acts on without fully understanding the model's reasoning — a condition Sendak et al. (2020) described as structurally inevitable given the opacity of such systems, noting that clinicians routinely treat model outputs as authoritative precisely because the underlying logic is inaccessible — the chain of supervisory accountability that respondeat superior requires simply does not exist in a traceable form. Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen (2020) made a similar point in their legal analysis of AI-driven healthcare, arguing that the combination of algorithmic opacity and workflow embeddedness produces a form of liability diffusion that existing tort frameworks cannot resolve without legislative or regulatory intervention. HHS has proposed no such intervention.⏎⏎The indeterminate causation problem is worth dwelling on, because it is not simply a legal technicality. It has direct consequences for patients seeking redress. Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert (2020) documented the relationship between malpractice liability exposure and care quality, finding that the threat of liability — however imperfect as a mechanism — does function as a check on clinical negligence. Remove the ability to assign liability clearly, and you remove one of the few external accountability pressures on clinical decision-making that the current system provides. Cohen, Amarasingham, Shah, Xie, and Lo (2014) raised this concern specifically in the context of predictive analytics in health care, arguing that the complexity of algorithmic decision support creates "accountability gaps" that harm patients' ability to seek legal redress and that existing informed consent frameworks do not close. The Department's RFI does not engage with this literature. It does not propose a mechanism for reconstructing accountability when AI intermediates clinical decisions at scale. It does not address how the 2023 HTI-1 Final Rule's algorithm transparency provisions (ONC, 2023, 88 Fed. Reg. 23746) interact with malpractice doctrine, despite the fact that those transparency requirements were in part designed to address the opacity problem that makes liability attribution so difficult. The RFI treats those as separate regulatory tracks. They are not separate problems.⏎⏎⏎Viz.ai | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 3⏎⏎⏎There is also a more granular operational concern that the Department should understand before issuing any final rule. Clinical decision support systems, even well-designed ones, generate alert fatigue at scale. Kesselheim, Cresswell, Phansalkar, Bates, and Sheikh (2011) documented this dynamic in their Health Affairs analysis, finding that the volume of automated alerts in clinical workflows causes clinicians to override or ignore a substantial proportion of them, and that modifying alert thresholds to reduce fatigue creates its own litigation risk because any modification can later be characterized as a deliberate choice to suppress a warning. That litigation risk currently falls on the hospital, because the hospital is the identifiable institutional actor. As AI systems become more deeply embedded in clinical workflows — and the Sancian data suggests that integration above 60% of eligible workflows is the threshold at which cost-avoidance gains become statistically meaningful — the hospital's ability to claim that a clinician made an independent judgment, rather than following an algorithmic prompt, becomes increasingly implausible. Workflow embeddedness and independent clinical judgment are, at some level of integration, in structural tension. HHS has not acknowledged that tension. The National Academy of Medicine's 2022 workshop proceedings on AI risks and benefits in health care identified this as one of the unresolved governance questions requiring federal attention before broad deployment, not after (National Academy of Medicine, 2022). Viz.ai shares that assessment.⏎⏎Obermeyer and Emanuel (2016) observed in the New England Journal of Medicine that machine learning tools in clinical medicine will inevitably produce predictions that are accurate at the population level but wrong for individual patients in ways that are difficult to anticipate or explain. That is not an argument against using such tools. It is an argument for building the accountability infrastructure before deploying the tools at scale, so that when the tool is wrong — and it will be wrong, for specific patients, in specific facilities, on specific dates — there is a human being or institution that can be identified as legally responsible for the decision that followed from that error. Dayan et al. (2021) demonstrated in their federated learning study that even sophisticated distributed AI architectures retain meaningful performance gaps across patient subpopulations, which means the patients most likely to be harmed by AI errors are not randomly distributed. They tend to be patients whose clinical characteristics are underrepresented in the training data. Those patients are disproportionately likely to already face systemic barriers to care and legal redress. HHS's proposal to accelerate deployment without an accountability framework is not neutral with respect to those populations.⏎⏎Viz.ai's specific request is this: HHS must condition any final rule or deployment pathway on the prior establishment of a regulatory framework that assigns clear legal accountability for AI-assisted clinical decisions to a named human or institutional party, specifies how that assignment interacts with existing respondeat superior doctrine and the vendor contractual structures that currently allow liability diffusion across the care delivery chain, and commissions dedicated legal research — through the Office of the General Counsel or a similar body with appropriate authority — on adapting malpractice doctrine to AI-intermediated clinical decisions before any acceleration of deployment pathways is finalized. The cost-avoidance data from the Sancian portfolio is real. The $4.2 million per facility figure is not disputed. But the CFO-level survey from Q2 2024 that produced that data also found that 78% of participating hospital finance leaders cited unclear reimbursement pathways as their primary scaling barrier — and what that number obscures is that the finance leaders who are most worried about liability exposure often declined to characterize it as a "barrier" because they have not yet been sued. The liability problem is not invisible because it does not exist. It is invisible because the cases that would make it visible have not yet worked their way through the courts in sufficient volume. HHS should not wait for that volume to accumulate before building the framework that would have prevented the harm in the first place. The ONC's HTI-1 transparency provisions are a start, but transparency about how an algorithm works does not, by itself, tell a patient's family who is responsible when the algorithm contributed to their relative's death. That question requires a regulatory answer, and the Department has not yet provided one.⏎⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Sandra Gonzalez⏎Chief Financial Officer⏎Viz.ai⏎On behalf of the Sancian LLC Hospital Finance Advisory Council⏎⏎sgonzalez@viz.ai⏎206-555-0173♔♔2026-02-21T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-21T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔organization♔high♔urgent♔Washington♔hospital CFO♔47♔A 2024 internal analysis across Sancian LLC's portfolio of 14 regional hospital systems found that AI-assisted clinical decision support tools reduced average length of stay by 1.3 days in facilities where integration exceeded 60% of eligible workflows, translating to an estimated $4.2 million in annual cost avoidance per facility. SYNTH-0087♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Deborah Ramirez♔University of Michigan Institute for Healthcare Policy and Innovation♔♔♔♔♔University of Michigan Institute for Healthcare Policy and Innovation⏎Comments Submitted to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Docket: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Deborah Ramirez, Assistant Professor, University of Michigan Institute for Healthcare Policy and Innovation⏎⏎— — —⏎⏎UMIHPI Comments | HHS AI RFI — Administrative Workforce | Page 1⏎⏎I. THE EFFICIENCY PREMISE DESERVES CLOSER SCRUTINY⏎⏎The goals articulated in this Request for Information are ones the University of Michigan Institute for Healthcare Policy and Innovation shares without reservation: reducing waste, improving patient experience, and deploying technology in ways that make the health system more responsive to the people it serves. What follows is not a rejection of those goals. It is, rather, an argument that the RFI's framing of administrative functions as a domain where AI automation constitutes a straightforward efficiency gain reflects a mischaracterization of what healthcare administrative workers actually do — and what patients stand to lose when that work is automated without adequate evidentiary grounding.⏎⏎The Institute's concern with deployment enthusiasm outrunning infrastructure readiness is not hypothetical. A 2024 American College of Cardiology survey of 2,817 cardiologist members found that 68% reported using at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or workflow tool in their clinical practice, while 54% identified inconsistent payer reimbursement policies as the primary barrier to broader integration. A Health Affairs Policy Task Force analysis of CMS claims data from 2021 through 2023 further documented that reimbursement denials for AI-augmented echocardiography interpretation increased by 31% over that period, even as peer-reviewed evidence supporting clinical utility continued to accumulate. These findings, while focused on clinical AI, establish a pattern the Institute believes HHS must take seriously before extending the automation impulse to administrative domains: the gap between deployment enthusiasm and the regulatory and reimbursement infrastructure necessary to sustain responsible adoption is already wide in clinical settings where the evidentiary standards are comparatively mature. In administrative settings, those standards are far less developed.⏎⏎UMIHPI Comments | HHS AI RFI — Administrative Workforce | Page 2⏎⏎II. WHAT ADMINISTRATIVE WORKERS ACTUALLY DO⏎⏎The RFI's framing treats administrative work — care coordination, patient navigation, prior authorization review, benefits counseling — as though these functions are primarily procedural, reducible to decision trees and structured data inputs that AI systems can replicate or improve upon. This assumption deserves empirical challenge. Michael Polanyi's foundational observation that skilled practitioners "know more than they can tell" (Polanyi, M., The Tacit Dimension, Doubleday, 1966) applies with particular force to healthcare administrative workers who navigate the intersection of insurance logic, clinical need, and patient circumstance simultaneously. A benefits counselor working with a Medicaid managed care enrollee in Providence, Rhode Island, for instance, does not simply apply a coverage rule; she interprets that rule in light of the patient's literacy level, her housing situation, the specific quirks of a particular managed care organization's prior authorization portal, and the informal relationships she has cultivated with case managers at that plan over years of repeated contact. This is institutional knowledge that does not exist in any training dataset.⏎⏎Yin and Bhatt's 2023 multi-state claims analysis documented the administrative complexity that Medicaid managed care patients face in navigating benefits — finding, among other things, that navigation burden falls disproportionately on patients with limited English proficiency, unstable housing, and multiple chronic conditions (Yin, W., & Bhatt, J., Health Affairs, 42(7), 2023, 1014–1023). The workers who absorb that burden on patients' behalf are doing something qualitatively different from processing transactions. They are providing what might be called relational brokerage: translating between the formal logic of the coverage system and the lived circumstances of individual patients in ways that require ongoing, context-sensitive judgment. Automating this work without understanding its actual structure risks eliminating the very functions that make the system accessible to its most vulnerable users.⏎⏎The Institute's own recent research is relevant here. Ramirez and Flores (2024) examined automation risk in Medicaid administrative workflows serving limited-English-proficiency populations, finding that even partial automation of prior authorization review generated measurable increases in denial rates for this population, driven by systematic misclassification of non-standard documentation submitted by community health workers and patient advocates (Ramirez, D., & Flores, M., Journal of Health Politics, Policy and Law, 49(3), 2024, 389–418). The errors were not visible at the aggregate level; they were concentrated among patients least able to identify and contest them. This is the pattern the Institute believes HHS must anticipate and design against.⏎⏎UMIHPI Comments | HHS AI RFI — Administrative Workforce | Page 3⏎⏎III. THE ERROR PROPAGATION PROBLEM AND ITS EQUITY IMPLICATIONS⏎⏎There is a well-documented body of literature on what happens when health information technology systems interact with complex, heterogeneous clinical and administrative environments. Ash, Berg, and Coiera's foundational 2004 analysis of patient care information system errors identified a category of "juxtaposition errors" — mistakes generated by the interface between automated systems and human workarounds — that are systematically harder to detect than the errors they replace (Ash, J.S., Berg, M., & Coiera, E., Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 11(2), 2004, 104–112). Atul Gawande made a related observation in his 2018 New Yorker essay on physician-computer interaction, noting that automation does not eliminate cognitive labor; it relocates it, often onto the workers least positioned to absorb it (Gawande, A., "Why Doctors Hate Their Computers," The New Yorker, November 12, 2018). The implication for administrative AI is direct: systems that automate prior authorization review or care coordination documentation do not reduce the total labor required to manage complex cases; they shift that labor onto patients, their families, and the remaining administrative staff who must correct machine errors — often without the institutional resources to do so systematically.⏎⏎The equity dimension of this error propagation problem is not speculative. Obermeyer and colleagues' 2019 Science analysis of a widely deployed population health algorithm demonstrated that racial bias embedded in training data produced systematic underestimation of Black patients' health needs, at a scale that affected millions of care decisions before the bias was identified (Obermeyer, Z., Powers, B., Vogeli, C., & Mullainathan, S., Science, 366(6464), 2019, 447–453). Veinot, Mitchell, and Ancker's 2018 review of informatics interventions reached a complementary conclusion: systems designed with good intentions and technically sound architectures can nonetheless worsen health inequity when they are deployed in contexts where the populations they serve have systematically different relationships to data infrastructure (Veinot, T.C., Mitchell, H., & Ancker, J.S., Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 25(8), 2018, 1080–1088). Administrative AI systems trained on claims data from commercially insured, English-speaking, high-health-literacy populations will not perform equivalently for the Medicaid populations who most depend on skilled human navigation. The Institute believes HHS should treat this as a predictable outcome, not an edge case.⏎⏎UMIHPI Comments | HHS AI RFI — Administrative Workforce | Page 4⏎⏎IV. ON THE WORKFORCE CONSEQUENCES OF ADMINISTRATIVE AUTOMATION⏎⏎The efficiency rationale for administrative AI rests on an assumption that is worth examining directly: that the administrative burden currently borne by health systems is waste that can be eliminated without disrupting the functions that burden currently performs. Himmelstein, Campbell, and Woolhandler's 2020 New England Journal of Medicine analysis estimated that administrative costs in the United States health care system consumed approximately 34.2% of total health expenditures in 2017, compared to 12% in Canada (Himmelstein, D.U., Campbell, T., & Woolhandler, S., New England Journal of Medicine, 382(15), 2020, 1483–1484). This is a real and serious inefficiency. But the question of which administrative functions constitute waste and which constitute protective infrastructure for patients navigating a fragmented system is one that cannot be answered by examining cost data alone. Casalino and colleagues' 2016 Health Affairs analysis found that physician practices spent more than $15.4 billion annually to report quality measures — a figure that looks like waste until one considers what quality reporting is actually accomplishing in specific clinical contexts (Casalino, L.P. et al., Health Affairs, 35(3), 2016, 401–406).⏎⏎The administrative workforce is already under serious strain. Sinsky and colleagues' 2017 Mayo Clinic Proceedings analysis of physician career satisfaction found that administrative burden was among the strongest predictors of burnout and intent to leave practice (Sinsky, C.A. et al., Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 92(11), 2017, 1625–1635). This finding is frequently cited to justify automation as a relief valve. What receives less attention is the parallel strain on non-physician administrative staff — patient navigators, care coordinators, benefits counselors — whose work is invisible in the burnout literature precisely because it is invisible in the professional prestige hierarchy of health care. Bhatt and Bathija's 2018 Academic Medicine analysis of health care access in vulnerable communities identified administrative navigation support as among the most effective interventions for reducing disparities in care-seeking behavior, and noted that this support depends on sustained, relationship-based human contact that cannot be replicated by asynchronous digital tools (Bhatt, J., & Bathija, P., Academic Medicine, 93(9), 2018, 1271–1275). Automating these roles in the name of efficiency relief may eliminate the very support structures that make the system accessible to patients who have no other advocate.⏎⏎UMIHPI Comments | HHS AI RFI — Administrative Workforce | Page 5⏎⏎V. A SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATION TO HHS⏎⏎The Institute respectfully urges HHS to take two concrete steps before issuing any sub-regulatory guidance on the automation of healthcare administrative functions.⏎⏎First, HHS should commission a program of ethnographic and qualitative research on administrative healthcare workflows, conducted in partnership with health equity researchers and frontline administrative workers, with particular attention to workflows serving Medicaid, dual-eligible, and limited-English-proficiency populations. The methodology should be grounded in institutional ethnography and workflow analysis, not claims data or administrative records, because the tacit knowledge and relational labor that make administrative functions effective are not captured in structured datasets. This research should be completed and publicly available before any guidance is issued that would create incentives — reimbursement-based or otherwise — for health systems to automate administrative roles.⏎⏎Second, HHS should establish an evidentiary standard for administrative AI that is equivalent in rigor to the standards currently applied to clinical AI. The Food and Drug Administration's framework for Software as a Medical Device provides a useful reference point, even though administrative AI systems fall outside its jurisdiction. The principle — that deployment should follow evidence, not precede it — applies with equal force to systems that determine whether a patient receives care coordination support as to systems that interpret a cardiac imaging study. The 31% increase in reimbursement denials for AI-augmented echocardiography documented in the Health Affairs Task Force analysis is a cautionary data point precisely because it shows what happens when deployment runs ahead of the reimbursement and regulatory infrastructure designed to govern it. The Institute believes HHS has an opportunity to prevent an analogous dynamic from developing in the administrative domain, where the populations at risk have fewer institutional resources to contest errors and fewer advocates with the visibility to document them.⏎⏎The Institute also notes, with some frustration, that the RFI does not ask specifically about administrative workforce impacts, which suggests that the framing of administrative AI as a workforce question rather than an efficiency question has not yet fully registered at the policy development level. This comment is submitted in the hope that it contributes to reframing that conversation. Questions about which administrative functions can be safely automated, under what conditions, with what monitoring requirements, and with what protections for the patients who depend on those functions — these are not technical questions that AI developers are best positioned to answer. They are⏎⏎UMIHPI Comments | HHS AI RFI — Administrative Workforce | Page 6⏎⏎empirical and ethical questions that require the kind of sustained, context-sensitive inquiry that the health services research community is equipped to conduct, if HHS chooses to commission it.⏎⏎The Institute would welcome the opportunity to provide additional technical assistance to HHS as it develops its response framework, and is prepared to share the underlying data from Ramirez and Flores (2024) with relevant program offices upon request. Contact information for the Institute's regulatory affairs office is available at ihpi.umich.edu/regulatory-affairs — though the Institute notes that the web form linked from the docket submission page did not appear to be functioning correctly as of the date this comment was prepared, and submitters relying on that channel may wish to confirm receipt through alternate means.♔♔2026-01-21T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-21T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Even administrative healthcare functions that appear routine require human contextual judgment that AI cannot replicate, and automating them will produce systematic errors that harm patients and workers.♔academic_organization♔high♔hopeful♔Rhode Island♔assistant professor♔62♔A 2024 ACC survey of 2,817 cardiologist members found that 68% reported using at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or workflow tool in their clinical practice, yet 54% identified inconsistent payer reimbursement policies as the primary barrier to broader integration. SYNTH-0088♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Charles Clark♔♔♔♔♔♔Comment of Charles Clark⏎Submitted to HHS Docket: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Rhode Island⏎⏎My cardiologist at Miriam Hospital retired in 2022. The physician who replaced him manages my warfarin dosing primarily through a risk-stratification algorithm. In March of this year, that algorithm rated my INR as within acceptable range. I ended up in the emergency department with a minor bleed. My previous doctor would have caught it by asking what I had been eating. I am seventy-five years old. I have worked in customer service for decades, and I know the difference between a system designed to serve people and one designed to process them. What I want HHS to understand is that my experience is not an outlier. It is a documented pattern, and the agency has been presented with that documentation repeatedly, and is now asking how to go faster.⏎⏎The question this RFI poses is, in effect: what regulatory, reimbursement, and research actions can HHS take to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care? I want to address that question directly, because I think the framing itself is the problem. HHS is asking how to accelerate something whose harms are already on the record. Obermeyer and colleagues published in Science in 2019 (Obermeyer et al., Science 366(6464):447-453) one of the most consequential findings in recent health policy research: a widely deployed commercial risk-stratification algorithm systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients by using healthcare cost as a proxy for health need. The algorithm was not a fringe product. It was managing the care of roughly 200 million people per year across health systems in the United States. The bias was not a software glitch. It was a design choice that encoded structural racism into the logic of the tool, and health systems deployed it anyway, and HHS did not require anyone to audit it before deployment or report disparate outcomes after. That paper was published five years ago. I am aware of it. I am a customer service representative from Providence, Rhode Island. The agency cannot claim it is not.⏎⏎Sjoding and colleagues published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 (Sjoding et al., NEJM 383:2477-2478) the finding that pulse oximeters overestimate oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin pigmentation. This is not a minor calibration issue. During the COVID-19 pandemic, clinicians were making triage and treatment decisions based on oximetry readings that were systematically wrong for a specific population. The reason this matters for an AI rulemaking is that AI systems trained on oximetry data inherit and amplify that bias. If you train a sepsis prediction model or a respiratory deterioration model on years of pulse oximetry readings that were artificially elevated for Black patients, the model learns a false baseline. It will underestimate deterioration risk for those patients. HHS is now considering how to accelerate the deployment of clinical AI. The agency should first explain what it intends to do about the fact that a substantial portion of the training data underlying these models is racially biased at the measurement level, before the algorithm even begins.⏎⏎The dermatology literature makes the same point in a different clinical domain. Adamson and Smith documented in JAMA Dermatology in 2018 (Adamson & Smith, JAMA Dermatol. 154(11):1247-1248) that AI systems trained predominantly on images of light-skinned patients perform substantially worse on darker skin tones, with documented misclassification of melanoma. Melanoma misclassification is not an acceptable error rate to optimize around. Vyas and colleagues published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 (Vyas et al., NEJM 383:874-882) a systematic review showing how race-adjusted clinical algorithms embed and perpetuate structural racism under the guise of precision medicine, affecting kidney function estimates, cardiac risk scores, and obstetric care decisions. These are not theoretical concerns from academic critics who have never seen a hospital. These are published findings in the flagship journals of American medicine, describing tools that are currently deployed in clinical settings that serve the patients who are already most vulnerable to inadequate care.⏎⏎Wong and colleagues published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021 (Wong et al., JAMA Intern. Med. 181(8):1065-1070) an external validation of the Epic Sepsis Model, which is one of the most widely implemented proprietary clinical AI tools in the country. Their finding was that the model performed far worse in real-world community hospital deployment than in the vendor's internal validation studies, with high false-positive rates that eroded clinician trust and consumed nursing resources. This is the gap that HHS is not adequately accounting for in this RFI: AI tools are validated at elite academic medical centers with clean structured data, trained research infrastructure, and dedicated clinical informatics staff, and then deployed at community hospitals, safety-net institutions, and rural clinics that have none of those things. The populations served by those community hospitals are disproportionately low-income, disproportionately non-white, and already receive measurably worse care by most outcome metrics. Accelerating deployment into those settings without mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing is not a neutral policy choice. It is a choice to extend and scale disparate outcomes. Cabitza and colleagues documented in JAMA in 2017 (Cabitza et al., JAMA 318(6):517-518) that clinicians systematically defer to algorithmic recommendations even when those recommendations conflict with their own clinical judgment, a phenomenon called automation bias. The combination of a biased model and a clinician trained to defer to it is not a hypothetical failure mode. It is a documented one. It is what happened to me in March.⏎⏎What I am asking HHS to require is specific and, I think, not unreasonable given the evidence base. No clinical AI tool should be deployed in a patient care setting without a pre-deployment equity audit that reports performance stratified by race, income, and geography, conducted by an independent party with access to the model's training data and validation methodology. That audit should be a condition of any reimbursement pathway HHS creates for AI-assisted clinical services, not a voluntary best practice that health systems can ignore when it is inconvenient. After deployment, health systems should be required to conduct ongoing bias surveillance and report disparate outcomes publicly, at a level of granularity that allows researchers and patients to see whether the model is performing differently across demographic groups in real-world conditions. The vendor's internal validation study is not sufficient evidence of real-world equity, as the Epic Sepsis Model findings make clear. HHS has the regulatory authority to require this. The agency is choosing not to. I want that choice named plainly in the record. I also want to note, because I think it is relevant to the reimbursement question this RFI raises, that I am on a fixed income. I do not know whether the reimbursement structures HHS is contemplating would result in higher costs to patients at the point of care. The RFI does not explain this clearly. If accelerating AI adoption means that AI-assisted visits are billed at a higher rate than standard visits, or that patients are steered toward AI-mediated care pathways because they are cheaper to deliver and more profitable to bill, I want HHS to say so explicitly, and I want the agency to explain what protections exist for Medicare beneficiaries who cannot absorb additional cost-sharing. That question is not answered anywhere in this request for information, and it is the question most directly relevant to the seventy-five year old patient in Rhode Island who is trying to figure out whether this rule is going to cost him money.♔♔2026-01-05T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-05T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔4♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔individual♔high♔angry♔Rhode Island♔customer service representative♔75♔My cardiologist at Miriam Hospital retired in 2022, and the practice brought in a younger physician who relies almost entirely on a risk-stratification algorithm to manage my warfarin dosing — something my previous doctor adjusted through forty years of clinical intuition and direct conversation with me. SYNTH-0089♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Amanda Robinson♔Disability Rights Advocates♔♔♔♔♔Disability Rights Advocates | HHS AI RFI Comment | Page 1⏎⏎Submitted to: HHS Office of the Deputy Secretary / ASTP-ONC⏎Re: Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitting Organization: Disability Rights Advocates⏎Contact: Amanda Robinson, Campaign Director⏎amanda.robinson@dralegal.org⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE CLINICAL PROMISE IS REAL. THE EQUITY PRECONDITIONS ARE MISSING.⏎⏎Disability Rights Advocates submits this comment with a degree of weary familiarity. We have watched federal health agencies, across multiple administrations now, frame technology adoption primarily as a speed problem — a matter of removing barriers, streamlining pathways, and accelerating uptake — while treating equity as a downstream consideration to be addressed once the tools are already embedded in clinical practice. This RFI follows that pattern closely enough that we feel obligated to say so plainly before proceeding to our specific policy recommendations.⏎⏎We do not oppose AI adoption in clinical care. Our own institutional evidence makes the clinical case more compellingly than we would prefer to have to argue. A 2024 survey of the National Multiple Sclerosis Society's network of approximately 940,000 individuals living with MS found that 67% reported delays of six months or more in receiving a confirmed diagnosis. Our Health Care Provider Council, comprising more than 600 MS specialists, documented in its 2023 annual policy review that facilities with integrated AI diagnostic support reduced mean diagnostic timelines by approximately 4.2 months compared to facilities operating without such tools. Our multi-site MS outcomes registry, tracking over 12,000 patient records across 38 states, found that earlier diagnosis correlates with a 31% reduction in first-relapse severity scores. These are not marginal findings. The clinical urgency is real, and we understand why HHS wants to move.⏎⏎But here is what the RFI's accelerationist framing does not adequately reckon with: the 4.2-month diagnostic advantage we documented has not been equitably distributed. It accrues primarily to patients receiving care at academic medical centers and well-resourced MS Comprehensive Care Centers. The underserved and rural communities where diagnostic delay is most severe — precisely the populations the RFI invokes to justify urgency — are also the communities least likely to be represented in the training data, validation cohorts, and deployment environments of the AI tools HHS is proposing to accelerate into widespread use. Acceleration, without equity preconditions, is a mechanism for widening the gap, not closing it.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Disability Rights Advocates | HHS AI RFI Comment | Page 2⏎⏎THE DOCUMENTED PATTERN OF EMBEDDED BIAS⏎⏎We want to be precise here, because the RFI's framing of AI bias risk is somewhat abstract. This is not a theoretical concern about future harms. The literature on embedded algorithmic bias in health care AI is extensive and specific, and it documents a consistent pattern across clinical domains.⏎⏎The most widely cited case remains Obermeyer et al.'s 2019 analysis in Science of a commercial algorithm used by health systems to identify patients for care management programs. The algorithm used health care cost as a proxy for health need — a methodologically defensible choice on its face — but because Black patients historically generate lower health care costs than white patients with equivalent illness burdens (due to documented disparities in access and utilization), the algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients. At a given risk score, Black patients were demonstrably sicker than white patients assigned the same score. The authors estimated that correcting this bias would more than double the proportion of Black patients receiving additional care (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. Science. 2019;366(6464):447-453). This was a tool already deployed across hundreds of health systems before the bias was characterized.⏎⏎Pulse oximetry is a different category of failure, and in some ways more troubling because the measurement error is physiological rather than algorithmic. Sjoding et al. demonstrated in 2020 that pulse oximeters overestimate arterial oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin tones at a rate three times higher than in patients with lighter skin tones, meaning that Black patients with occult hypoxemia were systematically missed by a device that clinicians treat as reliable (Sjoding MW, Dickson RP, Iwashyna TJ, Gay SE, Valley TS. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(25):2477-2478). When AI diagnostic tools are trained on data that incorporates pulse oximetry readings as a clinical variable — as many sepsis prediction and respiratory deterioration models are — the measurement error propagates into the model's predictions.⏎⏎Speaking of sepsis prediction: Wong et al. conducted an external validation of the Epic Sepsis Model at the University of Michigan Health System and found that the model performed substantially worse than reported in the vendor's internal validation, with an AUROC of 0.63 compared to claims of 0.76-0.83, and that it generated an enormous number of false positives that consumed nursing resources without improving outcomes (Wong A, Otles E, Donnelly JP, et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2021;181(8):1065-1070). The model had been widely implemented before this independent validation was published. This is the validation-deployment gap in concrete form: a tool validated at one type of institution, deployed broadly, and found to fail in ways that were not discoverable without independent evaluation.⏎⏎Dermatology AI presents yet another variant. Adamson and Smith documented in 2018 that the training datasets used for most skin lesion classification models were composed predominantly of images from patients with lighter skin tones, raising serious questions about performance in patients with darker skin tones — a population in which melanoma is more frequently diagnosed at advanced stages precisely because of delayed detection (Adamson AS, Smith A. JAMA Dermatol. 2018;154(11):1247-1248). The technical capability to build a diagnostic tool existed. The equity infrastructure to validate it across the relevant demographic range did not.⏎⏎Collectively, these cases — and they are cases, not hypotheticals — establish that embedded bias in health care AI is a documented pattern across clinical domains, measurement modalities, and institutional settings. Gianfrancesco et al. have described the structural mechanisms clearly: EHR data reflects historical patterns of care access and utilization, which means models trained on EHR data inherit and may amplify existing disparities (Gianfrancesco MA, Tamang S, Yazdany J, Schmajuk G. JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(11):1544-1547). Vyas et al. have further demonstrated that race corrections embedded in clinical algorithms — which appear in tools ranging from kidney function calculators to spirometry reference equations — encode contested assumptions about biological difference that lack adequate empirical grounding (Vyas DA, Eisenstein LEG, Jones DS. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(9):874-882).⏎⏎---⏎⏎Disability Rights Advocates | HHS AI RFI Comment | Page 3⏎⏎THE AUTOMATION BIAS PROBLEM⏎⏎There is a mechanism by which embedded bias in AI tools becomes harder to surface and correct than equivalent bias in human clinical judgment, and the RFI does not address it. The mechanism is automation bias.⏎⏎Cabitza et al. described the problem in JAMA in 2017: when clinical decision support tools present recommendations with numerical precision and an appearance of algorithmic objectivity, clinicians are less likely to override those recommendations than they would be to question equivalent recommendations from a human colleague (Cabitza F, Rasoini R, Gensini GF. JAMA. 2017;318(6):517-518). The authority of the number — a risk score of 0.84, a probability of 73% — carries a kind of epistemic weight that a colleague's intuition does not. Sendak et al. have documented in the fairness and accountability literature how this dynamic plays out in practice: clinicians who are uncertain about a patient's trajectory often defer to AI output precisely in the cases where the model is most likely to be operating outside its validation range (Sendak MP, Elish MC, Gao M, et al. Proc ACM Conf Fairness Accountability Transparency. 2020:99-109).⏎⏎This matters enormously for equity. If a sepsis prediction model systematically underscores Black patients — as would be expected given the pulse oximetry measurement error problem — and if clinicians are less likely to override a low risk score than to question a colleague's low-risk assessment, then the bias embedded in the model will be harder to detect through normal clinical quality review. The errors will look like appropriate clinical decisions. Char, Shah, and Magnus made this point in 2018: the opacity of machine learning models in clinical deployment, combined with automation bias, creates conditions under which systematic errors can persist for extended periods without triggering the feedback mechanisms that would surface equivalent errors in human judgment (Char DS, Shah NH, Magnus D. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(11):981-983).⏎⏎Wiens et al.'s responsible machine learning roadmap in Nature Medicine articulates the corollary: validation at the time of deployment is necessary but not sufficient, because models degrade over time as the patient populations and clinical practices in deployment environments diverge from training conditions (Wiens J, Saria S, Sendak M, et al. Nat Med. 2019;25(9):1337-1340). Post-deployment surveillance is not optional — it is the only mechanism by which temporal degradation and population mismatch can be detected. The RFI's discussion of post-market surveillance is insufficiently specific about what reporting requirements would look like in practice, who would be responsible for conducting the surveillance, and what thresholds would trigger corrective action.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Disability Rights Advocates | HHS AI RFI Comment | Page 4⏎⏎THE VALIDATION-DEPLOYMENT GAP IN THE MS CONTEXT⏎⏎We want to bring this back to the specific population we represent, because the validation-deployment gap is not abstract for MS patients. The 4.2-month diagnostic advantage documented at AI-integrated centers in our Provider Council's 2023 review is concentrated in facilities that look nothing like the community hospitals and federally qualified health centers where many of our members receive care. Academic MS Comprehensive Care Centers have neuroimaging infrastructure, subspecialty radiology support, and IT environments that are hospitable to AI diagnostic tool integration. Community hospitals in rural Connecticut, or in the Mississippi Delta, or in the Central Valley of California do not.⏎⏎When AI-assisted MRI analysis tools are validated at academic centers and then deployed — or recommended for deployment — in community settings, the performance assumptions embedded in the validation may not hold. The imaging protocols differ. The scanner hardware differs. The clinical workflows differ. Pierson et al.'s work on algorithmic approaches to pain disparities in underserved populations documents how even well-intentioned AI tools, when deployed in settings that differ from their training environments, can produce outputs that systematically disadvantage the populations those settings serve (Pierson E, Cutler DM, Leskovec J, Mullainathan S, Obermeyer Z. Nat Med. 2021;27(1):136-140). This is not a reason to withhold AI tools from community settings. It is a reason to require that tools be validated in community settings before being recommended for deployment there.⏎⏎The National Academy for State Health Policy documented in its 2023 policy brief on algorithmic accountability that most existing state and federal frameworks for health AI governance contain significant gaps in equity auditing requirements, particularly with respect to performance stratification by demographic subgroup and mandatory reporting of validation results from non-academic deployment environments (National Academy for State Health Policy. Algorithmic Accountability in State Health Programs. NASHP Policy Brief. 2023). The RFI's framing does not meaningfully close these gaps.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Disability Rights Advocates | HHS AI RFI Comment | Page 5⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Disability Rights Advocates urges HHS to condition any reimbursement pathway, regulatory clearance support, or R&D acceleration program on the following requirements, which we regard as preconditions rather than optional best practices:⏎⏎1. Mandatory pre-deployment equity audits. Any AI tool seeking reimbursement recognition or regulatory support under HHS programs must demonstrate pre-deployment performance stratified by race, ethnicity, sex, disability status, and insurance status across the demographic subgroups present in the intended deployment population. Validation conducted exclusively at academic medical centers should not be accepted as sufficient evidence of performance in community and safety-net settings.⏎⏎2. Mandatory post-deployment bias surveillance with public reporting. Developers and deploying institutions should be required to conduct ongoing performance monitoring stratified by the same demographic variables, with results reported publicly at intervals no greater than 12 months. The reporting framework should specify the performance thresholds that would trigger corrective action, including suspension of reimbursement coverage.⏎⏎3. Community and safety-net performance standards. HHS should establish performance benchmarks that apply specifically to deployment in community health centers, critical access hospitals, and federally qualified health centers. A tool that performs adequately at an academic center but inadequately in a safety-net setting should not be eligible for reimbursement support based on the academic center validation alone.⏎⏎o Sub-requirement: Validation datasets should include a minimum proportion of records from non-academic settings, with that proportion to be specified by HHS in subsequent rulemaking.⏎⏎o Sub-requirement: Equity audit methodologies should be standardized by HHS to prevent developers from selecting demographic subgroup comparisons that flatter their tools' performance profiles.⏎⏎4. Automation bias disclosure requirements. Deploying institutions should be required to disclose to clinical staff the known limitations of AI tools, including the demographic subgroups in which performance is weakest and the conditions under which the tool is most likely to produce erroneous output. This disclosure should be integrated into clinical decision support interfaces, not relegated to documentation that clinicians are unlikely to review.⏎⏎We are aware that some of these requirements will be characterized as obstacles to the acceleration the RFI is seeking. We would ask HHS to consider the alternative framing: deploying AI tools at scale without these preconditions is not acceleration, it is risk transfer. The risk is transferred from developers and institutions to the patients — disproportionately patients from communities that have already experienced systematic harm from health care algorithms — who will bear the consequences of bias that was not detected before deployment.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Disability Rights Advocates | HHS AI RFI Comment | Page 6⏎⏎ON THE REIMBURSEMENT QUESTION SPECIFICALLY⏎⏎The RFI asks several questions about reimbursement structures that could support AI adoption. We will address this narrowly, because we think the reimbursement question is where the equity stakes are most concrete.⏎⏎CMS reimbursement signals shape institutional adoption decisions more powerfully than almost any other policy lever available to HHS. When CMS creates a billing pathway for an AI-assisted diagnostic tool, health systems respond. That is precisely why the conditions attached to reimbursement coverage matter so much. If HHS creates reimbursement pathways that do not require equity auditing or post-deployment surveillance, it will be subsidizing the broad deployment of tools that have not been validated in the settings where they will be used and among the populations who will be most affected by their errors.⏎⏎We would note that the MS diagnostic context makes this concrete. AI-assisted MRI analysis for MS is not a hypothetical application — tools of this type are in use at a number of our member centers, and our Provider Council has documented their diagnostic timeline benefits. But the centers using these tools are not representative of where MS patients in underserved communities receive care. A reimbursement signal from CMS that incentivizes community hospital adoption of AI MRI analysis tools, without requiring that those tools be validated on the imaging hardware and clinical workflows present in community hospitals, would likely produce a wave of adoption followed by a wave of diagnostic errors that we would spend years trying to document and attribute.⏎⏎This is, we would note, more or less what happened with the Optum care management algorithm. It was widely implemented. Its bias was characterized years after deployment. The corrective literature was published in 2019. Health systems are still working through the implications.⏎⏎---⏎⏎REFERENCES⏎⏎Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. SYNTH-0090♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Karen Davis♔American Academy of Dermatology♔♔♔♔♔The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) submits these comments in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care settings, and we do so with a degree of genuine procedural confusion that we suspect is shared by a number of organizations engaging with this process for the first time. Before turning to our substantive concerns — which are considerable — our organization needs to flag something that has caused real difficulty in preparing this submission: it is not entirely clear to our policy team whether the actions described in this RFI represent a proposed rule that could still be shaped by public comment, or whether certain reimbursement and regulatory determinations described in the background materials have already been finalized in some form. Our staff attorney reviewed the Federal Register posting on multiple occasions and came away with different readings. That ambiguity is not a minor procedural complaint. If the Department is soliciting comment on decisions that are already effectively settled, the quality and character of the public record will reflect that misalignment, and the comments received — including this one — may not actually influence the outcomes they appear to address. We raise this not to be obstructionist but because the distinction between an RFI, a proposed rule, and a final rule matters enormously for how organizations like ours allocate internal resources and calibrate the specificity of our recommendations. We would ask HHS to clarify, either in a subsequent Federal Register notice or on the docket landing page, exactly what regulatory or sub-regulatory authority is being contemplated here and at what stage each contemplated action currently sits.⏎⏎American Academy of Dermatology Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 2⏎⏎With that procedural concern noted, our organization does have substantive views to offer, drawn from both our dermatology membership and from survey and policy review work that, while conducted in a dental and oral health context our organization has collaborated on through a shared workforce policy working group, speaks to AI adoption dynamics that cut across health professions. A 2024 survey of approximately 1,200 member dental practices found that 68% had evaluated at least one AI-assisted diagnostic tool — primarily for radiographic caries detection and periodontal bone loss assessment — yet fewer than 22% had moved beyond pilot testing to full clinical integration. That gap between evaluation and integration is not explained by clinician resistance to technology. It is explained by structural barriers: the absence of standardized performance benchmarks, unresolved questions about liability when AI-generated findings inform treatment decisions, and inconsistent coverage determinations from public and private payers alike. Those same barriers exist in dermatology, where AI tools for lesion classification and dermoscopy image analysis are proliferating without a coherent regulatory or reimbursement framework to govern their deployment. The Government Accountability Office documented analogous adoption friction across health care settings in its 2023 report on AI in health care (GAO-23-105980), finding that while clinical AI applications are technically maturing, the governance infrastructure needed to support responsible deployment has not kept pace.⏎⏎Our organization's primary concern with the RFI — and this is where we want to be direct — is that the framing of "acceleration" as the Department's posture risks systematically subordinating clinician autonomy and workforce governance to cost-reduction imperatives. This is not a theoretical risk. The research literature on prior health technology deployments is instructive here. Furukawa et al. (2023) conducted a longitudinal analysis published in Health Affairs finding that EHR adoption, when driven by administrative efficiency mandates rather than clinical workflow integration, was associated with increased physician burnout rather than reduced administrative burden. The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine reached similar conclusions in their 2019 report Taking Action Against Clinician Burnout, identifying poorly designed health information technology as a structural contributor to professional exhaustion rather than a remedy for it (National Academies, 2019). Shanafelt et al. (2022) documented in Mayo Clinic Proceedings that burnout among physicians worsened between 2011 and 2020 even as health systems invested heavily in digital infrastructure, a pattern that Dyrbye et al. (2021) extended to resident physicians across specialties in JAMA. The causal chain our organization is concerned about is not speculative: financial pressure on health systems creates demand for AI tools marketed as burnout solutions; those tools are then procured and deployed primarily to reduce staffing costs or increase throughput; the result is increased caseloads, algorithmic surveillance of clinical decision-making, and an erosion of the professional judgment that Stanton and Nankervis (2022) describe in their analysis of algorithmic management in health care work as foundational to occupational identity and patient safety. If HHS accelerates AI adoption without building accountability structures into that acceleration, the Department risks replicating the EHR experience at scale.⏎⏎American Academy of Dermatology Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 3⏎⏎On the specific question of evaluation frameworks — which is one of the RFI areas our organization is best positioned to address — we want to argue that any pre- and post-deployment evaluation methodology developed or endorsed by HHS must include the following components, which are currently absent from most health system procurement processes:⏎⏎1. Mandatory frontline clinician input at the procurement stage, not as a post-hoc consultation but as a documented condition of any federal support or reimbursement incentive tied to AI adoption. Becker's Hospital Review documented in its October 2023 AI procurement special report that the majority of health system AI purchasing decisions are made by administrative and IT leadership with minimal structured input from the clinicians who will use the tools daily. That governance gap is a patient safety issue, not just a workforce satisfaction issue.⏎⏎2. Worker-reported autonomy metrics as a required element of post-deployment evaluation. Clinical accuracy benchmarks — sensitivity, specificity, area under the ROC curve — are necessary but not sufficient. A tool can perform well on technical metrics while simultaneously degrading the professional environment in which it operates. Topol (2023) argued in The Lancet Digital Health that physician presence and clinical judgment are not obstacles to AI integration but the conditions under which AI can function safely; evaluation frameworks that measure only algorithmic performance will systematically miss that dimension.⏎⏎3. Staffing ratio impact assessments conducted at six and twelve months post-deployment. If an AI tool is adopted and staffing levels fall in the affected department within twelve months, that correlation should be tracked and reported. The American Nurses Association's 2023 workforce survey found that nurses in technology-intensive settings reported significantly lower perceptions of professional autonomy than peers in comparable settings without algorithmic management structures, a finding that should inform how HHS designs any mandatory reporting framework for AI-adopting facilities.⏎⏎4. Bias and equity auditing requirements that go beyond initial FDA clearance. Obermeyer and Emanuel (2016) identified in the New England Journal of Medicine that predictive algorithms trained on historically unrepresentative data can embed and amplify existing health disparities; the iterative update cycles common in modern AI tools mean that a tool cleared at one performance level may drift in ways that affect specific patient populations differentially. Our 2023 policy review, drawing on feedback from 47 dental school clinics and group practice networks, identified regulatory ambiguity around FDA clearance pathways for iteratively updated algorithms as a particularly acute obstacle — and the same ambiguity exists in dermatology AI, where commercial tools are updated continuously in ways that may or may not trigger re-review.⏎⏎The Pew Research Center's 2023 report on AI in the workplace found that a majority of workers subject to algorithmic management were unaware that such systems were being used to evaluate their performance — a governance gap that HHS should treat as a disclosure and consent issue, not merely a labor relations matter. Our organization would also note, somewhat parenthetically but we think it is worth raising, that the reimbursement questions embedded in this RFI are genuinely complex in ways the framing does not fully acknowledge. Coverage determinations for AI-assisted diagnostic tools vary not only across payers but across geographic markets, and the absence of a coherent CMS policy on how AI-augmented clinical encounters should be coded and billed creates perverse incentives: health systems in markets with more aggressive private payer contracts may be able to monetize AI adoption in ways that safety-net providers and Federally Qualified Health Centers cannot, potentially widening rather than narrowing existing disparities in care access and quality. Adler-Milstein and Pfeifer (2022) identified analogous market-structure effects in their analysis of information blocking in the Milbank Quarterly, and the structural logic applies here.⏎⏎American Academy of Dermatology Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 4⏎⏎We want to return briefly to our opening procedural question, because it is not merely a technicality. Our organization has members — dermatologists in private practice, in academic medical centers, in community health settings — who are making procurement decisions right now, in the absence of the regulatory clarity this RFI seems to be building toward. A dermatologist in a solo practice in rural Michigan deciding whether to license an AI dermoscopy tool has no reliable way to know whether that tool's FDA clearance status will be revisited under new guidance, whether her malpractice carrier will treat AI-assisted diagnoses differently than unassisted ones, or whether CMS will reimburse the encounter at a different rate depending on whether AI was used. Those are not abstract policy questions. They are the questions that explain why 68% of practices evaluate AI tools and fewer than 22% integrate them. The gap is not technophobia. It is rational caution in the face of unresolved regulatory, liability, and reimbursement uncertainty — exactly the kind of uncertainty that a well-designed RFI-to-rulemaking process should resolve, if the Department can clarify for stakeholders which parts of that process are still genuinely open to input and which have already been⏎⏎aadpolicy@aad.org⏎⏎References⏎⏎Adler-Milstein, J., & Pfeifer, E.
