SYNTH-0091♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Charles Nguyen♔American Diabetes Association♔♔♔♔♔American Diabetes Association⏎2451 Crystal Drive, Suite 900⏎Arlington, VA 22202⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Attention: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎February 14, 2025⏎⏎The American Diabetes Association (ADA) submits these comments in response to the Department's Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care settings. The ADA represents millions of people living with diabetes across the country, maintains affiliations with 214 research institutions, and has spent considerable organizational resources over the past two years examining precisely the adoption barriers HHS is now seeking to address. A 2024 benchmarking study conducted across our affiliated network found that 68% of institutions identified fragmented federal reimbursement pathways as the primary barrier to deploying validated AI clinical decision-support (CDSS) tools at scale, with an average implementation lag of 31 months between FDA clearance and first clinical deployment. A Q3 2024 policy survey of health system technology officers further revealed that institutions operating under value-based care arrangements were 2.4 times more likely to have piloted AI diagnostic tools than those in predominantly fee-for-service environments — a finding that aligns with the Government Accountability Office's October 2022 report (GAO-22-104629) on AI in health care, which similarly identified reimbursement architecture as a structural constraint on technology diffusion. The ADA does not dispute that these barriers are real. What the same benchmarking data also revealed, however, and what the Department's framing conspicuously omits, is that workforce consultation was absent from procurement processes in a majority of surveyed institutions. That absence is not incidental. It is the thread that, when pulled, unravels the entire accelerationist premise.⏎⏎ADA Comments | HHS AI RFI | February 2025 | Page 2⏎⏎The Department's RFI proceeds from an assumption that the primary problem is speed — that AI tools exist, that they are validated, and that regulatory friction is preventing their deployment at scale. The ADA urges HHS and ONC to examine that assumption with considerably more scrutiny than the RFI's framing invites. AI tools marketed to health systems as burnout-reduction and efficiency solutions are, in documented practice, being deployed primarily to justify reduced staffing ratios, increased caseloads, and the systematic extraction of productivity from clinical and administrative workforces. National Nurses United documented this pattern in their March 2023 research report, "Staffing Crisis and the Automation Illusion," finding that hospital AI procurement decisions in surveyed systems were made with no meaningful nurse consultation and were followed, in a majority of cases, by measurable increases in nurse-to-patient ratios within eighteen months of deployment. The American Medical Association's 2023 policy research report on physician perspectives on AI-assisted CDSS found that a significant share of responding physicians reported that AI tools reduced rather than preserved their clinical autonomy — a finding that directly contradicts the burnout-reduction narrative HHS appears to accept at face value. Shanafelt and colleagues, writing in Mayo Clinic Proceedings in 2022 (97[3]:491-506), documented that loss of autonomy and documentation burden — not workload volume per se — are the primary structural drivers of physician burnout between 2011 and 2020. Wachter and Goldsmith, writing in Harvard Business Review in March 2018, made the same argument specifically about EHR design. If the documented drivers of burnout are alert fatigue, loss of clinical autonomy, and EHR documentation burden, and if current AI deployment models in their dominant commercial form intensify all three of those conditions, then the claim that accelerating AI adoption will reduce burnout is not a hopeful projection — it is an empirically unsupported assertion that the Department is in danger of enshrining as policy. The ADA is concerned that the reimbursement and regulatory pathways HHS is considering would, without binding workforce protection standards, effectively subsidize deployment models that degrade the professional environments of the clinicians caring for people with diabetes and other chronic conditions.⏎⏎Kellogg, Valentine, and Christin, writing in the Academy of Management Annals in 2020 (14[1]:366-410), characterized algorithmic management as a "new contested terrain of control" in which workers subject to AI-driven performance monitoring experience measurable reductions in professional discretion and job satisfaction. The Pew Research Center's October 2023 report on AI in the workplace found that workers subject to algorithmic monitoring were substantially more likely to report stress and less likely to report that their employer trusted their judgment. These are not abstract workforce concerns. They are patient safety concerns. Dyrbye, Shanafelt, Sinsky, and colleagues, in their 2017 National Academy of Medicine discussion paper on burnout among health care professionals, drew a direct evidential line between clinician demoralization and adverse patient outcomes — a line the ADA believes HHS must incorporate into its regulatory calculus. Bates and colleagues, writing in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2020 (172[11 Suppl]:S137-S144), argued that machine learning interventions in clinical settings require rigorous prospective evaluation of workforce impact, not merely algorithmic performance metrics. Obermeyer and colleagues documented in Science in 2019 (366[6464]:447-453) that a widely deployed health management algorithm systematically underserved Black patients — a finding that raises the further question of who bears the consequences when accelerated deployment outpaces equity validation. ONC's own 2020 joint report to Congress on reducing regulatory and administrative burden acknowledged that poorly designed health IT deployment increases rather than decreases clinician burden. The ADA does not read that body of evidence as an argument against AI. Topol, writing in Nature Medicine in 2019 (25[1]:44-56), made a compelling case that the convergence of human and artificial intelligence, when structured around augmentation rather than replacement, can genuinely improve care. The operative phrase is "when structured around augmentation." That structure does not emerge automatically from market incentives. It requires regulatory architecture.⏎⏎ADA Comments | HHS AI RFI | February 2025 | Page 3⏎⏎The ADA therefore urges the Department to condition any federally endorsed or Medicare/Medicaid-reimbursed AI deployment in clinical settings on three demonstrated preconditions. First, health systems seeking reimbursement for AI-enabled CDSS or AI-assisted care coordination tools must document a structured workforce consultation process — not a post-hoc notification, but a genuine pre-procurement process involving clinical and administrative staff whose roles the technology will affect. Second, institutions must conduct and submit a staffing-ratio impact assessment projecting the tool's expected effect on nurse-to-patient and clinician-to-patient ratios over a 24-month post-deployment period, with a commitment to report actual outcomes and a mechanism for federal review if ratios deteriorate beyond projected thresholds. Third, deployed tools must meet autonomy-preservation standards — a regulatory concept the ADA acknowledges is underdeveloped and would benefit from a dedicated HHS working group that includes frontline clinician representatives, not only health system administrators and technology vendors. The ADA is aware that these preconditions will slow some deployments. The ADA's position is that deployments which cannot meet these standards should be slowed, because the harm they are likely to generate in workforce morale, patient safety, and health equity has not been adequately weighed against the efficiency gains their proponents project. A commissioned analysis released by the ADA Foundation in early 2024 estimated that regulatory ambiguity around AI algorithm updates costs health systems an aggregate $1.2 billion annually in duplicative validation expenditures. The ADA raises that figure not to argue for deregulation but to illustrate the scale of resources currently being consumed by processes that are not producing commensurately better outcomes for patients. SYNTH-0092♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Mark Harris♔Physicians for a National Health Program♔♔♔♔♔Physicians for a National Health Program | HHS AI RFI Comment | Page 1⏎⏎COMMENT OF PHYSICIANS FOR A NATIONAL HEALTH PROGRAM⏎Submitted in Response to HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information:⏎Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket No. HHS-AI-2024-RFI⏎⏎Submitted by: Mark Harris, Policy Director⏎Physicians for a National Health Program⏎Washington, DC | pnhp.org/policy⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE EQUITY PROBLEM HHS HAS NOT ADEQUATELY ADDRESSED⏎⏎The Department's framing of this RFI is, at its core, an acceleration agenda. HHS wants to know what regulatory, reimbursement, and research-and-development levers it can pull to move AI tools into clinical settings more quickly. Physicians for a National Health Program (PNHP) does not oppose that goal categorically, but we are compelled to register a concern that the RFI's structure largely presupposes the answer: that the primary constraints are administrative friction and misaligned incentives, and that resolving those constraints will produce better care. The evidence does not straightforwardly support that premise, and for the specific patient populations PNHP members serve — rural, safety-net, Medicaid-dependent, and historically marginalized communities — the risks of accelerating deployment ahead of demonstrated equity performance are not theoretical. They are documented, quantifiable, and in some cases already causing harm.⏎⏎The 2024 Texas Medical Association member survey of 4,200 licensed physicians found that 74% of respondents practicing in rural and safety-net settings expressed low confidence that available AI tools had been tested on patient populations comparable to their own (Texas Medical Association Policy Working Group on Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice, 2024). That is not a marginal finding. It means that the physicians closest to the populations most vulnerable to algorithmic failure are the ones reporting the least assurance of population-representative training data. The same survey found that fewer than 28% of physicians overall had received any formal institutional guidance on appropriate AI use, documentation standards, or liability implications. PNHP regards these figures as a reasonable proxy for the state of the field nationally, and they suggest that what HHS is proposing to accelerate is, in many practice environments, a set of tools whose equity properties have not been verified by anyone with regulatory authority to require that verification.⏎⏎The published literature on this point is now extensive enough that PNHP will not belabor it, but several specific findings warrant explicit mention because they are not edge cases — they are representative of how algorithmic bias operates in deployed clinical systems. Obermeyer and colleagues demonstrated in 2019 that a widely used commercial algorithm for managing care of high-cost patients assigned substantially lower risk scores to Black patients than to comparably ill white patients, because the algorithm used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, and historical cost data reflected decades of unequal access (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S., Science, 2019;366(6464):447-453). Sjoding and colleagues documented in 2020 that pulse oximeters — not AI systems per se, but a paradigmatic example of a clinical measurement tool validated in non-representative populations — systematically overestimated oxygen saturation in Black patients, with clinically meaningful consequences for COVID-19 care (Sjoding MW et al., N Engl J Med, 2020;383(25):2477-2478). Adamson and Smith identified in 2018 that dermatology AI classifiers trained predominantly on images of lighter-skinned patients performed substantially worse on images of darker-skinned patients, with the disparity largest in conditions that disproportionately affect Black and Hispanic populations (Adamson AS, Smith A., JAMA Dermatol, 2018;154(11):1247-1248). None of these findings emerged from adversarial research designed to find failure. They emerged from standard external validation attempts, which is itself part of the problem: the validation infrastructure was adequate to detect the bias only because researchers went looking for it. No regulatory requirement compelled the search.⏎⏎Physicians for a National Health Program | HHS AI RFI Comment | Page 2⏎⏎Wong and colleagues published in 2021 an external validation of a proprietary sepsis prediction model that had been implemented across hundreds of hospitals, finding that the model's performance in the validation cohort was substantially worse than the developer had reported, with a positive predictive value low enough to generate clinically problematic false-alarm rates (Wong A, Otles E, Donnelly JP et al., JAMA Intern Med, 2021;181(8):1065-1070). This is the distribution-shift problem in concrete form: a model trained and validated at academic medical centers may perform adequately in those environments while degrading significantly when deployed in community hospitals, rural critical-access facilities, or federally qualified health centers, where patient populations, documentation practices, and care workflows differ systematically from training environments. Wiens and colleagues described this dynamic explicitly in their 2019 roadmap for responsible machine learning in healthcare, noting that deployment in new clinical settings without prospective validation is one of the most consistent sources of observed model failure (Wiens J, Saria S, Sendak M et al., Nat Med, 2019;25(9):1337-1340). The Department's RFI does not, to PNHP's reading, propose any mechanism that would prevent this failure mode from recurring at scale.⏎⏎WHAT HHS HAS NOT PROPOSED AND SHOULD⏎⏎Gianfrancesco and colleagues identified in 2018 that electronic health record data used to train clinical machine learning models carries systematic biases reflecting differential access, documentation practices, and coding behaviors across patient populations, and that these biases propagate into model outputs in ways that are not visible from aggregate performance metrics (Gianfrancesco MA, Tamang S, Yazdany J, Schmajuk G., JAMA Intern Med, 2018;178(11):1544-1547). Char, Shah, and Magnus argued in the same year that addressing these ethical challenges requires institutional structures, not individual clinician vigilance, and that regulatory frameworks must require transparency about training data provenance as a precondition for deployment (Char DS, Shah NH, Magnus D., N Engl J Med, 2018;378(11):981-983). The ONC Data Brief on AI in health care, published in 2023, acknowledged these concerns but stopped well short of recommending mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing (ONC Data Brief No. 58, HHS, 2023). The TMA policy working group identified reimbursement uncertainty and the absence of standardized FDA-cleared performance benchmarks as the two most significant structural barriers to responsible AI adoption — and PNHP would add that the absence of mandatory equity auditing is a third structural barrier that the Department has so far treated as optional (Texas Medical Association Policy Working Group, 2024).⏎⏎The specific regulatory actions PNHP recommends HHS consider are the following:⏎⏎1. Mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing, with stratified performance reporting by race, ethnicity, language, insurance status, and geography, as a condition of CMS reimbursement for any AI-assisted clinical decision support tool. This should not be a voluntary attestation process. It should require submission of disaggregated validation data to a designated HHS office before any reimbursement pathway is activated.⏎⏎2. Post-deployment bias surveillance as a regulatory floor, not a best practice. Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones documented in 2020 the extent to which race-based corrections embedded in legacy clinical algorithms had propagated through the healthcare system for decades without systematic review (Vyas DA, Eisenstein LEI, Jones DS., N Engl J Med, 2020;383(9):874-882). A surveillance requirement would create the feedback loop that currently does not exist.⏎⏎3. Mandatory external validation in care settings that reflect the deployment environment, not the development environment. A model validated exclusively at an academic medical center should not be presumed valid for use at a rural critical-access hospital in, say, the Nebraska panhandle or the Mississippi Delta without prospective performance data from comparable settings. Sendak and colleagues have written about how the mismatch between development and deployment contexts is one of the most underappreciated sources of real-world model failure (Sendak MP, Elish MC, Gao M et al., Proc ACM Conf Fairness Accountability Transparency, 2020:99-109).⏎⏎Physicians for a National Health Program | HHS AI RFI Comment | Page 3⏎⏎4. Public reporting of model performance disaggregated by the demographic and socioeconomic characteristics listed above, updated on a defined schedule, and accessible to clinicians and patients. The automation bias problem — the well-documented tendency of clinicians to defer to algorithmic outputs even when clinical judgment would counsel otherwise — is substantially worsened when clinicians have no information about how a model performs in their specific patient population (Char DS, Shah NH, Magnus D., N Engl J Med, 2018;378(11):981-983; Pierson E, Cutler DM, Leskovec J, Mullainathan S, Obermeyer Z., Nat Med, 2021;27(1):136-140). Transparency about real-world performance is not a sufficient remedy for automation bias, but its absence removes even the possibility of informed clinical skepticism.⏎⏎THE ACCELERATION POSTURE AND ITS DISTRIBUTIONAL CONSEQUENCES⏎⏎PNHP wants to be clear that the concern here is not with AI in clinical care as a category. There are tools with genuine promise, and the membership includes physicians who have found specific applications — ambient documentation, image triage support, medication reconciliation — useful in practice. The concern is with the Department's apparent assumption that removing administrative friction is the binding constraint on equitable AI adoption. For a health system with no mandatory equity auditing requirement, removing administrative friction means removing friction for tools whose equity properties are unknown. The populations that will bear the cost of that unknown are not evenly distributed. They are, as the TMA survey data suggest, disproportionately the patients of physicians who already reported the least institutional support and the lowest confidence in training data representativeness. Pierson and colleagues demonstrated in 2021 that algorithmic approaches can actually reduce unexplained pain disparities in underserved populations when designed with equity as an explicit objective — which is exactly the point (Pierson E et al., Nat Med, 2021;27(1):136-140). The tools can be designed to reduce disparity. They can also be designed, or deployed without sufficient scrutiny, in ways that amplify it. HHS's acceleration agenda, as currently structured, does not adequately distinguish between these two possibilities.⏎⏎PNHP acknowledges that mandatory equity auditing and post-deployment surveillance will impose costs on developers and on the regulatory infrastructure. Those costs are real. But the alternative — detecting disparate harm retrospectively, after the harm has accumulated in patient populations that already carry a disproportionate burden of untreated and undertreated illness — is not a neutral default. It is a choice, and it is a choice with distributional consequences that fall most heavily on people who are least positioned to seek recourse. The Department has an opportunity, in responding to this RFI, to establish equity performance as a precondition for acceleration rather than as an aspiration to be addressed after the acceleration has occurred. PNHP urges HHS to take that opportunity seriously.⏎⏎One additional point that the RFI does not fully address: the question of which entities bear the cost of post-deployment surveillance. If that cost falls entirely on health systems and safety-net providers, it will function as a regressive tax on exactly the institutions serving the populations most at risk. The Department should consider whether developer-funded surveillance requirements, structured similarly to post-market surveillance obligations in the medical device context, would better align incentives without shifting costs to under-resourced institutions.⏎⏎REFERENCES⏎⏎Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. SYNTH-0094♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Barbara Wright♔Tempus AI♔♔♔♔♔Tempus AI | Government Affairs and Policy⏎350 North Orleans Street, Suite 950⏎Chicago, Illinois 60654⏎⏎www.tempus.com | policy@tempus.com⏎⏎October 14, 2024⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Hubert H. Humphrey Building, Room 120F⏎200 Independence Avenue, SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Attn: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information (HHS-ONC-2024-0001)⏎⏎Re: Comments of Tempus AI on the Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎Tempus AI submits these comments in response to the Department's request for information on regulatory, reimbursement, and research-and-development actions to accelerate artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings, published at 89 Fed. Reg. 22xxx (ONC 2024). Tempus AI operates at the intersection of clinical data infrastructure and AI-enabled decision support, and our perspective on this RFI is grounded in direct engagement with the hospital finance and governance leaders who are actually making procurement decisions about these tools. That grounding matters here, because the RFI's framing of acceleration as the primary policy objective omits what is, from our vantage point, the most consequential unresolved question facing health systems considering AI deployment at scale: who is legally and morally responsible when an AI-assisted clinical decision causes patient harm?⏎⏎We want to be direct about what is missing from this RFI. The Department asks extensive questions about reimbursement pathways, interoperability requirements, and R&D investment priorities. It does not ask, in any of the enumerated question sets, how liability should be allocated when an AI clinical decision support tool produces an erroneous recommendation that a clinician acts upon, and a patient is injured as a result. That silence is not a minor oversight. It is, in our assessment, a structural design flaw in the acceleration agenda the Department is proposing.⏎⏎Tempus AI | Government Affairs and Policy | HHS-ONC-2024-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎A 2024 internal benchmarking analysis conducted across EHY Consulting LLC's portfolio of 47 hospital CFO clients found that 68% had allocated budget for AI-enabled clinical decision support tools, yet fewer than 20% had successfully moved beyond pilot phases. Finance leadership at 83% of those institutions cited the absence of clear CMS coverage determinations as the primary barrier to capital commitment at scale. A Q2 2024 structured survey of that same CFO network identified payer policy inconsistency, not implementation cost, as the dominant factor stalling AI procurement within health system capital planning cycles. These findings are consistent with what the Government Accountability Office documented in its 2022 report on AI in health care, which found that liability ambiguity and governance gaps were among the most frequently cited barriers to sustained AI deployment in clinical environments (GAO-22-104629). The reimbursement problem is real, and we understand why the Department has focused on it. But the finance executives we work with are not primarily asking whether a CPT code will eventually cover an AI-assisted diagnostic workflow. They are asking what happens to their institution when that workflow produces a wrong answer.⏎⏎⏎ACCOUNTABILITY DIFFUSION AS AN INSTITUTIONAL LIABILITY PROBLEM⏎⏎The legal architecture governing clinical negligence presupposes an identifiable human decision-maker. Malpractice doctrine, as Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert documented in their 2020 JAMA review, is built around the standard of care as exercised by a reasonably competent clinician (Mello et al., 2020). When AI intermediates the relationship between clinical judgment and patient outcome, that foundational assumption breaks down in ways that existing doctrine has not resolved. Price, Gerke, and Cohen identified this problem with precision in their 2019 JAMA analysis: physicians using AI tools may face liability for failing to override a flawed recommendation, for deferring too readily to algorithmic output, or for not understanding the tool's limitations well enough to exercise independent judgment, while simultaneously having no clear legal recourse against the AI vendor whose product generated the error (Price et al., 2019). The result is that liability does not disappear; it diffuses across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in a way that makes it practically unassignable after the fact.⏎⏎Tempus AI | Government Affairs and Policy | HHS-ONC-2024-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen described this diffusion in their 2020 Academic Press chapter on ethical and legal challenges in AI-driven health care, noting that the multi-party nature of AI clinical tools, involving developers, training data curators, hospital IT infrastructure teams, and end-user clinicians, creates accountability gaps that no single legal theory currently bridges cleanly (Gerke et al., 2020). Product liability doctrine under the Restatement (Third) of Torts provides one potential avenue, particularly design defect theory, but courts have not settled on whether AI clinical tools are products subject to strict liability or services governed by negligence standards, and that unsettled question leaves health systems in an uncomfortable intermediate position (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability § 2, Am. Law Inst. 1998). Cohen, Amarasingham, Shah, Xie, and Lo raised an adjacent concern in their 2014 Health Affairs analysis: that the opacity of complex predictive analytics in clinical settings creates legal and ethical problems that go beyond malpractice, touching on informed consent, patient autonomy, and the right to an accountable human decision-maker (Cohen et al., 2014). That concern has not become less urgent in the decade since they wrote it.⏎⏎Health systems absorbing these tools into clinical workflows are not passive bystanders to this legal uncertainty. They are active parties to it. When a hospital signs a contract with an AI clinical decision support vendor, it typically accepts terms that limit vendor liability through warranty disclaimers and indemnification caps, while simultaneously assuming responsibility for how clinicians use the tool within the institution. The American Hospital Association's 2023 framework on trustworthy AI governance acknowledged this tension directly, noting that hospitals are often left holding accountability that neither the regulatory framework nor the vendor contract has clearly assigned (AHA, 2023). Dolin and Alschuler's work on semantic interoperability and system dependency, while focused on HL7 and EHR integration, is relevant here for a different reason: once an AI clinical tool is embedded in a workflow at sufficient depth, the practical ability to audit, override, or remove it is constrained by the same dependency structures that make the tool operationally useful (Dolin & Alschuler, 2011). The hospital that deploys an AI-assisted sepsis prediction tool across its ICUs is not in a position to simply turn it off when performance questions arise, because the workflow has been rebuilt around its outputs. That is an accountability lock-in problem, and the RFI does not address it.⏎⏎Tempus AI | Government Affairs and Policy | HHS-ONC-2024-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎⏎THE MALPRACTICE DOCTRINE PROBLEM IS NOT MERELY THEORETICAL⏎⏎Kesselheim, Cresswell, and Sheikh, writing in Health Affairs Scholar in 2023, argued that AI-assisted clinical decision making has produced accountability gaps that are not addressable through existing malpractice frameworks and that a purpose-built regulatory structure is needed before deployment scales further (Kesselheim et al., 2023). We think that assessment is correct, and we want to be specific about what the accountability gap looks like from the perspective of a hospital finance and legal team reviewing an AI procurement proposal.⏎⏎When a clinician makes an error unassisted, the accountability chain is relatively legible. The clinician's conduct is evaluated against the standard of care, the hospital may face vicarious liability, and malpractice insurance covers a known range of exposure. When an AI tool contributes to the error, the following questions are simultaneously unresolved:⏎⏎1. Was the clinician's reliance on the AI output reasonable given the information available about the tool's performance characteristics, and if so, does reasonable reliance insulate the clinician from liability or shift it to the institution that selected and deployed the tool?⏎⏎2. If the tool's output was the proximate cause of the error, is the vendor liable under product defect theory, and does it matter whether the error arose from a flaw in the model architecture, from model drift after deployment, or from a mismatch between the training data distribution and the patient population in which the tool was used?⏎⏎3. If the hospital modified the tool's default configuration, integrated it with EHR data in ways the vendor did not anticipate, or failed to implement the vendor's recommended monitoring protocols, has the hospital assumed liability that would otherwise have rested with the vendor?⏎⏎4. Does the patient have a cognizable claim against any of these parties under current doctrine, and if so, what discovery obligations arise with respect to the model's architecture, training data, and performance logs?⏎⏎Tempus AI | Government Affairs and Policy | HHS-ONC-2024-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎None of these questions has a settled answer in federal or state law. Obermeyer and Emanuel noted in their 2016 New England Journal of Medicine analysis that machine learning tools in clinical medicine operate through mechanisms that are often opaque even to their developers, which compounds the evidentiary problem in litigation: if the model's decision logic cannot be reconstructed post-hoc, causation may be practically unprovable even when the error is obvious (Obermeyer & Emanuel, 2016). The hospital's legal team knows this. The hospital's malpractice insurer knows this. The CFO knows this, because the CFO is the one signing off on the capital allocation that funds the deployment and reviewing the risk management analysis that should, in theory, quantify the tail liability exposure. The honest answer in most of those risk management analyses right now is that the tail liability exposure from AI clinical tool deployment is not quantifiable, because the legal framework for assigning it does not exist.⏎⏎We are not suggesting that AI clinical tools are without benefit. Tempus AI is in the business of developing and deploying these tools, and we have seen real evidence that well-designed, properly governed AI applications can improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce clinician cognitive burden in high-stakes environments. What we are saying is that the Department is proposing to accelerate deployment of these tools before the accountability infrastructure exists to make that deployment manageable from a legal, governance, and patient-rights perspective. That sequencing is a problem.⏎⏎⏎THE MORAL DIMENSION⏎⏎There is a dimension of this that goes beyond institutional liability management, and it deserves to be stated plainly. Patients who are harmed by errors in clinical care have a reasonable expectation that there is an identifiable human being who made the decision that harmed them, who can be held to account through legal and professional mechanisms, and whose accountability creates incentives for the system as a whole to perform better. That expectation is not sentimental. It is the foundation on which malpractice doctrine's deterrent function rests, as Mello and colleagues documented in their 2020 review of the relationship between liability and quality of care (Mello et al., 2020). When AI intermediates clinical decisions in ways that diffuse accountability across parties with conflicting interests and asymmetric information, the patient's ability to exercise that expectation is structurally undermined.⏎⏎Tempus AI | Government Affairs and Policy | HHS-ONC-2024-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎The Department's RFI does not acknowledge this. It treats AI adoption as a question of reimbursement alignment and regulatory pathway clarity, which are real problems worth addressing. But the patient on the receiving end of an AI-assisted diagnostic error is not primarily concerned with whether the tool was covered under a Medicare benefit category. That patient is concerned with whether anyone is responsible for what happened to them. The RFI's silence on that question is not a neutral omission. It is a policy choice to defer the accountability problem while accelerating the deployment that creates it, and health systems are being asked to absorb the consequences of that deferral.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING THE RFI'S FRAMING⏎⏎Tempus AI's comments focus primarily on the RFI's regulatory and governance questions rather than its reimbursement questions, because we believe the governance gap is more consequential and less acknowledged. We want to identify two specific framing problems in the RFI that we think should be corrected before the Department moves toward any formal rulemaking or guidance based on the responses it receives.⏎⏎First, the RFI treats accountability as a question of transparency and explainability, which conflates two distinct problems. Transparency and explainability are about whether clinicians and patients can understand how an AI tool reaches its outputs. Accountability is about who bears legal and moral responsibility when those outputs cause harm. A tool can be fully explainable and still produce errors for which no party is legally responsible under current doctrine. The Department should not allow progress on explainability requirements to be treated as a substitute for resolving the liability assignment problem.⏎⏎Second, the RFI's framing of "barriers to adoption" implicitly treats the absence of AI deployment as the problem to be solved. From the perspective of the hospital finance and legal teams we work with, the absence of a clear accountability framework is itself a barrier to responsible adoption, and it is a barrier that the Department has the authority to address through regulatory action. The Department could, for example, issue guidance establishing that hospitals deploying AI clinical decision support tools are responsible for maintaining auditable records of model performance, configuration, and any modifications made post-deployment, as a condition of Medicare participation. That would not resolve the full liability question, but it would create a baseline accountability infrastructure that does not currently exist.⏎⏎Tempus AI | Government Affairs and Policy | HHS-ONC-2024-0001 | Page 7⏎⏎⏎RECOMMENDATION⏎⏎Tempus AI recommends that the Department take the following procedural step before formalizing any acceleration pathway for AI clinical deployment: commission or formally solicit a legal analysis of the existing liability framework governing AI-assisted clinical errors, with specific attention to the gaps identified by Kesselheim, Cresswell, and Sheikh (2023) and by Price, Gerke, and Cohen (2019), and require that any reimbursement pathway or deployment guidance issued following this RFI be accompanied by a corresponding regulatory assignment of liability that specifies which party, whether the clinician, the hospital, the AI vendor, or some combination, bears primary responsibility for AI-assisted clinical errors under defined conditions.⏎⏎This is not a call to halt AI development. It is a call to sequence the regulatory work in an order that reflects the actual risks that health systems, clinicians, and patients are being asked to assume. The Department has significant authority to shape this sequencing. The question is whether it chooses to use that authority before or after the first wave of AI-assisted clinical errors produces litigation that forces the question through the courts on a timeline and in a forum that the Department will not control.⏎⏎The CFO network findings we cited at the outset are relevant here for a reason that goes beyond the reimbursement point. When 83% of hospital finance executives identify liability ambiguity as the primary barrier to AI procurement commitment, they are not describing a regulatory inconvenience. They are describing a rational response to a genuine structural risk. The Department's acceleration agenda, as currently framed, would ask those executives to set that rational response aside without providing the regulatory clarity that would make doing so responsible. That is not a reasonable ask, and the Department should not be surprised when health systems continue to stall at the pilot phase until the accountability question is answered.⏎⏎We appreciate the Department's engagement on these questions and remain available to discuss the governance and liability concerns raised in these comments.⏎⏎Sincerely,⏎⏎Barbara Wright⏎Chief Financial Officer, Tempus AI⏎Member, EHY Consulting CFO Advisory Network⏎350 North Orleans Street, Suite 950⏎Chicago, Illinois 60654⏎policy@tempus.com⏎312-555-0194⏎⏎Tempus AI | Government Affairs and Policy | HHS-ONC-2024-0001 | Page 8♔♔2026-02-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-12T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔8♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔organization♔high♔resigned♔Indiana♔hospital CFO♔47♔A 2024 internal benchmarking analysis conducted across EHY Consulting LLC's portfolio of 47 hospital CFO clients found that 68% had allocated budget for AI-enabled clinical decision support tools, yet fewer than 20% had successfully moved beyond pilot phases due to unresolved reimbursement pathway ambiguity. SYNTH-0095♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Stephanie Smith♔♔♔♔♔♔My cardiologist retired in 2022, and the practice that absorbed her patients assigned me to a nurse practitioner who spends our fifteen-minute appointments re-entering the same medication list I've had for six years because the system her office uses doesn't talk to the pharmacy, doesn't talk to the lab, and apparently doesn't talk to the system the cardiologist's old practice used either. I sit on that paper-covered table watching her squint at a screen and I think: this is what fragmentation looks like from the inside. Not a policy failure. A business model.⏎⏎I want to be clear that I read this RFI carefully and I understand what HHS is trying to do. The goals are reasonable on their face. Faster adoption, better reimbursement pathways, more public-private partnership. I don't think the people who wrote this are acting in bad faith. But I keep coming back to a question the RFI doesn't ask: who actually benefits when the federal government accelerates AI adoption in a market that is already heavily consolidated around a small number of vendors? Because from where I'm sitting, the answer is not me.⏎⏎⏎WHO BENEFITS FROM ACCELERATION⏎⏎The health IT market is not competitive in any meaningful sense. Gee and Bhatt wrote in Health Affairs in 2023 that concentration in the health information technology market has reached levels that would concern antitrust regulators in almost any other sector (Gee & Bhatt, 2023, Health Affairs, 42(3), 411-419). A handful of EHR vendors control the majority of hospital and large-practice market share, and those vendors have not competed primarily on interoperability or patient outcomes. They have competed on switching costs. The GAO documented this in 2023, finding that vendor lock-in and interoperability barriers in electronic health record systems are structural features of the market, not incidental technical problems (GAO-23-105412). Adler-Milstein and Pfeifer found in 2022 that information blocking behavior is correlated with EHR vendor market power, meaning the vendors with the most to lose from real interoperability are also the ones with the most leverage to resist it (Adler-Milstein & Pfeifer, 2022, Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 29(8), 1402-1408).⏎⏎So when HHS proposes to accelerate AI adoption through reimbursement modernization and public-private partnerships, I want to ask: which vendors are positioned to navigate complex federal billing and coverage processes? Which vendors have dedicated regulatory affairs teams who can engage with a CRADA negotiation? Which vendors already have preferential data access relationships with large health systems? The answer to all three questions is the same small group of incumbents who built the fragmented, incompatible systems that are currently failing patients like me. Acceleration, in this context, does not mean more competition. It means more of the same, faster.⏎⏎⏎ON REIMBURSEMENT MODERNIZATION⏎⏎The RFI asks about regulatory and reimbursement actions HHS can take to support AI adoption. I want to focus on this because I think it's where the political economy problem is sharpest. Dafny and Lee wrote in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2022 that federal reimbursement policy shapes AI vendor competition in ways that systematically favor incumbents who can absorb the cost of compliance and billing complexity (Dafny & Lee, 2022, NEJM, 387(14), 1311-1314). A smaller, community-based innovator who builds something genuinely better for patients in rural Texas or for people who see nurse practitioners in absorbed practices because their cardiologist retired, that innovator does not have the infrastructure to navigate a new AI reimbursement category. The large vendor does. So the reimbursement pathway that HHS designs to "accelerate adoption" functions in practice as a barrier to entry that protects the incumbents it was supposedly designed to displace.⏎⏎I'm not an economist and I don't pretend to know exactly how to fix this. But I know what the problem looks like from the patient side. The nurse practitioner I see now uses a system that was clearly designed to generate billing codes, not to support clinical decisions. The medication reconciliation workflow is so cumbersome that she re-enters my list by hand at nearly every visit. If HHS creates a new AI billing category and the incumbent vendor who sold her practice that system adds an AI module on top of it, that module will be optimized for the same thing the underlying system is optimized for: revenue capture. Not patient outcomes. Not interoperability. Certainly not the ability to pull my lab results from the lab system across town that uses a different vendor.⏎⏎⏎ON RESEARCH PRIORITIZATION AND PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIPS⏎⏎The RFI also asks about research and development priorities, and this is where I want to raise something that I think gets too little attention in these discussions. When HHS enters a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with a private vendor, what happens to the intellectual property that comes out of that collaboration? In most cases, the vendor retains proprietary control over the resulting product. Mazzucato and Roy argued in 2019 in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health that this is a systematic problem in health innovation: publicly funded research generates private value, and the public sees little of the return (Mazzucato & Roy, 2019, J Epidemiol Community Health, 73(6), 500-504). The vendor gets a product it can lock health systems into. The federal government gets a press release.⏎⏎I think HHS should ask itself whether the research it funds through CRADAs and public-private partnerships should be required to produce open-source, interoperable outputs. Not proprietary modules that get bolted onto existing locked systems, but actual infrastructure that any provider, any small practice, any community health center can use without paying a licensing fee to Epic or Oracle or whoever ends up winning the next round of consolidation. I recognize this is a harder political lift than signing a partnership agreement with a vendor who already has a Washington office. But it is the question that actually matters if you care about whether AI benefits patients rather than shareholders.⏎⏎There is also a fairness dimension here that I want to name even though I know it's handled in other parts of this RFI process. Obermeyer and colleagues published in Science in 2019 that a widely used health algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it was trained on cost data rather than health outcome data (Obermeyer et al., 2019, Science, 366(6464), 447-453). That algorithm was a product of exactly the kind of public-private research ecosystem that HHS is proposing to expand. The vendors who build these tools are not primarily accountable to patients. They are accountable to the health systems that pay for their contracts. When HHS accelerates adoption without building in meaningful accountability mechanisms that are independent of vendor self-reporting, it is accelerating the adoption of that accountability gap along with everything else.⏎⏎⏎WHAT I WOULD ACTUALLY LIKE TO SEE⏎⏎I want to be specific here because I think vague calls for "more accountability" don't help anyone.⏎⏎1. HHS should condition any new AI reimbursement pathway on demonstrated interoperability with at least two competing EHR systems, tested by an independent party, not self-certified. The existing certification frameworks have not produced real interoperability. A new pathway that relies on the same certification structure will not either.⏎⏎2. Any CRADA or public-private partnership that uses federal health data should require that the resulting model or tool be made available under an open license, or at minimum that the federal government retain a royalty-free license to deploy the tool in federally funded settings including community health centers and FQHCs.⏎⏎3. Reimbursement modernization for AI tools should include a small-practice carve-out that does not require a dedicated regulatory affairs team to navigate. The nurse practitioner who sees me works in a practice that absorbed patients from three retiring physicians in the span of eighteen months. She does not have a VP of Reimbursement Strategy. If the new billing pathway requires one, it will benefit exactly one category of provider: the large integrated health system that already has IT infrastructure, legal staff, and a vendor relationship with a major EHR company.⏎⏎4. HHS should commission an independent market analysis, not a vendor-sponsored white paper, of concentration in the health AI market before it designs acceleration policy. The Gee and Bhatt piece I cited earlier is a start, but it predates the most recent wave of AI-specific acquisitions. The market structure that acceleration policy will operate in is not the same market structure that existed when these academic analyses were conducted.⏎⏎5. There should be a patient feedback mechanism that is not routed through the vendor or the health system. Right now, if I want to report that my provider's EHR system is failing me, my options are essentially nothing. I can tell my nurse practitioner, who will shrug sympathetically and keep re-entering my medication list. I can file a complaint with my insurance company, which has its own vendor relationships and its own incentives. I cannot report to any federal body that a specific AI tool or EHR system is producing fragmented, dangerous care, because no such reporting mechanism exists for patients at the level of specific vendor products.⏎⏎⏎A NOTE ON WHAT I AM NOT ARGUING⏎⏎I want to be clear that I am not asking HHS to slow down because I am afraid of technology. I am sixty-nine years old and I work retail and I am not under any illusion that the status quo is fine. The status quo is the disconnected systems and the fifteen-minute appointments and the hand-entered medication lists. The status quo is already failing me. What I am asking is that HHS recognize that the entity most likely to benefit from acceleration, as currently designed, is not me. It is the vendor who sold my nurse practitioner's practice the system that doesn't talk to the pharmacy. Acceleration without structural reform in the underlying market is not a patient safety improvement. It is a subsidy.⏎⏎The RFI frames this as a question about how to get good technology to patients faster. I think the more honest framing is a question about who controls the infrastructure that AI runs on, who profits when that infrastructure gets embedded in federal reimbursement pathways, and what happens to patients when the answer to both questions is a company that has no direct accountability to them. I've been waiting two years for a system that works. I'm not holding my breath that a new AI reimbursement category will be the thing that finally makes my lab results visible to the person reading my EKG.⏎⏎I submitted this comment through regulations.gov and I am a private individual with no financial interest in any health IT vendor. My concern is that HHS will read comments from vendor coalitions and large health systems, which have the resources to submit detailed technical comments with economic modeling attached, and will weight those comments more heavily than the experience of someone who has watched her own care fall through the gap between incompatible systems for two years running. I don't know how to prevent that. I just wanted to put it on the record that the gap is real and that the people falling through it are not represented in most of the comments you will receive.♔♔2026-02-09T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-09T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔The AI healthcare market is dominated by a small number of powerful vendors whose commercial interests in rapid deployment conflict with patient safety, and HHS's acceleration agenda risks embedding those vendors permanently into critical healthcare infrastructure.♔individual♔high♔resigned♔Texas♔retail worker♔70♔My cardiologist retired in 2022, and the practice that absorbed her patients assigned me to a nurse practitioner who spends our fifteen-minute appointments scrolling through a system that clearly doesn't talk to the pharmacy or the lab. SYNTH-0096♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Barbara Young♔University of Washington Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science♔♔♔♔♔COMMENT SUBMITTED TO HHS DOCKET: HEALTH SECTOR AI REQUEST FOR INFORMATION⏎Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Cornell University AI in Health Initiative / Center for Health AI Trustworthiness⏎Contact: Barbara Young, Ph.D., University of Washington Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science (submitting on behalf of Cornell initiative research collaborators)⏎Docket Submission Date: 2024⏎⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎The Cornell University AI in Health Initiative, operating across the Weill Cornell Medicine campus and the Cornell Tech hub on Roosevelt Island, has conducted a 30-month evaluation of AI implementation patterns at 14 affiliated clinical partner sites. That assessment, completed in 2024, found that 68% of those sites identified reimbursement ambiguity and liability uncertainty as primary deployment barriers — a finding this comment does not contest and which is consistent with the regulatory reform priorities the RFI appears to have been designed to address. Cornell submits this comment, however, to raise a concern that the RFI does not adequately address and that the 30-month evaluation period has made difficult to ignore: the acceleration of AI adoption in clinical care, in the absence of mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing and post-deployment bias surveillance requirements, will predictably reproduce and entrench documented patterns of racially and socioeconomically disparate harm in health systems that are already failing the populations most likely to be affected. The empirical record on this question is not ambiguous. The policy posture implied by the current RFI — which frames acceleration primarily as a reimbursement and regulatory-burden problem without establishing equity safeguards as conditions of any new pathway — is not a neutral stance. It is a choice, and Cornell believes HHS should understand it as such before finalizing any regulatory or reimbursement action in this space.⏎⏎⏎SECTION 1: THE EMPIRICAL BASIS FOR CORNELL'S CONCERN⏎⏎Cornell's 30-month evaluation was not designed to produce an equity critique. It was designed to characterize implementation barriers, and it found what it found. But the same 240 clinical investigators and health systems researchers surveyed through our NIH-funded Center for Health AI Trustworthiness were also asked whether their institutions had conducted formal equity auditing of AI tools prior to deployment. Fewer than 12% reported that their institutions had done so in any systematic way. That number sits alongside a body of peer-reviewed literature that should, by this point in the policy cycle, be driving regulatory design rather than serving as background reading.⏎⏎The foundational work here is by now well-known. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan (2019, Science, 366(6464), 447–453) demonstrated that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to allocate health management resources systematically assigned lower risk scores to Black patients than to White patients with equivalent underlying illness burden, with the consequence that Black patients were effectively denied access to care coordination programs at scale. Sjoding, Dickson, Iwashyna, Gay, and Valley (2020, New England Journal of Medicine, 383(25), 2477–2478) documented that pulse oximetry devices — not a novel AI system, but a technology so entrenched in clinical practice that its outputs are treated as objective measurement — produced occult hypoxemia in Black patients at nearly three times the rate observed in White patients, a disparity that went largely undetected because aggregate performance metrics concealed subgroup failure. Adamson and Smith (2018, JAMA Dermatology, 154(11), 1247–1248) documented that dermatology diagnostic AI systems trained predominantly on images of lighter-skinned patients performed substantially worse on darker skin tones, a failure mode that was structurally predictable from the composition of training datasets and that was documented after deployment, not before.⏎⏎These are not edge cases in the literature. They are among the most-cited findings in the field, and they share a common architecture: a system that performs adequately on aggregate benchmarks, validated on datasets that do not adequately represent the populations most likely to experience harm, deployed into clinical environments where the authoritative presentation of algorithmic output creates conditions for what Cabitza, Rasoini, and Gensini (2017, JAMA, 318(6), 517–518) called automation bias — the tendency of clinicians to defer to machine-generated recommendations in ways that suppress the critical scrutiny that would catch equivalent errors in human judgment. The RFI solicits comment on how to accelerate adoption. Cornell's position is that acceleration without addressing this architecture is not a policy solution. It is a scaling mechanism for documented harm.⏎⏎⏎SECTION 2: STRUCTURAL UNDERREPRESENTATION AND THE COMMUNITY HOSPITAL PROBLEM⏎⏎Cornell University AI in Health Initiative | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎There is a dimension of this problem that receives less attention than the training-data bias literature and that Cornell's 14-site evaluation has made particularly concrete. AI clinical decision-support tools are predominantly developed and validated using data from large academic medical centers — institutions with well-resourced informatics infrastructure, relatively homogeneous patient populations by some sociodemographic dimensions, and clinical workflows that reflect the particular practices of high-volume tertiary care. The external validity problem this creates is not subtle. Wiens, Saria, Sendak, Ghassemi, Liu, Doshi-Velez, and Goldenberg (2019, Nature Medicine, 25(9), 1337–1340) described this as one of the central unsolved challenges in responsible clinical AI deployment: performance on held-out test sets from the same institution that generated the training data does not predict performance in genuinely external settings, particularly settings that differ in patient population, EHR system, documentation practices, or clinical workflow. This is not a theoretical concern. Wong, Otles, Donnelly, Krumm, McCullough, DeTroyer-Cooley, and Singh (2021, JAMA Internal Medicine, 181(8), 1065–1070) externally validated a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model — a tool that had been adopted by hundreds of hospitals on the basis of internal validation performance — and found that its real-world performance was substantially worse than reported, with poor positive predictive value and significant variation across subpopulations.⏎⏎Of the 14 sites in Cornell's evaluation, six were community hospitals or safety-net institutions. Those six sites reported the highest rates of uncertainty about AI tool performance in their specific patient populations, and they were also the sites least likely to have access to the institutional resources — biomedical informatics staff, data science capacity, legal counsel — needed to conduct independent equity auditing prior to deployment. Seyyed-Kalantari, Zhang, McDermott, Chen, and Ghassemi (2021, Nature Medicine, 27(12), 2176–2182) documented precisely this dynamic in their analysis of chest radiograph AI systems: underserved patient populations experienced higher rates of underdiagnosis, and the disparity was most pronounced in settings that most closely resembled the resource-constrained institutions where the tools were being deployed without site-specific validation. This pattern is not incidental to how clinical AI markets currently operate. It is a structural consequence of development practices that treat academic medical center data as a reasonable proxy for the full range of clinical environments and patient populations the tools will eventually encounter.⏎⏎Gianfrancesco, Tamang, Yazdany, and Schmajuk (2018, JAMA Internal Medicine, 178(11), 1544–1547) identified several mechanisms by which EHR-derived training data introduces systematic bias into clinical AI, including differential rates of missing data across sociodemographic groups, the encoding of historically unequal treatment patterns as ground-truth labels, and the use of proxy variables that carry racial or socioeconomic content without explicit encoding. Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones (2020, New England Journal of Medicine, 383(9), 874–882) extended this analysis to the specific problem of race correction in clinical algorithms, demonstrating that the use of race as a biological variable in algorithmic risk estimation encodes historical medical racism into automated systems in ways that are difficult to detect and correct after deployment. Char, Shah, and Magnus (2018, New England Journal of Medicine, 378(11), 981–983) argued that these ethical challenges are not incidental to machine learning implementation in healthcare but are structural features of how the technology interacts with existing health system inequities, requiring proactive regulatory attention rather than post-hoc correction.⏎⏎Cornell University AI in Health Initiative | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎The consistent thread across this literature — and across Cornell's 30-month evaluation — is that the institutions least equipped to detect algorithmic harm are disproportionately the institutions serving the populations most likely to experience it. The RFI's framing of acceleration as primarily a reimbursement and regulatory-burden problem does not engage with this dynamic, and Cornell believes this is a significant gap in the regulatory analysis underlying the solicitation.⏎⏎⏎SECTION 3: WHAT THE CURRENT RFI DOES NOT REQUIRE⏎⏎Cornell has reviewed the RFI with attention to whether it proposes, or even solicits comment on, mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing or post-deployment bias surveillance as conditions of any new reimbursement or regulatory pathway. It does not. The RFI solicits comment on how to reduce regulatory burden, how to clarify reimbursement pathways, and how to accelerate the translation of validated AI tools into clinical practice. Ferryman and Pitcan (2018, Data & Society Research Institute, https://datasociety.net/library/fairness-in-precision-medicine) identified, in the context of precision medicine, a pattern that applies with equal force here: the framing of equity as a downstream consideration — something to be addressed after deployment, if disparities become visible — rather than as a precondition of deployment systematically disadvantages the populations most likely to be harmed. The RFI reproduces this framing.⏎⏎Cornell's specific concern is that any new CMS reimbursement pathway for AI clinical decision-support tools, or any streamlined FDA regulatory pathway for such tools, that does not include mandatory equity auditing requirements will create financial incentives for deployment at scale before subgroup performance is characterized. This is not a speculative concern. The sepsis prediction model documented by Wong et al. (2021) was adopted by hundreds of institutions before external validation revealed its performance limitations. The pulse oximetry disparity documented by Sjoding et al. (2020) persisted for decades before systematic analysis surfaced it as a clinical safety concern. The dermatology AI disparities documented by Adamson and Smith (2018) were identified by researchers examining training data composition, not by clinical surveillance systems that detected patient harm. In each case, the absence of mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing and post-deployment surveillance created conditions in which harm could scale before it could be measured.⏎⏎⏎NUMBERED RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Cornell respectfully submits the following specific recommendations to HHS, addressed to the RFI's solicitation of comment on regulatory and reimbursement actions:⏎⏎1. Any new CMS reimbursement pathway for AI clinical decision-support tools should require, as a condition of reimbursement eligibility, documented pre-deployment equity auditing that characterizes tool performance across subgroups defined by race, ethnicity, sex, insurance status, and primary language. The auditing methodology should be publicly disclosed and should include external validation in settings that differ from the primary development environment.⏎⏎2. Any new FDA regulatory pathway for AI clinical decision-support tools should require post-market surveillance protocols that include subgroup performance monitoring, with mandatory reporting of performance degradation in subpopulations to FDA within a defined timeframe. The current framework for Software as a Medical Device does not adequately address this requirement.⏎⏎3. HHS should fund, through the NIH or AHRQ, the development of standardized equity auditing protocols that community hospitals and safety-net institutions can apply without requiring large biomedical informatics infrastructure. The current literature provides methodological foundations (see Wiens et al., 2019; Gianfrancesco et al., 2018) but no operationalized standards accessible to resource-constrained institutions.⏎⏎4. Any HHS guidance on AI adoption in clinical care should explicitly address the problem of automation bias (Cabitza et al., 2017) and require that AI tool deployments include documented clinician training on the conditions under which algorithmic outputs are most likely to be unreliable, including in subpopulations underrepresented in training data.⏎⏎5. HHS should commission a systematic review of currently deployed AI clinical decision-support tools to characterize the extent of subgroup performance disparities in real-world settings, with findings made publicly available as a condition of any federal investment in AI acceleration infrastructure.⏎⏎⏎Cornell University AI in Health Initiative | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎⏎SECTION 4: A NOTE ON THE FRAMING OF THIS SOLICITATION⏎⏎Cornell recognizes that the RFI is responding to real and documented barriers to AI adoption — the 68% of partner sites that identified reimbursement ambiguity as their primary concern represent a genuine regulatory failure that HHS is right to address. The concern this comment raises is not that acceleration is wrong as a policy goal but that the framing of the current solicitation treats equity considerations as outside the scope of what is being asked. The questions the RFI poses are almost entirely about how to remove barriers to adoption. They do not ask whether the tools being adopted perform equitably across the populations they will encounter, or what mechanisms would allow disparate harm to be detected before it scales.⏎⏎This framing matters because it shapes what kinds of comment the agency is likely to receive and, by extension, what kinds of recommendations are likely to inform the final regulatory action. Researchers who have spent years documenting algorithmic bias in clinical AI — and the list of relevant work cited in this comment represents a fraction of the available literature — are not the natural constituency for an RFI framed around regulatory burden reduction. Cornell is submitting this comment because the 30-month evaluation, and the survey of 240 clinical investigators conducted through the Center for Health AI Trustworthiness, produced findings that make it difficult to participate in a policy process organized around acceleration without raising the question of what is being accelerated and for whom.⏎⏎The internal assessment completed in 2024 found that the six community hospital and safety-net sites in the evaluation cohort were, on average, receiving AI tools that had been validated exclusively on academic medical center data, without site-specific performance characterization, and without any systematic mechanism for detecting subgroup performance failure after deployment. Those six sites collectively serve patient populations with substantially higher proportions of Medicaid enrollees, non-English primary language speakers, and patients from racial and ethnic minority groups than the academic medical center sites where the tools were developed. The performance gap that Seyyed-Kalantari et al. (2021) documented in chest radiograph AI — where underserved populations experienced systematically higher rates of underdiagnosis — is the kind of harm that would not be visible to a clinician relying on aggregate performance metrics, would not trigger any existing reporting requirement, and would not be addressed by any of the regulatory or reimbursement reforms the RFI proposes.⏎⏎Cornell does not believe HHS intends to institutionalize this dynamic. But the absence of mandatory equity auditing and post-deployment bias surveillance from the current RFI's framework means that the regulatory and reimbursement actions the agency takes in response to this solicitation will, in practice, create incentives for deployment without the safeguards that the empirical record indicates are necessary. The appendix to this comment, which is not attached to this submission but is available upon request from the Cornell Tech research office, includes the full dataset from the 14-site evaluation and the survey instrument used with the 240 clinical investigators, along with a more detailed methodological account of the equity auditing gap finding.⏎⏎HHS is asked to treat mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing and post-deployment bias surveillance not as optional features of a responsible AI ecosystem but as preconditions of any reimbursement or regulatory pathway the Department creates. The question of how to operationalize those requirements at institutions that currently lack the capacity to conduct them independently — which is to say, at most of the institutions where the populations most likely to be harmed by algorithmic bias actually receive care — is a genuinely difficult implementation problem, and Cornell would welcome the opportunity to contribute to a more targeted technical assistance process if HHS elects to convene one. The standardized auditing protocol recommendation above (Recommendation 3) is offered in that spirit, though the methodological details would require substantially more space than this comment format allows to develop adequately, and the existing literature on fairness metrics in clinical AI does not yet converge on a single approach that would be appropriate across all tool types and clinical contexts, which is itself an argument for federal investment in the development of such standards before, rather than after, large-scale deployment is incentivized through new reimbursement pathways.♔♔2026-01-09T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-09T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔8♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔academic_organization♔high♔resigned♔Utah♔public health researcher♔46♔Cornell University's multidisciplinary AI in Health Initiative, spanning the Weill Cornell Medicine campus and the Cornell Tech hub on Roosevelt Island, has documented implementation patterns across 14 affiliated clinical partner sites over a 30-month evaluation period.
