SYNTH-0097♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Kevin Hernandez♔American Society of Clinical Oncology♔♔♔♔♔AMERICAN SOCIETY OF CLINICAL ONCOLOGY — SUPPLEMENTAL SUBMISSION⏎HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted on Behalf of: Kevin Hernandez, Senior Policy Analyst⏎Organization: American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO)⏎Docket Reference: HHS-ONC-AI-RFI-2024⏎⏎⏎THE DIAGNOSTIC PROMISE DOES NOT JUSTIFY IGNORING THE DENIAL MACHINE⏎⏎There is genuine, well-documented reason to believe that AI-assisted diagnostic tools can materially reduce suffering for patients with complex, difficult-to-diagnose conditions. The National MS Society's 2024 cross-analysis of CMS claims data and Society-funded research found that earlier, more accurate diagnosis is associated with a 34% reduction in avoidable relapse-related hospitalizations within the first two years of disease-modifying therapy initiation (National MS Society Policy Research Team, Internal Policy Brief, 2024). ASCO recognizes that finding as representative of a broader pattern: algorithmic tools that support clinical decision-making, when properly validated and deployed, can compress diagnostic timelines and reduce the access disparities that disproportionately affect rural and low-income patients. The 4.3-month longer wait for neurological consultation in non-metropolitan areas, documented in that same analysis, is exactly the kind of structural inequity that well-governed AI could help address.⏎⏎That acknowledgment, however, is not a license for HHS to proceed as though the dominant commercial deployment of AI in American healthcare is diagnostic assistance. It is not. The dominant deployment — the one generating the most revenue, the most administrative friction, and the most documented patient harm — is prior authorization denial automation. HHS's RFI frames AI reimbursement policy largely as a tool to "foster competition among clinical care AI tool builders," and that framing is a category error that this comment is compelled to name directly. STAT News reported in November 2023 that UnitedHealth Group's nH Predict algorithm was being used to systematically deny elderly patients post-acute care, often after hospital stays for serious conditions, with denial rates that internal reviewers acknowledged were inconsistent with individual clinical presentations (Mukherjee and Ross, STAT News, November 2023). The U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations documented in its November 2024 report, "Denial, Delay, Disappear," that Medicare Advantage insurers were deploying algorithmic prior authorization tools in ways that generated denials at scale with minimal individualized physician review — a finding that corroborates earlier Kaiser Family Foundation analysis showing that prior authorization in Medicare Advantage affected a substantial share of beneficiaries and that denial rates varied dramatically across plans without clear clinical justification (Koma, Cubanski, and Neuman, KFF Issue Brief, March 2023). The American Medical Association's 2023 prior authorization physician survey found that 94% of physicians reported delays in care attributable to prior authorization, and 33% reported that a patient experienced a serious adverse event as a direct result (AMA Policy Research Perspectives, 2023). These are not edge cases. They are the operational reality of AI in healthcare as it exists today, in 2024, at scale.⏎⏎ASCO — Comments on HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎⏎What makes this moment genuinely dangerous is that HHS's acceleration agenda, absent explicit and enforceable accountability requirements, will function as a regulatory endorsement of the denial-automation use case. Insurers are not passive actors waiting for HHS guidance; they are actively expanding algorithmic prior authorization capacity because the financial incentives favor it. The insurer cost-containment incentive structure is not subtle — as Dafny, Gruber, and Ody (American Journal of Health Economics, 2015) documented, competitive pressure in insurance markets does not reliably constrain the use of administrative mechanisms to limit care when those mechanisms are opaque and the affected populations lack bargaining power. Elderly, disabled, and low-income patients — including a substantial share of the MS patient population ASCO works alongside — are structurally unable to navigate multi-step appeals processes. A denial generated by an algorithm and nominally subject to appeal is, for many of these patients, functionally final. The Colorado Division of Insurance's October 2023 market conduct examination (DORA Report No. 2023-MC-14) found that AI-assisted prior authorization tools in commercial and Medicare Advantage plans operating in that state exhibited patterns of denial concentration among high-cost, chronically ill beneficiaries that warranted further investigation — and Colorado is not a regulatory outlier. Fuse Brown, Adler-Milstein, and Durbin, writing in Health Affairs Forefront in January 2024, have made the case for mandatory explainability requirements in prior authorization AI with considerable rigor, and their framework deserves direct engagement in HHS's final policy response. The equity dimension cannot be separated from the accountability question: Obermeyer and colleagues demonstrated in Science (2019;366[6464]:447-453) that widely deployed health algorithms embedded cost-containment proxies that produced racially disparate outcomes, and there is no structural reason to believe that prior authorization AI is immune to that dynamic. Ndugga, Artiga, and Pham (KFF, April 2023) have documented the compounding effect of such disparities on already-disadvantaged populations.⏎⏎ASCO's specific demands are as follows. HHS must require that any AI system used in insurance coverage or prior authorization decisions disclose its training objectives, the cost-containment metrics incorporated into model development, and the demographic composition of training data — prior to deployment and on a continuing basis. Independent audits for cost-containment bias must be mandatory, not voluntary, and results must be publicly accessible. Beneficiaries must have an enforceable right to meaningful human review of any algorithmically generated denial, with "meaningful" defined to exclude rubber-stamp processes in which the reviewing clinician has no access to the patient's actual clinical record. HHS should further consider whether a moratorium on AI-generated prior authorization denials is appropriate absent demonstrated clinical appropriateness standards validated against⏎⏎ASCO — Comments on HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎outcomes data. CMS's own rulemaking at 88 Fed. Reg. 22120 (CMS-4201-P, April 12, 2023) acknowledged the administrative burden problem in behavioral health contexts; the logic of that acknowledgment applies with equal force here. The Department has the authority and the obligation to act on it.⏎⏎asco_hhs_ai_rfi_comments_hernandez_2024.pdf⏎policy@asco.org♔♔2026-01-06T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-06T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔3♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI-powered insurance decision-making automates prior authorization denials and coverage restrictions in ways that are opaque, unappealable, and systematically biased against vulnerable patients.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔frustrated♔Colorado♔senior policy analyst♔60♔A 2024 survey of 1,100 individuals living with multiple sclerosis conducted by the National Multiple Sclerosis Society found that 68% reported delays of six months or longer in receiving definitive diagnoses, with neurologist respondents in a parallel clinician survey identifying inconsistent MRI interpretation and limited access to subspecialty expertise as the primary drivers of that delay. SYNTH-0098♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Matthew Walker♔Evolent Health♔♔♔♔♔Evolent Health | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLIN | Page 1⏎⏎Matthew Walker, MD⏎Chief Medical Officer⏎Evolent Health⏎Salt Lake City, Utah⏎⏎Submitted in Response to: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary / ASTP/ONC⏎Docket Submission Date: [filed electronically]⏎⏎mwalker@evolenthealth.org⏎⏎⏎PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS: WHAT THE DATA ACTUALLY SHOWS⏎⏎Evolent Health operates across a broad network of affiliated clinical deployment sites, and the internal data we have collected over the past two years tells a story that is considerably more complicated than the efficiency narrative that tends to dominate federal AI policy discussions. Our Q2-Q3 2024 implementation review, which covered 47 affiliated clinical sites and was structured around standardized feedback protocols, found that 61% of AI-assisted diagnostic tools in active use had encountered at least one reimbursement barrier that delayed or prevented full integration into standard care workflows (Newton's Tree Health Network, 2024). That figure is not a marginal finding. It suggests that the infrastructure for AI adoption in clinical settings is not simply immature — it is actively distorted by incentive structures that have very little to do with clinical value.⏎⏎The same audit found that fragmented documentation requirements, varying by payer and by state, produced an estimated 34% increase in administrative burden per AI-assisted encounter compared to conventional care pathways. Thirty-four percent. That number does not come from a policy simulation or a modeled projection. It comes from structured workflow data collected at real deployment sites. We are raising it here not to complain about regulatory complexity in the abstract, but because it bears directly on the question HHS is implicitly asking: why is adoption lagging, and what would actually fix it? Our view is that the Department's current framing — which treats regulatory timidity and reimbursement ambiguity as the primary obstacles — misidentifies the structural problem and risks making it considerably worse.⏎⏎⏎THE MARKET CONCENTRATION PROBLEM HHS IS NOT NAMING⏎⏎Evolent Health | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLIN | Page 2⏎⏎The healthcare AI market is not a competitive marketplace in the conventional sense. A relatively small number of large technology vendors and EHR platform companies control the dominant share of clinical AI deployments, and that concentration has consequences that go well beyond pricing. Jiang, Bhatt, and Fonarow, writing in Health Affairs in 2023, documented how vendor concentration in clinical AI creates procurement dynamics that systematically disadvantage health systems — particularly those without dedicated AI procurement infrastructure — and insulate incumbent products from the kind of performance-based competition that would otherwise drive improvement (Jiang et al., 2023, Health Affairs, 42(4), 511-519). The Federal Trade Commission reached a similar conclusion in its 2023 staff report on generative AI and the healthcare sector, noting that dominant platform positions in health IT create structural barriers to entry that are not adequately addressed by existing competition policy frameworks (FTC, 2023).⏎⏎What concerns Evolent Health about the current RFI is that several of the mechanisms HHS is considering — accelerated reimbursement pathways, public-private partnerships, Cooperative Research and Development Agreements — are precisely the kinds of policy instruments that incumbent vendors are best positioned to exploit. Navigating complex billing and coverage processes requires legal and regulatory infrastructure that smaller, often clinically superior vendors simply do not have. When HHS creates a new reimbursement pathway for AI-assisted clinical decision support, the first organizations through that door will be the ones with established CMS relationships, dedicated government affairs staff, and the resources to absorb compliance costs during the transition period. Schulman and Richman made this point directly in a 2023 JAMA Health Forum analysis of Medicare coverage pathways for clinical decision support, arguing that the political economy of AI reimbursement reform systematically advantages large incumbents and that the cost-reduction framing that typically accompanies these proposals obscures substantial value transfer from health systems to technology companies (Schulman & Richman, 2023, JAMA Health Forum, 4(9), e232847).⏎⏎Gans and Stern, in a 2022 analysis published in the Journal of Health Politics, Policy and Law, used the term "regulatory capture" to describe the process by which incumbent digital health platforms shape emerging AI governance frameworks in ways that appear to be modernization but actually function to entrench existing market positions (Gans & Stern, 2022, J Health Politics, Policy and Law, 47(3), 389-414). That framing is uncomfortable, but it is accurate. The comment process for this RFI will itself be a data point: large vendors with government relations capacity will submit detailed, technically sophisticated comments that map their existing product roadmaps onto HHS's stated priorities. Smaller vendors and health systems will be underrepresented, not because they lack relevant perspectives, but because they lack the institutional infrastructure to engage at this level consistently.⏎⏎⏎VENDOR LOCK-IN AND THE EHR INTEGRATION PROBLEM⏎⏎Evolent Health | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLIN | Page 3⏎⏎There is a specific mechanism through which market concentration in clinical AI becomes self-reinforcing, and HHS's acceleration agenda risks deepening it. When AI tools are bundled into EHR platforms — which is increasingly the dominant deployment model — health systems face switching costs that have nothing to do with clinical performance. Beaulieu-Jones, Finlayson, and Yuan documented this dynamic in a 2023 npj Digital Medicine analysis, finding that EHR-integrated AI tools create competitive moats through workflow dependency, data format lock-in, and contract structures that make replacement economically prohibitive even when superior alternatives exist (Beaulieu-Jones et al., 2023, npj Digital Medicine, 6(1), 88). This is not a hypothetical concern. Evolent Health has encountered this directly: at multiple affiliated sites, procurement teams have identified AI tools with demonstrably better diagnostic performance than the bundled EHR-native option, and the switching cost analysis has nonetheless favored staying with the incumbent product.⏎⏎The ONC's own 2023 data brief on health IT market concentration documented how interoperability barriers function as a form of vendor protection, preventing health systems from substituting better-performing tools without incurring integration costs that can run into the millions of dollars (ONC Data Brief No. 58, 2023). What this means in practice is that the market does not reliably select for clinical quality. It selects for integration depth, contract leverage, and the ability to absorb implementation costs — all of which favor large incumbents. Dafny and Lee, writing about healthcare market concentration dynamics in the New England Journal of Medicine, observed that in concentrated markets, the normal mechanisms of competitive discipline break down and quality improvement becomes decoupled from market success (Dafny & Lee, 2016, NEJM, 374(19), 1804-1806). Clinical AI markets are exhibiting exactly this pattern, and HHS's acceleration agenda, if it proceeds without structural safeguards, will accelerate the concentration alongside the adoption.⏎⏎The licensing and maintenance cost question also deserves more direct attention than it has received in the RFI framing. Sarah Kliff and Adam Satariano published a detailed examination in The New York Times in November 2023 of how hospital AI licensing fees, implementation costs, and long-term maintenance contracts are consuming a substantial share of the efficiency gains that AI vendors claim their products will deliver (Kliff & Satariano, Nov. 14, 2023, NYT). The cost-reduction narrative that HHS has adopted largely uncritically is, in many cases, a vendor marketing claim that has not been subjected to independent verification at scale. Evolent Health is not in a position to put a precise dollar figure on this across the full network, but our procurement teams have flagged it consistently as a concern that the aggregate cost picture for AI-assisted care is less favorable than headline efficiency estimates suggest.⏎⏎⏎Evolent Health | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLIN | Page 4⏎⏎⏎PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIPS AND THE DISTRIBUTION OF BENEFITS⏎⏎The RFI's discussion of public-private partnerships and CRADAs as mechanisms for accelerating AI development raises a question that Evolent Health believes deserves a direct answer: who captures the value from federally funded AI research? Adler-Milstein and Pfeifer examined this question in a 2022 Milbank Quarterly analysis and found that public-private data partnerships in health AI systematically privatize the benefits of federally funded research while socializing the costs — particularly the costs of data infrastructure, privacy compliance, and the clinical validation work that health systems perform without compensation (Adler-Milstein & Pfeifer, 2022, Milbank Quarterly, 100(2), 447-471). The pattern they identified is not unique to health AI, but it is particularly acute in this sector because the underlying training data — patient records, clinical notes, diagnostic images — is generated through publicly subsidized care delivery and then contributed to AI development processes whose commercial outputs accrue entirely to private vendors.⏎⏎Evolent Health does not oppose public-private collaboration in principle. There are genuine areas where federal investment in shared infrastructure, federated data environments, and algorithm validation frameworks would benefit the sector broadly. But the CRADA model as it currently operates tends to produce arrangements where the federal partner contributes data access and regulatory facilitation while the private partner retains intellectual property rights and commercialization upside. HHS should be explicit about what it expects from these arrangements in terms of public benefit requirements — open licensing conditions, price constraints on federally assisted products, mandatory publication of validation data — rather than leaving these terms to individual negotiation where the private partner consistently has more leverage.⏎⏎There is also a workforce dimension to this that the RFI does not adequately address. The administrative burden our audit documented — that 34% increase per AI-assisted encounter — falls disproportionately on clinical staff and on the health systems that employ them. When AI tools generate documentation requirements, prior authorization workflows, and payer-specific coding demands, the labor cost is absorbed by the health system, not the vendor. This is a real transfer of value that does not appear in vendor efficiency claims, and it is one reason Evolent Health is skeptical of aggregate cost-reduction projections that do not account for implementation-level administrative friction.⏎⏎⏎REGARDING ALGORITHMIC BIAS AND MARKET INCENTIVES⏎⏎Evolent Health | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLIN | Page 5⏎⏎This comment has deliberately set aside clinical safety arguments, which are being addressed in other organizational submissions. But one dimension of the safety question is inseparable from the market structure analysis above: algorithmic bias in commercial AI products is not simply a technical failure. It is, in many cases, a predictable consequence of the incentive structures under which these products are developed and deployed. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan documented in a 2019 Science paper how a widely deployed commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients — not because the developers intended to discriminate, but because the algorithm was trained on cost as a proxy for health need, and cost is itself a biased variable in a healthcare system with deep structural inequities (Obermeyer et al., 2019, Science, 366(6464), 447-453). The market did not correct this. The algorithm remained in widespread use for years after the bias was documented in the academic literature.⏎⏎Evolent Health raises this not to relitigate a well-known case but to make a structural point: when AI vendors face limited competitive pressure and health systems face high switching costs, there is no reliable market mechanism that forces performance improvement or bias remediation. The only mechanisms that reliably work in this environment are regulatory requirements — mandatory auditing, public disclosure of performance data stratified by demographic group, and reimbursement conditions that tie payment to demonstrated equity in outcomes. HHS's acceleration agenda should build these requirements in from the beginning rather than treating them as add-ons to be negotiated later.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Evolent Health's experience across 47 clinical deployment sites, combined with the academic and regulatory literature cited above, leads to the following specific recommendations for HHS consideration. These are not offered as a comprehensive list but as the areas where we believe HHS has the most direct leverage and where the structural risks are most acute.⏎⏎1. Condition reimbursement modernization on open interoperability standards. Any new Medicare or Medicaid reimbursement pathway for AI-assisted clinical decision support should require that covered tools comply with open interoperability standards that prevent EHR bundling from foreclosing competition. Health systems should be able to substitute better-performing tools without prohibitive switching costs. ONC has the regulatory authority to define these standards and should do so as a precondition for reimbursement eligibility rather than a separate, downstream policy process.⏎⏎2. Require mandatory algorithmic auditing by independent third parties. Self-reported performance data from AI vendors is not adequate for reimbursement decisions. HHS should establish a requirement that any AI tool seeking reimbursement under federal programs submit to independent algorithmic auditing that evaluates performance across demographic subgroups, documents false positive and false negative rates in real-world deployment conditions, and assesses model drift over time. The auditing methodology should be publicly specified and the results should be publicly disclosed.⏎⏎3. Adopt anti-concentration provisions in CRADA and public-private partnership agreements. Federal agreements with AI vendors should include provisions that prevent dominant EHR vendors from bundling federally assisted AI tools in ways that foreclose competition from smaller vendors. This could take the form of non-exclusivity requirements, open licensing conditions for federally funded components, or mandatory interoperability commitments as a condition of federal partnership.⏎⏎4. Establish a reimbursement review process that accounts for total cost of adoption. HHS should develop a methodology for evaluating the total cost of AI adoption — including licensing fees, implementation costs, maintenance contracts, and administrative burden — rather than relying on vendor-supplied efficiency projections. This methodology should be applied consistently across reimbursement applications and the underlying data should be available for public review.⏎⏎o A related concern: the documentation and coding requirements that payers are currently imposing on AI-assisted encounters vary so significantly across payers and states that they are functioning as de facto barriers to adoption — but the burden falls on health systems and clinical staff, not on the vendors whose products generate the documentation requirements. HHS should convene a cross-payer working group to standardize documentation requirements for AI-assisted encounters, with a specific mandate to reduce the administrative burden differential our audit identified.⏎⏎5. Create a structured pathway for smaller and mid-size vendors to access reimbursement modernization. If HHS proceeds with accelerated reimbursement pathways, it should include explicit provisions — reduced compliance costs, technical assistance, phased implementation timelines — that allow clinically validated tools from smaller vendors to access these pathways without the regulatory infrastructure advantages that large incumbents bring. The FTC's 2023 report on competition in health AI recommended exactly this kind of structural accommodation, and HHS should coordinate with the FTC in designing it.⏎⏎⏎Evolent Health | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLIN | Page 6⏎⏎The concern that animates all of these recommendations is not that AI in clinical care is a bad idea. The concern is that the specific policy mechanisms HHS is considering will produce a version of AI adoption that concentrates market power, transfers value from health systems to technology companies, and insulates underperforming products from competitive accountability — all while the Department describes the process as modernization. Evolent Health has seen this pattern operate at the site level, in procurement decisions, in payer negotiations, and in the administrative burden our clinical staff absorbs every day. The 61% reimbursement barrier figure from our 2024 audit is not primarily a story about regulatory timidity. It is a story about a market structure that is not organized around clinical value, and about documentation and billing requirements that have become a competitive moat rather than a quality assurance mechanism.⏎⏎HHS has real authority here, and the RFI process suggests genuine interest in getting this right. The Department can condition reimbursement modernization on structural safeguards. It can require independent auditing. It can build anti-concentration provisions into its partnership agreements. It can work with ONC to make open interoperability a precondition rather than an aspiration. None of these steps require new statutory authority, and all of them would materially improve the probability that AI adoption in clinical care produces outcomes that are good for patients rather than primarily good for the vendors who are best positioned to navigate a complex regulatory environment.⏎⏎What Evolent Health would find genuinely useful, and what is not currently contemplated in the RFI, is a formal mechanism for health systems to report reimbursement barriers and documentation burden increases in real time — something analogous to the adverse event reporting infrastructure that exists for device safety. The data our audit produced was gathered through significant internal effort, and it covers only our affiliated network. There is almost certainly a much larger dataset sitting in the operational experience of health systems across the country that HHS is currently not collecting. A standardized reporting mechanism, even a voluntary one, would give the Department better signal on where the structural problems are concentrated and would make it considerably harder for the efficiency narrative to go unchallenged when the underlying cost and burden data tells a more complicated story.⏎⏎The specific documentation inconsistency problem — varying requirements by payer and by state — is the one area where Evolent Health would most strongly urge immediate action, even ahead of broader reimbursement reform. Our clinical informatics team has spent an estimated 2,300 staff-hours since January 2024 managing payer-specific documentation variants for AI-assisted encounters across the network. That is not a quality assurance cost. It is a pure administrative waste that does not benefit patients, does not improve AI performance, and does not serve any legitimate regulatory function. It exists because no one has taken responsibility for standardizing it, and because the vendors whose tools generate the documentation requirements have no incentive to push for standardization when the burden falls on health systems.♔♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔9♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔The AI healthcare market is dominated by a small number of powerful vendors whose commercial interests in rapid deployment conflict with patient safety, and HHS's acceleration agenda risks embedding those vendors permanently into critical healthcare infrastructure.♔organization♔high♔hopeful♔Utah♔chief medical officer♔38♔A 2024 internal analysis across Newton's Tree's 47 affiliated clinical deployment sites found that 61% of AI-assisted diagnostic tools in active use had encountered at least one reimbursement barrier that delayed or prevented full integration into standard care workflows. SYNTH-0099♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Lisa Lee♔Johns Hopkins Malone Center for Engineering in Healthcare♔♔♔♔♔Malone Center for Engineering in Healthcare | Johns Hopkins University | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 1⏎⏎The question the RFI does not ask is, in some ways, the most consequential one: when an AI system contributes to a patient harm, who is accountable, and under what legal and institutional framework is that accountability enforced? The Department's Request for Information, published in 2024, solicits extensive comment on regulatory pathways, reimbursement structures, and research priorities — and does so with evident enthusiasm for accelerating clinical adoption. The Malone Center for Engineering in Healthcare at Johns Hopkins University shares that enthusiasm in principle. There is genuine and well-documented potential for AI-assisted tools to improve diagnostic accuracy, reduce preventable errors, and extend the reach of clinical expertise into under-resourced settings, as Topol (2019) and Obermeyer and Emanuel (2016) have each argued at length. But the RFI's framing of "barriers to adoption" treats reimbursement uncertainty and regulatory ambiguity as the primary structural obstacles, and in doing so it systematically avoids the harder question of whether the institutional conditions necessary for responsible deployment actually exist. The Malone Center's position, developed through sustained engagement with both clinical implementation research and the health economics of technology adoption, is that they do not — and that proceeding to accelerate adoption before those conditions are constructed is not a calculated risk but a sequencing error with compounding consequences.⏎⏎To be precise about the evidentiary basis for this concern: a 2024 survey of 214 computing research departments affiliated with CRA member institutions found that 67% of faculty conducting health AI research identified reimbursement uncertainty as the primary barrier preventing clinical translation of validated algorithms. That figure is real and worth taking seriously. But the same research infrastructure has produced a related finding that receives far less attention in policy discussions: fewer than 12% of health AI tools developed in academic settings successfully reached even a pilot clinical implementation stage, and in post-project faculty debriefs conducted through the Computing Community Consortium, reimbursement structure was identified as the dominant structural obstacle. The Taulbee Survey documented a 34% increase in health-focused AI dissertations between 2021 and 2023, which means the pipeline of validated tools is growing substantially. The gap between pipeline volume and clinical deployment is therefore widening, not narrowing. The Department's instinct to address this gap through reimbursement reform and regulatory streamlining is understandable. What that framing misses, however, is that many institutions capable of deploying these tools are choosing not to — not primarily because reimbursement codes are unavailable, but because the liability exposure associated with AI-assisted clinical decisions is genuinely unresolved, and no institution's legal counsel is prepared to advise deployment into that vacuum.⏎⏎This is, at its core, an institutional economics problem as much as a legal one. The standard account of technology adoption in healthcare, drawing on work by Cohen, Amarasingham, Shah, Xie, and Lo (2014), treats legal and ethical uncertainty as exogenous friction that slows otherwise-desirable diffusion. The Malone Center's view is that this framing inverts the actual causal structure. Legal uncertainty around AI-assisted harm is not friction applied to a functioning adoption mechanism — it is a signal that the adoption mechanism itself is missing a load-bearing component. When a physician makes a clinical error, the malpractice system, whatever its well-documented limitations (Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert, 2020), at least provides a legible framework for assigning responsibility, compensating injured patients, and generating deterrence signals that feed back into clinical practice. That system was designed around a model of identifiable human agency. AI intermediation fractures that model. The algorithm that recommended the treatment is a product, not a person. The physician who accepted or declined the recommendation may have done so in good faith, relying on a system they neither designed nor fully understood. The hospital that deployed the system may have conducted reasonable due diligence. The developer may have validated the tool on a population that differed from the deployment context in ways that were not disclosed in the product documentation. Under current doctrine, the result is a diffusion of responsibility across actors none of whom is clearly liable, which is functionally equivalent to no one being liable.⏎⏎Malone Center for Engineering in Healthcare | Johns Hopkins University | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 2⏎⏎M.C. Elish's (2019) concept of the "moral crumple zone" is the most precise analytical description of what happens in this configuration. Elish's argument, developed through case analysis of human-machine systems in aviation and autonomous vehicles before being extended to healthcare contexts, is that when accountability is formally distributed across a human-machine assemblage, the human operator absorbs the moral and legal consequences of system failures regardless of the actual causal structure — not because the human is most responsible, but because the human is most legible to institutional accountability mechanisms. In clinical AI deployment, this means that frontline clinicians become the default repositories of liability for failures that originated in algorithmic design, training data composition, or deployment context mismatch. Sendak, Elish, Gao, Futoma, and colleagues (2020) documented exactly this dynamic in their study of deep learning deployment in clinical decision support — the institutional tendency to position the human clinician as the "final check" is not a safety mechanism so much as a liability-laundering mechanism, one that preserves the appearance of human oversight while in practice creating conditions under which no actor has adequate information or authority to exercise meaningful control. Pasquale (2020) has argued that this architecture is not accidental: it is a predictable consequence of deploying systems whose internal logic is opaque even to their developers, in institutional contexts where the pressure to deploy outpaces the development of governance infrastructure.⏎⏎The RFI text does not mention malpractice liability, accountability assignment, or the legal doctrine of learned intermediary as it might apply to AI-assisted clinical recommendations. This is a documentable omission, not an inference. The Department asks extensively about reimbursement models, about interoperability standards, about FDA regulatory pathways for software as a medical device — all legitimate questions. It does not ask who is legally responsible when an AI-assisted recommendation contributes to patient harm, how that responsibility should be allocated across the developer-deployer-clinician chain, or what institutional infrastructure would need to exist before deployment could be considered responsible rather than merely expedient. Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen (2020) have identified precisely this gap in their systematic review of legal and ethical frameworks for AI-driven healthcare: existing tort doctrine, products liability law, and professional liability standards were not designed to accommodate the causal complexity introduced by learning systems, and none of the major regulatory frameworks currently in force in the United States assigns clear accountability for AI-assisted harm in a way that would be enforceable at the point of clinical deployment. Doshi-Velez, Kortz, Budish, and colleagues (2017) made a related argument in the context of explainability requirements: accountability under law requires that decisions be attributable to identifiable agents, and AI systems that cannot explain their outputs in terms legible to legal and institutional accountability mechanisms are, in a meaningful sense, operating outside the accountability frameworks that those mechanisms were built to enforce.⏎⏎The practical consequences of proceeding without accountability infrastructure are not speculative. They are already visible in the pattern of institutional behavior around AI deployment. Hospitals and health systems that have attempted to deploy AI-assisted clinical tools — and there are a growing number of documented cases — have found themselves navigating a liability landscape that their legal and risk management teams describe as genuinely uncharted. Price and Cohen (2019) identified this as a structural feature of medical data ecosystems more broadly: the legal frameworks governing data use, model development, and clinical deployment were constructed in different eras for different purposes, and their interaction in the context of AI-assisted care creates zones of genuine legal ambiguity that institutional actors rationally respond to by either avoiding deployment or by deploying in ways that minimize their own exposure rather than maximizing patient safety. The latter dynamic — deployment structured to manage institutional liability rather than patient risk — is, from a health economics perspective, exactly the wrong incentive structure to build into the foundation of a new clinical technology. Kearns and Roth (2019) have argued that the design of accountability mechanisms is as consequential for social outcomes as the design of the algorithms themselves, and that systems deployed into poorly-designed accountability structures tend to optimize for the wrong objectives. The Malone Center finds this argument persuasive and sees no reason why healthcare AI would be an exception.⏎⏎Malone Center for Engineering in Healthcare | Johns Hopkins University | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 3⏎⏎What would adequate accountability infrastructure look like? The Malone Center does not propose to resolve this question in a comment of this length, and the Department should not expect any single commenter to do so. But the minimum components are identifiable, and their absence from the RFI is what makes the accelerationist posture of the document so difficult to endorse. At minimum, responsible deployment of AI-assisted clinical tools would require:⏎⏎1.  A legally enforceable framework specifying how liability for AI-assisted patient harm is allocated across the developer, the deployer (typically a hospital or health system), and the treating clinician — with allocation rules that reflect actual causal contribution rather than defaulting to the most legally legible human actor.⏎⏎2.  Mandatory pre-deployment disclosure standards requiring developers to specify the population on which a tool was validated, the conditions under which its performance estimates are reliable, and the clinical contexts in which deployment is contraindicated — analogous to, but more detailed than, existing labeling requirements for pharmaceutical products.⏎⏎3.  A post-deployment surveillance mechanism with mandatory adverse event reporting for AI-assisted clinical failures, structured to generate the kind of feedback signal that the malpractice system theoretically provides for human clinical error — without the well-documented access barriers and underreporting problems that characterize that system (Hoffman and Podgurski, 2013).⏎⏎4.  An institutional credentialing or certification process, administered either by HHS or by accreditation bodies operating under HHS authority, that conditions clinical deployment of AI tools on demonstrated compliance with the above requirements.⏎⏎None of these components currently exists in enforceable form. The Department's RFI proceeds as though their absence is a detail to be addressed downstream, after adoption pathways have been established. The Malone Center's concern is that this sequencing is backwards in a way that will become increasingly difficult to correct. Once reimbursement codes exist, once clinical workflows have been redesigned around AI-assisted decision support, once EHR vendors have embedded specific tools into standard interfaces, the institutional and economic cost of imposing accountability requirements retroactively will be substantial — and the political economy of that moment will favor incumbent deployers over patient safety advocates. This is not a hypothetical pattern; it is the pattern that characterized the introduction of electronic health records under HITECH, where the pressure to achieve rapid adoption led to certification standards that locked in interoperability failures that have taken more than a decade to partially address. The analogy is not perfect, but the institutional dynamic is recognizable.⏎⏎The Malone Center therefore urges HHS to condition any reimbursement pathway, regulatory safe harbor, or accelerated approval mechanism for AI-assisted clinical tools on the prior establishment of a clear, legally enforceable accountability assignment framework meeting at minimum the components described above. This is not a request to slow AI adoption for its own sake. The research pipeline documented through the CRA surveys represents genuine scientific progress, and the clinical problems that health AI tools are designed to address — diagnostic errors, care coordination failures, preventable readmissions — are serious and warrant urgent attention. But the value of that pipeline is contingent on deployment conditions that make responsible adoption legible to the institutions, clinicians, and patients involved. Without an accountability framework, what the Department will accelerate is not the translation of validated tools into clinical benefit — it is the embedding of an accountability vacuum into clinical infrastructure at a scale and depth that will make it structurally very difficult to excavate later. The reimbursement question and the accountability question are not sequential; they are interdependent, and treating them as sequential is the design flaw the Malone Center is most concerned about.⏎⏎The Malone Center appreciates the Department's evident commitment to improving patient outcomes through technology adoption and recognizes the genuine complexity of the regulatory task the RFI is addressing. Correspondence regarding these comments may be directed to the Malone Center for Engineering in Healthcare at Johns Hopkins University. SYNTH-0100♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Charles Davis♔CVS Health♔♔♔♔♔CVS Health | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 1⏎⏎In response to the Request for Information: Accelerating the Adoption and Use of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Care Settings⏎⏎Submitted by: Charles Davis, Chief Financial Officer, CVS Health⏎⏎I. THE EQUITY INFRASTRUCTURE PROBLEM⏎⏎CVS Health operates across a network of clinical settings that spans well-resourced suburban facilities and safety-net institutions serving Medicaid-dominant patient populations, and our review of AI-assisted clinical tools over the past three fiscal years has produced a consistent and troubling finding: the tools that perform best in vendor demonstrations and academic validation studies perform materially worse when deployed in the community hospitals and federally qualified health centers where our most vulnerable patients actually receive care. This is not a theoretical concern. It is a documented pattern in the peer-reviewed literature, and the RFI as currently structured contains no mandatory mechanism to detect it before patients are harmed at scale.⏎⏎The evidence base here is substantial. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan (Science, 2019, 366(6464), 447-453) documented that a widely used commercial health-management algorithm systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients by using healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, effectively diverting care resources away from a population that faced greater structural barriers to accessing that care in the first place. Sjoding, Dickson, Iwashyna, Gay, and Valley (New England Journal of Medicine, 2020, 383(25), 2477-2478) found that pulse oximeters, a device so routine it is easy to forget it involves measurement algorithms, produced clinically significant overestimates of oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin pigmentation, a finding with direct implications for any AI system that ingests pulse oximetry data as a training feature. Wong, Otles, Donnelly, et al. (JAMA Internal Medicine, 2021, 181(8), 1065-1070) conducted external validation of a proprietary sepsis prediction model that had been implemented at hundreds of hospitals and found that real-world performance degraded substantially compared to internal validation metrics, with the model generating high false-positive alert burdens that fell disproportionately on already-strained nursing staff at lower-resource institutions. Seyyed-Kalantari, Zhang, McDermott, Chen, and Ghassemi (Nature Medicine, 2021, 27(12), 2176-2182) demonstrated that AI algorithms applied to chest radiographs produced systematically higher underdiagnosis rates for underserved patient populations, including patients on Medicaid and patients with limited English proficiency. Adamson and Smith (JAMA Dermatology, 2018, 154(11), 1247-1248) identified that dermatology machine learning datasets were heavily skewed toward lighter skin tones, producing models that performed substantially worse on patients of color. Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones (New England Journal of Medicine, 2020, 383(9), 874-882) documented how race-corrected clinical algorithms embedded in EHR systems propagate structural bias through what appears to be objective clinical decision support. Gianfrancesco, Tamang, Yazdany, and Schmajuk (JAMA Internal Medicine, 2018, 178(11), 1544-1547) catalogued the specific mechanisms by which EHR-derived training data encodes socioeconomic and racial bias into downstream model outputs.⏎⏎CVS Health | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 2⏎⏎What this body of literature establishes, collectively, is not that AI in clinical care is inherently problematic but that AI systems trained on historically biased clinical data will reproduce that bias at deployment scale unless there is deliberate infrastructure to detect and correct it. The RFI does not propose such infrastructure. This is the gap that concerns our institution most.⏎⏎II. SPECIFIC REGULATORY CONCERNS AND REQUESTS⏎⏎The RFI asks broadly what regulatory actions HHS can take to accelerate adoption. Our submission focuses on two connected concerns rather than attempting to address every question the RFI poses.⏎⏎First, on pre-deployment auditing: CVS Health requests that HHS establish mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing as a condition of any reimbursement pathway for AI-enabled clinical decision support tools. Char, Shah, and Magnus (New England Journal of Medicine, 2018, 378(11), 981-983) articulated the ethical obligations that attach to clinical AI deployment, and Wiens, Saria, Sendak, et al. (Nature Medicine, 2019, 25(9), 1337-1340) offered a practical roadmap for responsible ML deployment that includes prospective bias assessment. The ONC HTI-1 Final Rule (88 Fed. Reg. 23746, 2023) established algorithm transparency requirements that move in the right direction, but transparency is not the same as auditing. Knowing that an algorithm exists and knowing whether it performs equitably across race, insurance status, language preference, and geography are different things.⏎⏎o Pre-deployment auditing requirements should mandate stratified performance reporting across race, ethnicity, and payer type.⏎⏎o Audit datasets must include patient populations drawn from community hospitals and safety-net institutions, not only academic medical center cohorts.⏎⏎o Vendors should bear the burden of demonstrating equity performance, not health systems.⏎⏎Second, on automation bias: Our financial modeling of AI-assisted clinical trial enrollment, which showed a 34% reduction in time-to-enrollment and surfaced trial opportunities for 22% of patients who would otherwise have been missed under standard workflows (Massive Bio, 2024, utilization review across 47,000 patient records), also revealed something that does not appear in the headline statistics: when AI tools surface a recommendation, clinicians at community sites defer to that recommendation at rates substantially higher than clinicians at academic sites. This is consistent with the automation bias literature. The authoritative presentation of AI outputs, particularly in EHR-embedded clinical decision support, makes errors harder to detect and challenge than ordinary human clinical errors, because the error appears to have been validated before it reaches the clinician. HHS should require post-deployment bias surveillance as an ongoing condition of reimbursement, not a one-time certification event, with reporting intervals no longer than twelve months and stratified outcome data submitted to a centralized registry that allows cross-institutional pattern detection.⏎⏎CVS Health appreciates the opportunity to submit comment and requests that HHS treat the equity auditing and bias surveillance requirements described above as threshold conditions for any accelerated reimbursement pathway rather than as optional best practices.
